stories.Headline: The Next AI Chip Shortage May Be the Machines That Make HBM
stories.Summary:
Applied Materials announced on October 26, 2026, an agreement to raise its ownership of the Dutch advanced assembly equipment maker BE Semiconductor Industries, known as BESI, to about 20% of outstanding shares. BESI makes assembly equipment, including technologies used in hybrid bonding. The deal expands a strategic relationship between the two companies that began in 2020. The proposed increase is still subject to regulatory requirements, so the 20% figure is the announced target and not a completed transaction.

Several equipment makers have reported strong recent results tied to memory and packaging demand. Lam Research posted September-quarter 2026 revenue of $8.22 billion, up 54.4% from a year earlier and 22% from the prior quarter, with a GAAP operating margin of 40.0%. Camtek reported September-quarter revenue of about $161 million, up 28%, and projected revenue above $800 million in 2027, against roughly $595 million expected in 2026. KLA reported $4.14 billion for the September quarter, up 28.9%, and Applied Materials reported $9.12 billion for the July quarter, up 25.0%.

Japan's TOWA reported orders of ¥32.97 billion for July to September 2026, up 125.8% from a year earlier, while sales rose 14.1% to ¥17.53 billion. That put its order-to-sales ratio at roughly 1.88. TOWA raised its forecast for the fiscal year ending March 2027, lifting expected revenue from ¥64 billion to ¥71 billion and operating profit from ¥10.24 billion to ¥13.15 billion. The extra ¥7 billion in revenue comes with ¥2.91 billion in extra operating profit, an implied incremental margin of 41.6%. South Korea's Wonik IPS, based in Pyeongtaek, reported preliminary third-quarter revenue of about ₩337.8 billion, up 25.8%, with operating profit of about ₩66.7 billion, up 142.0%, for a margin of roughly 19.7%.

Analyst Robert Castellano, writing for 24/7 Wall St., said high-bandwidth memory production is creating a second investment opportunity in the equipment makers, beyond the chip and memory suppliers that have dominated attention. He said HBM demand comes from conventional capacity expansion by SK hynix, Samsung and Micron, and from rising manufacturing complexity as each generation needs more advanced deposition, etching, bonding and process-control tools. Lam attributed its sequential growth to demand from both foundry and memory customers, not HBM alone, and TOWA also serves other packaging applications. Castellano also noted that Applied's BESI stake carries a financial risk, because BESI's growth depends partly on the timing and economics of hybrid bonding adoption.

The articles describe why these tools matter. HBM differs from conventional DRAM because multiple DRAM dies must be thinned, connected through vertical structures called through-silicon vias, stacked, bonded and inspected before the memory can be paired with an AI accelerator. Each added step brings equipment needs, processing costs and potential yield losses. Reuters reported on November 6 that research firm Yole Group expects advanced packaging revenue to pass conventional packaging revenue for the first time in 2026, with related capital spending near $28 billion.

Packaging capacity is also becoming a bottleneck for finished AI accelerators, according to Korea IT Times. TSMC's CoWoS packaging is widely used by Nvidia and AMD, and TSMC is producing it at a scale of 5.5 reticles, with a 14-reticle platform planned for 2028 to hold about 10 large computing chips and 20 HBM stacks. Reuters cited industry sources saying Nvidia is providing billions of dollars to expand CoWoS capacity at SPIL, a subsidiary of ASE Technology, though the companies have not confirmed the terms. Taiwan's Powertech Technology is developing panel-level packaging and pursuing a roughly $400 million joint venture with Broadcom in Singapore, with production targeted for 2028.

stories.Headline: geniosAI Raises $19.1 Million to Bring Traceable AI Analysis to Financial Institutions
stories.Summary:
Financial intelligence startup geniosAI has come out of stealth with $19.1 million in combined seed and Series A funding, according to an announcement made on Monday, Nov. 9. The money comes from FactSet, Zoom and General Catalyst, and FactSet led the Series A round. FactSet also serves as the company's strategic partner. The startup is betting that banks and investment firms will pay for AI that shows how it reached its answers as well as producing them.

The company is building AI products for corporate finance teams, investment professionals and the office of the CFO. Its central idea is that financial institutions need a way to preserve the assumptions, calculations and review decisions behind their analyses. That would let employees verify results, challenge conclusions and build on earlier work. Through the FactSet partnership, geniosAI will bring FactSet's financial data into its platform. Zoom will support the conversations where financial decisions take place, including internal finance reviews and earnings calls.

The company said its technology is already used by finance and investment teams at Fortune 500 banks and technology companies. Those teams use it to prepare for earnings, compare results with analyst expectations and identify questions investors may raise. FactSet CEO Sanoke Viswanathan said the value of data depends on how decisively people can act on it. He added that combining FactSet's data with geniosAI's traceable analysis could help financial teams decide with greater confidence and speed.

PYMNTS described the timing as part of a wider shift in enterprise finance, where companies must connect systems, preserve controls and decide which capabilities to own. For CFOs, it said, the cost of a modern finance stack often lies less in software licenses than in the work of keeping applications, data and processes connected. A PYMNTS Intelligence study found that at least half of surveyed financial services firms were using AI in 27 of 75 business tasks examined. Revenue recognition led adoption at 65%, with credit risk assessment and sales forecasting at 60% each. Fragmented or poor-quality data remained the biggest obstacle to wider deployment for 30% of financial services leaders.

Banks are also finding ways to add AI without replacing the technology they already run. Sutherland and FlowX.AI are putting more than 220 AI agents to work on top of existing banking systems, targeting lending, onboarding and anti-money laundering reviews. One European lender reportedly cut manual credit-workflow handoffs by 80%. Separately, a WilmerHale analysis published on JD Supra on Nov. 10 noted that AI systems are increasingly designed to act, not just answer. It cited a UK Financial Conduct Authority review, The Mills Review, published on 6 July 2026, which found that one in five UK adults was already open to AI making decisions for them.

stories.Headline: Environmental activists set to rally outside Schumer's office over AI data center bill
stories.Summary:
Environmental activists planned to rally on Monday, November 9, 2026, outside Senator Chuck Schumer's Midtown Manhattan office, starting at 10 a.m. They want the New York Democrat to oppose legislation they say would speed up the growth of unregulated artificial intelligence data centers. ABC7 New York reported the protest as the Senate was expected to take up a bill that would quicken approvals for data center projects. The measure has bipartisan support in Congress.

Mashable described the bill somewhat differently, saying the Senate was preparing for a pivotal procedural vote on legislation that would speed approvals for energy projects. According to that account, the bill would also require large data centers to carry more of the costs they place on the power grid. The outlet called it a bipartisan bill that would add much-needed regulation of data centers, though some politicians believe it may also encourage more construction. Mashable noted that Congress was returning to Washington that week.

Pete Sikora of New York Communities for Change spoke for the protesters, calling data centers enormous energy hogs that use large amounts of water and power. He said they produce huge amounts of pollution, including water pollution, because the facilities use water and pollute it. He added that they also cause air pollution from the gas turbines used to power them. The protesters argue that the projects would increase energy use, water use and pollution.

Supporters of expansion say more data center capacity is needed to meet growing demand for AI technologies and to keep the United States competitive. Eyewitness News contacted Schumer's office for comment and had not received a response when the story was published. Mashable's piece was an opinion column, and its writer, John Casey, argued that restrictions could slow the rollout of AI products and that companies might shift blame onto lawmakers. He also wrote that data centers can bring economic benefits if technology companies invest in the communities that host them.

The political backdrop, as Mashable tells it, is last week's midterm elections, which it called sweeping and history-making. It said voters sent a message to the AI industry to stop building data centers, and across the country local communities are pushing to stop, restrict or set conditions on development. Many Democrats campaigned on limiting data center development, responding to voter worries about electricity costs and water use. Citing Reuters, Mashable reported that some Democrats believe provisions in the bill could encourage more data centers, which would leave incoming lawmakers explaining why their campaign promises no longer apply. Mashable also linked to a report that voters approved more than 40 measures to slow or ban data center growth, and noted that one town voted yes on data centers.

stories.Headline: State Superintendent Tony Thurmond Convenes Summit on AI in Education, Emphasizes Innovation, Student Safety, and Educator Leadership
stories.Summary:
State Superintendent of Public Instruction Tony Thurmond convened educators, students, school district leaders and technology experts in Sacramento to examine the opportunities and challenges artificial intelligence presents for California schools. The event was called the AI & Education Innovation Summit: Moving the Needle for California Students. It was held on a day that the Van Nuys News Press dated November 9, 2026, and it was streamed online for anyone who wanted to watch. The summit looked at how emerging technologies can support literacy and mathematics instruction and prepare students for a changing workforce.

Speakers also took up questions about student privacy, safety and equity, along with the role of educators in an increasingly AI-driven world. Thurmond was joined by school administrators, school information technology staff, teachers and students. Representatives came from CodeAI, Microsoft, Nvidia, Google, Digital Promise, Amira Learning, Carnegie Learning, Curriculum Associates and the Center for Outcomes Based Contracting. The summit was described as reflecting a balanced state approach, one that explores AI's potential to support student achievement while recognizing the need for safeguards, equitable access, educator involvement and accountability for results.

Thurmond said California has an opportunity to lead the nation in showing how AI can be used responsibly to strengthen teaching and learning. He said innovation cannot come at the expense of student safety, privacy or the human connections that are essential to education. In his words, the state must be thoughtful about when and how the tools are used, keep educators at the center of instructional decisions, and demand evidence that technology is actually improving student outcomes. He added that the goal is not simply to bring more AI into classrooms, but to make sure any technology introduced serves students, supports teachers and expands opportunity for all.

The summit is part of wider state work on a framework for AI use in K-12 education. Senate Bill 1288, sponsored by Thurmond, established a statewide AI working group. That group is charged with developing guidance and a model policy for local educational agencies. The work is meant to help schools handle emerging technologies while addressing student privacy, data security, academic integrity and the appropriate role of AI in teaching and learning. For more information, the announcement points readers to the California Department of Education's Artificial Intelligence Guide.

A separate event in Orange County showed students taking part in AI work. The Orange County Department of Education held its third annual Student AI Convening on Nov. 6 at the OCDE Conference Center in Costa Mesa. About 100 middle and high school students attended, along with 20 adults including educators, parents and community members. The event was designed and led by students, and it featured an opening keynote, six interactive breakout sessions and a closing panel.

Participants explored machine learning, AI-powered study tools, educational games, computer programming and responsible technology use. Denise Duong of Fountain Valley High School led a workshop on machine learning using Teachable Machine, a web-based tool for building AI models without coding experience. Laguna Beach High School student Ollie Rankin presented Storyscape, an educational game meant to help students develop their writing skills. Branson Lewis and Dean LaDuke of Legacy Magnet Academy in the Tustin Unified School District led a session on responsible AI use that introduced a learning tool called Clyde AI.

Wes Kriesel, OCDE's AI education lead, said the students did not just attend but led. He said that when builders on the closing panel were asked what building taught them, they spoke of pushing through frustration, staying up until 4 a.m. to finish a game, and believing in themselves. He also recalled one student's remark that a person in motion beats a person at rest, even if that person is a hundred times smarter. The convening extends OCDE's Student AI Network, which connects middle and high school students across the county, and students in grades seven through 12 can learn more at ai-student-network.web.app.

stories.Headline: Nvidia spy scandal revives push to write China chip export limits into the defense bill
stories.Summary:
Reports that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had a relationship with a woman U.S. officials suspect of working for Chinese intelligence have given Washington's chip hawks a fresh argument, and they are pressing it in this year's defense bill. Lawmakers and advocates told Reuters that Congress is now more likely to pass limits on China's access to AI chips, with three measures possibly headed into the National Defense Authorization Act for fiscal 2027. On Monday, Nov. 9, House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said he strongly supports chip restrictions in the final bill, after a classified briefing for congressional leaders. The woman is Alice Huang, a former executive at Megaspeed, one of Nvidia's big Southeast Asian customers, and she has not been charged. Huang has admitted being unfaithful to his wife, and Nvidia's board has opened an investigation into whether he was targeted by foreign intelligence.

The three measures already sit in the Senate's manager's package for the defense bill, after the House Foreign Affairs Committee advanced all of them earlier this year. The AI Overwatch Act would treat AI chip sales to adversary nations much like arms sales: Commerce would have to notify two congressional committees at least 30 days before licensing chips such as Nvidia's H200, and Congress could block a sale by joint resolution. Blackwell-class chips would face mandatory denial, and the House text would end existing licenses for covered exports. The Chip Security Act would require companies to track their chips to fight smuggling, and its House version passed committee unanimously.

The MATCH Act would push U.S. allies to restrict more chipmaking equipment sales to China. Senators Elizabeth Warren and Jim Banks said in a joint statement that Huang's relationship with a suspected spy makes the national security concerns even more urgent, and they urged Congress to pass the AI Overwatch Act. Nvidia declined to comment and says it follows export laws, while its board says it has no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised. China's foreign ministry calls the spying allegation unsubstantiated.

The White House did not comment on the bills, though The Information reported that its officials shared feedback with congressional staff in late October. President Donald Trump has backed Huang, calling him an amazing guy and saying Huang told him he had no idea the woman was a spy. Congress has been here before: a similar Senate provision, the GAIN AI Act, was dropped from last year's final defense bill after lobbying by the White House and Nvidia. A former congressional staffer told Reuters that Nvidia is the biggest opponent of the Chip Security and AI Overwatch Acts, and an industry group that counts Nvidia as a member also opposes them.

If the provisions are dropped again, they would return to a Congress run by Democrats from Jan. 3, with chip hawks such as Chris Coons and Warren in line for key chairmanships. Nvidia's licensed H200 sales to China were under 1% of data center revenue last quarter, so a congressional veto would mainly cap future sales. Huang was asked to give House Republican chairmen a closed-door briefing on Nov. 18, and Nvidia reports third-quarter results on Nov. 17. Nvidia shares fell about 5% on Monday, more than 20% below their peak a month earlier.

stories.Headline: Sarvam AI Appoints Ex-Google Cloud India MD Sashikumar Sreedharan as President and CBO
stories.Summary:
Indian AI startup Sarvam AI has appointed Sashikumar Sreedharan, who until recently was Managing Director of Google Cloud India, as its President and Chief Business Officer. The announcement was reported on November 9, 2026, and he will also join the company's board of directors. Sreedharan will lead Sarvam's business across enterprises and government institutions, and will oversee its work with digital-native companies, developers and partners. His remit also covers marketing, finance, forward-deployed engineering, service delivery and commercial operations.

The articles differ slightly on his background, though both describe a long career in technology. One puts his experience at more than three decades, while another says roughly 35 years. Before Google he led Microsoft India's enterprise business as Managing Director for more than five years, and one report adds earlier stints at IBM, Wipro and Happiest Minds Technologies. Sarvam says more than 100 enterprises and government institutions are already building with its full-stack AI offering, and the hire comes as it tries to widen that base.

In a statement on his appointment, Sreedharan said India should be a maker of the intelligence the world runs on, and that joining Sarvam was a commitment to that opportunity. He said he looks forward to working with the team and customers on products that become part of how industries and governments operate. Sarvam said its next phase of growth will focus on advancing its research, developing products for global markets and scaling its operations. The company is also making enterprise ownership of AI central to its strategy, keeping enterprise data, models and agents inside organisations so they retain control over their AI systems and the value those systems create.

Sarvam was founded in 2023 by Pratyush Kumar and Vivek Raghavan, and it builds foundational AI models, computing infrastructure and enterprise applications. It is introducing new products including Sarvam 105B, Sarvam Vision 2.1, Saaras V4 and Bulbul V4 Flash. Earlier this year it raised $234 million in the first close of a $300 million Series B round, which valued the company at $1.5 billion. Investors include HCLTech, Bessemer Venture Partners, Khosla Ventures and Peak XV Partners. Sarvam also believes enterprise requirements will feed its research, with industry demands driving research and breakthroughs helping to create new industries.

stories.Headline: Samsung, SK hynix Jump Over 5% in Premarket as U.S. Chip Stocks Rebound
stories.Summary:
Samsung Electronics and SK hynix both rose more than 5% in premarket trading on Nextrade on the 10th, reclaiming the 200,000-won and 1.2 million-won levels respectively. As of 8:12 a.m., SK hynix traded at 1.213 million won, up 6.78% from the previous session. Samsung Electronics stood at 201,000 won, a gain of 5.85%. The rise followed bargain hunting in U.S. chip stocks overnight and a steep drop in oil prices.

On Wall Street the day before, all three major indexes climbed more than 2%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average closed at 52,389.75, up 2.15%, and the S&P 500 ended at 7,549.94, up 2.35%. The Nasdaq Composite finished at 25,253.14, up 2.74%. Chip stocks that had fallen sharply the previous week led the rebound, with AMD up 13.26%, Marvell Technology up 9.49%, Broadcom up 8.78% and Micron Technology up 6.25%. SK hynix's American depositary receipts gained 5.53%, and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index, which had dropped more than 12% in a single session on the 5th, rose nearly 7%.

Nvidia fell 4.27% amid controversy surrounding Chief Executive Jensen Huang. The stock slid as low as $170.24 during the session, a decline of as much as 8.79%. Its closing market value shrank by about $192.1 billion, roughly 258 trillion won, in one day. Nvidia's board has maintained that no leak of confidential information or breach of national security has been confirmed.

Oil prices also supported the rebound after U.S. President Donald Trump said the chances of large-scale additional strikes on Iran were very low. That raised expectations that tensions in the Middle East would ease. West Texas Intermediate futures settled at $86.85 a barrel, down 4.38%, and Brent crude futures closed at $92.57, down 5.85%. With the December Federal Open Market Committee meeting approaching, lower oil prices fueled expectations that price pressures could ease.

Analysts said the strength in major chip and artificial intelligence stocks apart from Nvidia showed that the market is separating the controversy over Huang from the broader flow of AI investment. They see little chance that the controversy will prompt large cloud providers to delay AI investment schedules or cut orders for graphics processing units. Han Ji-young, an analyst at Kiwoom Securities, said the sharp recent correction has already priced in much of the concern about the AI industry and the earnings outlook for chipmakers. She added that easing Middle East tensions could lower the market's sensitivity to existing negatives. The U.S. consumer price index for October due this week, along with earnings from AI cloud provider CoreWeave, could become a trigger for a recovery in investor sentiment, she said.

stories.Headline: Samsung, Hyundai Motor Deepen Physical AI Alliance
stories.Summary:
Samsung Electronics hosted the "HMG Appreciation Day" for key executives of Hyundai Motor Group at its Seocheon Training Institute on Nov. 9. It was the first time Samsung Electronics has held such a large-scale invitation event for a major domestic conglomerate. Held under the theme "One Harmony Toward the Future," the gathering drew 177 people, including executives, officers and spouses from key affiliates of both groups. Samsung Electronics Vice Chairman Jun Young-hyun, who heads the Device Solutions Unit, and Hyundai Motor Group Vice Chair Chang Jae-hoon were among those present. The articles describe the move as a "one team" step to secure leadership in future advanced industries.

Other Samsung attendees included Roh Tae-moon, head of the Device eXperience Unit, Park Yong-in of System LSI, Han Jin-man of the Foundry Business, Samsung Display President Lee Chung, Samsung SDI President Choi Joo-sun and Samsung Electro-Mechanics President Chang Duck-hyun. From Hyundai Motor Group, Seo Gang-hyun, president of planning and coordination at Hyundai Motor Company, Manfred Harrer, head of the Hyundai Motor and Kia R&D Division, and Park Min-woo, head of the Advanced Vehicle Platform Division, took part. The two groups are widening cooperation that already covers semiconductors, batteries and automotive electronics to robots and artificial intelligence. The plan combines the electronics and semiconductor strengths of one group with the automotive strengths of the other to move first in future mobility and physical AI markets. Analysts cited in the report say pairing Samsung's semiconductor, sensor and battery technologies with Hyundai's robotics and autonomous driving could strengthen its future mobility competitiveness.

In his welcoming speech, Jun called the two groups reliable partners who have written the history of South Korean industry together. He said he hoped Hyundai's vision for future mobility would meet Samsung's technology, which spans components to finished products, to open up wide possibilities. Chang said the two sides are extending cooperation beyond automotive electronics, audio and batteries into future fields such as robots and energy. He added that bringing together the strengths each group built over three generations will create greater synergy.

The cooperation has already produced concrete business results. Samsung Electronics has agreed to supply its Exynos Auto V920 in-vehicle infotainment chip to Hyundai Motor Company. Samsung SDI signed its first long-term electric vehicle battery supply contract with Hyundai Motor Company in 2023, and its high-nickel NCA prismatic batteries will go into Kia's compact electric SUV EV and Hyundai's Ioniq 3. Samsung SDI's prismatic batteries will also be used in the GV90, the flagship electric SUV from Hyundai's premium brand Genesis. Samsung SDI and Hyundai Motor and Kia have also begun jointly developing batteries made only for robots.

The ties between the two groups run back through three generations. In 1985, Samsung founder Lee Byung-chull attended the 70th birthday banquet of Hyundai founder Chung Ju-yung despite illness and gave him a white porcelain piece he had chosen himself. In 2001, the late Samsung Chairman Lee Kun-hee met privately with then Hyundai and Kia Motors Chairman Chung Mong-koo at Seungjiwon, Samsung's guesthouse. That same year Samsung began buying Hyundai's Equus luxury sedan as company cars for affiliate presidents, and Hyundai Motor Group partly adopted Samsung Cards for corporate card use. Samsung Electronics Executive Chairman Lee Jae-yong and Hyundai Motor Group Executive Chair Euisun Chung met twice in 2020, at Samsung SDI's Cheonan plant and Hyundai's Namyang Research and Development Center, to discuss future mobility cooperation including next-generation electric vehicle batteries.

Separately, Nvidia opened its "Nvidia AI Day Seoul 2026" at COEX in Seoul's Gangnam District on Monday for a two-day run. It announced wider physical AI cooperation with South Korean companies including Hyundai Motor Group, Doosan, SK Hynix and LG Electronics. With Hyundai Motor Group, Nvidia is jointly developing robot simulation for automotive manufacturing processes using its Omniverse and Isaac platforms. Kakao Mobility signed a memorandum of understanding with Nvidia on Level 4 autonomous driving and plans to adopt a compute unit built on two DRIVE AGX Thor chips, with the technology first going into Kia's purpose-built vehicle models.

stories.Headline: What California’s new law means for legal teams using AI and whether other states could follow suit
stories.Summary:
California has become the first state to regulate, by statute, how attorneys use artificial intelligence, through Senate Bill 574, which takes effect January 1, 2027. Senator Tom Umberg, chair of the state's Senate Judiciary Committee, introduced the bill in February 2025. After two rounds of amendments in the Senate and four in the Assembly, it passed both chambers on the last day of the session. Governor Gavin Newsom signed it on September 30, 2026.

The law's central rule is that attorneys may use generative AI to assist in the practice of law but may not hand the practice of law over to it. It also sets limits for arbitrators and tightens citation rules for filings in California courts, whether or not AI was involved. Attorneys cannot enter confidential or personal identifying information into an AI system unless access is limited to them and their authorized people. They must verify AI output and correct errors before relying on it, and must disclose AI use on documents submitted to a court. Every citation in a filing must be personally verified by the responsible attorney, and arbitrators cannot delegate any part of their decisions to AI.

The law applies to every attorney licensed in California, including in-house counsel, and its citation rule reaches anyone filing in a California court. Courts can sanction attorneys and their firms, and firms are generally responsible for violations by their lawyers and staff. Attorneys usually receive 21 days to withdraw or fix a challenged filing before sanctions apply. The bill does not spell out separate penalties for the other duties. An earlier version required attorneys to read every cited source personally, but lawmakers removed that requirement before passage.

The law leaves several points unsettled. It does not draw a firm line between assisting and delegating, nor say which AI tools trigger a disclosure or what a disclosure should contain. It also does not say which attorney is responsible for citations on large filings with many contributors, leaving firms to decide. The State Bar first issued AI guidance for attorneys in 2023, and the Judicial Council followed in 2025 with rules for judges and court staff. In May 2026 the Bar updated its guidance to address agentic AI, which can carry out tasks with little human direction.

Other states may act, though most state supreme courts regulate the practice of law, so future rules are more likely to come from courts than legislatures. New York's court system adopted a statewide rule on attorney AI use in June 2026, while similar disclosure bills in its legislature have stalled in committee. The Florida Supreme Court updated its practice rules so that signing a filing certifies its cited authorities exist and are cited accurately. The Illinois Supreme Court decided its existing rules were sufficient and does not require disclosure of AI use if lawyers review the output. Citation verification appears the most likely rule to spread, while disclosure is where states are expected to keep disagreeing.

stories.Headline: Meta, TikTok join Google to push back on Indonesia’s planned AI copyright law revisions
stories.Summary:
Indonesia's government has proposed revisions to its copyright law that would require digital platforms to pay publishers for displaying news content and would set rules for artificial intelligence. Google, Meta and TikTok have each pushed back against the proposals in parliamentary hearings. If the bill passes, Indonesia would become the first country in Southeast Asia to incorporate AI into its copyright law, as governments worldwide struggle with how the technology affects copyright rules. Reuters first reported the planned revisions in July, citing a draft of the bill. The hearing at which the companies spoke took place on Wednesday, November 11, 2026, in Jakarta.

The core dispute concerns compensation for news. Under the proposal, platforms would have to pay compensation for showing links to news content from publishers. Agung Pamungkas, Google's Indonesia government affairs and public policy manager, told the hearing that this requirement would limit Indonesians' access to news. Berni Moestafa, Meta's public policy head in Indonesia, said that publishers could lose readership traffic as well as potential advertising and subscription revenue. He argued that directing readers to an article differs from reproducing or republishing the article itself.

On AI, TikTok's head of public policy in Indonesia, Noudhy Valdryno, told lawmakers that disclosure requirements should not apply where AI is used only in an assistive capacity rather than to fully create content. He also urged lawmakers to preserve safe-harbour protections. He said platforms cannot reliably determine copyright ownership or licences, which is the reason he gave for keeping those protections. The articles do not say which lawmakers or ministry officials responded to these arguments, nor whether any changes to the draft have been made since the hearing.

The articles give little further background beyond the July draft. They describe the use of human-created work to train AI models as one of the issues governments are grappling with globally. They do not describe the existing wording of Indonesia's copyright law or the history of the revision effort. The articles also do not say when the bill is expected to be voted on or what steps would follow its passage.

stories.Headline: Governor Hochul Declares NY Will Lead the Nation in AI Science and Safety; Launches New Research Institute
stories.Summary:
Governor Kathy Hochul launched the New York Center for AI Responsibility and Research, based at State University of New York's Binghamton University, to advance AI science and safety. The announcement was made on November 10, 2026, and the Center is meant to bring together academic expertise to advance AI safety research, accelerate scientific discovery, and independently test advanced AI systems for safety and security. The Center will convene more than 80 leading scientists from colleges and research institutions across New York State who have expertise in AI safety, security and computer science. It is supported by Empire AI, Governor Hochul's $500 million public-private initiative to drive AI research for public good.

Greg Morrisett of Cornell Tech and Jeannette Wing of Columbia University will serve as interim co-directors of the Center. The Center's work will include independent testing of frontier AI systems, foundational scientific research, and the training of a new generation of AI safety experts. One of its first objectives is a national recruiting effort for experts in areas such as formal methods and verification, interpretability and alignment, and biosecurity. The Center will also give state officials objective evidence to inform policy decisions about AI safety and accountability. Separately, the state's Office of Digital Innovation, Governance, Integrity, and Trust (DIGIT) opened an online portal for large frontier AI developers to register by January 1, 2027.

Governor Hochul said that while the federal government fails to act, New York is leading the way on AI safety and holding big tech accountable. Tom Secunda, Empire AI Board Chair, said independent testing will help researchers understand what increasingly powerful systems can do and how to use them safely. SUNY Chancellor John B. King Jr. said SUNY would help ensure New York State is a national and global leader in advancing AI safety and security. Binghamton University President Anne D'Alleva thanked Governor Hochul and Secunda, a Binghamton alumnus and Bloomberg LP co-founder, for their support. The New York State Department of Financial Services Acting Superintendent, Kaitlin Asrow, said DFS is leading implementation of the RAISE Act through the DIGIT Office.

The RAISE Act requires large frontier AI developers to register with the state and meet strict safety, transparency and reporting standards. New York's requirement to report any critical safety incident within 72 hours is the strongest in the nation, according to the state. Beginning in January, large frontier developers must publish safety frameworks on their websites, and all frontier developers must report critical safety incidents and publish model transparency reports. The Center was first announced in January with a $30 million philanthropic gift from a group of donors led by Tom Secunda, along with a $25 million research investment from SUNY and operating capital from New York State. The announcement builds on Governor Hochul's broader AI safety agenda, which includes implementation of the RAISE Act.

At the state's request, the Center will be able to provide expertise, assessments and evidence to help inform state policymaking and oversight of frontier AI developers. The Center will coordinate with DIGIT to begin reviewing developers' published safety frameworks and recommending ways to strengthen requirements. Governor Hochul said that in the coming months she will continue exploring ways to build on the RAISE Act. SUNY describes itself as the largest comprehensive system of higher education in the United States, with 64 colleges and universities. The system's research expenditures were nearly $1.5 billion in fiscal year 2025.

stories.Headline: ‘AI-generated’ book purchase case: DMK’s Paranthamen moves Madras High Court seeking registration of FIR by DVAC
stories.Summary:
On November 10, 2026, the Madras High Court's Madurai Bench, comprising Justices G.R. Swaminathan and M.D. Sumathi, directed the Directorate of Vigilance and Anti Corruption (DVAC) to immediately register a First Information Report over alleged fraudulent procurement of books for public libraries across Tamil Nadu. The Bench also flagged fake and AI-generated books in public libraries and ordered their removal. It further froze the bank accounts of Agal Vilakku Publication, its proprietor Mohan and others involved in the alleged scam. The order followed a writ petition filed by I. Paranthamen, joint secretary of the DMK Legal Wing, seeking a direction for the FIR.

The Bench ordered the State government to initiate disciplinary action, including suspension, against officials responsible for the fraudulent procurement. It directed authorities to identify the officials involved, remove suspect books and disclose procurement expenditure. The Court observed that compliance with its June 2024 transparency directions could have prevented the scam. The matter is to be heard next on November 11.

The Bench said that crores of rupees had gone out of the public exchequer and that such a crime could not have taken place without the active involvement of government servants. It said that both the BNS provisions and the Prevention of Corruption Act were attracted. The Court also held that AI-generated and plagiarised books could fall within the expression "doubtful taste" under the Tamil Nadu Public Libraries Rules, 1950. It noted that the State Public Prosecutor, R. John Sathyan, had asked for time for the DVAC to complete its detailed enquiry, and when asked, did not dispute that a crime had been committed.

Paranthamen's affidavit, filed through advocate A. Damodaran, said the Periyar Arivulagam library in Coimbatore cost ₹300 crore, including ₹50 crore for procurement of books. The Tamil Nadu government had constituted a 112-member book recommendation committee on November 5, 2025, and purchase orders were issued on February 2, 2026. The library was inaugurated on October 16, 2026, after which a controversy erupted over the quality of the books. Writer Perumal Murugan, a member of the committee, wrote an article on November 6, 2026, saying the library was filled with "AI generated" books carrying fictitious author names.

Paranthamen said he lodged a complaint with the DVAC on November 7, 2026, but the agency had neither registered an FIR nor informed him of a preliminary inquiry. In his complaint, he said Agalvilakku Publications and Phoenix Publications appeared to have supplied books generated using AI tools, with ISBNs obtained in bulk blocks rather than title-wise. The Court recorded that the State government had acknowledged serious irregularities, that IAS officer Jayanthi had been relieved as Director of Public Libraries, and that existing procurement orders had been cancelled. The DVAC had begun a detailed enquiry on November 7, 2026, on a complaint lodged by the School Education department on November 6, 2026.

stories.Headline: AI Debt Under Pressure: Credit Spreads Widen as Democrats Target AI Regulation - News and Statistics
stories.Summary:
Investors in the bond market have grown more cautious about debt tied to the artificial intelligence boom, Reuters reported, as worries mount that a Democrat-controlled Congress will try to slow AI investment and data center growth. During last Thursday's stock-market selloff, US high-yield credit spreads reached 348 basis points, according to ICE BofA US Corporate Index data, the widest level since May 2025. By Friday those spreads had tightened to 342 basis points. Larry Holzenthaler, a senior portfolio manager at Catalyst Funds in New York, said the market was clearly nervous and that further swings in high yield and loans would not be a surprise. Investment-grade spreads stood at 93 basis points last Thursday, compared with 91 the session before.

Democrats are set to take control of Congress in January and intend to introduce a large batch of legislation aimed at AI systems and data center development. Republican President Donald Trump has repeatedly rejected calls for mandatory AI rules. After his party suffered a historic midterm defeat over the weekend, however, he indicated a willingness to consider safeguards. Analysts said that a broader rethink of AI-related risk could widen credit spreads across both high-yield and investment-grade debt. Ali Hassan, a portfolio manager at Thornburg Investment Management, said investor appetite has grown more careful and selective.

Political and regulatory scrutiny is driving a reassessment of credits across the AI supply chain, from developers to contractors to suppliers, Hassan said. Data center bonds, heavily represented in the BB and single-B tiers of the junk bond market, have faced renewed strain in recent weeks, especially amid the technology selloff. Analysts said single-B spreads widened 35 basis points to 367 basis points, driving the high-yield deterioration and reaching their highest levels since March. Peter Yanulis, a multi-asset portfolio manager at Loomis Sayles, said any slowdown in the AI buildout would produce a second-order effect on power producers, electrical contractors, equipment makers and data center developers.

The pressure is visible in individual bonds. On November 5, Galaxy Helios Data Center bonds dropped to 89.25 cents on the dollar, pushing yields to 13% from the 9.875% offered when Galaxy Digital's wholly owned unit sold the B+ rated debt in late July. The bonds' price decline and the rise in yield show how quickly investors have repriced debt linked to data center construction. Analysts have pointed to the broader technology selloff as the backdrop for the strain. Solid corporate fundamentals remain supportive, according to analysts and portfolio managers, even as the risk outlook shifts.

stories.Headline: SoftBank swings to first-half loss as AI ambitions face fresh setbacks
stories.Summary:
SoftBank Group reported a first-half net loss on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, after swinging from profit, according to the articles. The company said it faces growing uncertainty over its ambitious artificial intelligence strategy, following political setbacks in the United States and regulatory hurdles in China. One specific setback mentioned is that China blocked SoftBank's $5.4 billion deal to acquire ABB's robotics division. The articles frame the loss as a sign that the company's AI hopes are running into fresh obstacles.

The articles say the setbacks touch several parts of SoftBank's growth plan, including its investments in robotics and data centers. A U.S. election has raised questions about the company's data center plans. The robotics deal, which would have added a major industrial automation business, is now blocked by Beijing. Investors are watching closely to see whether the artificial intelligence strategy can still deliver the growth the company has promised.

The articles identify SoftBank Group as the company responsible for the strategy and the reported loss, with its reporting covered by Nikkei Asia's Tsubasa Suruga. The reporting describes the company's position as one of increasing uncertainty rather than quoting specific executive statements on the outlook. The articles also note that investors are focused on whether the AI growth strategy succeeds. Beyond the blocked robotics deal and the data center questions, the articles do not give further detail on the company's response.

The broader context is that SoftBank has tied much of its recent expansion to artificial intelligence, through stakes in OpenAI and related infrastructure projects. The articles also report that SoftBank's shares fell 11 percent after OpenAI said it would not go public this year. What happens next is not specified in the articles beyond continued investor attention to the strategy.

stories.Headline: Georgia students raise privacy concerns over AI smart glasses
stories.Summary:
Meta's AI-powered smart glasses can translate conversations, send texts, take calls and record video, and concerns are growing about people being recorded without their knowledge as the technology spreads. The glasses look like traditional eyewear but have built-in cameras, and an LED light is designed to indicate when recording is underway. Georgia Tech students told WSB-TV they are uncomfortable with how easily someone could record them without knowing it. Earlier this year, University of Georgia police investigated complaints from students who said people wearing smart glasses secretly filmed them on campus.

Under Georgia and federal law, recording people in public places is generally legal because there is no expectation of privacy. Recording in private spaces, including restrooms, locker rooms or private homes, can bring criminal or civil consequences. Smart glasses and other personal electronic devices are banned in Georgia schools under a law that took effect this year. The technology could let students photograph tests, according to Georgia Schools Superintendent-elect Dr. Lydia Powell, who said it could also be used to record others in restrooms.

Kade Crockford, director of the ACLU's Technology and Justice Programs, said people still expect some level of privacy and anonymity in public spaces. Privacy advocates also worry that facial recognition could be added to the glasses, and the ACLU says that could let wearers covertly identify people and store that information. Meta acknowledges it is exploring facial recognition but says no final decision has been made. According to Meta, the recording indicator light cannot be turned off or disabled, and if it is blocked, the camera will not work.

Elsewhere, misuse of the technology has drawn charges. This summer in Boston, a registered sex offender was charged with using camera-equipped sunglasses to record children changing at a playground. In June, Milton police arrested Christopher Hall on felony eavesdropping and surveillance charges after a mother found smart glasses on top of her car, pointed toward her 13-year-old daughter's bedroom window. Hall's friend told Channel 2 that he believed there was an innocent explanation, saying Hall may have gotten drunk at a party and left the glasses behind.

stories.Headline: TSMC October revenue hits record $17.81 billion
stories.Summary:
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, known as TSMC, reported its highest-ever monthly revenue for October, reaching about $17.81 billion. The figure was up 59.7 per cent from a year earlier and rose 14.7 per cent from September. The world's largest contract chipmaker posted consolidated revenue of NT 586.89 billion for the month. October's total beat the company's previous monthly record of $15.63 billion, set in August.

Revenue for January through October totaled $140 billion, a 43.3 per cent increase over the same stretch last year. The company credited the growth to strong demand for advanced semiconductors, particularly chips used in artificial intelligence infrastructure. Its 2-nanometre technology has entered commercial production and is contributing to sales. High-performance computing rose 22 per cent from the previous quarter and now makes up 68 per cent of total revenue, while the 2nm process accounted for 8 per cent of wafer revenue in the third quarter.

TSMC also raised its full-year 2026 revenue growth forecast to about 44 per cent in US dollar terms, up from an earlier projection of slightly above 40 per cent. The company attributed the revision to robust demand for its advanced manufacturing processes during its October earnings conference. For the fourth quarter, it expects consolidated revenue between $52.3 billion and $54.3 billion. The company's shares closed 2.24 per cent higher on the Taiwan Stock Exchange on November 10.

The results come as the chipmaker's customers face their own scrutiny. TSMC manufactures chips for several technology companies, including NVIDIA, whose shares fell 4.3 per cent on November 9, wiping out about $190 billion in market value according to Reuters. That drop followed reports of an investigation involving NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang and his relationship with an accused Chinese spy, as well as a proposed shareholder lawsuit. The articles do not say how these developments will affect TSMC's future orders.

stories.Headline: Databricks' new Genie tool is the latest sign of the AI industry's full court press for knowledge workers
stories.Summary:
Databricks, a San Francisco data and AI company, announced on Wednesday, November 11, 2026, a second generation of its Genie assistant that operates as an always-on, autonomous agent for enterprise work. Users can give Genie a goal, and it takes ownership of the work, delegates to subagents, tracks progress, follows up on missing inputs, and reaches out when a person needs to make a decision. A new priority inbox highlights items needing attention, and Genie emails users when they are away. The launch came a day after Anthropic released its own set of AI productivity tools aimed at corporate users. Databricks CEO Ali Ghodsi said the agents run in the background at all times.

The new Genie is grounded in Genie Ontology, which captures a company's horizontal context, including definitions, metrics, people and processes, and keeps it current as the business changes. Genie Search expands to more than 100 enterprise data sources, including Google Drive, Jira and Confluence, and indexes content in place without moving or copying it. Genie runs within a company's existing Databricks environment and is governed by Unity Catalog and Unity Gateway, so every action stays within existing controls. Genie now runs in autonomous mode on its own compute, and every action is fully auditable. Ontology Manager, a new feature, lets teams manage and govern business context.

Ghodsi, who co-founded and leads Databricks, said Genie has made him a "10x more productive CEO" and that he uses it every hour of the day. He said it can work because it knows how the company operates, including what counts as revenue and which numbers are official. Ghodsi also said Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is an amazing CEO and should remain in that role after the revelation of Huang's extramarital affair with a woman U.S. officials believe to be a spy for China. Ghodsi said he thinks the industry will weather the storm. Databricks, still privately held, raised $5 billion at a $190 billion valuation in August.

The industry is pushing harder into corporate work because AI has transformed software programming but remains experimental in other business functions where returns are less clear. Anthropic's prospectus for its initial public offering said the work of knowledge workers represented more than $40 trillion in economic value globally in 2025. Anthropic's IPO, expected the following week, could value the company at $1.4 trillion, and many in the industry are watching it closely. Anthropic's tools include a spreadsheet application that competes with Microsoft Excel and Google Sheets, and a feature that lets Claude join video calls. Some believe recent advances in AI agents and model capabilities may let the technology capture a broader part of the market.

stories.Headline: Fed’s Bowman Warns of Stock Correction If AI Bets Don’t Pan Out
stories.Summary:
Federal Reserve Governor Michelle Bowman warned in written remarks delivered Tuesday local time at the Council on Foreign Relations in Washington that U.S. stock valuations could face a sharp correction if returns on artificial intelligence investments fail to meet expectations. She also singled out a sharp rise in private long-term interest rates as another potential trigger. The same day, the U.S. Department of Labor reported that October core consumer price index rose 0.3% month-over-month, above market expectations. Bowman said weakening stock prices could erode consumer spending, and rising borrowing costs would squeeze the housing market and small-business investment. She said that inflation persistence has exceeded her earlier assessment and that there is still work to do to bring inflation back to the 2% target.

Bowman said that persistent inflation pressure and tightening labor market conditions left her open to another rate hike at the December meeting. The Fed held rates steady at its October 27-28 meeting after a 25-basis-point hike in September, the first since 2023. Bowman said she supported holding rates steady last month to give policymakers time to assess the transmission of the September hike to the real economy. Governor Christopher Waller argued in a London speech that December should seriously consider a 50-basis-point hike if inflation data remain hot. Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan, who holds a vote this year, said in Houston that the Federal Open Market Committee needs at least two more 25-basis-point hikes.

Bowman also expressed concern about AI-related debt, which she said is expected to exceed $800 billion this year in corporate bonds, private credit and project finance. She highlighted how large technology companies and hyperscalers use their strong credit ratings to enable smaller, higher-risk companies to pledge assets as collateral for data centers and accelerated computing equipment. She noted that cloud giants and chip designers have made equity investments in smaller companies that buy their products, creating what she called the appearance of revolving financing. She warned that once markets come under pressure, this web of capital linkages could amplify risk transmission.

The officials' hawkish remarks and hot inflation data pushed U.S. Treasury yields higher across the board. The 2-year yield surged 19 basis points to 4.75% on the day, its largest single-day increase since the reciprocal tariff measures in April 2025 triggered global market turmoil. Federal funds rate futures showed investors betting on a 25-basis-point hike in December and another in January, while Christopher Hodge of Natixis said the data are not strong enough to justify a 50-basis-point hike. Christopher Phelan, chairman of the White House Council of Economic Advisers, publicly opposed the aggressive approach, saying there is no reason to raise rates by 50 basis points in December. Before the December meeting, Fed officials will still receive one employment report and full inflation data.

stories.Headline: Mashup Ventures Raises 25.9 Billion Won Fund for AI, Deep Tech Startups
stories.Summary:
Seoul-based early-stage investor Mashup Ventures said on November 11, 2026, that it has closed a 25.9 billion won ($17.6 million) fund, called Mashup First Believer Venture Investment Fund No. 5, without government policy money. The firm will use the fund to back promising startups in artificial intelligence and deep tech. Partners at Mashup Ventures are its largest contributors, and the fund also drew money from successful founders, startups, information technology and manufacturing companies, and financial institutions. The fund has a 10-year life and will focus on pre-seed companies, whose founders are still preparing to launch, and seed-stage companies, which are raising their first outside capital.

Its main investment areas are physical AI, vertical AI tailored to specific industries, energy and aerospace. The firm plans to expand its deep tech investments under Chief Investment Officer Park Eun-woo, who previously led global expansion as chief strategy officer at autonomous drone company Nearthlab. Mashup Ventures was led by Lee Taek-kyung, a co-founder of Daum, and has invested in about 220 companies since 2013, being the first institutional investor in 87% of them. Its portfolio includes Bucketplace, operator of the interior design platform Ohou, as well as MyRealTrip, Remember & Company, Wrtn Technologies and ScatterLab. More recently it has widened its scope to space, advanced materials and energy, with investments in O&B Space, NanoForge AI and Biologen.

The firm has also added specialists to strengthen its capacity to invest in technology startups. This year it recruited AI partner Yang Sung-min, a former engineer who has founded and sold companies, and venture partner Lee Sang-won, a co-founder of Silicon Valley deep tech company Quixo. The two will review the technology of early-stage portfolio companies and support product development and overseas expansion. Lee said the firm believed in founders who jumped into an uncertain market even as the paradigm shifted from the internet to mobile. He added that with AI now moving into robotics, energy and space, the firm intends to be the first investor to back founders before their technology is proven.

Separately, a Proximal Ventures fund was reported on November 10, 2026, by TechCrunch. Its founder, Sahir Raoof, a former SignalFire investor, raised $27.5 million for his first solo VC fund. The firm is betting that AI can automate the tools, infrastructure and services that support drug development, which pharmaceutical companies have historically outsourced. Proximal plans to write checks from $500,000 to $1.5 million to pre-seed and seed-stage startups, and has already backed seven startups.

stories.Headline: The AI Regulation Fight Is About Speed. It Should Be About Measurement
stories.Summary:
Washington is split between those who want AI development slowed and those who want the United States to stay ahead of China, but two Wharton-affiliated scholars, Burcu Esmer and N. Bugra Ozel, argue the more pressing need is measurement. They say the core problem is that firms, regulators, investors, and the public lack a reliable system for identifying, comparing, and tracing AI's consequences. In September, Anthropic and Accenture each said they expect to invest at least $1 billion over five years in embedded evaluation, but Anthropic acknowledged that no standards govern what outside evaluators may see or how they report. Google DeepMind's CEO, Demis Hassabis, has proposed a U.S. oversight body modeled on FINRA, though the authors note that such a body would be toothless without reporting authority and direct access. Labs currently choose their own benchmarks and hold most of the underlying data.

The authors propose a narrower first federal step: a standardized harm ledger with a common reporting architecture for recording what AI systems do, whom they affect, and how often consequential failures occur. Duties would scale with size and risk, leaving most startups and research labs outside the regime. They urge Congress to pass an AI Measurement and Incident Reporting Act before the current session ends. Under that proposal, NIST's Center for AI Standards and Innovation would publish common definitions and reporting forms within a year. Frontier developers above a capability threshold would file standardized pre-release evaluations and serious-incident reports, while large hospitals, employers, and lenders would report consequential errors and outcome disparities to their existing regulators.

Independent auditors would verify the reports, and aggregate results would be public. The authors argue that delay carries two costs. First, harms accumulate unseen, and the FBI's 2025 internet-crime report, the first to include an AI section, logged 22,364 complaints and nearly $893 million in reported losses, yet it shows only that AI was mentioned, not that it caused the losses. Quieter harms such as a screened-out job applicant or a denied loan have no comparable national record. Second, delay shifts power toward leading developers, which the authors describe as some of the world's most valuable companies, giving them more wealth, lobbying capacity, and control over the evidence regulators will later need.

They point to industrialization and the years before 2008 as precedents, noting that federal child-labor limits arrived in 1938 and modern workplace-safety rules in 1970, after costs were already entrenched. Europe has already written post-market monitoring and serious-incident reporting for high-risk systems into law, and a declaration issued during UN General Assembly week shows a growing group of governments wants shared standards. The authors conclude that the first constraint on AI need not limit innovation but should limit opacity, so that the industry does not become powerful enough to define harm on its own terms. They present their case as a response to a debate they say has been framed too narrowly around speed. Their proposal, however, remains a recommendation, and the articles do not report any congressional action on it.

stories.Headline: KT Token Factory: Only Seven of 73 AI Models Run on Own Hardware as KT Plans More GPUs
stories.Summary:
KT Corp. said on its third-quarter earnings call on November 10, 2026, that it will expand its own GPU investment to produce more AI tokens for Token Factory, its enterprise AI platform. Token Factory launched on October 30 with 73 models, but only seven of them run as inference services on GPUs in KT's domestic data centers. The other 66 are global models reached through KT's partnership with the US model marketplace OpenRouter. KT did not disclose a GPU count, an investment amount or a capacity figure, which leaves enterprise buyers unable to size the production side of the business.

Park Sang-won, head of KT's AX business division, answered a KB Securities analyst's question about AX costs and Token Factory. He said KT will expand its own GPU investment to strengthen token production and, over the long term, become a domestic hub for producing and distributing tokens. He also said running models on domestically hosted infrastructure carries a significant sovereignty advantage, and that KT will grow self-hosted and brokered models in balance. Management gave no quantitative Token Factory targets on the call, though Park said KT's telecom billing capabilities could create synergy revenue for the platform.

The seven self-hosted models are KT's Midm K 3.0 Pro, Upstage's Solar Pro 4, Motif Technologies' Motif 3, Nvidia's Nemotron 3 Ultra, Google's Gemma 4 31B, Z.ai's GLM 5.3 Flash and Moonshot AI's Kimi K3, according to Digital Today. Three come from Korean developers, two from US companies and two from Chinese developers, and KT calls them sovereign AI models in a sense that describes where the model runs, not who built it. KT executive Lee Jin-hyung said the seven were chosen from widely used models in South Korea and the latest models from domestic startups. KT plans to expand the self-hosted lineup to 12 models next year, according to Digital Daily, though SBS reported about 10.

KT says running models in its data centers keeps enterprise data processing in Korea, but that argument covers only the self-hosted tier. The Korea Herald reported that most models supplied through OpenRouter process requests overseas, and KT said it will disclose each model's provider and operating region. KT applies a no-storage, no-training policy to the seven self-hosted models, and AX platform head Won Man-ho said prompts are not stored by default. Customers who need prompts for internal audits can opt in to storage and lookup.

Token Factory bills by usage, and Lee said KT generates a token detail record using a technique modeled on the call detail record that telecom billing relies on. KT applies each model's pricing, issues one consolidated bill and accepts payment in Korean won. KT says its internal testing found about 20% savings from prompt compression and about 5% from automatically switching a request to a cheaper capable model, for a target of up to 25%. KT did not disclose the criteria for those tests, and the reporting reviewed cites no independent benchmark.

KT described a hardware architecture at a September 11 briefing on the government's Modu-ui AI project that splits inference into two phases. Prefill, where the model reads the prompt, runs on GPUs, while decode, where it writes the answer token by token, runs on domestic AI chips. KT says 100 government-supplied GPUs would deliver the work of about 121 through Token Factory and that throughput rises about 31%, with prompt compression cutting input tokens by up to 80%. KT said it would start with 32 domestic AI chips and invest more as their performance improves, and the report cites no independent testing of these figures.

Because Token Factory charges by usage, every token a customer saves is a token KT does not bill. Digital Daily noted that lower token consumption can shrink KT's revenue, which is why KT is betting on margins from producing tokens itself rather than on brokerage fees. Lee said global model intermediaries typically charge about 5% and that KT's main revenue model is not fee-based. KT has named no customers and says it may disclose contracted companies after reviewing usage through December, and it has not disclosed revenue targets or paying-customer numbers.

KT is also discounting the capacity it wants to fill. A 30% promotion on usage fees for the seven self-hosted models runs through November 30 for corporate customers that completed verification and product contracts. The reports reviewed do not say what the promotion costs KT or how much of the self-hosted capacity is in use. Other carriers have chosen differently: STL Partners reports that AT&T treats tokens mainly as a cost to manage, while China Mobile's MoMA gateway offers more than 300 models. That same analysis argues that standalone gateways are hard to differentiate and that operators fare better bundling them with connectivity, compute, security and sovereignty.

stories.Headline: Hands-on experience prepares Wayne State engineers for Michigan’s AI-powered manufacturing future
stories.Summary:
Wayne State University is giving engineering students hands-on experience with robots, conveyor systems, machine vision and generative AI, and that experience is already helping graduates land jobs in the field. The work takes place in part in IntelliMake, a new research hub and pilot-scale factory being developed in partnership with Kyndryl to advance AI-driven manufacturing. Students at the James and Patricia Anderson College of Engineering learn to make manufacturing smarter, more flexible and more efficient. The article was published on November 10, 2026.

The initiative addresses a workforce challenge for Michigan, where manufacturing remains central to the economy. According to the state's AI and Workforce Plan, an estimated 75% of manufacturing jobs will require some form of upskilling as artificial intelligence and automation become more prevalent. The state estimates that responsible AI adoption could generate up to $70 billion in economic impact and support 130,000 jobs. Wayne State says preparing that workforce means giving students chances to experiment with these technologies, understand their limits and apply them to real engineering problems.

Dr. Ratna Babu Chinnam, professor and chair of industrial and systems engineering and co-director of IntelliMake, said the university is trying to create a pipeline of students who can address that need. Raj Sohmshetty, co-director of IntelliMake and instructor of IE 6000: Digital Automation, redesigned the course to combine classroom learning with hands-on work in the IntelliMake lab. Chinnam said computer science students may understand AI but do not know how to think about the real need, and that the lab bridges that gap. The article notes that traditional industrial robots follow programmed instructions and may fail when a part's position or geometry varies slightly.

The article reports that about 10 students spent substantial time in the lab during fall 2025, and several subsequently secured positions with leading companies. One recent graduate of the artificial intelligence master's program, Gokula Kumaran Kiruthiga Gopal, became an AI engineer with Panasonic. Kiruthiga Gopal said the IntelliMake experience was part of the reason she landed that position, and that Panasonic was especially interested in a factory-monitoring system her team developed. Chinnam said that in one recent class about 70% of students were already working engineers or other professionals, including people employed by automotive companies.

Sushant Lingras, an operations manager for PHINA, formerly Delphi Technologies, is pursuing a master's in artificial intelligence. He said he developed an AI-powered agent that helps employees quickly access plant information, standard work and operational knowledge, which eliminated several manual data-entry tasks. Derek Stringfellow, an applications analyst at Great Lakes Water Authority and a Wayne State graduate student in AI, said the class shows how such systems are built, how they fail and how a person still has a significant role. The article says that at IntelliMake students can test ideas and refine solutions in a controlled environment, which is impractical at a production plant. As the facility develops, Wayne State plans to extend the approach to quality control, production control, facilities design and operational optimization.

Articles.Title: Hands-on experience prepares Wayne State engineers for Michigan’s AI-powered manufacturing future

stories.Headline: Stony Brook FinTech Workshop Explores AI’s Impact on Finance, Announces New Industry Partnership
stories.Summary:
Stony Brook University held its FinTech Workshop on November 6 in the New Computer Science Building, where researchers and industry leaders discussed how artificial intelligence is changing financial analysis, software development and investment decisions. The event was organized by Karina Torres Castro, manager of research and innovation and assistant research professor in mechanical engineering, and it included the announcement of a new AI Innovation Lab in partnership with the financial technology company Broadridge. Students and faculty will work alongside industry experts in the lab to tackle challenges in AI and finance. The workshop included academic research presentations, industry perspectives and a panel discussion, and it was sponsored by the College of Engineering and Applied Sciences, the Long Island Manufacturing Extension Partnership, the Center of Excellence in Wireless and Information Technology and the AI Innovation Institute.

Amy Erickson, executive director of the Long Island Manufacturing Extension Partnership, said AI-driven financial modeling can help small and mid-sized manufacturers reduce waste and make better investment decisions without replacing skilled workers. She described the workshop as the first of several AI-focused programs her organization is rolling out for regional manufacturers. Andrew C. Singer, dean of the college, welcomed participants and introduced keynote speaker Robert J. Frey, research professor and founder of the university's Quantitative Finance Program. Frey, who has held leadership roles at Renaissance Technologies and other financial firms, compared the rise of AI with earlier technological advances that disrupted industries, saying some adjustments can be painful in the short term. He argued that stagnation is not the answer.

At Broadridge, AI is taking on more complex software development tasks, including some once assigned to entry-level employees. Roger Burkhardt, the company's chief technology officer of capital markets and AI, said the career ladder is changing and that new employees may be expected to define problems, evaluate AI-generated code and recognize security vulnerabilities. He encouraged students to experiment with AI development tools while learning to assess their output, and he said critical thinking and communicating with users are lasting skills. Jill Scher, managing director at CBIZ Advisors, began her accounting career in 1994 working with paper ledgers and red pencils, and she now uses AI to analyze financial statements and prepare for client meetings. Frey said that when AI is used properly, students will see it as a force multiplier that increases productivity rather than replacing them.

Pawel Polak, a faculty member in the Department of Applied Mathematics and Statistics, presented research on an international competition that attracted more than 1,000 registered participants to develop AI agents capable of writing code, forecasting financial trends and simulating markets. Some agents significantly improved the speed of existing software, but others struggled with unfamiliar problems. Teams that incorporated financial knowledge and agents required to explain their predictions generally performed better on new tasks, and Polak said human involvement definitely helps. Lav Varshney, professor of electrical and computer engineering and inaugural director of the AI Innovation Institute, argued that opaque "black box" AI may be less helpful because its inner workings are unknown. He described research using explicit, verifiable rules, with one possible application being financial transactions that fail to settle as expected, a context where traceability matters in regulated industries.

The afternoon panel, moderated by Yvette Wohn, inaugural chair of the Department of Technology, AI and Society, included Polak, Burkhardt, Scher and Melissa Brown, managing director of investment decision research at SimCorp. Brown said her team helps investors understand how unexpected economic developments might affect their portfolios, and she described an exercise considering what could happen if the Federal Reserve lost its independence. She said that work once took hours of searching historical data but now can be done by asking AI to identify similar past circumstances, which "takes five minutes rather than a day." Scher said some clients arrive with AI-generated tax analyses and ask her to confirm them, even when those analyses may overlook changing regulations or individual circumstances. Samir Das, chair of the Department of Computer Science, closed the workshop by announcing the AI Innovation Lab, which he said will focus on experiential learning and on how universities and industry can work together.
