stories.Headline: Digital Health and AI: Key Regulatory, Reimbursement and Policy Developments
stories.Summary:
Last week, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services finalized its 2027 Hospital Outpatient Prospective Payment System rule and its Medicare Physician Fee Schedule rule, both of which address digital health and artificial intelligence. In the outpatient rule, CMS coined the term "Software as a Medical Service" for software that supports clinical decisions through algorithmic analysis. CMS also created an interim payment pathway, assigning qualifying services to New Technology Ambulatory Payment Classifications and establishing a new status indicator, O1. The policy does not guarantee separate payment for every AI-enabled tool, since payment still depends on service and coding requirements. CMS also finalized separate payment for certain stand-alone algorithmic analyses of previously completed laboratory data, including secondary analyses of genomic sequencing results.

The physician fee schedule rule did not create an AI-specific payment pathway, but it signals growing attention to how technology affects physician work and quality measurement. CMS issued a Request for Information seeking industry input on technology-enabled primary care and on how Medicare payment might account for clinical AI. The rule cites an estimated 25 percent penetration of AI documentation tools, such as ambient scribes, among U.S. physicians. CMS also said more than 40 percent of U.S. physicians had self-reported using OpenEvidence, an AI application that answers clinical questions from peer-reviewed sources. Many commenters expressed skepticism and urged CMS to ensure that any Medicare-paid AI demonstrates proven clinical value.

CMS said it would consider that feedback in future rulemaking. CMS addressed AI in the Medicare Annual Wellness Visit, stressing that a physician or other health professional must still perform the visit and that clinicians must retain responsibility for clinical decisions. The agency said AI may support components such as administering the Health Risk Assessment, reconciling medications for clinician verification, and drafting a personalized prevention plan for clinician review. CMS said it was not aware of how AI could conduct a cognitive assessment under the current standard.

Beneficiary-facing software used to implement a prevention plan must not constitute the practice of medicine or replace the beneficiary-clinician relationship, and it must comply with fraud and abuse laws, including the Anti-Kickback Statute. CMS may issue further guidance in future rulemaking. CMS also tightened oversight of remote patient monitoring and remote therapeutic monitoring after findings by the Office of the Inspector General about potential fraud, waste and abuse. The rule extends the established-patient requirement to remote therapeutic monitoring, so practitioners must furnish a separately reportable initiating face-to-face visit, in person or via telehealth, before monitoring begins.

CMS also finalized a requirement that clinical staff performing these services be directly employed by the billing practitioner or practice, subject to incident-to requirements. That requirement may materially affect digital health companies that provide outsourced monitoring services. CMS delayed its implementation until Jan. 1, 2029, giving providers and vendors more time to adjust their operating models. Separately, the Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology streamlined portions of the federal health IT certification framework, and the American Medical Association released a clinical AI liability framework.

The AMA framework would allocate responsibility among clinicians, AI developers and deploying healthcare organizations based on each party's authority, access to information and ability to control or mitigate risk. It rejects the assumption that keeping a physician "in the loop" automatically shifts responsibility away from developers or health systems. Congress has also extended several Medicare telehealth flexibilities through Dec. 31, 2027, including audio-only telehealth and access from beneficiaries' homes. Pending legislation, including the PATIENT AI Act and Doctors Not AI Act, reflects continued congressional attention to AI reimbursement, oversight and privacy.

Articles.Title: Digital Health and AI: Key Regulatory, Reimbursement and Policy Developments - JD Supra

stories.Headline: Taiwan Creative Content Fest Takeaways: ‘Avatar’ VFX House Brings Its AI Ambitions to Taipei as Character IP Booms
stories.Summary:
Taiwan Creative Content Fest (TCCF) wrapped its 2026 edition in Taipei with animation and character IP companies moving to the front of the show floor. They made up the largest exhibitor group, at 29 of 107 exhibitors, up from 19 in 2025, according to post-event figures from organizer the Taiwan Creative Content Agency (TAICCA). Of this year's exhibitors, 69 were Taiwanese and 38 came from overseas, compared with 117 exhibitors in total last year. Television and media networks rose from 20 to 22 exhibitors, while new media, streaming and entertainment companies grew from six to eight.

Film and TV production and distribution companies dropped from 22 to 16, digital tech, VFX and immersive media fell from 15 to eight, and publishing, comics and webtoons went from 12 to five. The Pitching program presented 93 projects and stories to industry participants from 28 countries, including entries from TAICCA School. TAICCA is still compiling buyer attendance and the value of business done. The headline deal came on opening day, Nov. 6, when New Zealand visual effects company Weta FX signed a memorandum of understanding with TAICCA.

The agreement aims to make Taiwan an AI hub for Asia's content industries. Weta FX will partner with Taiwanese animation and VFX outfit Moonshine Studio and set up a technology platform to back Taiwanese film and TV projects. The deal also includes exchanges and internships for young Taiwanese filmmakers. Weta FX CEO Daniel Seah said studio legal departments had ruled out any use of generative AI on their projects early last year. By the turn of the year, clients were asking about Weta's AI strategy, mostly to find out how much money the technology could save.

Seah said AI had become a national strategy in Taiwan on the back of the island's semiconductor industry, and Moonshine had been moving quickly as a result. Japanese studios also brought their AI work to Taipei. Toei, the studio behind "Kamen Rider" and the Super Sentai series, has adopted rules for generative AI and is already using it for backgrounds, according to president Yoshimura Fumio. At a TCCF panel on AI in animation, OLM Digital board director Yotsukura Tatsuo presented a coloring tool that learns a show's look from three hand-painted frames. Taiwanese technology company imCore Corp. launched Core Studio, an AI filmmaking platform with more than 24 specialized agents, at TCCF on Nov. 7.

Southeast Asia ran through the program. K7 Media's Trang Nguyen presented a study of Indonesia, Southeast Asia's biggest film market with box office revenue of $352.9 million in 2025, and pointed to horror as a natural meeting ground for Taiwanese and Indonesian producers. The top Pitching prize, the $35,000 TAICCA × CNC Feature Film Grand Award, went to "Somewhere in the South," a Malaysian feature written and directed by Tan Ce Ding and produced by Anthony Chen. Grace Chan, a program planner at Taiwan Television Enterprise (TTV), said the broadcaster had seen a significant increase in Vietnamese buyers this year, after Korean buyers had been the largest group last year.

Japan was also looking at Taiwan. Cinematographer Wayne Lo, at TCCF for the first time, met several Japanese teams and found that up-and-coming filmmakers see working directly with TAICCA as a route to getting projects made. Toei's Yoshimura said Japanese films were the most-released titles in Taiwan in 2025 and second only to U.S. films at the box office. Toei is also launching a games label whose first three titles are originals rather than adaptations of its existing IP. Publishing, comics and webtoon exhibitors were down, but Mirror Fiction's "The Three Witches of Shetou" won both the TAICCA Award: Best Story and the friDay Video Original Story Award.

TAICCA presented the slates of its four joint-venture funds, which have backed 27 projects and drawn NT$4.9 billion in private capital alongside NT$740 million from the agency, about $180 million in all. The Chunghwa Digital Cultural and Creative Fund, majority owned by Chunghwa Telecom, totals NT$1 billion ($32 million). Enjoy Entertainment, a partnership with telecom Far EasTone, invested in 15 projects in its first 10 months. "The Rope Curse 4: Kuntilanak," a Taiwan-Indonesia horror collaboration that Toei also invested in, took NT$80 million ($2.6 million) at the Taiwanese box office, a franchise record.

Articles.Title: Taiwan Creative Content Fest Takeaways: ‘Avatar’ VFX House Brings Its AI Ambitions to Taipei as Character IP Booms

stories.Headline: Denver, Aurora schools to get $350K for AI tool
stories.Summary:
The DSST Public Schools charter network will receive a $350,000 grant to build AI tools across its 16 campuses in Denver and Aurora. The grant comes from Multilingual by Design, a philanthropic group based in Washington, D.C., which is financially backed by the Bezos Family Foundation and pairs education nonprofits with AI developers. The group picked DSST as one of three grant recipients from applicants across the nation. The announcement was published on November 10, 2026. The Denver Gazette reported the details.

DSST will use the money to pilot a tool called Premo, which helps K-8 teachers plan grade-level math lessons so multilingual students can take on content while building academic English. Premo aligns each lesson to established English language development frameworks and creates teaching strategies matched to each student's English proficiency level. The tool will roll out across all 16 DSST campuses over the coming year, and teachers will receive coaching, technical assistance and support. Throughline Learning, a Rhode Island-based nonprofit, will partner with DSST to implement the tool and help teachers understand how it works in classrooms. More than 65% of students at the 16 campuses are current or former multilingual learners.

Some of those campuses are part of Denver Public Schools and others part of Aurora Public Schools. Sandra Licon, fund director at Multilingual by Design, said teachers are short on time and working hard to help multilingual learners keep up in math and early literacy. She said the three funded teams started with close attention to what students and teachers experience day to day. Angie McPhaul, director of youth success at Gary Community Ventures, a financial backer of the group, said every child deserves a classroom where they are understood and supported. She said the projects center the strengths multilingual students bring to schools.

Both statements praised the grant recipients' focus on students' needs. The grant is part of a broader effort by Multilingual by Design to fund tools that support multilingual learners in classrooms. The articles do not describe how the results of the pilot will be measured or whether the tool will be expanded beyond the 16 campuses after the first year. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Denver, Aurora schools to get $350K for AI tool - Denver Gazette

stories.Headline: 6 Members of Congress Set for 'Broadband and AI' as Reps. Pramila Jayapal and Jennifer McClellan Join Keynote Lineup
stories.Summary:
Broadband Breakfast announced that two House Democrats who are writing artificial intelligence legislation, Reps. Pramila Jayapal of Washington and Jennifer McClellan of Virginia, will deliver keynotes at its Broadband and AI in the Next Congress conference. Their additions raise the number of members of Congress on the program to six. Rep. Greg Landsman of Ohio will take part in a fireside chat with the outlet's editor and publisher, Drew Clark. Sen. Ed Markey, Rep. Buddy Carter and Rep. Nanette Barragán were announced earlier as keynote speakers.

The announcement was published on November 10, 2026. The conference is set for Tuesday, December 1, at the National Press Club in Washington. Registration for in-person attendance costs $245, and Breakfast Club members receive an additional $100 off. The program begins at 9 a.m., with doors opening no later than 8:30 a.m., in the Grand Ballroom.

Comcast and Broadband Nation Expo are gold sponsors, and INCOMPAS is a silver sponsor. Full program details and registration are available on the event page. Jayapal has represented Washington's Seventh District, which includes most of Seattle, since 2017, and she co-leads the House version of the AI Civil Rights Act. That bill would bar companies from using biased algorithms in high-stakes decisions and require testing before and after deployment.

In October 2026 she released a framework for a national AI charter that would require AI companies to meet public-benefit conditions. McClellan has represented Virginia's Fourth District, which includes Richmond, since 2023, and in March 2026 she introduced the bipartisan AI-Ready Networks Act with Rep. Jay Obernolte. That bill, H.R. 7783, would direct the National Telecommunications and Information Administration to report on how AI is being adopted in U.S. commercial telecommunications networks. Landsman has written legislation requiring data centers to cover the full cost of their energy and infrastructure needs, while Barragán introduced the Artificial Intelligence Environmental Impacts Act with Rep. Don Beyer.

Markey, who authored the Telecommunications Act of 1996 in the House, released an AI Accountability Agenda in July 2026. Carter is the lead sponsor of the American Broadband Deployment Act, H.R. 2289. The conference is organized around four panels covering catastrophic AI risk, permitting reform, data center power and ratepayer protection, and federal preemption versus state AI rules. Additional speakers are still to be announced.

Articles.Title: 6 Members of Congress Set for 'Broadband and AI' as Reps. Pramila Jayapal and Jennifer McClellan Join Keynote Lineup

stories.Headline: K Altman Law Highlights School Artificial Intelligence Controls and Questions for Families
stories.Summary:
Google said on November 3 that it plans to turn off access to the Gemini application, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom, and Google Search for kindergarten through twelfth-grade student accounts until school administrators explicitly enable them. The company described these changes in an announcement about administrator controls and new learning features in products used by schools. It said it would provide schools with further details in the coming months, before the changes roll out. The announcement also described learning features in Search and Classroom, along with the timing of the proposed updates.

K Altman Law, a firm led by Keith Altman, has highlighted questions for families and schools as artificial intelligence tools become more common in educational technology. The firm says that artificial intelligence features may appear in standalone applications, classroom products, or search experiences, and that disabling one product does not automatically disable every such feature in another. Availability and controls can depend on the product, the school's configuration, the account, and the timing of any changes. The firm suggests that a clear school technology policy can explain which tools are available and how students are expected to use them.

Altman said that families should have understandable information about the technology students can access through school accounts. He said schools and parents can support informed use by discussing available controls, privacy expectations, and the appropriate ways for students to seek help from trusted adults. The release does not name any official responsible for enforcing these changes beyond Google's own announcement. Google's plans were described as proposed, and the release does not say how those plans will apply to any particular school district.

The firm recommends that families ask schools which artificial intelligence tools and search features are available through a student's account and device. It also suggests requesting the school's current technology-use, privacy, monitoring, and parent-notification policies, including any anticipated changes. Families are advised to ask whether separate controls apply to standalone applications, classroom tools, and search, and when changes are expected locally. The release notes that students who use accessibility tools or receive disability-related services should ask how any technology changes will affect their access. The release is general information, not legal advice, and laws and procedures vary by jurisdiction.

Articles.Title: K Altman Law Highlights School Artificial Intelligence Controls and Questions for Families

stories.Headline: Bill Kurtis: AI stole my voice — and I want it back
stories.Summary:
Chicago broadcaster Bill Kurtis, a longtime television journalist and narrator, has said in a column published by the Chicago Tribune on November 10, 2026, that artificial intelligence companies have copied his voice without his permission. The discovery began on October 1 of this year, when a viewer emailed him about a cable show whose voiceover she suspected was AI generated. Kurtis said his own reporting turned up more than 200 voice-over examples that used a replicated version of his voice, and he said he was never asked or contacted about them. He added that some of the offending operations appeared to be based outside the United States.

Kurtis described the replication as part of a wider problem in which AI firms have collected material from libraries, books, television and universities, often without payment, and then sold access back to customers. He said these companies argue the practice is "fair use" and needs no compensation. Chicago attorney Ross Kimbarovsky of Loevy & Loevy has filed 13 proposed class actions against companies including Google, Amazon, Meta, Nvidia, Microsoft, Apple and ElevenLabs. Kimbarovsky called the conduct an illegal and unethical exploitation of talent on a massive scale and one of the largest violations of biometric privacy ever committed.

Several legal tools are now in play, according to Kurtis. Two Illinois laws prohibit using AI to create and distribute digital replicas of a person's voice, image or likeness, and another bars training an AI voice model on audio without notice and permission. A federal bill called the No Fakes Act, supported by the entertainment union SAG/AFTRA, was approved by the U.S. Senate Judiciary Committee and is awaiting a vote by the full Senate. Kurtis warned that if many people can obtain his voice for free, it will lose its value as a source of income, which could end a career built over 60 years on integrity and ethical standards.

Kurtis is a television producer and host and a former CBS network and WBBM-Ch. 2 news anchor, and he has framed the dispute as one over both his voice and his journalistic reputation. He said he will not give that reputation away. The column notes that the courts will have to resolve the many pending class actions, and it leaves open how the Senate vote on federal legislation will turn out.

Articles.Title: Bill Kurtis: AI stole my voice — and I want it back

stories.Headline: AI in Practice: AI Helped DHL Save More Than $1 Million in Outside Counsel Fees in One Year
stories.Summary:
The article is a feature profile published by Law.com on November 10, 2026, written by Trudy Knockless, about DHL Supply's general counsel Mark Smolik and his department's use of artificial intelligence. The piece opens with Smolik's early work organizing DHL's legal files nearly two decades ago, which he initially saw as a filing task rather than the foundation for later AI work. That groundwork eventually supported an initiative that let the legal department bring employment-related legal work in-house. The result, according to the headline, was savings of more than $1 million in outside counsel fees in a single year.

The article's full body is behind a subscription wall, so the visible text offers only the opening of the story. From what is shown, the change is a shift of employment-related legal work from outside firms to DHL's own lawyers, enabled by AI tools built on the earlier document organization. The savings figure is stated as more than $1 million in one year, and the period is described as a single year without a specific date range in the visible text. The visible excerpt does not describe which AI tools were used, how many matters moved in-house, or what staffing changes were made.

Smolik is the general counsel of DHL Supply and is the person the article centers on, and the excerpt quotes no statements from him. The visible text also does not give his specific comments on the savings or the AI program. Two related Law.com pieces appear in the page navigation: a November 9, 2026 article by Tony Thompson on research from WorldCC, Deloitte and Ironclad about the gap between individual AI productivity gains and organization-level results, and a November 6, 2026 article by Brendan Pierson on copyright suits over AI training against Meta. Neither is about DHL, and the visible text does not connect them to this story. The visible material does not say what comes next for DHL's program.

Articles.Title: AI in Practice: AI Helped DHL Save More Than $1 Million in Outside Counsel Fees in One Year

stories.Headline: Scott Wiener was the AI-safety world’s congressional pick. Can the freshman find his voice on Capitol Hill?
stories.Summary:
Scott Wiener, the San Francisco congressman-elect, authored the country's first major state AI safety law, and he won his race to replace Nancy Pelosi on November 6, 2026. Democrats resoundingly took control of the House, with some viewing that as a mandate to craft comprehensive AI regulation that could reach President Donald Trump's desk in the upcoming session. Wiener is a freshman, and rookie members do not usually get the most coveted and powerful committee assignments on Capitol Hill. The main question is whether Trump would sign such legislation.

Rep. Zoe Lofgren, ranking member on the House Committee on Science, Space and Tech, said the president may not care about what good can be accomplished, but the midterms showed Americans want responsible action on AI. The House Committee on Energy and Commerce has been a main venue for AI-safety fights, and AI safety experts and lobbyists doubt Wiener will get a spot on it. Instead, they say his likelier route is Lofgren's committee, which is open to first-timers, or a new select committee House Democrats have been mulling. Lofgren told Mission Local she welcomes all excitement over joining the committee. Wiener told MIT Technology Review he would be eager to serve on a select AI committee if one is created, and he declined to comment for the article.

The timing is pertinent because, the day after Wiener won, a team of outside AI evaluators released a report claiming San Francisco-based Anthropic's own use of artificial intelligence had dramatically sped up the company's research. Anthropic redacted major portions of the evidence reviewed by Model Evaluation and Threat Research, or METR, a Berkeley-based nonprofit. METR said AI is not yet able to make highly significant and fully autonomous contributions to the most important parts of model training. Responses to the November 5 report ranged widely, with Jake Mendel of Coefficient Giving saying he needed to call his family and Dane Sherburn saying he felt sick. George Mason University economist Robin Hanson wrote that it looked more like a one-time speedup than continuous acceleration.

Last year, Wiener authored successful state legislation setting transparency and reporting requirements for AI models, and he has opposed more hardline stances, such as a moratorium on data centers. His campaign received millions of dollars in support from Public First Action, an Anthropic-backed AI safety nonprofit, along with direct cash from Anthropic and OpenAI employees. Wiener has insisted there was no Anthropic money in the race, and the company said it earmarked its giving to Public First Action for non-political purposes. Sacha Haworth, executive director of the Tech Oversight Project, said Energy and Commerce will most likely deal with the biggest AI issues, but it is a highly competitive panel to join. Haworth also said the Veterans Affairs committee could act on AI scams, since AI is everywhere.

Other questions remain about how Democrats in power will handle AI regulation. An unnamed D.C. lobbyist said progressives may want to focus more on oversight investigations, while moderates look to repair the party's relationship with big tech and its money. The federal question of preemption could void state laws such as Wiener's legislation, which have sprung up in the absence of a comprehensive federal law. The articles do not say which committee Wiener will be assigned to, or whether a federal AI law will pass.

Articles.Title: Scott Wiener was the AI-safety world’s congressional pick. Can the freshman find his voice on Capitol Hill?

stories.Headline: Elvis AI Voice Lawsuit, Olivia Rodrigo’s ‘Take Me Home,’ BTS Song Case & More Top Music Law News
stories.Summary:
I can't produce this as a single news story from the article, because the source is a weekly roundup of several unrelated legal items rather than one event. I can write the Elvis Presley estate's lawsuit against Suno, which is the only item the article develops with enough detail for three paragraphs of four to five sentences each. Elvis Presley Enterprises, the company that owns the intellectual property of Elvis Presley, filed a lawsuit against Suno, described as the leading AI music firm, in the week before the November 10, 2026 newsletter. The suit accuses Suno of stealing Presley's likeness by letting users clone his singing voice, which the filing calls "unmistakable and iconic." It says that all of the humanity, history, despair and triumph that make up Elvis's identity was stolen and stored on Suno's servers to make large sums of money.

The complaint is the second such action from the same rights owners, following a case filed about two weeks earlier against Anthropic. The earlier cases against Suno brought by music companies center on the use of copyrighted material to train AI models, while this one invokes likeness rights. Likeness rights are state-level protections meant to guard a person's name, image and voice against commercial exploitation. The lawsuit cites the ELVIS Act, a state law, in support of its claims.

The article notes that Suno may raise counter-arguments but does not say what they are. The article does not describe Suno's response to the new filing beyond noting that it is a potential defense. Days before the Presley case was filed, Suno asked a judge to dismiss a separate lawsuit brought by Jason Isbell and other musicians over similar name-and-likeness claims. The newsletter's author, Bill Donahue, points readers to a full Billboard story and video for further detail on the new lawsuit and the arguments Suno may make.

Articles.Title: Elvis AI Voice Lawsuit, Olivia Rodrigo’s ‘Take Me Home,’ BTS Song Case & More Top Music Law News

stories.Headline: Our AI Problem Isn’t Too Little Regulation. It’s Too Much.
stories.Summary:
This is an opinion essay rather than a news report, so there is no discrete event to write up as a news story. Published on November 10, 2026, on the Learn Liberty website and co-written by Alex Tokarev, an associate professor of economics and philosophy at Northwood University, and Kristin Tokarev, a producer for Stossel TV, the piece argues that the United States faces too much AI regulation rather than too little. The authors say that lawmakers respond to new technology with alarm, hearings, and calls for restrictions, and they claim that America led in AI because entrepreneurs, investors, and engineers were free to act without government direction. They note that 13 of the top 15 AI applications are American, with the most successful Chinese ones ranked fourth and tenth.

The authors contend that China is investing across the AI ecosystem, including semiconductors, cloud computing, autonomous systems, and energy infrastructure, with the aim of controlling the technology stack. They argue that Washington should not answer with more central planning, pointing to the Soviet Union's failure to match Silicon Valley as evidence. Their main example of regulatory harm is Defense Department procurement, which they say buys software as though it were aircraft carriers, so that contracts can take years to clear reviews and the technology is outdated by delivery. They say that compliance burdens favor large companies able to employ armies of compliance officers, and they urge a risk-based approach, arguing that software predicting helicopter engine failures should not face the same scrutiny as software used in lethal targeting. They also say that cybersecurity standards, accountability, and human supervision for autonomous weapons are appropriate, while maintaining that not every application carries the same risk.

The essay does not identify any specific pending bill, rule, or agency action, and it does not name a particular lawmaker whose proposal it opposes. It concludes that America's advantage has come from free enterprise rather than central planning, and that the AI contest is about whether free societies can out-innovate authoritarian ones. The article itself says it expresses only the authors' opinion and not the position of Students For Liberty, the organization that hosts it. It also promotes the group's Local Coordinator Program and invites readers to join. The piece does not describe any subsequent developments, so what happens next is not reported.

Articles.Title: Our AI Problem Isn’t Too Little Regulation. It’s Too Much.

stories.Headline: Antonio Bravo (BBVA): “AI Will Help Us Build a Better, More Profitable Bank With Greater Growth Potential”
stories.Summary:
BBVA's Global Head of AI Transformation, Antonio Bravo, spoke at two London events organized by Bloomberg and the Financial Times, laying out how the bank plans to deploy artificial intelligence across its organization. The article is dated November 11, 2026. Bravo said the bank has already spent more than a year developing AI agents and now has AI tools available across the group. He added that the first AI solutions are being rolled out and that the pace of launches will speed up next year.

The bank is moving from early, project-by-project development toward a model for scaling the technology safely, with governance and controls built in. Its next step is to industrialize that capability through a new framework for deploying AI agents systematically, using common standards for security, governance and quality. A system will monitor and evaluate every operation and response its agents produce, measuring them against benchmark datasets known as "golden datasets" that set the required quality thresholds. Deviations are meant to be detected and errors corrected, combining the technology with human oversight. The article also notes that the change requires new ways of working, with employees supported by training and room to experiment.

Bravo said the strategy is driven from the top and affects every business area, and that the bank wants AI to make it more profitable and give it greater growth potential in the countries where it operates. He told the Bloomberg Tech Week audience that AI can remove bottlenecks and bring its benefits into the daily experience of customers and employees. He also argued that control, governance and security are compatible with the speed and innovation the bank needs. He stressed that security and service quality are non-negotiable for keeping customers' trust, which he described as one of the most valuable assets of an institution with nearly 170 years of history.

The early work is already producing results in Spain and Mexico, where BBVA is building solutions for customer service, relationship manager support and risk analysis with OpenAI, under a strategic partnership. The article reports a 30% reduction in the time spent on certain tasks in preparing enterprise financial risk programs. It also says early versions of the mobile AI assistant already handle about half of the text-based queries that previously went to relationship managers. The bank expects to accelerate the rollout of new agents, products and features over the coming months, with the aim of a more proactive, personalized banking model that anticipates customer needs.

Articles.Title: Antonio Bravo (BBVA): “AI Will Help Us Build a Better, More Profitable Bank With Greater Growth Potential”

stories.Headline: VerticalScope Turns 2 Billion Forum Posts Into AI Shopping Revenue
stories.Summary:
VerticalScope, a Toronto-based operator of enthusiast forums, reported in its third-quarter 2026 results on Tuesday, November 10, that AI-powered shopping recommendations lifted affiliate commerce revenue 29% from a year earlier. The company runs more than 1,200 communities holding over 2 billion user-generated posts. Overall revenue still fell 11%, and monthly active users averaged 76.8 million, down from 83 million a year earlier. VerticalScope attributed the audience decline to lower organic search traffic.

The AI recommends products inside discussion threads drawn from what members have written about items they own, and VerticalScope earns an affiliate commission when a reader follows a link and completes a qualifying purchase. By August, affiliate commerce revenue on the forums was up 13% year over year and approaching a $1 million annual run rate, double the level given in May. The company has not disclosed the specific mechanics of the shopping experience or how much revenue the AI generated on its own. CEO Chris Goodridge said on the earnings call that AI can repeat product specifications but cannot convey what it is like to own something for ten years.

VerticalScope signed its first two data agreements with frontier AI labs in October, without naming them. One is a non-exclusive license to train models on a selection of communities, with fees tied to the volume of content delivered. The other pays VerticalScope when its content contributes to an AI-generated answer, and it began in November with a subset of communities. Goodridge said AI companies, AI search engines and AI agents made 115 million attempts to access the communities over the past 30 days, and that VerticalScope blocks any company that tries without an agreement.

The shift comes as Reddit faces similar pressure, with its search referrals reportedly falling by more than 1 million a week on average in October. Reddit began testing an AI shopping experience in February that places product carousels with prices and purchase links in its search results. A PYMNTS Intelligence survey cited in the coverage found about 61 million U.S. consumers, or 23%, now start online retail research with AI, but Amazon closed 60% of respondents' most recent AI-assisted purchases. The articles do not say how VerticalScope's model will perform as its AI licensing revenue begins, which the company expects in the fourth quarter.

Articles.Title: VerticalScope Turns 2 Billion Forum Posts Into AI Shopping Revenue

stories.Headline: Why an ex-Cohere leader doesn’t want you to call his new law firm “AI-native”
stories.Summary:
Blackletter, a law firm founded by former Cohere and Blue J leaders, announced on Tuesday that it has raised $6 million USD in seed funding. The company was started by Jonathan Rosenbluth and David Stewart, both ex-Cohere product and engineering leaders, along with former Blue J COO Avi Brudner. Its goal is to run a law firm on top of its own AI legaltech platform. The firm is based in Toronto and New York City and uses fixed-fee, outcome-based pricing instead of the hourly billing common in the industry. It says it can deliver quality legal work faster and at lower cost than traditional firms.

The seed round is meant to help the company hire more lawyers and engineers. Blackletter is building tools for its own lawyers to use fully, which Rosenbluth says contrasts with vendors selling software to firms whose lawyers have little incentive to use it. The round was led by Lerer Hippeau, a New York City venture capital firm, with participation from Seven Stars, Maple VC, Garage Capital, and Ripple Ventures. Cohere co-founders Aidan Gomez, Ivan Zhang, and Nick Frosst also took part, as did TwelveLabs CEO Jae Lee and Adaption CEO Sara Hooker. Rosenbluth said the company has worked with 75 clients since emerging from stealth in June.

Rosenbluth rejects the description of Blackletter as an "AI-native law firm." He told BetaKit that calling it that suggests cheap and fast service, and that the firm is simply hiring strong lawyers. He compared the label to calling a firm Microsoft-native because it uses Microsoft Word. Clients named by the company include TwelveLabs, Fanatics, and Toronto-based Ada, though Rosenbluth declined to say whether Blackletter helped with Ada's recent $600 million CAD merger with Dialpad.

He said the idea for Blackletter came to him while at Cohere, when it became clear that AI should be improving legal services but he was not seeing that benefit as a client. Rosenbluth believes building the firm in both Canada and the United States will help make top-tier legal services more widely available. He expects the company to push the rest of the legal sector to innovate. The article does not describe any further timeline or plans beyond the seed funding and hiring.

Articles.Title: Why an ex-Cohere leader doesn’t want you to call his new law firm “AI-native”

stories.Headline: OpenAI's Q3 results and Nvidia's scandal impact on the AI ecosystem
stories.Summary:
OpenAI reported third-quarter revenue of $10 billion, up from about $6.7 billion in the prior quarter, according to a Yahoo Finance interview published November 10, 2026. The network's host, Deidre Bosa, said that growth was nearly 50 percent and almost triple the 18 percent growth OpenAI posted in the second quarter. Anthropic, which the host said is about to go public, reported $17 billion in third-quarter revenue, with 47 percent growth after 144 percent in the prior quarter. Bosa said the two companies' quarterly growth rates were now close to each other for the first time this year. She added that the exact size of Anthropic's lead was hard to pin down because the companies account for cloud sales differently.

Vinod Khosla, a founder of Khosla Ventures and one of OpenAI's earliest backers, was interviewed on the show about the comparison. He said his firm invested in OpenAI at a $1 billion valuation and chose not to invest in Anthropic. Khosla argued that quarter-over-quarter results matter less than the trajectory over the coming years. He said OpenAI invests heavily in research and compute, which he described as giving it a cost advantage. He also argued that token usage, rather than prices or revenue, is the better measure of real demand and of whether a bubble exists.

Bosa pressed Khosla on the rise of open-source models, which she said are taking a growing share of developer usage. Khosla responded that open-source models are not cheaper to run, because Nvidia's chips carry a premium of about five times the cost. He said OpenAI's own silicon would lower its per-token costs as it comes online over the next few years, and that Google's TPUs have begun competing with Nvidia. Bosa noted that companies such as Fireworks and Base 10 help serve open models efficiently, and asked whether chips developed for in-house use were lowering compute costs for others. Khosla said they were not, because Nvidia and Google both price their chips at a premium while a silicon shortage lasts for a couple of years.

The interview also included Bosa's separate conversation with OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar about the company's push into enterprise AI, its "dots" rollout, and the global AI model race. The episode was introduced as Deirdre Bosa Live, which airs daily at 4 p.m. The same broadcast flagged a hot consumer price index report that day that pushed markets lower, and said Nvidia and Microsoft were among the day's biggest stocks. The broadcast also said poor results from neo clouds were expected shortly. The articles do not say what follows OpenAI's results or Anthropic's public listing.

Articles.Title: OpenAI's Q3 results and Nvidia's scandal impact on the AI ecosystem

stories.Headline: Microsoft Corporation (MSFT) Is Pouring Billions Into AI: Could Massive Spending Weigh on Future Returns?
stories.Summary:
Moon Capital Management, an investment firm, released its third-quarter 2026 investor letter, which focused largely on the heavy spending on artificial intelligence by major technology companies. The letter reported that the firm's equity portfolio gained about 4% in the first nine months of 2026, compared with roughly 12% for the S&P 500 over the same period. It noted that market gains had been narrow, with nearly half of S&P 500 constituents declining and the median stock rising only about 4%. The firm also said it had avoided direct AI investments because it is unsure which companies will ultimately capture the economic benefits.

The letter says the major hyperscalers are expected to spend about $1.2 trillion on capital expenditures in 2027 and another $1.4 trillion in 2028. Semiconductor demand has been strong, with the S&P Global Semiconductor Index rising about 95% through September. Moon Capital questioned whether these infrastructure investments would generate adequate returns. The firm said it remains focused on businesses whose economics it can assess with confidence and whose shares trade at meaningful discounts to estimated intrinsic value.

The letter named Microsoft Corporation, which develops software, cloud services, personal computing products, and enterprise solutions, as one of the holdings it highlighted. Microsoft's stock closed at about $545.18 per share on November 9, 2026, giving it a market capitalization of $3.96 trillion. Its one-month return was 1.9%, and its shares traded between $352.83 and $555.80 over the past 52 weeks. In the letter, Moon Capital said that while AI-related investment accounts for a large share of U.S. GDP and S&P 500 earnings growth, it remains to be seen whether the eventual returns will justify the capital committed.

Articles.Title: Microsoft Corporation (MSFT) Is Pouring Billions Into AI: Could Massive Spending Weigh on Future Returns?

stories.Headline: AI lending surge tests credit insurance capacity as banks seek cover
stories.Summary:
Three of the world's largest banks have recently explored or bought credit insurance to hedge their exposure to AI infrastructure loans, according to the Financial Times. Barclays has been asking insurers about default protection on more than $10 billion of such loans, and HSBC has also looked at using credit insurance on data center debt. JPMorgan Chase considered the approach but ultimately declined it. The moves suggest that the rapid growth in data center financing is pushing against the limits of what bank balance sheets can carry alone.

Concentration limits, which cap how much a bank can lend to a single company, project or sector, are restricting lending at the same time that hyperscalers want ever-larger loan packages. Credit insurance eases that constraint by shifting part of the default risk to insurers. In a typical deal, a bank cedes 20% to 50% of its exposure, which frees capacity to approve bigger facilities or more deals. Azi Larsen of Marsh Specialty told the FT that the rising cost of credit default swaps and the scale of AI debt issuance have led US lenders to look at insurance as a cheaper route to exposure relief.

The number of credit insurance providers for project finance has grown from a handful a decade ago to more than 70, including AIG, Chubb and Axa, according to the FT. Premiums for data center exposure run at 50% to 70% of what banks earn on that part of their loan portfolios, the report says. A Willis Towers Watson survey released in May 2026 found that several non-trade credit insurers were approaching sector limits or were already full on data center exposure. Willis Re also reported that direct credit insurance premium at Lloyd's rose by roughly a quarter in 2025 to about £1.6 billion, after Lloyd's removed premium income limits on credit and financial guarantee business in July 2025.

Charlie Radcliffe of BPL Global, a specialist credit and political risk broker, told the FT that banks will pay premium rates to secure majority lender status or to show support for a client. Willis Re has warned that reinsurers will scrutinize data center concentrations closely at the January 2027 renewals. The specific insurers approached by Barclays and HSBC have not been named, and several of the transactions remain exploratory. Even so, credit risk transfer on AI infrastructure has begun to look like a recurring placement category, where insurer selectivity and capacity management will shape outcomes as much as price.

Articles.Title: AI lending surge tests credit insurance capacity as banks seek cover

stories.Headline: Innocean turns Seoul billboards into outdoor AI art galleries
stories.Summary:
Innocean, the Seoul advertising agency, said on Wednesday that it has launched a public art project that shows works by AI artists on large digital billboards across the city. The Innocean Open Museum project is led by the agency's AI creative research team, i-Lab, and it departs from ordinary outdoor advertising by showing artists' work instead of promoting brands or products. The first installations appeared in mid-October at The Monte Gangnam and Shinsegae Gangnam Gate DS at Central City. Works were also shown at Central City Underworld DS throughout October, and the K Finance screen in Myeong-dong joined in November.

Under the inaugural theme "Open," three artists and creative teams explore different approaches to AI-driven art. Designer Kim Ji-young's "Alien Beauty" challenges conventional beauty standards through unusual skin textures. Kim Ji-hyun of the creative studio Anreal presents "Aperture," which draws on the growth and dispersal of dandelions. The creative duo Neither.I offers "Behind," which combines video, photography and electronic music to reveal scenes beyond a large curtain. Innocean has adapted each work to the dimensions of its billboard, and it will document the artists' creative processes through interviews and an online archive.

The project follows a concept called "Open Inquiry," which lets artists experiment freely with AI as a creative tool, a collaborator or a subject. Innocean's CEO, Kim Jung-ah, said that AI is changing creative methods and possibilities and that the company wanted to open its capabilities and urban screens to artists. She added that the initiative would grow through partnerships with artists and brands. The article does not give further detail on how those partnerships will be structured.

The installations will run through the end of the year, and new works are scheduled to follow during that period. Innocean also plans to recruit more AI artists and to explore collaborations that connect artists' creative visions with brands. The article does not say how many new works or artists are planned, or what the project will cost. Its launch comes as AI tools move further into commercial creative work, and the company presents the project as a way to give those tools a public audience in the city.

Articles.Title: Innocean turns Seoul billboards into outdoor AI art galleries

stories.Headline: PATIENT AI Act targets FDA, reimbursement gaps for AI-enabled health technology - Hogan Lovells Cadwalader
stories.Summary:
Sen. Bill Cassidy, MD (R-LA) released a discussion draft of the Protecting Americans Through Intelligent, Ethical, and Transparent Artificial Intelligence in Health Care Act, known as the PATIENT AI Act, which would establish a federal framework for AI-based health technologies. The articles describe the draft as the first comprehensive health AI proposal released in Congress. Stakeholders may submit feedback on the discussion draft through December 1. The article is dated November 10, 2026, and Cassidy is due to leave Capitol Hill at the conclusion of the 119th Congress.

The bill would direct the Department of Health and Human Services to create a coverage evaluation framework and a coverage evaluation pathway for applications reviewed under an expanded third-party review scheme, and to develop proposed payment methodologies for reimbursement. It would direct the Center for Medicare and Medicaid Innovation to establish a payment model for AI applications that deliver care autonomously. HHS would also set up a process to create Healthcare Common Procedure Coding System Level II codes for AI-based services. For the FDA, the bill would extend the predetermined change control plan framework, currently limited to postmarket changes, to software changes during premarket review, expand third-party review to low- to moderate-risk software, and require a voluntary pilot program to modernize postmarket surveillance. The bill would also broaden the Certified Health IT framework to cover clinical research technology and AI applications that are not FDA-regulated devices, and direct HHS to issue privacy and security guidance under HIPAA for AI use in health care.

The articles identify Sen. Cassidy as the sponsor and say the draft follows HHS's "OneHHS" AI strategy, released in December 2025, which directs FDA and other agencies to build one Department-wide AI infrastructure. The articles also note that in October the Senate passed the Health Care Cybersecurity and Resiliency Act by unanimous consent, and that in July the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, chaired by Cassidy, unanimously passed the Health Information Privacy Reform Act. The authors, Cybil Roehrenbeck, Victoria Wallace and Kristin Zielinski Duggan of Hogan Lovells, write that AI-based health technology developers often face a gap between FDA authorization and a viable path to coverage and reimbursement. They add that the bill does not appear to establish a comprehensive framework for allocating liability when AI contributes to patient harm.

The articles state that the draft could affect HHS coordination among its components, FDA oversight of iterative software changes, and the scope of companies subject to the Certified Health IT framework. They say it is unclear how the new processes would affect coding and payment, since existing mechanisms already exist for reimbursing autonomous AI services and creating temporary HCPCS and CPT codes. The authors note that the discussion draft is likely to shape future federal AI health proposals even if Cassidy leaves Congress. Stakeholders who wish to comment must do so by December 1.

Articles.Title: PATIENT AI Act targets FDA, reimbursement gaps for AI-enabled health technology - Hogan Lovells Cadwalader

stories.Headline: With AI, Korea faces balancing act between driving growth and disgruntling public
stories.Summary:
Korea's exports hit a record in September, with total shipments topping $120 billion for the first time, driven almost entirely by demand for AI-related memory chips. Semiconductor exports more than tripled from a year earlier to a record $60.3 billion, and chips made up 49.9 percent of total exports. Memory shipments rose from $11.79 billion to $54.07 billion in one year as data centers bought more and prices climbed. Exports from January to September reached $814.5 billion, already surpassing last year's full-year record of $709.3 billion.

The gains, however, are concentrated in a few companies. Samsung Electronics and SK hynix together control more than 80 percent of the global high bandwidth memory market, while less than 1 percent of Korea's workers are in the chip sector. Employment among people aged 15 to 29 fell by 285,000 between June 2022 and June this year, according to a Bank of Korea report released in August. About 94 percent of those drops came from industries where AI usage is prioritized. The Yongin chip cluster, where Samsung and SK hynix are building new labs, will need around 15 to 16 gigawatts at full operation, reportedly about 25 percent of Seoul's electricity demand.

Samsung's loss-making foundry division and system large-scale integration divisions skipped entry-level hiring in both rounds of recruitment last year. SK hynix paid employees a performance bonus worth 2,964 percent of their monthly base salary for 2025. Samsung Electronics Vice Chairman Jun Young-hyun said at the company's March shareholders' meeting that the chip division's bonus payout rate falls short of competitors. The Bank of Korea's employment research team head, Oh Sam-il, said AI is accelerating the trend of a diminishing career ladder for young people.

The Semiconductor Special Act, which gives chipmakers bigger tax credits and priority access to electricity and water, passed in January without an exemption from the 52-hour weekly work cap that chipmakers had sought for R&D engineers. In a union survey last year, 90 percent of Samsung's unionized R&D staff opposed the exemption. Industry Minister Kim Jung-kwan said at an August 6 forum that the current 52-hour system must be revised. The Korea Electric Power Corporation is pursuing a 37 trillion won project to move coastal power plants to inland Yongin, scheduled to finish in 2036, and residents in the affected area are resisting the relocation.

Articles.Title: With AI, Korea faces balancing act between driving growth and disgruntling public

stories.Headline: Grab, SoftBank to invest $1.85bn in Malaysia AI infrastructure
stories.Summary:
Grab and SoftBank Group announced on Monday, November 10, 2026, that they will invest $1.85 billion in artificial intelligence infrastructure projects in Malaysia, including data centers. The announcement came from the companies themselves, and the articles describe the investment as two projects. The companies say the goal is to capture the growing demand for digital services across Southeast Asia. The article is datelined Singapore and was written by Kentaro Takeda for Nikkei Asia.

The projects involve building data centers in Malaysia to support AI services. The article describes the investment as aimed at serving regional demand rather than only Malaysian demand. The related coverage in the same feed indicates that SoftBank's work includes an AI infrastructure development in Malaysia's Sarawak state. Other linked stories describe Grab expanding its AI functions across its services. The articles give no figures beyond the $1.85 billion total and the reference to a separate plan of $50 billion attributed to a Malaysian prime minister.

Grab and SoftBank are the companies responsible for the investment, and their announcement is the source of the figures. The coverage reports that the companies are seeking to capture demand as Southeast Asia's digital economy expands. The articles do not supply direct quotations from company executives in the portion provided. Context in the feed includes Grab's pending acquisition of Atome Financial for $1.49 billion and a Taiwan deal that the articles say was blocked, which the article links to Grab's wider AI ambitions. The articles do not say when the data centers will be completed or what the next steps will be.

Articles.Title: Grab, SoftBank to invest $1.85bn in Malaysia AI infrastructure

stories.Headline: LCPS launches AI pilot program at 7 schools
stories.Summary:
Seven Loudoun County public schools are taking part in a generative artificial intelligence pilot program with Google, according to an article published by the Loudoun Times on November 10, 2026. The program is being launched by Loudoun County Public Schools, known as LCPS. The schools named in the article are Clarke Lightfoot, Brambleton Middle, Lansdowne High, Loudoun Valley High, and Sterling Elementary. The article says the program is intended to allow students and staff to use generative AI tools in a responsible and ethical way.

It describes the program's aims as expanding the district's understanding of artificial intelligence, examining its benefits and risks, and developing guidelines for its use. Participants will reportedly be asked to test AI-powered tools in classroom settings and provide feedback. The article notes that LCPS did not say how long the program will last. The Loudoun County School Board's Curriculum and Instruction Committee has reportedly been drafting policies governing district use of generative AI and data privacy.

The article identifies the pilot as one of several steps the district is taking alongside its broader technology plans. The program is overseen by the LCPS Office of Instructional Technology, and a district spokesperson was quoted describing the initiative as a careful, measured approach. Some parents and community members reportedly expressed concern at a recent board meeting about student data privacy and whether AI tools could affect academic integrity. The article says the district responded that data protections are a central part of the pilot's design.

It also notes that Loudoun County has been a leader in technology integration in its schools for several years. The article indicates that the district expects to share findings from the pilot with the school board and the public once initial results are available. It does not give a date for that report. Additional schools may be added to the program depending on the outcome of the initial phase, according to the article.

Articles.Title: LCPS launches AI pilot program at 7 schools - Loudoun Times-Mirror
