stories.Headline: TSMC, Microsoft executives debate AI's impact on Day 2 of Nikkei Dialogue
stories.Summary:
TSMC and Microsoft executives were scheduled to speak on Wednesday, November 11, 2026, on the second day of Nikkei's 2026 Global Management Dialogue in Tokyo. The event, which opened its second day in the Japanese capital, was set to keep artificial intelligence at the top of its agenda. Among the participants was a senior executive from Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., the world's largest contract chipmaker. Other speakers were also scheduled to take part in the program. The articles describe the session mainly as a forum for discussing AI's broader effects.

The event is the second day of a multi-day gathering organized by Nikkei, and the articles present it as a platform rather than a source of new rules or policy changes. The conference also features speakers from fitness and martial arts, according to the subheading of the coverage. Nikkei's reporting connects the discussion to wider industry concerns, including memory chip prices and AI-driven demand that other coverage in the same publication has covered. The articles do not state any formal requirement, deadline, or change arising from the debate. No specific figures, commitments, or outcomes from the sessions were reported in the material available.

Responsibility for the program rests with Nikkei, which organized the dialogue and commissioned the related content through its Global Business Bureau. The articles do not include direct statements from the TSMC or Microsoft executives in the form of quotations, so their positions on AI are not reported here. The coverage notes that other executives at the event have expressed views on AI, such as the Siemens CEO saying that AI will not take jobs but those who can use it will, and a Foxconn chief downplaying bubble concerns. Those remarks come from separate reports and are not drawn from the TSMC or Microsoft sessions. The articles carry no further information about what will follow the event beyond the conclusion of the dialogue.

Articles.Title: TSMC, Microsoft executives debate AI's impact on Day 2 of Nikkei Dialogue

stories.Headline: Andhra Pradesh Cabinet clears policy frameworks to attract investments in AI, electronics, renewable energy
stories.Summary:
The Andhra Pradesh Cabinet, chaired by Chief Minister N. Chandrababu Naidu at the Secretariat on Tuesday, approved a series of proposals aimed at drawing investment in artificial intelligence, electronics, renewable energy, pharmaceuticals and manufacturing. The approvals covered the Animation, Visual Effects, Gaming, Comics and Extended Reality policy for 2026 to 2031 and the Robotics and Physical AI policy for 2026 to 2036. The Cabinet also cleared amendments to the Semiconductor and Display Fab Policy for 2024 to 2029. Decisions on infrastructure, education and administration were taken alongside these investment measures.

Among the largest approvals is a ₹31,387 crore investment by AM Intelligence for a 512 MW green integrated AI data centre at Amanam in Bheemunipatnam mandal of Visakhapatnam district. The Cabinet also cleared a ₹4,000.20 crore advanced materials project by Carbon Cosmo at Naidupeta and allotted land in Tirupati to Dixon Technologies for a ₹700 crore investment. About 25 acres were allocated to Reliance Industries for a gigascale AI data centre at Bhogapuram in Vizianagaram district. An ₹570.20 crore Epack unit at Rambilli in Anakapalli district is expected to employ 2,565 people, and Hetero Group received 173.82 acres in the Nakkapalli Bulk Drug Park.

The Cabinet approved the creation of a Directorate of Traffic Management and Road Safety under the Director-General of Police, with its headquarters at Mangalagiri. It also sanctioned a ₹236.92 crore expansion of Ravali Spinners in West Godavari district, expected to employ 1,569 people, and a 30-acre industrial park for women entrepreneurs at Jaggayyapet in NTR district. Compressed biogas plants were approved for NTR, Prakasam and Vizianagaram districts, and the government agreed to study small modular nuclear reactors as an alternative to thermal power. The Cabinet also transferred 5.50 acres of APGENCO land to the Vijayawada Municipal Corporation for a 15 MW waste-to-energy plant.

The articles do not name anyone outside the Cabinet as responsible for the decisions beyond the Chief Minister, who chaired the meeting. The Hindu's report, published on November 11, 2026, attributes the investment figures to sources in the government. Other measures included a 30-year lease of 192.68 acres of Wakf land in Anantapur district for a solar project, a Kendriya Vidyalaya site in the capital region, and the withdrawal of earlier land allotments made to Websol Renewables and Metro Decorative at the Naidupeta Special Economic Zone. The articles do not describe any next steps or timelines for these approvals.

Articles.Title: Andhra Pradesh Cabinet clears policy frameworks to attract investments in AI, electronics, renewable energy

stories.Headline: Riverside Council Enshrines Temporary Data Center Ban Language While City Researches AI
stories.Summary:
On Tuesday, November 10, 2026, the Riverside City Council voted 5-2 to adopt a resolution barring the city from accepting data center proposals. The council took this step because data centers are not currently included in city code as an allowed land use. Councilmembers Chuck Conder and Sean Mill cast the two votes against it. The council chose this option over a second one that would have imposed a 45-day temporary moratorium.

The resolution has the city state that it is technically prohibited from accepting data center proposals for now, while a council-led AI working group researches policies. That group, created the day after a September 14 Land Use Committee meeting, was given 13 months to develop a forward-looking strategy on AI's growth and how the city should use the technology. Councilmember Steven Robillard, who leads the group, said it plans to tackle data center policies in the coming months. The next AI ad hoc committee meeting is scheduled for December 3, and the group is set to present policy recommendations to the full council later next year.

Councilmember Philip Falcone championed the restrictions and told the council that pausing development lets the city set regulations and parameters before acting, rather than doing both at once. He was pushed to request the ban after a nonprofit's agreement with the city mentioned a possible data center, which its CEO had described as a community-use facility for training residents on emerging technologies. Falcone said a ban would preserve commercial land for job-producing sectors, prevent an electrical grid overload, and protect the city's water supply. Robillard said there are currently no proposals on the table and that approving a data center makes no sense until the broader AI conversation is complete.

The decision drew mixed reactions during public comment, as residents and environmental advocates supported restrictions over concerns about long-term harm to the community. Several union representatives opposed a ban, citing recently signed California laws that already restrict these facilities and arguing that prohibitions would cost union members jobs. Conder, a supporter of data centers during his reelection campaign, argued the technology is improving and can be built to minimize harm, and he suggested opposition was partly funded by foreign governments, a claim an NPR investigation found little evidence to support. The city's position is set out in the resolution, with the working group continuing to meet over the next year on AI topics including data centers.

Articles.Title: Riverside Council Enshrines Temporary Data Center Ban Language While City Researches AI - The Riverside Record

stories.Headline: Elon Musk wants to build a s $24 billion gas-powered AI supercomputer in Texas company town
stories.Summary:
Starbase, Texas, which hosts SpaceX's Starship rocket program, has posted notice of a public hearing on a gas-fired power plant and supercomputing facility within the city limits. The project carries an initial cost of $24 billion and will apparently be owned by SpaceX. Tom's Hardware reported the project on November 11, 2026, and described it as a 10 gigawatt site that goes up for approval in December. Bloomberg reports that the project could face resistance from incoming Texas governor Gina Hinojosa.

Hinojosa campaigned against approving new data centers until the state's legislature enacts stronger protections against potential harms from those projects. The $24 billion figure covers only the "initial phases of the projects," and the company says the plan could "include future expansions." Starbase is essentially a company town for SpaceX, since the city mostly sits on land owned by SpaceX and its population mostly comprises the company's own employees. That arrangement may draw less local opposition than the company's Memphis facilities did.

SpaceXSI, the company behind the plan, has been building out its Colossus I and Colossus II data centers near the Mississippi-Tennessee border. Those projects have faced backlash, including a lawsuit from area residents that aims to curb pollutants produced by the large number of gas turbines required to power them. The project appears to be part of SpaceX's push to build 10 gigawatts of compute in 2027 alone. Hinojosa's arrival in the governor's office could override the local regulatory climate the company likely hoped for.

Beyond its terrestrial plans, SpaceX is also working on launching data centers into space. Musk has laid out plans for a first-generation AI1 compute satellite with a 150kW peak compute payload. The company has also submitted a proposal to the FCC to build a 1-million-satellite Orbital Data Center System. Musk wrote in a post on X after the recent U.S. midterm elections that "data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now," and that work could accelerate after data center measures lost big in the polls.

Articles.Title: Elon Musk wants to build a s $24 billion gas-powered AI supercomputer in Texas company town

stories.Headline: Softbank loses $3.7 billion on canceled AI data center gas turbine orders days after denying Elon Musk’s claim it was defaulting
stories.Summary:
SoftBank, the Japanese technology investment firm, has taken a $3.7 billion loss after canceling orders for gas turbines meant to power AI data centers, according to a report published by Tom's Hardware on November 11, 2026. The article, citing The Wall Street Journal, says the company had reserved more than 13 gigawatts of turbine capacity, roughly equal to more than six Hoover Dams. The cancellations, which the article says SoftBank made voluntarily, came days after the company denied a claim by Elon Musk that it had defaulted on turbine orders. SoftBank now plans to unwind its remaining reservations with GE Vernova, its turbine supplier, along with contracts for orders that were too far along to cancel.

The turbines were intended for gas-fired power plants supporting data centers. The article reports that SoftBank had planned a 9.2-gigawatt power plant in Ohio, with construction scheduled for early 2027 and a cost of $33 billion, to supply a neighboring eight-gigawatt data center. That data center was to be leased to OpenAI, and the article says Nvidia had entered discussions about guaranteeing around $250 billion of financing for the project. The article says SoftBank initially planned to use the turbines for future gas plants but later changed direction.

SoftBank Chief Financial Officer Yoshimitsu Goto responded to Musk's claim, reportedly saying, "This is simply not correct at all," and "There is no such default." Musk had made his claim in a post on X, which the article identifies as a social network. On an earnings call, SoftBank told investors the orders had been placed to secure power generation equipment in anticipation of shortages. The article attributes the turbine reservation details to unnamed people familiar with the orders.

The article says turbine manufacturers typically charge customers tens of millions of dollars per gigawatt, and that orders must be placed years before the equipment is needed. SoftBank had bet on demand outstripping supply, which the article says would have left it holding valuable orders. By early 2026, the article notes, the company had reserved more power generation capacity than the entire state of Connecticut after securing a large share of global gas turbine production. The article does not say what the cancellations will mean for the Ohio project or the OpenAI lease.

Articles.Title: Softbank loses $3.7 billion on canceled AI data center gas turbine orders days after denying Elon Musk’s claim it was defaulting

stories.Headline: OpenAI and Georgia county leaders hit with Mafia-style RICO racketeering lawsuit over $30 billion AI data center
stories.Summary:
A residents' group in Effingham County, Georgia, has filed a Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act lawsuit against county commissioners, county leaders, OpenAI and its affiliates over the proposed "Project Camellia" data center. The plaintiffs are Dr. Michelle Finch-Mincey, Lehman Mincey Jr. and Raymond Carver, who are seeking civil damages. They say the project has harmed their property values and that purchase offers for nearby residential properties have dropped or been withdrawn since the data center was announced. The filing reported by the Effingham Herald alleges a conspiracy to advance the project through confidential negotiations and closed-door decisions.

The lawsuit names all six Effingham County Commissioners as defendants, including Chairperson Damon Rahn, Forrest Floyd, Roger Burdette, Jamie DeLoach, Elizabeth Helmly and Phil Kieffer. It also names County Manager Tim Callanan, Effingham County Industrial Development Authority CEO Brandt Herndon, and the IDA itself. The defendants further include OpenAI, Octans GA LLC, which operates the data center on OpenAI's behalf, and Savannah Industrial Development LLC, which was involved in the sale of IDA property to Octans and OpenAI. The plaintiffs allege fraud and concealment through non-disclosure agreements and misleading public statements, along with improper land transactions, zoning violations and civil racketeering.

Project Camellia is one of OpenAI's largest planned data centers in Effingham County, with an expected cost between $20 billion and $30 billion. The project is to be built across five phases with a planned compute capacity of 3.2 gigawatts. OpenAI has said it will pay the full cost of all required infrastructure upgrades so the community's utility costs are not affected, and that its closed-loop water system will keep water use minimal. The residents opposing the project contend that the county sought land, tax incentives and zoning approvals without informing the public until key decisions were finalized and contracts signed.

The federal RICO Act was originally designed to counter organized crime, and Georgia's version is less stringent than the federal one. Georgia's statute has been used in the 2023 election racketeering case against Donald Trump and 18 others, and in Young Thug's trial over the alleged YSL Records street gang. Georgia State University criminal justice professor Volkan Topalli, quoted by Atlanta Magazine, said critics consider the state law too encompassing and say it has been used against defendants in more ordinary felony cases. The articles also note that data center developers have used non-disclosure agreements during negotiations, and that an AWS data center in Gilroy, California, drew scrutiny after residents learned of its nature only when construction began.

Articles.Title: OpenAI and Georgia county leaders hit with Mafia-style RICO racketeering lawsuit over $30 billion AI data center

stories.Headline: ‘Children are not a pilot programme’: Lucy Calkins on use of AI in schools
stories.Summary:
Lucy Calkins, a Columbia University professor who created the reading and writing curriculum Units of Study, spoke with The Hindu about the use of AI in schools, and her interview was published on November 11, 2026. Calkins had given a lecture at Shiv Nadar School in Gurugram on October 31, 2026, and the piece carries a photo credit to a special arrangement. Her curriculum is used in thousands of schools across the United States. The article's central concern is that the literacy crisis has grown especially urgent in both India and America.

In the interview, Calkins argues that developing deep reading and writing skills in children matters more than ever now that AI can generate text in seconds. She is quoted saying that by the time children reach middle school, they can let AI take over their reading lives entirely. Her remark frames the problem as one of habit and skill formation rather than access to technology. The article presents her view as a warning to educators and families rather than a list of prescribed policy changes. The excerpt does not spell out specific measures schools should adopt.

Calkins is the person whose views the article reports, and the interview was conducted by Nivedita S. for The Hindu. The piece is labeled as an interview under the education category, and it appears in the paper's education coverage. The article does not report any formal response from school authorities or government bodies. Calkins's central point, as the headline makes clear, is that children should not be treated as subjects of an experiment with AI tools. The text available does not describe further developments or follow-up actions.

Articles.Title: ‘Children are not a pilot programme’: Lucy Calkins on use of AI in schools - The Hindu

stories.Headline: AI has made it ‘close to impossible’ to assess university coursework, regulator says
stories.Summary:
The Office for Students, England's higher education regulator, has concluded that artificial intelligence has made it close to impossible to assess university coursework fairly. Its investigation, published on 11 November 2026, found that lecturers are struggling to grade essays, dissertations and open book exams because AI use is widespread and often goes undetected. The regulator is urging universities to return to traditional exams and in-person presentations as a way to grade students. It warned that the credibility of degrees in England is under threat.

The regulator said institutions that fail to design valid and reliable ways of measuring students' knowledge and skills to counter AI could breach their conditions of registration. Such failures could lead to sanctions being imposed on the institutions. Josh Fleming, the OfS director of strategy and delivery, described AI in higher education as a generational risk that threatens both learning and the ability to assess students. He said the sector needs far greater use of AI-free assessment. The regulator said it will keep working with universities and colleges to capture AI's benefits while managing its risks.

The findings come from a report by the OfS and Advance HE, a charity that promotes university governance and teaching, which interviewed more than 300 students and staff at 127 universities and colleges this year. Many institutions have already changed how they assess students, using more in-person written exams, oral examinations known as vivas, and process-based assessments in which students explain how they researched and produced their work. The report also cited students who said peers completed assessments with AI in a few minutes and still received grades similar to those who did not use it. Academics described receiving large numbers of near-identical submissions that cited the same literature and shared a style. A Department for Education spokesperson said universities should take the issue seriously and that the OfS should enforce existing standards and make its framework on AI explicit, strong and durable.

Articles.Title: AI has made it ‘close to impossible’ to assess university coursework, regulator says

stories.Headline: Ohio likely won’t pass AI regulations before year ends
stories.Summary:
Ohio has no substantial artificial intelligence regulations, and lawmakers from both parties are trying to pass some before their December deadline. One Republican leader is blocking them, saying none of the bills are ready for a vote. As AI chatbots become more mainstream, wrongful death lawsuits have appeared across the country, and court documents say the victims all received help from a bot. State Rep. Christine Cockley, D-Columbus, said, "We aren't preventing deaths right now."

The latest case involves a 13-year-old whose parents are suing after Google's AI Gemini allegedly helped the child make a suicide plot over a matter of weeks. The child survived, but the parents and Cockley say it shouldn't have gotten to this point. Cockley, Republican state Rep. Ty Mathews of Findlay, and a bipartisan group of legislators introduced House Bill 524. The bill would establish penalties for developers whose AI models generate content encouraging self-harm or violence.

Under House Bill 524, the state could investigate and impose civil penalties of up to $50,000 per violation. The money collected would go to the state's 988 crisis hotline and consumer protection enforcement. House Technology and Innovation Committee Chair Thad Claggett, R-Licking County, said after hearing bills Monday that the problem is not the developers, because the harm comes generations down the line through a bot acting through its systems. Claggett said he wants "really good law" rather than legislation that must be quickly amended.

Lawmakers have tried to tackle AI policy for years, but it continues to stall. Eight bills on the topic sit in Claggett's committee, including measures that would require watermarks on AI-altered images, make it a crime to generate AI child sexual abuse material, and prevent AI marriage. Claggett said none of the bills are ready for a vote, and he said he knows of no bill in his committee that lacks problematic issues involving liberty or unnecessary burdens. Claggett blames the intricacy of the topic for the delay.

Cockley believes tech companies are spending money to delay legislation, saying that money in politics instills fear in legislators. She also cited fear of big tech, fear of going against the status quo, and fear of the unknown. Cockley said new leadership could allow regulations to be put in place, pointing to Governor-elect Amy Acton and an end to the superminority. The lawmakers have until mid-December to pass guardrails, and Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine has repeatedly pushed for safety regulations.

Articles.Title: Ohio likely won’t pass AI regulations before year ends

Sen. Elizabeth Warren, a Massachusetts Democrat, is said to be set to take over as chair of the Senate Banking Committee in January. Her financial and housing priorities are also outlined in the coverage. Crypto businesses tied to President Donald Trump's family are expected to be a key focus of her oversight. The articles describe these as areas where she would seek to use committee authority, though they do not spell out the specific bills or steps she would take.

Those points, however, rest on reports that have not been fully confirmed. The coverage is based on a November 9, 2026 report, and the articles do not describe any formal announcement from Warren or the committee. stories.Headline: AI voice company WellSaid retools for agents while keeping its commitment to human actors
stories.Summary:
WellSaid, the AI voice company that spun out of Seattle's Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence in 2019, has launched WellSaid Producer, a product that connects its voiceover tools to AI assistants such as Claude and Microsoft Copilot. Corporate users can now ask an assistant for a voiceover for a training or marketing video, and the assistant sends the script to WellSaid, which generates the audio with its licensed voices. The launch is part of a broader overhaul of the business, which has moved away from individual users to focus on companies. The company has about 30 employees, down from more than 70 in late 2024, and CEO Benjamin Dorr told GeekWire it has become profitable.

Producer uses the Model Context Protocol, a standard that lets AI assistants connect to other software, and it works with Claude, ChatGPT, Copilot and Atlassian's Rovo. Companies can set style guides so brand names and technical terms are pronounced the same way in every file. When a script changes, Producer can update every affected voiceover in one pass, and each finished file carries a record of its license. WellSaid also says it is the first voiceover platform to generate audio natively at 48 kHz, the standard for film and video, and its Studio app will remain available. Producer is sold on credits for minutes of finished, licensed audio, and Dorr said the company wants to price more like the traditional voiceover industry, where pricing depends on length, reach and run time.

Dorr, who joined as chief financial officer in 2024 and became chief executive in spring 2025, leads a team that includes several executives he brought from Cordial, a San Diego marketing software company. He succeeded Brian Cook, who led the company for about 16 months, and co-founder Matt Hocking remains on the board. Dorr described the new direction as "Act II," with Producer as its opening scene, and acknowledged that the cast is much smaller. WellSaid is keeping its practice of building voices from recordings of professional actors, who receive royalties when businesses use their voices. The company says nearly half of the Fortune 100 are customers.

Dorr argues that voiceover is only one step in a larger production process and that AI agents will let companies combine specialized tools from vendors they trust rather than rely on a single app. He said agents that work on their own will be able to use Producer by the end of the year. The company's licensing approach sets it apart in a sector where many models are trained on audio scraped from the internet. The articles do not say how many customers use Producer so far or what revenue the company reports.

Articles.Title: AI voice company WellSaid retools for agents while keeping its commitment to human actors

stories.Headline: Inside Greece's new AI Act framework
stories.Summary:
Greece has set up its national framework for enforcing the EU AI Act through Law 5321/2026, which took effect on its 20 July publication date unless a provision says otherwise. The law spreads oversight across existing sectoral regulators instead of creating a new standalone AI authority. Its publication came about two weeks before the European Commission and national authorities began enforcing the AI Act on 2 August, when new transparency rules took effect. The bill moved quickly, opening for public consultation on 21 June, with the text finalized and enacted within two weeks after consultation closed on 6 July.

The Hellenic Data Protection Authority has been designated as the market surveillance authority for prohibited AI practices, Annex III high-risk systems and Article 50 transparency obligations. It also serves as Greece's single point of contact with the Commission and other member states. As a result, enforcement of the AI Act and the EU General Data Protection Regulation sits with the same regulator. Legal commentators have pointed out that many AI systems covered by Annex III process personal data or directly affect fundamental rights, which gives the authority's existing data protection expertise direct relevance to its new role.

The article was written by Aspasia Xirou, a data privacy risk specialist at the International Monetary Fund, and it was published by the IAPP. The author's analysis describes the structure of the law and its timing rather than attributing new decisions to any particular official. The Greek Ministry of Digital Governance handled the bill's public consultation and its passage. The article does not report any direct statements from ministry officials or from the data protection authority about how they plan to carry out the new duties.

The move reflects a broader choice available to EU member states, which have discretion over how to organize the national authorities that the AI Act relies on. Greece chose to build on an existing regulator rather than create a new body, and the article presents this as a distributed model in contrast to other approaches. The article does not describe specific enforcement actions, penalties, or a timetable for further guidance beyond the dates already noted. Further developments on how the framework operates in practice are not covered in the article.

Articles.Title: Inside Greece's new AI Act framework - IAPP

stories.Headline: Judge rules Novig's sports event contracts are not swaps, letting New York enforce its gambling law
stories.Summary:
A federal judge in Manhattan has denied sports prediction market Novig's request for a preliminary injunction that would have stopped New York from enforcing its gambling laws against it. In a filing dated November 10, U.S. District Judge Colleen McMahon of the Southern District of New York ruled that Novig's sports event contracts are not swaps under the Commodity Exchange Act, according to The Block. Because the contracts fall outside that definition, she concluded, federal commodities law does not preempt New York's gambling and sports-wagering rules. The ruling was reported on November 11, 2026. The practical effect is that New York can now require Novig to obtain a state gambling license or stop listing and trading the contracts.

McMahon wrote that the contracts "bear more than a passing resemblance to sports betting," and she reasoned that they do not depend on events with a financial, economic or commercial consequence, which is the test for a swap. Novig, whose legal entity is Ludlow Exchange LLC, had sued New York Attorney General Letitia James and state Gaming Commission officials on August 5, arguing that the Commodity Futures Trading Commission has exclusive jurisdiction over event contracts. The CFTC had designated Ludlow as a contract market in June, and Novig began offering sports contracts to New York customers in August. The ruling is narrower than it might first appear, though it goes further than an earlier decision against Kalshi. In July, Judge Analisa Torres of the same court denied Kalshi a preliminary injunction while assuming, without deciding, that its sports contracts were swaps.

A finding that such contracts are not swaps at all would undercut the starting point of the preemption argument that Kalshi, Polymarket and others rely on. Lawyer Daniel Wallach told The Block that federal courts in the Second Circuit have now issued 10 rulings in sports prediction-market litigation, all favoring the states. The ruling does not end Novig's lawsuit, and the company is litigating the same issue in several other states. The Block said it had asked Novig for comment.

Articles.Title: Judge rules Novig's sports event contracts are not swaps, letting New York enforce its gambling law - MLQ.ai

stories.Headline: From teacher workloads to student work, Boise schools navigate AI
stories.Summary:
The Boise School District plans to give its teachers and staff access to ChatGPT for Teachers, a tool built by OpenAI, with a rollout set for spring 2027. The district is weighing how to protect student privacy, review AI-generated materials, and help teachers handle concerns about cheating as the technology spreads through classrooms. Teachers could use the tool to draft practice quizzes, prepare assignments, or turn spoken instructions into lesson plans for substitutes. The story was reported by Riley Shoemaker of Idaho News 6.

Ryan Gravett, the district's chief technology officer, said the tools could ease teachers' workloads. He gave the example of a teacher who wakes up sick and must prepare someone else to teach the day's lessons, saying a teacher could simply dictate what a day would look like. Gravett also said AI-generated materials still need human review before they reach students. Data privacy, he said, was a major part of the agreement with OpenAI, and the district asked who owns the data, what is done with it, and where it is stored.

According to the article, OpenAI says information entered into the district's workspace will not be used to train its AI models. Gravett said parents and students trust the district with the tools it provides, which is why those questions matter. The new workspace is meant for staff, but students are already using AI, so teachers face the question of whether students did their own work. Gravett said teachers can review how a document developed over time, allowing them to see how an essay took shape. He said the district is leaving judgments about possible AI misuse to individual teachers.

The district is also asking parents to share their views on AI in schools through a survey posted on its website. The article does not say how many parents have responded or what the district will do with the results. It also does not describe any incidents, costs, or formal policies beyond what Gravett described. The rollout in spring 2027 is the next milestone the article identifies.

Articles.Title: From teacher workloads to student work, Boise schools navigate AI

stories.Headline: OCC Gives Bank Examiners a New Playbook for Reviewing AI
stories.Summary:
The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency released a new guide on November 4 called the "OCC Supervisory Framework on Bank Use of Super Intelligence," which is meant to help its examiners review how banks use artificial intelligence. The guide focuses on generative AI, which creates text and other content, and agentic AI, which can act without a person stepping in each time. The agency used the term super intelligence because the executive branch adopted it in place of artificial intelligence, following a September 29 executive order signed by President Donald Trump. Some AI tools now handle credit decisions, customer service and fraud detection, which prompted the agency to set out how examiners should check them. The article frames the release as a response to the growing amount of work banks are handing to these systems.

The guide does not create new rules for banks, according to an analysis from the law firm Ballard Spahr, and it works as a resource for examiners instead. Banks will not treat AI as a separate risk category, and examiners will instead look at how AI changes risks banks already manage, including fraud, privacy, cybersecurity and work with outside vendors. The OCC built the guide around six areas, asking what an AI system is allowed to do, what happens when it makes a mistake, what guardrails exist, who is watching, how a bank recovers from failure, and whether safety checks keep working over time. The guide also ties risk to how much freedom a system has, and it lays out four risk levels, with autonomous payment bots and instant credit decisions at the top and internal tools that never touch customer data at the bottom. The OCC warned that a person who simply clicks approve does not provide real oversight, and reviewers need the skills, facts and power to reject or stop what the AI does.

The OCC's position is that banks remain responsible for their AI systems, and a bank is still on the hook if its AI breaks the law, the analysis said. The agency pointed to customer harm from chatbots that give wrong answers about fees, interest rates or account balances, which could lead to legal trouble. Because many banks buy their AI from outside companies, vendors face extra scrutiny, and the guide asks whether contracts spell out who pays when an AI tool causes harm. It also asks whether vendors must warn banks before changing how their AI works, since a vendor could add new AI features to an old product without the bank noticing the new risks. In a bulletin released with the guide, the OCC said the document sets no binding standards and banks are not expected to use it to grade their own AI programs.

Even without binding force, the analysis said banks should not ignore the guide, which offers a clear preview of what examiners may ask in future bank exams. Banks are encouraged to study it and check whether current risk and compliance programs already cover the issues the OCC raised. Institutions that find gaps now may have an easier time when examiners arrive, the analysis suggested. The article does not say whether the OCC plans further guidance or enforcement actions tied to AI, so those details remain unclear.

Articles.Title: OCC Gives Bank Examiners a New Playbook for Reviewing AI - PYMNTS.com

stories.Headline: Mercedes Lawyer Joins AI Native Compound Law
stories.Summary:
Compound Law, an AI-native law firm based in Berlin, has hired Marc Schuba, a former White & Case lawyer who most recently served as Legal Counsel at Mercedes-Benz, and Philipp Brandt, a business lawyer with more than 20 years of experience, who joins as a partner. The firm was co-founded by the former General Counsel of Zenjob, Julian Jantze, who is now its Chief Legal Officer. The article reports the hires on November 11, 2026. The move is notable because it involves an experienced in-house lawyer from a major corporation joining a firm built around a model that avoids the billable hour and puts AI at the centre of its work. The firm runs on two linked companies: a regulated law firm that advises clients and is responsible for the legal work, and a technology company that builds Compound OS, its AI platform.

Compound OS uses AI agents to prepare research, carry out analysis and draft documents, after which a lawyer reviews every result and is accountable for the final output to the client. Work is billed at fixed prices agreed up front rather than at hourly rates. The new hires will cover IT and AI law, data protection and intellectual property. The firm's focus is Germany and the EU, where, according to the article, the top 100 German law firms billed more than €10bn last year, and it plans to extend into further markets as it grows. Schuba told the publication that the traditional law firm model is out of date because it sells the same judgment repeatedly by the hour.

He argued that good legal judgment can be captured, refined and applied at scale, so that the firm codifies it once, lets its agents apply it, and improves it with each matter, which he said makes competitive fixed pricing possible. Jantze said that both new partners have long built their own software and online tools, and that clients with questions on software contracts, the EU AI Act, trademarks or a crisis will be routed directly to a partner with years of experience in the field. The article places the hires within a wider pattern in which experienced lawyers leave traditional firms to work in firms that do not bill by the hour, and it notes that these so-called NewMod firms are increasingly taking on complex, high-value work rather than only startup contracts or bulk review. The author suggests that large commercial firms are still using AI within a billing model that often works against its wider adoption, and expects more AI-native firms to appear. The article does not say what further steps Compound Law will take or when it will enter new markets.

Articles.Title: Mercedes Lawyer Joins AI Native Compound Law - Artificial Lawyer

stories.Headline: Anthropic agrees to strict AI privacy rules in schools
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, the AI company, has agreed to a set of strict privacy rules for schools that use its tools, according to a report published November 11, 2026, by District Administration. The standards apply automatically to schools that use Claude for Teachers, the article says. They ban AI providers from training their models on data belonging to students and staff. The agreement was reached with the American Federation of Teachers and the United Federation of Teachers, the two unions named in the report.

The article gives no further figures, dates for when the rules take effect, or penalties for violations, so those details cannot be reported here. What the report does establish is the core change: schools using the product are protected from having student and staff information used to train the company's models. The rules cover the schools that use Claude for Teachers rather than all AI tools in education. Beyond that, the report offers only the headline terms of the deal.

The article names Anthropic and the two teachers' unions as the parties to the agreement, and it does not include direct statements from any of them. Micah Ward is listed as the reporter. The piece appears alongside related coverage on AI in schools, including a separate story about Google restricting its search engine in schools that ban AI, but those stories are not part of this agreement. More to follow.
