stories.Headline: AI giant Anthropic sets prices for initial public offering
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, the artificial intelligence company, still plans to go public later this month, according to a Wall Street Journal report cited by Gizmodo published on November 9, 2026. The company's shares, which would trade on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT, could become available as soon as October 19 or 20, though the report's dates appear inconsistent with its November timing. Expectations for the offering have fallen sharply, with the valuation once speculated at roughly $2 trillion now seen by investors as nearer $1.5 trillion, and CNBC reporting on a range of $1 trillion to $1.25 trillion as more likely. The shift followed a rough stretch for AI-linked stocks, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq posting its worst month in quite a while in October.

Those market losses have hit chipmakers particularly hard, and Nvidia's share price fell from an all-time high of $243.37 on October 6 to $204 at the end of that month and closed at $178.67 on Monday, November 9. Nvidia also faced separate turmoil that day after reports that CEO Jensen Huang had an extramarital affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy, and investors worry he may have harmed U.S. national security by selling AI technology to an intermediary for the Chinese government. Huang has publicly apologized to his wife and children. President Donald Trump said at a press conference that the FBI was investigating the matter, and he expressed hope that no problem existed while describing Huang as suffering greatly.

Anthropic's regulatory filings show $33 billion in revenue from January to September 2026, and those same filings state that AI could pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity. The article notes that investors are nervous about the AI trade overall, since the fortunes of major stock market indexes depend heavily on these companies succeeding. Rival OpenAI confidentially filed to go public in June, but the article says it will not list before the end of the year. The author suggests the more probable danger is an AI arms race that places powerful hacking tools in the hands of bad actors, which could disrupt the U.S. financial system.

stories.Headline: Google Acquires Crusoe’s Wyoming Data Center Site
stories.Summary:
Google has acquired Crusoe's data center site in southeast Wyoming, Crusoe announced on November 6, 2026, from Denver. The sale ends Crusoe's pre-development work on the project, which covered site selection, governmental approvals and a power strategy. Crusoe's co-founder and CEO, Chase Lochmiller, said the pre-construction effort of origination, entitlement and de-risking has set the project up for construction and eventual operation. Crusoe is a Denver-based developer recently valued at $30.9 billion. Google did not disclose the price.

Google said it will invest $17 billion to develop the campus, which is in Laramie County. The site is planned to use air cooling and 702 megawatts of Bloom Energy fuel cells. It was announced in July 2025 at 1.8 gigawatts, expandable up to 10 gigawatts. The power strategy was developed with Tallgrass Energy and combines fuel cells, grid power and natural gas turbines. It also carries a long-term roadmap for carbon capture through Tallgrass's regional CO2 sequestration hub.

Crusoe and Tallgrass started the campus through joint development of power and data center infrastructure. That parallel process required simultaneous coordination across energy systems design, data center engineering, site development and hyperscaler engagement. Tallgrass is backed by Blackstone. Lochmiller said Crusoe is in the business of activating gigawatts for intelligence, with more than 6 GW contracted and over 40 GW in its pipeline.

One report said Crusoe had tried and failed to sign Google as a customer for the site. It added that Google is taking over development after reportedly raising concerns about cost and construction timelines under Crusoe's management. The same report said the deal underlines how hard it is for independent developers to deliver massive AI projects on time and on budget. It pointed to challenges in securing equipment and power and to growing local opposition. Another report said the transaction separates Crusoe's technical preparation from Google's investment, which must still turn the site into construction and operation.

Google and Crusoe continue to work together elsewhere. Crusoe recently announced that it is the developer of Google's data center campus under construction in Armstrong County, outside Amarillo, Texas. Crusoe also serves Oracle and OpenAI at its Abilene, Texas, campus and is building a 900-megawatt campus for Microsoft. Meta is a customer, and Jane Street reportedly signed a $13 billion cloud deal with the company. Crusoe was founded by Lochmiller and Cully Cavness, secured $3.9 billion in September and added Redwood Materials founder JB Straubel to its board.

stories.Headline: 1 Stock-Split AI Stock to Buy Before It Soars 328%, According to a Wall Street Analyst
stories.Summary:
Sandisk, the memory chip maker, announced an 8-for-1 stock split that takes effect on November 19, 2026. The split follows a share price that has more than tripled this year after a 559% gain last year, driven by a memory chip supply shortage tied to the AI boom. Its share price was $885 when the Motley Fool article was published on November 11, 2026, and the company had traded at $1,330 when the split was announced on October 29. Splits, according to the article, are often seen as signs of quality businesses because they usually come only after sustained price gains.

Bank of America research cited in the article found that stocks rose an average of 25.4% in the 12 months after a split announcement from 1980 to 2023, compared with 11.9% for the S&P 500 over the same periods. Applying that average to the October 29 price of $1,330 would put Sandisk at $1,667, about 98% above its current price. Wall Street's median target of $2,100 per share, drawn from 34 analysts, implies about 150% upside, and Ben Reitzes of Melius Research has a $3,600 target. The article also notes that Sandisk plans to begin sampling a product called high-bandwidth flash next year.

Sandisk reported first-quarter fiscal 2027 revenue of $11 billion, up 378%, and non-GAAP earnings of $49.51 per diluted share, up 40-fold from a year earlier. The company has signed long-term supply agreements with at least eight customers covering about two-thirds of expected NAND flash production in fiscal 2028. Goldman Sachs analysts estimate high-bandwidth flash could cut inference costs by 30% and create a market worth $40 billion to $150 billion by 2030. The article's author, Trevor Jennewine, says the company's pricing power reflects the current shortage rather than a durable competitive advantage.

The bear case in the article rests on the cyclical nature of the memory industry, where NAND prices dropped 70% during the last downturn. Every major chipmaker is expanding capacity, which the article says would likely lead to a supply glut and falling prices. Sandisk held an 11% NAND flash market share in the June quarter, placing it sixth behind Samsung (28%), SK Hynix (19%), Micron (15%), Kioxia (14%) and YMTC (14%), according to Counterpoint Research. The author says Sandisk trades at 6.7 times earnings, and that earnings will decline when the next downturn arrives.

Trevor Jennewine concludes that patient investors might buy a small position while accepting volatility, but he prefers market leaders with durable competitive edges, which he says Sandisk does not have. A separate Live Trading News piece dated November 9, 2026, by Shayne Heffernan, reports that the broader market fell sharply on November 5 after Democrats won both chambers of Congress in the November 3 midterms. The Nasdaq Composite fell 5.5% that day and the PHLX Semiconductor index fell 12.25%, with Nvidia down 9.26%. Heffernan describes the sell-off as an overreaction concentrated in AI hardware stocks, which he attributes to worries about data-center moratoriums.

Heffernan cites the Artificial Intelligence Data Center Moratorium Act, introduced by Senator Bernie Sanders on March 25, 2026, and by Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez on June 24, which would halt construction of AI data centers until Congress legislates. Neither bill has moved past committee, and New York enacted a state pause in July. Heffernan expects the bill will not become law within two years, since overriding a presidential veto would require two-thirds of each chamber. He also notes that Goldman Sachs estimated Democratic state and local wins could bring short-term moratoriums affecting about 45% of planned US data-center capacity expansion.

stories.Headline: Vanta Buys Pillar to Tie AI Governance to Real-Time Controls
stories.Summary:
Vanta, a platform for security, risk and compliance management, has agreed to buy Pillar Security, an Israeli AI security startup, in a deal valued at about $150 million paid through a mix of cash and shares. The agreement was reported by Calcalist on November 9, 2026. Once the acquisition is complete, Pillar will become Vanta's research and development center in Israel, and its more than 20 employees are expected to join that center. Pillar's technology will be built into Vanta's platform, which serves more than 20,000 customers, and Pillar's founders, Ziv Karliner and Dor Sarig, will stay on to lead its AI security work.

Pillar, founded in 2023, has raised $9 million, with its April 2025 seed round led by Shield Capital. Its platform helps organizations find the AI systems and agents they run, test them against attacks and protect them while they operate. Vanta plans to add an AI inventory tool in January that will map an organization's AI applications, models, agents and related components to owners, approved uses, data access and risks. It also plans to launch runtime monitoring and detection in January, which would flag suspicious activity and violations of set safeguards. Throughout 2027, Vanta expects to release further capabilities drawn from Pillar's technology, and the company says its AI governance product, introduced in July 2026, has drawn more demand than it can accommodate.

Christina Cacioppo, Vanta's CEO and co-founder, said that customers, regulators and auditors want evidence that a company's AI behaves as described, and that a policy document alone does not provide it. Ziv Karliner, Pillar's CEO and co-founder, said Pillar tests AI systems the way attackers would and stops them when they step outside their limits. Vanta's own research found that 65% of IT and business leaders say their use of agentic AI is moving faster than their understanding of it, and fewer than half have a framework for deciding how much autonomy AI should have. Pillar's researchers also found flaws that could let attackers bypass safeguards in AI development tools including Cursor, Codex and Gemini CLI, and the affected vendors patched them after being notified.

The deal is Vanta's third acquisition, following Trustpage in January 2023 and Riskey in July 2025. Vanta says it serves three-quarters of the companies on the Forbes AI 50 list and that daily users of its Vanta Agent rose 253% over the past three quarters. The company reported surpassing $300 million in annual recurring revenue in April 2026, up 63% from the year before. The articles do not say when the acquisition is expected to close.

stories.Headline: Gix Internet: Quantum X Labs Expands AI-Powered Quantum Error Correction Program to Three IBM Quantum Processors
stories.Summary:
Quantum X Labs, a Nasdaq-listed quantum technology company, announced on November 9, 2026 that it had expanded its AI-powered quantum error correction program to datasets from three IBM quantum processors: IBM Fez, IBM Kingston and IBM Pittsburgh. In preliminary benchmarks using experimental data from these processors, the company reported up to 20% fewer logical decoding failures. The company said the results came from its noise-model calibration method, which is meant to help decoders find and fix errors that occur during quantum computations. A later release dated November 10, 2026 repeated these findings from Gix Internet Ltd., which holds about 13% of the company, or 2,818,585 shares. The expanded work builds on earlier research that used experimental surface-code datasets linked to Google's quantum hardware.

The expansion matters because the company is testing its approach across more than one hardware vendor and code family. Its stated goal is hardware-agnostic error correction that can adapt to different architectures and noise characteristics. The benchmarking workflow now connects experimental quantum measurements, noise-model calibration, GPU-accelerated AI training and decoder performance evaluation. The company described the work as one step toward more reliable and scalable quantum computing systems. Quantum processors are sensitive to environmental interference, hardware imperfections and operational noise, which can introduce errors and limit their practical reliability.

Prof. Nir Sharon, the company's Chief Quantum Scientist, said that improving logical decoding performance on different processors is an important step toward fault-tolerant quantum computing across the industry. He said that as processors grow in size and complexity, efficient error correction is expected to become essential to practical systems. The releases attribute the announcements to the company itself and to Gix, with Gix describing the results as preliminary and warning that any benefit to QXL may not translate into value for Gix's investment. Both releases include forward-looking statements and caution that actual results may differ materially.

The articles do not say whether the results have been independently verified or when the company expects them to be published in peer-reviewed form. Gix Internet, a separately listed technology company focused on hospital logistics automation through its deliverz.ai subsidiary, presented the milestone as part of its minority stake in Quantum X Labs. The articles frame the work as part of a broader strategy to develop quantum infrastructure and software for more commercially viable platforms. They do not describe specific product launches, commercial timelines or further benchmark dates beyond the current preliminary results.

stories.Headline: An analysis of the tech job market in late 2026: product managers seem to be benefiting most in the AI era, demand for engineers is plateauing, and more (Lenny Rachitsky/Lenny's Newsletter)
stories.Summary:
Lenny Rachitsky's newsletter published a report on November 10, 2026, titled "State of the tech job market: late 2026," analyzing hiring trends at tech companies. The report is based on two datasets: TrueUp, which tracks global job openings at more than 9,000 tech companies, and Live Data Technologies, which tracks job changes for 124 million professionals, with hiring figures specific to the United States. Rachitsky said the report is his second of 2026 and the most surprising of the five he has produced over the past few years. Product managers appear to be benefiting most in the AI era, according to the report. Open PM roles are at their highest level in nearly four years, up 75% from the March 2023 low, and PM openings grew 56% since the start of 2023, compared with 43% for engineering.

PM's share of hiring rose from 16% in 2021 to 21% today, even though hiring for every core product role has been flat or declining. Rachitsky wrote that this suggests growing demand for PMs but that landing strong candidates is getting harder. Engineering demand has plateaued, the report says. Open engineering roles grew 29% through 2024, 15% through 2025, and just 2.5% in the past year, and there are fewer open engineering roles today than in March. U.S. companies hired about 113,000 software engineers between May 2025 and April 2026, less than half the 2022 peak of 239,000, and the number has dropped every year since 2022.

Rachitsky pointed to recruiter openings, which are up nearly 300% since mid-2023, as a possible sign that engineering hiring could reaccelerate. He also noted the rise of forward deployed engineer roles, with about 1,500 open globally after a 4.6x increase over the past year. Design and user research roles are declining sharply, according to the report. There are about 1,900 open product design roles at tech companies globally, the lowest since tracking began and down 28% from a year ago, and U.S. companies hired about 12,600 product designers in the past 12 months, less than half the 27,600 hired in 2022. User researcher hiring fell 66% from 5,300 in 2022 to about 1,800 over the past year, and only 108 UXR jobs are open globally.

Rachitsky attributed the decline to faster product development, with teams releasing products earlier and relying more on post-launch iteration, along with better tools that let non-researchers conduct user research. The report also tracks skills and location trends. "LLM" is now the most mentioned skill in PM job descriptions, while "Claude" is the second most mentioned skill in designer job descriptions this spring. Fifteen percent of open tech roles are now based in the Bay Area, up 43% from a year ago, and only 14% offer a remote option, the lowest on record and down from 21% in late 2022. Rachitsky said the report's final takeaway, that the tech job market is growing outside of software roles, was reserved for paid subscribers, so the article's text available here does not describe it.

stories.Headline: Not funny: US comedians say 'sexualized' AI personas steal jokes
stories.Summary:
Several American stand-up comedians say AI-generated social media personas are copying their jokes, according to an Agence France-Presse report published on November 11, 2026. Julia Jasunas, a Los Angeles-based comedian, said an account called "Aylen Skye" lifted a joke about kissing a roommate that she had spent years developing. AFP found several similar sexualized AI personalities on Instagram and TikTok that were reusing material from real comedians, and it was unclear who was running them. Some of the accounts appeared to drive traffic to subscription services that host pornography.

The Aylen Skye account gathered more than 230,000 Instagram followers and a Meta verified checkmark before it was removed, while the TikTok version still exists and links to Fanvue, a subscription platform with adult content from AI models. New York comedian Olivia Carter said a copycat video used her joke about asking out a personal trainer, a bit she once performed on Jimmy Fallon's show, and she has stopped posting new material online. California comedian George Brett Olson said an account called "Tiffany Sloane," with over 370,000 followers, copied his joke, his outfit and his stage setup. Experts quoted in the report describe the problem as part of a wider pattern in which AI systems take creative work from painters, musicians and others without payment or credit.

The comedians said platform owners should do more to stop this, and Jasunas argued that companies with the money and technology have a duty to tighten their rules. Meta did not immediately comment, while a TikTok spokesperson pointed to community guidelines that bar sharing content that violates another user's intellectual property rights. Meta's head, Adam Mosseri, responded to Olson's complaint by saying that banning AI was not practical but that the company wanted to direct more traffic to original creators. He added that Meta should work out what it could do about wholesale copying, though he said he was not sure what that would be. Olson called the response a "big nothing-burger."

Carnegie Mellon University professor Michael Smith told AFP that comedians once policed one another's jokes informally, but large language models scraping the internet have made that difficult to enforce. Smith warned that the accounts siphon clicks and money from artists who rely on social media to build audiences and win bookings, which could weaken the early stages of comedy careers. Olson said he sees the issue as a choice made by the companies rather than something that cannot be avoided. The report does not say whether any platform has announced new measures in response.

stories.Headline: Testing the new generation of AI-enabled fire-extinguishing drones
stories.Summary:
Fire crews in Aspen, Colorado are training to pilot a new generation of drones made by the California-based company Seneca, and the Aspen Fire Protection District will be the first fire department in the country to operate them independently once training is complete. The drones are about 10 by 12 feet wide, have four large arms with propellers, and are designed to work in a swarm. Five of them can carry 500 to 1,000 gallons of finished fire foam, and firefighters reported they were easy to operate. Andy Fisher, deputy chief of Aspen Fire, said the department's program could launch as early as next year. So far the drones have only been used on prescribed burns in California with support from Seneca's staff.

Fisher wants to send the drones to hard-to-reach fires, such as remote lightning strikes, before firefighters arrive. The city of Aspen is surrounded by dense forests and has few evacuation routes for residents and visitors. Seneca's founder, Stuart Landesberg, said the drones have a range of 5 to 10 miles, double that when empty, and can cross steep or treacherous terrain quickly. Hovering over a fire, an AI-supported sensor suite calculates distance and wind speed, then releases water or retardant at a specific angle and velocity. Landesberg said the drones will not replace air tankers on big fires but can carry tools, monitor fires and help extinguish hot spots.

Landesberg said the drones could make aerial firefighting far cheaper than helicopters, saying they could be "the next best thing at two orders of magnitude less cost." Aspen Fire says it will pay about $2.5 million over the next five years, with private donors covering the bill. Joe Stutler, a firefighter with nearly 60 years of experience who is not affiliated with Aspen Fire or Seneca, said he is a "big proponent of technology" and hopes the drones can fight fires overnight, when manned aircraft are often grounded. He also hopes they will reduce risk to pilots flying helicopters and air tankers. Stutler remains skeptical, saying he has not seen results from real wildfires and that claims need to be backed by data.

The FAA granted Aspen Fire a waiver in late October, allowing the department to fly the drones up to 200 feet in Pitkin County once training is complete. The drones cannot fly over populated areas, and someone must keep eyes on them at all times, including a spotter on a ridgeline who can communicate with the pilots. If the drones prove useful, Aspen Fire hopes to expand the waiver and help fight fires elsewhere in the state. Before other fire departments invest in the technology, many are watching Aspen to see how effective the drones can be.

The company attributed the gain mainly to a growing contribution from its generative AI platform, which it acquired through the Ask Sage transaction in December 2025, along with stronger revenue. Gross profit climbed about 83% to $13.6 million from $7.4 million, which the article says highlights improving operating economics.

The generative AI platform is described as a key growth and margin catalyst. It lets government agencies and critical industries securely access advanced AI models, develop agentic workflows and process sensitive information in secure environments. Adoption across federal agencies, including the FBI, NASA, U.S. Coast Guard and Department of Energy, strengthens its expansion opportunities. BigBear.ai secured more than 25 contracts worth over $225 million since the second quarter, and backlog rose 22% sequentially to $330 million. Management raised its 2026 revenue guidance to $150-$165 million.

Profitability challenges remain, according to the article. Adjusted EBITDA was still negative at $9.1 million, and selling, general and administrative expenses increased to $31.3 million. The article says sustained generative AI adoption, favorable revenue mix and effective cost management will be crucial to turning gross margin gains into stronger operating profitability. The company's management issued the revenue guidance, and the article notes the company's own figures for these results.

The article says BigBear.ai's improving revenue mix and generative AI adoption could strengthen its position against C3.ai.

Revenue rose 168% to $3.66 billion, and backlog climbed to $132.5 billion from $104 billion in June. Peers Iren Ltd and Nebius rallied 4.5% and nearly 9% respectively. He said the company expects to finance most of the remaining capital spending through delayed draw term loans matched to specific customer contracts. Intrator also said more than 75% of committed capital expenditure through 2027 is tied to investment grade and enterprise customers. He added that he sees no impact from the Democrats' win in Congress, which many believe will slow data center buildout.

CFO Nitin Agarwal acknowledged that the company operates in "a dynamic macro environment" but argued that today's environment is very profitable for companies with demand for differentiated technology that can execute. Futurum Group CEO Daniel Newman wrote in an X post that the quarter reminded the market that CoreWeave's demand and growth prospects remain positive. stories.Headline: Tester joins AI, data and surveillance company with MAGA ties
stories.Summary:
Former Montana U.S. Senator Jon Tester has taken a job as a senior advisor at Palantir Technologies, an artificial intelligence, surveillance and data analytics company with ties to the GOP and the Trump administration. The company's software is used by U.S. immigration enforcement and the Israeli military, drawing scrutiny from the American Civil Liberties Union. Palantir was co-founded by billionaire conservative Trump ally Peter Thiel. The Palantir opportunity reached Tester's desk in July.

Tester said working for Palantir is not the same as working for data centers, though the two are connected. He said data centers are "screwed up big time" because they can overload energy grids, and he argued that communities need to be driving the decisions about them. He called for complete transparency from data center operators. He also said there will be congressional hearings, accountability and oversight on AI.

Tester said he hopes to use his experience as a third-generation organic grain and crop farmer to streamline the paperwork-heavy parts of food production with AI. He said AI could let the U.S. Department of Agriculture and crop insurers interact without overlapping paperwork. He pointed to medical record sharing between Veterans Affairs facilities and the private sector, where Palantir is already active. He said his official role is limited to advising on real-world uses of AI and improving efficiency and ease of use.

The Chronicle asked Tester about earlier statements by Palantir CEO Alex Karp that AI could disrupt white-collar jobs such as coding, writing and legal work. Tester said he did not reach his decision overnight and had talked with Karp before accepting the position. He said people at the company he spoke with one-on-one respected civil liberties and privacy. Karp has contended that only vocational or technical workers and neurodivergent individuals with out-of-the-box problem-solving skills can thrive in an AI-driven world.

Tester said Congress needs to put "sideboards" on AI and that it "bears watching." On July 23, Democratic California representative Ted Lieu and Texas Republican Nathaniel Moran introduced an AI Kill Switch Act, which remains in limbo. Polling from The AI Policy Institute found that 86% of voters support legislating a guaranteed shutdown capability. Tester-endorsed Democratic Representative-elect Sam Forstag proposed a kill switch during an Oct. 26 visit to Montana State University, and Tester said he had not compared notes with Forstag but likes him a lot.

stories.Summary:
On November 10, 2026, the Cloud Native Computing Foundation announced that Vultr had upgraded its CNCF membership to Platinum, at a time when cloud native and AI infrastructure are converging on shared, open interoperability. The announcement was made at KubeCon and CloudNativeCon North America, held in Salt Lake City. The upgrade builds on Vultr's deepening partnerships with CNCF projects and on the recently launched Vultr Open Source Alliance. The alliance brings together work across open infrastructure, cloud native technologies, AI, and developer ecosystems.

The move centers on the idea that developers should be able to choose the infrastructure, frameworks, models, tools, and protocols that suit their workloads without being tied to a single technology stack. Vultr contributed both CPU and GPU infrastructure capacity to support CNCF project testing. Its Vultr Kubernetes Engine is a CNCF Certified Kubernetes product. Vultr also serves as a member of the Agentic AI Foundation, a separate Linux Foundation initiative that stewards open standards for the agentic AI stack.

Chris Aniszczyk, CTO of CNCF, said AI factory infrastructure should be open and fungible rather than another walled garden, and he described Platinum membership as a real commitment to building that open future. Kevin Cochrane, Chief Marketing Officer of Vultr, said open source is the foundation of modern AI infrastructure and that developers should be free to choose their frameworks, models, and infrastructure. Cochrane said the Platinum upgrade builds on five years of work alongside the CNCF community. Vultr's engineering team has worked directly with maintainers on CNCF projects including Kubernetes and Kubeflow.

Vultr first joined CNCF as a Silver Member in 2021. Its infrastructure runs heterogeneous GPU and CPU capacity that supports open source frameworks, including PyTorch for model training and Kubernetes for inference. The engineering work includes contributing feedback and improvements upstream rather than only consuming the technology downstream. The CNCF describes itself as hosting critical components of the global technology infrastructure, including Kubernetes, Prometheus, and Envoy. It is supported by nearly 800 members and over 200 startups, and it is part of the nonprofit Linux Foundation.

stories.Headline: AI hoaxes are deceiving 911 dispatchers, and they're only getting harder to detect
stories.Summary:
In August, a caller made a bomb threat to Wheatland Union High School in Yuba County, California. Police responded overnight, classes were canceled, and no bomb was found and no one was hurt. Authorities said the call was part of a series of hoax calls, also called swatting, made to schools across the country over the summer. What set this incident apart was that the caller's voice was generated by artificial intelligence.

Swatting calls can be placed to 911 or police departments, with callers reporting a bomb threat, mass shooting or another life-threatening emergency in order to set off a large emergency response. According to the FBI, the aim is to harass or retaliate against targets such as public officials. Such calls usually trigger a big, chaotic police response that pulls resources away from real emergencies. Mel Maier, CEO and executive director of APCO International, notes that people have been killed and injured in swatting attacks.

Maier says AI-generated voices have changed these hoaxes. Earlier swatting voices were fairly easy to recognize, but now they sound natural, with pauses and filler words such as "uh" and "um." APCO and NENA: The 9-1-1 Association, which together represent 911 dispatchers, have voiced growing concern about how bad actors could use AI. In June, APCO and the Public Safety Threat Alliance published findings from 766 responses from public safety communications professionals, and about 14% of dispatchers said they had been targeted using AI tools. Maier says he expects that figure to keep rising as the tools improve.

Brandon May, an assistant professor of forensic psychology at the Florida Institute of Technology, says companies such as ElevenLabs offer synthetic voice software that is cheap and easy to get. He says he can clone his own voice on ElevenLabs for less than $20 and change its intonation, pitch and pauses. May says it is no longer simple to tell from a voice or video that it is AI, and he says elaborate fraud callers using AI chatbots are even tricking people out of their life savings. He says the fakes will be nearly impossible for dispatchers to detect during high-stakes calls.

April Heinze, NENA's vice president and chief of 911 operations, says most swatters do not dial 911 directly, because 911 supplies location, a callback number and the phone owner's name, and spoofing a location on 911 is essentially impossible. Swatting calls are usually made to police departments or courthouses and then transferred into 911 centers, which makes them hard to trace. Heinze and Maier both decline to describe their dispatcher training in detail, saying more public information would make it easier to train AI to fool dispatchers. Maier says APCO is developing caller interrogation criteria that ask questions granular enough that an AI could not pull the answers from public databases or social media. Both Maier and Heinze stress that dispatchers will always treat reports of life-threatening situations as real and send emergency resources, with Heinze saying, "if it's a life-or-death situation, you cannot ever take chances on that."

stories.Headline: Intel and Altera Simplify Sensor Integration for Edge and Physical AI
stories.Summary:
Intel and Altera announced on November 11, 2026, that they will collaborate on a flexible, real-time sensor bridge for edge and physical AI systems. The announcement came from Santa Clara, California, and combines Intel compute, connectivity and software with Altera FPGAs. The companies say the work aims to help equipment makers connect and act on data from increasingly sensor-rich environments. The partnership targets healthcare, aerospace and defense, and robotics applications. The collaboration centers on modular reference solutions that pair programmable hardware with a consistent Intel compute and software foundation.

The articles say these designs are meant to handle sensor data that must be merged while meeting requirements for timing, performance, power and cost. Some applications need very high bandwidth or flexible form factors that place input and output away from the compute board. In those cases, sensor data must be streamed rapidly into memory for the host Intel processor to use. The companies say this approach should let manufacturers adapt as applications and sensors change and move more efficiently from prototype to deployment. Dan Rodriguez, corporate vice president and general manager of Intel's Edge Computing Group, said customers need a simpler way to turn real-world data into timely action as sensors multiply.

Farhad Shafai, head of business solutions and marketing at Altera, said physical AI systems must sense, decide and act in real time, and that Altera FPGAs supply the connectivity, data processing and deterministic control needed for that. Shafai added that the FPGAs remain programmable as sensors and AI models evolve. Both executives framed the combined offering as a flexible foundation that manufacturers can tailor to their needs. The companies plan to apply the work in three areas. In healthcare, they are jointly developing a reference solution aimed at the strict latency and real-time requirements of advanced equipment.

In aerospace and defense, they are working on reference solutions for next-generation mission systems with a focus on size, weight and power for converged AI and signal-processing workloads. In robotics, they plan to combine Intel compute, connectivity and robotics software with Altera FPGA technology to address complex sensing and timing needs. Developers will reach these capabilities through Intel's Open Edge Platform SDK and an Altera SDK. The articles do not give timelines for when the reference solutions will be released.

stories.Headline: Coframe, which uses AI to make websites that test and personalize themselves for each visitor, raised a $25M Series A, bringing its total funding to $35M (Ben Bergman/Business Insider)
stories.Summary:
Coframe, a startup that uses AI to build websites that test and personalize themselves for each visitor, raised a $25 million Series A, bringing its total funding to $35 million, according to Business Insider. The round was co-led by Khosla Ventures and Hanabi Capital, and the valuation was not disclosed. Khosla Ventures had also backed the company at the seed stage. The company describes its goal as turning websites into what it calls the "living internet."

Billionaire venture capitalist Vinod Khosla said AI has made extreme customization possible, arguing that one-size-fits-all websites are becoming outdated. He criticized Amazon, saying its shopping experience has gotten worse over the past 15 years because it pushes what it wants to sell rather than what is most relevant to each user. Khosla added that writing custom code for every page is too expensive and too slow, which is why AI is needed. He called the idea of a customized page for every user "a really good idea."

Coframe was founded in 2023 by Josh Payne, an AI researcher and entrepreneur who studied mathematics and computer science at Stanford and previously co-founded the sports and entertainment startup Autograph. Payne said the company grew out of manual, labor-intensive work he encountered while trying to grow a consumer business. He said that when ChatGPT came out, he saw generative AI could be the solution. He described websites as static, noting that they are built once and then take a great deal of effort to improve.

Payne said Coframe's advantage will come from learning what drives a particular customer to click and buy, rather than simply generating a more attractive landing page. He said the company gives consumers a more relevant experience that better represents what a business does. Coframe says it has generated more than $300 million in incremental revenue for customers including Dropbox, BCG, Block, Backcountry, and Sur La Table. The company says conversion rates rose 158% at Dropbox, 410% at Replit, and 60% at Cash App.

Payne described marketing technology as a category that has rarely drawn strong interest from venture capitalists, with the market dominated by giants such as Adobe and Salesforce along with many vendors selling testing and measurement tools. He noted that Optimizely, once a Silicon Valley favorite, was acquired for an undisclosed sum in 2021. Payne said he believes AI can give the category a second act. He added that the technology is catching up quickly enough to deliver the kind of living internet Coframe is pursuing.

stories.Headline: Veterans tour Washington war memorials using AI glasses
stories.Summary:
On Tuesday, November 10, 2026, a group of veterans from across the country toured Washington's war memorials using special sets of AI glasses to help them locate fallen service members. The trip was an honor flight sponsored by Meta, and the veterans spent three days in the capital. Many of them were blind or visually impaired, so each received a pair of Ray-Ban Meta AI glasses to help them move through the memorials built in their honor. The glasses use built-in cameras, microphones and AI to sense the wearer's surroundings and describe them aloud.

The glasses could be used to read details about the memorials and to explain what the wearers were facing. Meta has committed to donating 130,000 pairs to visually impaired and blinded veterans nationwide. According to John Bockstanz, an Innovation Policy Manager at Meta, the glasses are already helping users regain independence in places like busy airports, restaurants and clothing stores. He described the effort as an ongoing, year-round commitment rather than a single flight.

John Bockstanz, who is also an Iraq War veteran, said the company worked with the veterans so they could ask the glasses what they were seeing and get more information about each memorial. Victor Dunham, a Vietnam veteran from Texas, used his pair to research a friend named Anthony, known as Tony, who died while serving beside him. The glasses helped him locate Anthony's name on the Vietnam Memorial wall. Dunham said the experience closed a loop he had carried for decades.

The trip also gave Dunham a chance to share the experience with his son Mark, an Iraq War veteran who came along. Dunham called the visit wonderful and said he appreciated it beyond belief. He described it as the most meaningful thing he had ever done with the company. The articles do not describe any further plans for the trip beyond the three days in Washington.

stories.Headline: IBM report finds 94% of surveyed enterprises faced a sovereignty challenge, with AI the most common
stories.Summary:
The IBM report, Proof, Not Promises: The Digital Sovereignty Index, was released on November 11, 2026, and it finds that 94% of the enterprises it surveyed faced at least one sovereignty challenge over the previous three years. Those challenges included AI-provider failures, regulatory conflicts, critical vendor disruption, government restrictions such as export controls, and data-access problems. Of the organizations affected, 81% had to supply formal evidence of control to regulators, customers, auditors or internal stakeholders. IBM describes the gap it has found as an "overconfidence gap," in which leaders believe they can prove sovereign control but the evidence often falls short of the Index's highest standards.

The report measures whether an organization can retain and prove control over its critical AI, technology, operations and data, especially when conditions change or dependencies come under pressure. It assesses six areas: responsibility, which asks whether the organization can prove who was accountable; trace, which asks whether it can show exactly what happened; constraint, which asks whether it can prove its controls were working; intervention, which asks whether it can show how it responded and recovered; legitimacy, which asks whether it can explain and justify decisions under scrutiny; and exit, which asks whether it can prove it could change provider or recover operations if needed. The findings suggest that the difficulty is less about control itself than about sovereignty efforts not being built to answer these questions smoothly under pressure. Only a third of respondents, 33%, test their ability to demonstrate sovereignty continuously or as part of regular governance and assurance processes.

IBM's Senior Vice President and Chief Global Affairs Officer, Jonathan Adashek, said that sovereignty should expand future choices rather than restrict them, and that boards need to show how they can adapt, change strategy or change critical provider. He added that the next step is stronger evidence that governance works, including testing exit capabilities, understanding critical dependencies and focusing on where a loss of control would have the greatest impact. Emmanuel Frenehard, Chief Digital Officer at Sanofi, said that digital sovereignty is a business reality rather than a compliance checkbox, and that it is a matter of business continuity as AI becomes embedded across the enterprise. The report itself does not say which organizations or regulators, beyond these two executives, took any position on the findings.

AI emerged as the most common sovereignty problem, with AI-related issues, including incorrect outputs, explainability problems, model or provider failures and governance concerns, cited by 44% of respondents. That figure was ahead of significant provider changes at 35%, formal audit or regulatory events at 38%, data-access or transfer issues at 33%, and government restrictions such as export controls or sanctions at 30%. An average of 82% of respondents said they were very or extremely confident they could provide evidence of sovereign control. However, only 26% of enterprises reached the Index's Leading Digital Sovereignty tier, and enterprises in that tier were more than twice as likely to resolve their most testing challenge without material disruption, at 52% compared with 22% of establishing enterprises.

The research behind the Index combined a review of 27 sources, including legislation, standards, governance frameworks and academic research, with 25 interviews with policymakers, regulators, public-sector officials and policy experts, and perspectives from 17 senior customer leaders across five countries. Its quantitative survey covered 2,003 senior decision-makers at large enterprises in the United States, United Kingdom, Germany, France, Saudi Arabia, India and Japan. Among the barriers that respondents reported to proving sovereignty were manual or time-consuming evidence collection, cited by 56%, and fragmented evidence across teams and systems, dependence on third parties for records, and legacy systems or inconsistent standards, each cited by 53%. Half of respondents, 50%, pointed to untested controls, recovery or exit arrangements. The report does not describe any specific steps that organizations are scheduled to take next.

stories.Headline: Australian companies face 'AI washing' claims after wave of job cuts, offshoring
stories.Summary:
Australian blue-chip companies are increasingly citing artificial intelligence as they cut jobs and move work offshore, according to unions and experts, a trend that complicates the government's efforts to support employment in a slowing economy. On Tuesday, Qantas said it would cut 850 jobs and outsource some corporate functions offshore as part of an AI-driven overhaul with consulting firm Accenture, a move that has drawn accusations of "AI washing." The term describes companies attributing layoffs to AI when the primary driver may be broader cost-cutting, such as shifting jobs offshore. Tech companies WiseTech and Atlassian have cut jobs this year and attributed the losses to AI. Telstra has also cut jobs from an AI joint venture with Accenture, with some work moved to India.

Other firms across corporate Australia have slashed domestic headcounts while expanding operations in India, the Philippines and Vietnam, though they did not explicitly mention AI in their announcements. When asked about the Qantas cuts, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said AI "represents an enormous opportunity and a major economic issue." Labour unions argue that Australian workers are not being replaced by AI but by lower-paid offshore employees. The Australian Council of Trade Unions' Melissa Donnelly said unions are concerned that companies are using AI as cover to cut Australian jobs without accountability. The Australian Services Union, which represents affected Qantas workers, accused the airline of "using AI to launder their cuts to Australian jobs."

A Qantas spokesperson said the airline would continue to consult with unions and was focused on "redeployment opportunities" and support for affected staff, but did not respond to the concerns about AI washing. Senator Barbara Pocock of the Australian Greens said on Wednesday she was concerned to see big companies engaging in AI washing, saying AI "is transforming our workplaces and economy but that's no excuse to let it run rampant." Atlassian, WiseTech and Telstra did not immediately respond to requests for comment. University of Sydney Business School professor Uri Gal said a growing number of companies were blaming job cuts on AI and that accepting AI as the primary explanation should be approached with caution. He said that Qantas's decision appeared to reflect conventional outsourcing, since the work is first being transferred to Accenture, primarily in India.

Further job cuts could pose difficulties for Australia's centre-left Labor government, whose approval ratings have steadily fallen in recent polls amid high cost-of-living pressures. The central bank has raised interest rates five times so far this year, to their highest level in 18 years, amid persistent inflation, while the latest data showed unemployment at a five-year high of 4.7%. The Reserve Bank of Australia said this week that AI had not yet led to widespread job losses, though it noted "tentative signs of adjustment," with job ads weakening in AI-exposed occupations. A government spokesperson said it expects Australian workers to benefit from new technologies and that employers should invest in upskilling them to adopt AI.

stories.Headline: AI Opportunity Fund Expands AI Skills Training Across Asia Pacific with 28 Phase Three Local Implementing Partners
stories.Summary:
AVPN, Asia's largest platform for social impact, announced on November 11, 2026 the 28 organisations selected as local implementing partners for phase three of the AI Opportunity Fund: Asia-Pacific, supported by Google.org and the Asian Development Bank. The new cohort extends the Fund's AI skills training into schools, universities and workplaces across 19 markets, including through organisations taking part in AI Ready ASEAN, led by ASEAN Foundation. Most of the new partners will work directly with K-12 teachers, university students and faculty, reaching the educators who shape the next generation of workers. Other partners will reach healthcare workers, agricultural and service-sector workers, and employees of micro, small and medium-sized enterprises. The same day, AVPN also launched the AI Opportunity Learning Platform.

The platform gives learners access to localised AI training and recommended learning pathways in 16 languages, with a pathway suggested after a short assessment. Certification is available on completion of training. A Gemini-powered assistant helps users navigate the platform and provides guided learning. For phase three, AVPN brought on two new strategic partners: the Raspberry Pi Foundation, which will help local partners localise its Experience AI content, and the Ayala Foundation, which will give educators and students in the Philippines access to Google AI learning resources and support local partners there. Among the funded organisations, Pratham Education Foundation in India will train teachers to use AI critically, JA Korea will pair Google's AI training with formal certification for public school educators, and AI Edu Corp in Vietnam will support embedding AI literacy into national teacher standards.

AVPN chief executive Naina Subberwal Batra said that AI tools are already entering classrooms and workplaces across the region, and that the challenge is helping people use them well and know when not to rely on them too heavily. She said local organisations understand the languages and communities they serve and can adapt training in ways a regional programme alone cannot. Marija Ralic, head of Google.org APAC, said access to AI skills depends on whether people can find relevant training in a language and setting that works for them, and that the platform brings training and local partners together in one place. The Fund was launched in 2024 with a USD 15 million commitment, received a further USD 10 million in phase two in May 2025 and another USD 10 million in phase three in May 2026, bringing Google.org's total commitment to USD 35 million. To date, the Fund has trained more than 850,000 workers and 63,000 small businesses through almost 60 local implementing partner organisations, delivering programmes in more than 30 local languages.

stories.Headline: Rackspace and Together AI Announce Strategic Agreement to Support Enterprise AI Inference
stories.Summary:
Rackspace and Together AI announced an initial multiyear strategic AI infrastructure agreement on November 10, 2026, in San Antonio. Under the deal, Rackspace expects to provide and operate dedicated NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 infrastructure, connected with NVIDIA Spectrum-X Ethernet networking, to support Together AI inference workloads. Deployment is planned for 2027, subject to certain conditions. The companies also signed a separate, non-binding letter of intent to explore a joint go-to-market approach for enterprise-focused AI solutions. Rackspace is described as the operator of the full enterprise AI stack.

Rackspace expects to supply the dedicated NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra infrastructure, including power, liquid cooling, networking and storage. Together AI expects to provide the managed cloud platform running on that infrastructure, including access to open source models, inference optimizations and developer tools. The parties expect to evaluate additional security, governance and compliance controls for future offerings, depending on customer requirements. Rackspace intends to build a repeatable model to support AI platform companies, systems integrators and enterprises. Its approach is to seek contractual commitments for dedicated capacity and manage related financing with the goal of aligning to expected customer demand and the useful life of the hardware.

Gajen Kandiah, Chief Executive Officer of Rackspace, said that enterprise AI requires more than compute, and that success depends on bringing compute into production and operating it reliably. He said Rackspace brings more than 25 years of experience operating complex enterprise environments. Vipul Ved Prakash, founder and CEO of Together AI, said that scaling in the enterprise requires infrastructure that can grow with the company's ambitions. Raj Mirpuri, Vice President of Global AI Clouds and Infrastructure Ecosystem at NVIDIA, said that Rackspace and Together AI can run inference workloads efficiently with NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra. Rackspace, an NVIDIA Cloud Partner, plans to operate the deployment in a purpose-built, liquid-cooled facility.

Effective November 6, 2026, Rackspace entered into a share purchase agreement with an investor group led by Voss Capital, LP, providing for an aggregate $66 million private placement of common stock. Rackspace expects to use the net proceeds for general corporate purposes, working capital, capital expenditures and growth capital, including GPU-related initiatives. Rackspace expects to seek separate financing for the NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 systems and is in active discussions with potential lenders. However, no definitive GPU financing commitment had been obtained as of the release date. The release states that Rackspace's obligations to proceed with the deployment are subject to the financing condition and other conditions in the definitive agreement.

Together AI, described as the AI Native Cloud, was founded in 2022 and says it powers over two million developers. The release says the non-binding letter of intent contemplates evaluating how Together AI's inference, post-training and reinforcement learning capabilities could be combined with Rackspace's infrastructure and engineering services. Any joint offerings would depend on further agreement between the parties and applicable customer requirements. The release also says that the availability of any deployment configurations, including data residency and compliance features, would be determined by the specific offering. The release does not say what happens next beyond the planned 2027 deployment and the exploration of joint offerings.

stories.Headline: CoreWeave AI Cloud Revenue Climbs 168% as Backlog More Than Doubles
stories.Summary:
CoreWeave reported its third-quarter 2026 results on November 10, 2026, showing revenue up 168% from a year earlier to $3.661 billion. Its revenue backlog reached about $132.5 billion, and the company raised its full-year outlook. The AI cloud provider's net loss widened to $709 million as interest and depreciation costs rose. Those figures came in the company's earnings presentation.

The company credited strong execution, favorable pricing and customer demand for its AI cloud platform for the growth. Backlog rose 138% from $55.6 billion a year earlier, with AI labs, hyperscaler customers, enterprises and AI-native companies all adding to it. Backlog represents committed future revenue under contracts rather than revenue already earned. CoreWeave expects 36% of it to be recognized within 24 months, 38% in months 25 through 48 and 26% after 48 months. Active power exceeded 1.7 gigawatts after more than 200 megawatts were added during the quarter.

Operating income improved to $207 million from $52 million, lifting operating margin to 6% from 4%. Net interest expense rose to $846 million from $310 million, and depreciation and amortization climbed to $1.889 billion from $630 million. Those increases explain why the net loss widened from $110 million despite the stronger operating result. Company-defined capital expenditures reached $14.5 billion, compared with $1.85 billion a year earlier.

CoreWeave raised full-year 2026 revenue guidance to $13.0 billion to $13.3 billion from the previous $12.4 billion to $13.2 billion. Full-year capital expenditures are now expected at $37 billion to $39 billion, with the low end raised from $35 billion because the company expects to deploy infrastructure sooner than planned. During the quarter it raised about $4.2 billion in convertible notes and closed a $2.6 billion term-loan facility. CEO Michael Intrator said about $9 billion in customer prepayments and deposits is expected over the next three months.

stories.Headline: The AI Interview: Chris Bergey, EVP of Edge AI at Arm
stories.Summary:
Chris Bergey, Executive Vice President of Edge AI at Arm, was interviewed by AI Magazine and published on November 11, 2026, in an interview written by Adam Pond and Tom Chapman. He said the arrival of more AI inference and the desire to have intelligence closer to where people use it, on the devices they carry and wear, marks another inflection point. Bergey leads Arm's Edge AI business, which spans smartphones, PCs, wearables and intelligent endpoints. The article cites Arm figures of more than 350 billion Arm-based chips shipped to date, more than 22 million software developers building on the Arm compute platform, and 99 percent of the world's smartphones powered by Arm architecture. Bergey stressed that making AI tasks more efficient does not reduce total computing, because efficiency opens new experiences.

Bergey described how AI on smartphones has moved from discrete tasks such as image enhancement and speech recognition toward continuous interaction, multimodal understanding and AI agents. He said an agent may need to interpret speech, retrieve information, maintain context and coordinate multiple applications, so the overall activity grows even as each operation becomes more efficient. Arm sees a similar shift in graphics, where AI reconstructs images and generates frames within mobile power limits. Bergey argued that performance for Arm is no longer about how fast one workload runs but about sustaining complex AI functions across the whole system. He added that agentic AI differs because a single request can involve several stages, applications and models.

Bergey said agentic AI demands sustained performance, efficient memory access and the ability to run multiple workloads concurrently within tight power and thermal limits. He identified the CPU as the orchestration engine coordinating AI models, applications and accelerators. The article says this is a major focus of Arm's new Arm CSS for Mobile 2 platform, which pairs the Arm C2 CPU cluster with SME2 technology, an AI-native Mali GPU with Arm Neural Technology, system IP and software. Asked whether latency, privacy or power drives moving inference to the edge, Bergey said power efficiency is the fundamental enabler, though he called all three critical. He said processing locally can reduce the need to send sensitive personal data elsewhere, and he does not see edge and cloud as an either-or choice.

Bergey said the challenge is shifting from accelerating individual models to coordinating the complete workload efficiently. He also said Arm still sees software as important, pointing to SME2 acceleration in its CPUs, Arm Neural Technology in its latest Mali GPUs, KleidiAI, which helps developers optimise AI workloads, and its AI Portal. He said sustained responsiveness and power efficiency will matter more than peak compute. Bergey said delivering edge intelligence depends on partnerships, citing MediaTek for smartphones, Snap and Meta for wearables, and Microsoft and NVIDIA for PCs, with NVIDIA on the NVIDIA RTX Spark. He concluded that success will be measured by how seamlessly these devices fit into daily life.

stories.Headline: 5 Best Artificial Intelligence (AI) ETFs to Buy in 2026
stories.Summary:
The Motley Fool has published a guide to five artificial intelligence exchange-traded funds that investors may consider buying in 2026, with the article last updated on November 10, 2026. The funds bundle stocks so that investors do not have to rely on a single company for exposure to AI growth. Artificial intelligence is already changing how companies operate, from recommendation engines and logistics software to chatbots and automation tools. Interest has grown since generative AI tools such as ChatGPT reached the mainstream. AI ETFs have existed for longer than the boom that began with ChatGPT's launch in late 2022, and many of them invest in robotics and semiconductors.

The article's first pick is the Global X Artificial Intelligence and Technology ETF, which the article calls the largest AI ETF, with assets of $9.73 billion and an expense ratio of 0.68%. It launched in 2018 and holds 88 stocks, and its top 10 holdings made up about 33% of the fund in November 2026. Its largest positions include Microsoft, Palantir, Space Exploration Technologies, Tesla and Amazon. According to Global X, the global AI market is expected to grow from $184 billion in 2024 to $826.7 billion in 2030. The article notes that the fund has outperformed over its history, in part because of strong performance by big tech stocks.

The second pick is the Global X Robotics and Artificial Intelligence ETF, established in 2016, which holds 81 stocks and has assets of $3.04 billion. Its top holdings include Intuitive Surgical, FANUC, Keyence, ABB and Nvidia, and the top five made up more than 40% of the fund. The article says the fund is actively managed, carries an expense ratio of 0.68%, and has underperformed the S&P 500 since its 2016 launch. The third pick is the Robo Global Robotics and Automation Index ETF, which holds 79 stocks, has an expense ratio of 0.95% and assets of $1.89 billion. The article says it has also trailed the S&P 500 since its 2013 inception.

The fourth pick is the iShares Future AI and Tech ETF, formed in 2018, which has an expense ratio of 0.47%, the lowest of the five, and about $3.65 billion in assets. It holds 50 stocks, and its top holdings as of October 2026 included Nvidia, Advanced Micro Devices, Broadcom, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing and Oracle. The article says the fund has recently outperformed the S&P 500 because of a surge in semiconductor stocks, after underperforming for most of its history. The fifth pick is the First Trust Nasdaq Artificial Intelligence and Robotics ETF, which holds 111 stocks, carries an expense ratio of 0.65% and has assets of $723.4 million. Its holdings include Intuitive Surgical, Ocado Group, Tempus AI, Appian and Meta Platforms.

The article's author is Jeremy Bowman, and the piece was fact-checked by Frank Bass. The article cautions that most AI ETFs have lagged the S&P 500, a broad U.S. stock index, so investors should compare returns and holdings before buying. It also advises comparing annual fees, noting that ARTY charges 0.47% while the robotics-focused ROBO charges 0.95%. The article does not say what the funds will do after 2026.

stories.Headline: Should You Buy SoundHound AI Stock After Its 83% Plunge? The Answer Might Surprise You.
