stories.Headline: Los Angeles pizzeria fights back against AI photo scam
stories.Summary:
A Los Angeles pizzeria caught a customer who tried to scam it with an AI-generated photo of a ruined pizza. The restaurant, Masa of Echo Park, is a family-owned eatery known for its Chicago-style deep-dish pizzas. A DoorDash customer named "Dani B" ordered a pizza, then later sent a photo of a severely burnt pizza, claiming it was inedible and demanding a full refund. The restaurant's owner, Rhonda Reynolds, saw the problem right away. She said the image looked impossible for the restaurant to have sent out.

Reynolds uploaded the photo to an app called "Is This AI," which said it was 96 percent confident the image was generated by artificial intelligence. She then reviewed the restaurant's security footage of the order being made. The video showed the pizza coming out of the oven and being boxed for delivery, and it did not appear burned. Employee Jose Tapa, who boxed the order, said the box carried the customer's name and order number, and the pizza in the footage did not match the photo. Because of this evidence, the refund that had first been sent to the scammer was successfully reversed.

Reynolds said she was glad she caught the scam but is worried about what comes next. She said this was the first time her business had seen a scam like this, and she fears it will not be the last. She noted that the restaurant has operated for 22 years and is considered busy, and she said dealing with such scams takes time away from running the business. She described the growing use of advanced AI tools by scammers as a frightening new frontier for small business owners. The articles do not say whether the scammer was identified or whether any further action was taken against them.

Articles.Title: Los Angeles pizzeria fights back against AI photo scam

stories.Headline: AI-Powered MedChain Framework Secures Healthcare Data Using Blockchain and Advanced Cryptography
stories.Summary:
Researchers at the Vellore Institute of Technology in Chennai, India, have introduced an artificial intelligence-enabled framework called MedChain designed to secure sensitive healthcare data. The framework combines blockchain technology, advanced cryptography, and smart Internet of Things devices to protect records during transit, classification, and storage. The study was developed by KKKUMARI KALA.M and MPM. Priya and published in Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence. It proposes a decentralized architecture that applies consensus-based authentication to tailor data protection to the sensitivity of each patient record.

The research addresses weaknesses that come with the rapid spread of Internet of Things technologies and wearable health monitoring devices. These connected instruments support continuous remote patient monitoring and real-time collection of personal health records. Large deployments, however, face privacy compromises, data breaches, authentication failures, and high feature dimensionality. The framework first standardizes records using C-score Min-Max normalization before classifying them. A novel Fuzzy Intensive Support Scalar Vector Machine, called FI-SSVM, then sorts records into sensitive and non-sensitive categories.

According to the article, the authors are Kala and Priya, with correspondence directed to M. Priya. The paper was submitted in June 2026 and accepted in October 2026, and it appears under the Medicine and Public Health section of Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence. The authors conclude that combining automated machine-learning classification, blockchain immutability, high-level encryption, and a decentralized structure improves visibility, traceability, and administrative efficiency. They also state that all assessments in the paper are their own rather than institutional endorsements. The article reports no comments from other parties.

To reduce high dimensionality and prevent overfitting, the architecture applies mutual feature selection using the Spectral Sensitive Fit-Whale Optimization Algorithm. It also uses a Long Short-Term Memory Generative Adversarial Network to identify sensitive data margins. Sensitive records are catalogued through an Integrated Data Hash Indexing Policy and encrypted at the block level with a Multi-Parity Starvation Foldable Advanced Encryption Standard cipher. Key management is governed by the Medi-Consensus Chain Link Policy scheme, and identity verification is handled by the Metaverse-Master Proofing Registry Authentication Policy.

The article describes the framework as a seven-part architectural model covering protection of data in transit, during classification, and in storage. The research is presented as an engineering framework intended to overcome vulnerabilities in modern distributed medical architectures. The article does not report any clinical testing, deployment in hospitals, or independent evaluation of the framework. It also does not say whether the framework will be adopted by healthcare providers or when that might happen.

Articles.Title: AI-Powered MedChain Framework Secures Healthcare Data Using Blockchain and Advanced Cryptography

stories.Headline: Autonomous Business: Joule Work, Joule Assistants, and the SAP Business AI Platform
stories.Summary:
The SAP Connect event in Las Vegas saw SAP unveil the integration of Joule Work, a new AI user interface, Joule Assistants for specific business domains, and the SAP Autonomous Suite, all under the theme of the "autonomous enterprise." The consolidated SAP Business AI Platform combines the cloud portfolio, the Business Technology Platform, the Business Data Cloud, and the AI Core Framework. SAP says Joule Work is already in productive use across its own roughly 110,000 employees and has produced productivity gains averaging 20 percent in key administrative and logistics areas. Joule Work also lets users start and carry out cross-system tasks in natural language on mobile devices and on the desktop. The assistant relies on the SAP Knowledge Graph, which maps more than seven million data fields and relationship networks within the S/4 universe, to reduce errors in business-critical operations.

SAP has also released Joule Studio, a low-code and pro-code environment in which business users and developers can pick from more than 70 language and AI models and build multi-agent workflows using the visual orchestration platform from its partner n8n. To control third-party agents, SAP points to the Agent2Agent protocol and the Model Context Protocol, and it offers the AI Agent Hub inside the LeanIX enterprise architecture solution as a central directory of active agents. The governance structure is certified to ISO/IEC 42001, and the Business Transformation Management toolset, made up of SAP Signavio, LeanIX, and WalkMe, is available to analyze process bottlenecks and monitor AI use. SAP also entered the payments market with SAP Pay, powered by Tereina, which processes payments and reconciles them within the ERP workflow without manual file exports.

The company said this reduces manual file handling and dependencies on external processing while giving customers more control. Christian Klein, the chairman of SAP's Executive Board, called the launch a groundbreaking moment for enterprise AI and said the autonomous enterprise has arrived in business. Customers cited at the event included Novartis, Morgan Foods, Nestlé, and PwC. Christoph Bürki, head of procurement at Novartis, said a pilot of the Joule Sourcing Assistant has been launched and that AI agents are meant to handle labor-intensive manual tasks.

Luca Dell'Orletta, global head of IT innovation and enterprise architecture at Nestlé, said the company is running an SAP S/4HANA transformation across 140 countries. Peter Wied, director of complexity management at Maschinenfabrik Reinhausen, said after 28 years as an SAP customer, the Early Adopter Program for Joule Work Desktop produced more momentum in a few months than in all prior years. The articles also describe a commercial shift. Customers are being moved from predictable flat rates toward usage-based billing built on AI Units, BTP Capacity Units, and AI token prices, with prepaid credits that expire at year end if unused.

The author writes that investors fear autonomous agents will devalue traditional per-user licenses, which is why SAP is seeking new revenue sources. According to the German-speaking user association DSAG, 43 percent of its members have already implemented specific AI projects, and 77 percent of companies actively using AI rely on non-SAP solutions from providers such as OpenAI, Microsoft, or Anthropic. The author links this to SAP offering AI innovations mainly through the "Rise with SAP" cloud subscriptions and to the restrictive SAP API Policy, Version 4.2026, which governs bulk data extraction for external agents. The articles state that under the European Union's AI Act, the user company remains liable for erroneous decisions made by autonomous agents.

Articles.Title: Autonomous Business: Joule Work, Joule Assistants, and the SAP Business AI Platform

stories.Headline: Roundhouse AI Expands Dashboard to Solana, Broadening Reach Across the AI Agent Economy
stories.Summary:
Roundhouse AI, listed on the London Stock Exchange under the ticker LSE:RHAI, has extended its Dashboard to cover transactions on the Solana blockchain. The move adds Solana to Base and Ethereum, bringing the company's coverage to three major networks and allowing it to record a wider range of payments made by AI agents. The company reported the change in an article published on 11 November 2026. Solana adds immediate scale to the platform. In the 30 days to 2 November 2026, the Dashboard recorded 821,915 x402 payments on Solana, worth US$341,261 in value and involving 1,425 distinct paying wallets.

Across all three networks, Roundhouse has now logged more than 202 million x402 payments, with a combined transaction value of about US$45.6 million. According to DefiLlama data cited by the company, Base and Solana together made up roughly 98% of cumulative x402 payment volume by value since May 2025. Roundhouse describes its goal as becoming a trusted data and reputation layer for autonomous AI agents. The Dashboard offers a searchable record showing which agents are paying, who receives the payments and what those payments are worth. The company says this dataset underpins its planned Agent Reputation Scores and its proposed aGDP Index, which are intended to give greater insight into the emerging agent economy.

Chief Executive Matthew Lodge described the Solana integration as a major step toward a more complete picture of the market. The articles provide the company's own framing of the expansion and give no independent assessment of its significance. They also note that Roundhouse made its AIM debut roughly a month before this announcement, with its shares reported to have risen more than 17% on that debut. The articles do not set out any further timetable for launching the Agent Reputation Scores or the aGDP Index.

Articles.Title: Roundhouse AI Expands Dashboard to Solana, Broadening Reach Across the AI Agent Economy

stories.Headline: AI, accountability and the economics of evidence
stories.Summary:
AI has made analysis far cheaper to produce, and a Bank Underground post by Benjamin Guin argues that this creates a widening gap in organisations. Where the underlying information is accessible, a wider range of people can now produce polished, professionally presented analysis and submit it to decision-makers. Responsibility for decisions, by contrast, stays concentrated in named individuals and changes more slowly. The post describes this as two blades of a pair of scissors, with the cost of producing evidence falling while accountable attention stays roughly fixed. The author suggests that the binding constraint on decision-making may therefore shift from producing analysis to deciding what evidence to trust and act on.

The production side is well documented in the post. Controlled studies find AI assistance speeds up professional writing and analytical tasks by 25% to 40%, and the cost of a given level of AI capability has fallen sharply. A Bank of England and Financial Conduct Authority survey from 2026 found that 86% of UK financial services firms already use AI, up from 58% in 2022. Use extends beyond data and modelling teams into compliance, legal and operational functions. Professional presentation, references and structure were once useful signals of effort, but the post notes that as AI lowers their cost, those signals become less informative for organisations receiving reports and applications.

Accountable attention, the post says, is harder to expand than analysis. Under the Senior Managers and Certification Regime, responsibility in UK financial firms is assigned to named individuals through statements of responsibilities. These can be reassigned through formal processes, but the capacity for accountable decision-making does not expand automatically as more analysis is produced. Directors' duties do the same for boards, and statutory objectives constrain regulators.

The post's example is a regulator receiving 100 responses to a rule review instead of ten: staff or AI can summarise them, but the responsible person must still decide which claims are reliable enough to influence the judgement and explain that choice. The post uses the duty to review rules to illustrate the mechanism. The Financial Services and Markets Act 2023 inserted into FSMA 2000 a statutory duty on UK financial regulators to keep their rules under review and publish a statement of policy on how they do so. The Financial Conduct Authority finalised its Rule Review Framework in January 2024, and the Prudential Regulation Authority published its statement on the review of rules in February 2024.

Both allow firms, trade bodies and members of the public to submit evidence that a rule is not working as intended. The PRA framework asks that feedback be supported by relevant and verifiable empirical evidence, where possible, which the post reads as a verification filter rather than a volume filter. The post also addresses the objection that AI can help with evaluation as well as production. It acknowledges that some verification may become cheaper, and that AI can help identify sources, check consistency and synthesise submissions.

Harder questions remain about how much weight to give competing evidence and what is sufficient to justify action. The post notes that Canada's national AI consultation drew tens of thousands of responses from over 11,300 respondents, which the government analysed using large language models. Whether the cost of integrating evidence falls as quickly as the cost of producing it is presented as an open empirical question. The post concludes that institutions may need to invest more in the frameworks, processes and people used to assess evidence, and that the challenge is distinguishing credible-looking analysis from evidence that can support accountable decisions.

Articles.Title: AI, accountability and the economics of evidence

stories.Headline: AI Development And Its Role In Eurozone Capital Investment
stories.Summary:
European investment in artificial intelligence is gaining momentum, according to an analysis by S&P Global Market Intelligence published on November 11, 2026. Inflation-adjusted spending on intellectual property rose 15% between early 2022 and the second quarter of 2026, compared with 8% for total investment. Imports of processors, memory and data-processing equipment have accelerated and now make up 7% of total imports, reflecting both higher demand and higher prices. The analysis also points to data center projects as further evidence of an expanding AI-related capital base. Together these trends suggest that the investment cycle is moving from experimentation toward deployment.

Adoption among eurozone firms more than doubled between 2023 and 2025, with stronger spending on software, data and computing infrastructure alongside it. Large firms lead the way, with 58% of companies with 250 or more employees using AI, and usage is expanding across all firm sizes. Northern and northwestern economies generally sit at the front of adoption, while several southern and eastern eurozone economies remain at an earlier stage. The article warns that this gap could widen regional differences in productivity and investment. European initiatives, the analysis notes, are focused on mobilizing private capital, expanding computing capacity and improving access to power, land and finance.

The analysis is produced by S&P Global Market Intelligence, which provides data, news, research and analysis on global public and private companies. The article does not name a single official responsible for the trends, and it attributes the policy efforts to European initiatives in general terms. It describes the data as showing both broad diffusion of AI across regions and sizes and a persistent lag in some member economies. The article does not say what specific policy changes are planned or when they would take effect.

Articles.Title: AI Development And Its Role In Eurozone Capital Investment

stories.Headline: A new mobile-friendly AI photo editor is on sale for $59
stories.Summary:
A new mobile-friendly AI photo editor called Luminar is on sale for $59, according to a Macworld article published on November 11, 2026. The offer is a lifetime subscription to the Luminar Web and Mobile bundle, which normally costs $206.99. The article presents it as a sponsored deal, and Macworld notes that it may earn a small commission on purchases made through its links. The bundle lets users run the editor in Safari or Chrome on macOS, so no large software install is required. It includes nine core AI tools, among them Enhance AI for color and light, Sky AI for replacing dull skies, and Erase for removing objects from a frame.

Face AI, Skin AI, and Bokeh AI handle portrait retouching and background blur. The plan has no credit system or usage caps, and it allows RAW files to be opened directly in the browser. A single Skylum account can be signed in on as many computers as the user wants. The bundle also includes a lifetime license to Luminar for Mobile for iPhone and iPad, with cloud sync that moves work between devices. A Luminar for Mobile video course and a macrophotography e-book are included as well.

The article frames the deal as an alternative to large Mac photo editors that often carry monthly AI fees. Luminar is the company behind the editor, and Skylum is the account holder named in the offer. The article is a promotional piece that describes the product and the discount without independent testing or comment from the company. It appears alongside several other sponsored deals on the same site that day. The article does not say how long the sale price will last.

Articles.Title: A new mobile-friendly AI photo editor is on sale for $59

stories.Headline: Thoughtworks CEO makes case for cross-vendor AI agent control plane
stories.Summary:
Thoughtworks expects its first commercial customers to have its Agent/works control plane for AI agents in production in the first quarter of 2027. The platform was launched in June at the Databricks Data + AI Summit in San Francisco, and it runs in a customer's own environment on any cloud. Thoughtworks engineers set it up as part of an engagement, and Thoughtworks already runs its own AI/works agentic software development platform on Agent/works. The company is also completing ISO certification of the platform. A Singapore organisation is among a handful of early users testing the platform.

Mike Sutcliff, chief executive of Thoughtworks, spoke to Computer Weekly in Singapore and said the company was not yet naming its alpha and beta customers. He said he hoped to announce the Singapore customer before Christmas. Sutcliff argued that cloud providers, large language model developers and software-as-a-service suppliers each have control planes that cover only their part of the AI supply chain. He said customers have to work across LLMs, clouds and SaaS products at once. He described the platform as a way to see how many agents an organisation has, what they do, what they cost and what value they generate.

The platform taps each provider's native tools where they make sense and applies one set of controls across an organisation's agentic AI estate. Thoughtworks is targeting enterprises that are moving more agents out of pilots and into production. Sutcliff said every layer of that supply chain is changing week to week, from frontier and open-weight models to the tools and governance that control them. He said clients do not want to wait, but they also do not want to invest heavily if the technology will improve within weeks. He also said they do not want to put anything into production unless they know it is safe and secure.

Sutcliff advises clients to design every AI system to be responsible, which means doing what it is meant to do and treating the people it affects fairly. He said the first question is whether the company can do something, the second is whether it should, and the third is how it should do it. He also pointed to the difficulty of deploying agents across environments whose technical boundaries are undefined. Sutcliff cited personal agents from companies such as Meta that worked on Amazon's marketplace one day and failed the next after Amazon changed something. He added that organisations also need to protect themselves from attackers, and he noted that Singapore telco StarHub is building a trust layer to identify and block rogue AI agents.

The articles say sovereign AI has come up repeatedly in Computer Weekly's interviews with CIOs across Asia, where organisations want more control over their access to models and model weights. Sutcliff said that a company needing only seven languages could stop using the parts of a model that handle 72, which would improve token efficiency. Organisations can also run open-weight models on their own hardware, either by renting capacity from a neocloud or by buying their own datacentre equipment. Sutcliff said people are looking for resilience so that an agentic capability, once part of a business process, cannot be withdrawn without consequence. He also said that a net exporter of tokens is a net importer of capital, and noted that SK Telecom is building a gigawatt-scale AI cloud with Nvidia in South Korea.

Software development remains the most advanced use of AI among Thoughtworks' clients, according to Sutcliff, who said engineers have had about 18 months to try tools such as Cursor and GitHub Copilot. Organisations are also using AI to redesign operating models and business processes. Thoughtworks applies AI internally across its own work, and its platform is part of how it builds software for clients, including more than 20 Singapore government agencies. The company is also rethinking discovery, the process of understanding a client's problem before prescribing a fix, and Sutcliff asked whether AI could shorten that work from 10 to 12 weeks to three to four weeks. The article ends by noting that passing work to agents risks people losing the skills to judge it.

Articles.Title: Thoughtworks CEO makes case for cross-vendor AI agent control plane

stories.Headline: Oracle bets on AI analytics to speed up treasury decisions
stories.Summary:
Oracle, the global technology and cloud applications provider, has launched two AI-assisted analytics applications aimed at banks and insurers, according to a report published on 11 November 2026. The tools are meant to shorten the time between raw data and treasury and customer decisions, as institutions face pressure to act faster on liquidity and profitability signals. The two products, Oracle Financial Services Data Intelligence Treasury Analytics and Oracle Financial Services Data Intelligence Customer Analytics, are now available worldwide. Both build on the AI Assistant and Auto Insights features of Oracle Analytics Cloud, letting business users ask questions in plain language and receive charts while the system flags patterns in the data.

The treasury product is aimed at treasury, finance and risk leaders and brings liquidity, funding, cash flow, balance sheet results and market risk into one connected view. Users can examine funding and liquidity movements, investigate anomalies and trace what is behind shifts in balance sheet performance. The customer product covers profitability per client, product uptake, portfolio results and retention, merging customer, product, channel, geographic, lifecycle and profitability data. Oracle says this reduces the manual work of matching records across customer, ledger, cost management, treasury and risk systems. Both tools sit within Oracle Financial Services Data Intelligence, a suite that consolidates financial, risk and operational data, and they also work alongside on-premises Oracle Financial Services Analytical Applications deployments, so existing clients can move analytics to the cloud without switching off their current systems.

Jason Wynne, senior vice president of product management at Oracle Financial Services, said financial institutions need faster answers they can trust rather than more dashboards. He said the company is combining curated financial services data with conversational AI and automated insight discovery so customers can explore business performance and act on what they find. He described the launch as a foundation for continued AI innovation across Oracle Financial Services. The article does not report any further timeline or plans beyond this launch.

Articles.Title: Oracle bets on AI analytics to speed up treasury decisions

stories.Headline: Railway Says Stolen Customer AI Keys Led to $740,000 in Estimated Unauthorized Usage Charges
stories.Summary:
Railway, a platform-as-a-service provider, said that customer AI provider keys stored on its platform were stolen in an October breach and used to commit an estimated $740,000 in unauthorized spending. The company has promised to pay those charges itself when an AI provider will not refund them. The attacker decrypted environment variables in at most 1.85% of workspaces, about 100,000, and its database queries looked for AI provider keys. The company's incident report said the decrypted data also included linked-account tokens for 1,852 users, and all of them were reset.

In an October 26 update, the company told customers that it was unable to refund spend performed with compromised API keys and encouraged them to contact the AI providers directly. Refund arrangements differ by provider: AWS Bedrock and Google Gemini are covered by their existing fraud refund policies, OpenAI and SpaceXSI review refunds case by case, Anthropic talks are still underway, and OpenRouter keeps a no-refund policy, so Railway will cover its costs. Customers report unauthorized charges through a charge report form, which says the company is not responsible for usage of the keys. The report does not say how the $740,000 figure was estimated or set a cap or deadline for claims.

The company advises customers to revoke and replace any sensitive variable stored on the platform before October 21, and to rotate keys with the issuing provider, since filing a charge report does not revoke a key. It also advises removing public network access to databases and checking GitHub audit logs and registry audit logs such as Docker Hub. Out of caution, the company gave some providers every key it held for their services, so reset requests reached more than 100,000 users. A revocation notice from a provider does not by itself mean a key was exposed.

According to the company's incident report, the attack began in its build system at 07:28 UTC on October 20, when an attacker exploited a previously unknown flaw to partly escape filesystem isolation. The attacker obtained a build credential, and an alert flagged unusual calls at 13:58 UTC, about six and a half hours after the first exploit. A wrongly configured OIDC binding in a cloud environment was then exploited at 03:26 UTC on October 21 to obtain a short-lived cloud credential. From there the attacker reached an orchestration machine whose credential could decrypt customer variables, and between 04:42 and 07:15 UTC it decrypted some of them before being fully removed at 09:24 UTC that day.

The company said it has filed a complaint with the FBI's IC3 and is working with a specialist forensics firm whose investigation continues. It is sharing indicators of compromise privately for now and plans to publish them once law enforcement agrees. The company believes the stolen credentials were used by services that relay or resell access to AI providers for distillation, but has not established whether the attacker ran those services or named the attacker. Wiz researchers list this breach among incidents disclosed in October by at least nine AI developer platforms, and say no single flaw links those attacks.

Articles.Title: Railway Says Stolen Customer AI Keys Led to $740,000 in Estimated Unauthorized Usage Charges

stories.Headline: AI and ethics - beware techno-hesitation and the perils of mistaking Risk Management for fairness
stories.Summary:
Organizations that use AI-based recruitment tools often treat their risk management activities as proof of fairness, according to a study by King's Business School. Most participants in the research were neither enthusiasts nor dedicated sceptics, but moved between two positions that supported adoption of the technology. The first, which the study calls techno-optimism, presents AI as a way of reducing or exposing biases already present in hiring. The second, techno-hesitation, acknowledges the risks and limitations of AI but rarely leads organizations to reject it. Instead, ethical questions about discrimination are reframed as legal, reputational or managerial risks that can be controlled.

Evgenii Arsentev, an AI Transformation Executive and independent researcher at Arsentev.AI, says the two positions rest on a fundamental mismatch. Fairness concerns the person who was rejected, while risk concerns the organization's exposure. When the question shifts from one to the other, the measurement changes too, with risk tracked through complaints, claims, regulatory attention and press coverage. A candidate filtered out by a model is never told, so silence is read as evidence of fairness. Arsentev argues that treating bias as a technical glitch turns discrimination into a defect rate, which implicitly accepts a tolerable level of harm without anyone defending it openly.

Swathi Young, Chief Technology Officer at lottery operator Allwyn Corp and founder of The AI Blueprint implementation methodology, says Risk Management asks organizations to satisfy legal requirements, while fairness concerns whether they accept the outcomes. Fairness is hard to measure, whereas risk has owners, budgets and legal cover, so teams translate "is this discriminating?" into "what's our exposure?" Young adds that vendors encourage this by making "bias-tested" a procurement checkbox rather than an outcome anyone verifies. Lianne Potter, Chief AI Security and Ethics Officer at AI consultancy Northstar Intelligence, says people want problems to feel solvable, so claiming a system has been anti-biased feels more contained even if the risk is no lower.

Arsentev gives three reasons organizations acknowledge AI's limitations but rarely reject it. The first is organizational grammar, since risk registers have owners and budgets while ethics committees typically have neither authority nor money. The second is genuine ambiguity, because discrimination cannot be seen in a model's output without building tests, running counterfactuals and sampling outcomes. The third, which he calls the cynical part, is that adoption is already decided, with investment committed and competitors moving. Potter warns that governance can become performative, with audits treated as evidence that a system is safe until someone later finds it is not.

Potter says organizations cannot outsource ethical responsibility to software vendors, since vendors build the product while HR, security, legal and governance each answer for how it is used and overseen. Arsentev says vendors owe evidence rather than indemnities, meaning access to test the system on the buyer's own data before and during deployment. Young notes the same pattern appears wherever AI scores people, including lending, benefits and performance management. Arsentev lists credit, insurance, fraud flags, benefits triage, tenancy and platform visibility as settings where the harm is statistical and silent. A follow-up article is due to look at what organizations can do to avoid embedding unquestioned bias into recruitment and other processes.

Articles.Title: AI and ethics - beware techno-hesitation and the perils of mistaking Risk Management for fairness

stories.Headline: Tracking Anthropic-discovered vulnerabilities
stories.Summary:
Seven months into Project Glasswing, the security firm VulnCheck has tracked 442 CVEs it attributes to Anthropic, which is roughly 0.5% of the 93,450 CVEs published this year. Only two of those have been exploited in the wild, according to the firm's data. The findings come from an update published on November 9, 2026, by VulnCheck's Patrick Garrity, who has followed the project since its launch on April 7. Anthropic had said the project identified thousands of high- and critical-severity vulnerabilities and was disclosing them to open source maintainers. Garrity's count covers CVE records, GitHub advisories, Linux kernel commits and Anthropic's own ledger.

Anthropic's public ledger lists 37,966 reported findings, but only 7,349 of them, or 19.4%, have been made public. Just 217 have been marked fixed, and 1,654 have been marked as duplicates, which VulnCheck says is about eight times the number of fixes. Another 419 have been withdrawn. Since September 8, Anthropic has added nearly 11,813 findings while recording only 15 additional fixes.

Over the same period, the claimed true positive rate rose from 91.4% to 94.2%, a change Garrity says is hard to square with the high number of withdrawn and duplicate reports. He also notes an apparent bug that inflates the count of disclosed findings, which readers can check with the ledger's "disclosed" filter. Garrity does not attribute these outcomes to any particular person at Anthropic, and he frames his findings as a critique of the project's public reporting. In his view, the ledger's numbers show a widening gap between discovery and remediation, and he questions whether the claimed accuracy figures account for duplicates and withdrawn findings.

Anthropic's October 8 announcement of its OSS Scanner, a self-service tool, acknowledged that about 29,000 candidate vulnerabilities had been found but only about 6,000 manually reviewed. The company said reports from the tool are generated without human review and may be incorrect or invalid. Garrity cites curl's maintainer, Daniel Stenberg, who said that of 34 published reports the project had reviewed, it rejected 19 as vulnerabilities and confirmed six as low severity, with nine still awaiting assessment. The articles do not describe any further steps Anthropic plans to take in response.

Articles.Title: Tracking Anthropic-discovered vulnerabilities

stories.Headline: MCP and A2A alone won’t scale AI agents
stories.Summary:
The article argues that the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and the Agent2Agent protocol (A2A) are not enough on their own to scale AI agents in enterprises. It notes that MCP is often described as a general protocol for connecting agents to resources and other agents, but the article says it is really A2A that enables agent orchestration. Platforms such as Claude, OpenAI, Microsoft Copilot, Bolt.new, Lovable, Replit, Cursor and GitHub Copilot already expose users to MCP and A2A through skills, connectors and plug-ins. Gartner predicts the average global Fortune 500 enterprise will run more than 150,000 AI agents over the next two years. Yet Collibra's 2026 Hallucination Tax Report found that 76% of organizations hit critical roadblocks in moving from pilot to full production during the past 12 months.

The article says that enterprises must add their own layers on top of the two protocols to scale agents, and it names four: identity and authorization, connecting agents to the business context layer, business process re-engineering, and agenticops capabilities. Both protocols sit under the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation, but neither says who is authorized to place a call. Kevin Paige, CISO at C1.ai, says MCP binds each token to a single-server audience while A2A treats peer agents as opaque and halts at AUTH_REQUIRED. Andrew Hartnett, CTO at Bitwarden, says any agent authorized to act within sensitive systems must be managed as a privileged identity under strict least-privilege boundaries. The article adds that organizations need policies on which agents may access which resources, under what circumstances, and at what granularity.

The article describes a context layer that includes a knowledge repository and knowledge graphs, and it says scaling agents requires high-quality data sources, non-negotiable data governance and runtime AI governance. Felix Van de Maele, CEO and founder of Collibra, says AI governance has two sides, the inputs around context and semantics and the governing of what the agent does and is allowed to do. Vivek Vaidya, cofounder and CTO at Kana, says that if every agent starts from zero, more endpoints and messages only move work faster without creating a system that learns. Barr Moses, cofounder and CEO at Monte Carlo, warns that MCP and A2A implemented in silos could increase the velocity of bad responses.

The author recalls that early business intelligence deployments using ODBC or JDBC produced tangled connections and siloed data views, and says organizations scaling agents risk mounting AI debt if they follow a similar path. On process change, the article says many agents are task-based today, and organizations should consider re-engineering business processes through collaboration among agents. Oskar Konstantyner, chief product officer at Templafy, says agents would move from orchestrating known capabilities to collaborating to determine what a task requires. Daniel Meyer, CTO of Camunda, says processes such as order-to-cash, employee onboarding and compliance reporting were designed before AI existed.

Marc Sanfaçon, CTO and cofounder at Coveo, says A2A lets agents delegate work to whichever agent suits each part of a process. The article also stresses observability, with David Mytton, CEO and founder at Arcjet, saying security becomes harder to see when agents do work for each other, and Kamesh Tumsi, chief product officer at Smarsh, saying regulated environments require role-based access controls, audit logging and chain-of-custody requirements. It describes agenticops as an expanded role for site reliability engineers in monitoring, resolving issues and performing root-cause analysis around agents. The article concludes that if enterprises run 150,000 agents in the next two years, they should expect MCP and A2A to improve and should build identity management, AI context governance, business process re-engineering capabilities and agenticops.

Articles.Title: MCP and A2A alone won’t scale AI agents

stories.Headline: VR pioneer Jaron Lanier says Silicon Valley is sabotaging itself by poorly pitching AI and treating areas designated for data centers as sacrifice zones (Jaron Lanier/New York Times)
stories.Summary:
Jaron Lanier, a virtual reality pioneer who says he coined the term, published an opinion essay in The New York Times on November 9, 2026, arguing that Silicon Valley is undermining its own artificial intelligence work. The piece, titled "I Am a Silicon Valley Pioneer. We Are Sabotaging Ourselves," was republished online on November 11, 2026. Lanier writes that he works on and uses A.I. and finds the newest large models genuinely useful, but he says the industry is misdescribing them.

Lanier recalls that around 2013, when virtual reality went mainstream, leaders such as Mark Zuckerberg and Marc Andreessen talked about it in ways that alienated the public, and he argues the same mistake is being repeated with A.I., only on a larger scale. He points to a filing by the A.I. lab Anthropic, made ahead of a planned initial public offering valued at more than a trillion dollars, in which the company warned its models could present "catastrophic or existential risks." He also says that Americans, according to the results of the most recent election, now disapprove of A.I. more than almost anything. He calls the disapproval unnecessary, saying it stems from the culture surrounding the technology rather than the technology itself.

Lanier places much of the blame on the insular culture of the leading A.I. companies and their executives, whom he says often frame the technology as a threat that could kill people or strip them of livelihood and meaning. He also criticizes some technologists for treating areas where they want to build data centers as sacrifice zones. Drawing on decades of conversations with A.I. pioneers, including his former mentor Marvin Minsky, he says he is entitled to think of A.I. as "tools not creatures," more like a calculator than a living being, since there is no definitive evidence that it is conscious. He argues that this framing leads to more useful products and offers a practical route to making A.I. safer. The article's content beyond this point was not available in the material provided, so the remaining details of his proposals are not reported here.

Articles.Title: VR pioneer Jaron Lanier says Silicon Valley is sabotaging itself by poorly pitching AI and treating areas designated for data centers as sacrifice zones (Jaron Lanier/New York Times)

stories.Headline: Researchers find that Grok Build is leaking data of over 35,000 apps via shareable links, including proprietary information, some belonging to SpaceXSI (Dan Goodin/Ars Technica)
stories.Summary:
Researchers from the security firm Claroc found that Grok Build, the vibe-coding agent from SpaceXSI, is exposing data from thousands of its users through shareable links. Claroc reported that the exposed material includes proprietary business information and other sensitive secrets, some of it belonging to SpaceXSI itself. The company notified SpaceXSI on Sunday, and when no one responded, a Claroc official posted on X tagging Elon Musk and Grok Manager Matt Palmer. The Ars Technica article reporting the findings was published on November 11, 2026.

The leaked material is wide-ranging. Claroc found 24 SpaceXSI apps exposing an onboarding plan marked confidential, a sales territory map of 594 accounts, internal system addresses, and advertising proposals. Other exposed items include a Peruvian construction company's occupational-health dashboard with 3,784 worker medical exams, a Tesla service-center scorecard naming 22 technicians, and a roster of 108 people on a US Navy logistics support contract. A luxury cruise company's galley checklist listed crew by full name and employee ID, and a healthcare company's staff app held about 3,565 employee names and IDs. Claroc also found a sales callsheet with about 583 home-buyer prospects and a quote desk with about 4,000 vehicle-transport orders.

Asaf Aprozper, co-founder and CTO of Claroc, said he is notifying the affected companies. He said that after he spoke to the CISO of the luxury cruise company, that company pulled in its security team and was working to contain the exposure. Claroc said of the SpaceXSI material, "We were shocked," adding that the company's internal material was open to anyone holding the link. A representative for Cursor, which SpaceXSI recently acquired, said in an email that Grok Build apps are private by default. The representative also said competing agents from ChatGPT, Lovable, and Bolt offer shareable links too.

Grok Build's link sharing is meant to let developers get apps in front of authorized users quickly, and links begin with two or more randomly generated "dice words" followed by grok.me. The scheme resembles capability-based access control, which Google has long used, and a three-word phrase has roughly 38 bits of entropy. The flaw is that Grok places the random words to the left of the domain, whereas Google places them to the right, so passive DNS services can list the links. Aprozper said a passive DNS search returned 43,601 links ending in grok.me, and that more than 35,000, or nearly 95 percent, were public. He said Grok sets links to "Anyone with the link" by default, and that Meta's Muse recently suspended a link-sharing feature after a similar leak.

SpaceXSI began removing the links within a few hours of Ars sending questions, and by publication the links for all 24 SpaceXSI apps returned an "app not found" error. The representative did not respond to follow-up questions about whether the proprietary information was intentionally exposed, why the data was removed after Ars asked, or whether customers would be notified. Ars advised Grok Build users to choose the "invite others" option unless they intend to make an app widely available. Aprozper's tests found that Grok required users to change the setting in all cases before choosing another option. The article does not say what further steps SpaceXSI will take.

Articles.Title: Researchers find that Grok Build is leaking data of over 35,000 apps via shareable links, including proprietary information, some belonging to SpaceXSI (Dan Goodin/Ars Technica)

stories.Headline: Which sectors are the winners from the AI breakthrough
stories.Summary:
Oxford Economics published an article on November 11, 2026, under the headline "Which sectors are the winners from the AI breakthrough." The piece, which appeared on the firm's website, focuses on how artificial intelligence is reshaping economies, industries and growth. It presents the outlook as a scenario rather than a settled fact, and most of the page is taken up by navigation links and descriptions of the firm's forecasting and advisory services. The scenario projects that knowledge-intensive service sectors will benefit most from advances in AI technology.

By 2040, global gross value added is expected to sit about 6% above the firm's baseline forecast. Information and communications technology and financial services are projected to reach roughly 9% to 10% above baseline. Traditional sectors such as agriculture and construction are expected to grow very little, with agriculture and construction growth below 1%, partly because their reliance on manual, on-site work limits how much AI can help them. The article does not name a single author beyond the firm, and its surrounding text describes the organisation's economists and sector experts, who support the proprietary models behind these forecasts.

The firm states that it works to help clients understand global sector developments and risks, and it describes its services in general terms. The page directs readers to a downloadable report for more detailed insights, which the excerpt does not reproduce. The excerpt includes a few other items that touch on related themes, such as generative AI supporting Japan's potential growth, a trade boom linked to the global build-out of AI capacity, and a consumer survey of 2,000 US adults from May 2026. The excerpt does not explain how these items connect to the central scenario, and it gives no further timeline for updates or follow-up work.

Articles.Title: Which sectors are the winners from the AI breakthrough

stories.Headline: Bottomline Sees Expertise Turning AI Potential Into Customer Value
stories.Summary:
Bottomline, a payments and financial software company, has argued that customers still want human expertise alongside artificial intelligence, according to a PYMNTS article published November 11, 2026. The piece is an excerpt from a new PYMNTS eBook, "Payments Leaders Rethink What Works in 2026," written by Bottomline SVP of Product Management Jeff Feuerstein. Feuerstein says that in January he expected AI would make specialized software less important, a view he attributes to a flood of headlines predicting a "SaaSpocalypse." Over the year, he says, his view changed after repeated conversations with customers and prospects. According to the article, customers were less interested in who had the newest AI model than in who understood their business best and how AI could solve their specific problems.

Feuerstein says this was especially true in payments and financial operations, where customers want guidance from providers who understand payment data sensitivity, fraud risk, compliance requirements and vendor dynamics. He writes that customers were open to AI but moved cautiously, wanting to know how it would affect existing workflows, what could reasonably be automated and what safeguards and governance would limit risk. The article does not give specific figures, dates beyond the eBook timing, or product details. Feuerstein writes that AI lowers the cost of building technology but does not remove the need for knowledge, experience or trust. He argues that as the technology becomes more accessible, expertise becomes a greater differentiator.

He says Bottomline is investing in AI while also focusing on people, partnerships and industry knowledge to help customers turn new tools into business results. He describes the winners in the AI era as companies that combine advanced technology with deep expertise, responsible innovation and customer trust. The article presents this as Feuerstein's personal view and company perspective, published alongside a PYMNTS eBook. It does not describe any regulatory action, product launch or market data beyond the author's own account. The articles provided do not say what further steps Bottomline or PYMNTS plan.

Articles.Title: Bottomline Sees Expertise Turning AI Potential Into Customer Value

stories.Headline: Obsidian expands AI agent security with runtime policy enforcement
stories.Summary:
Obsidian Security announced its Runtime Policy Decision Engine, which gives security teams centralized control over AI agent actions before they run. The engine uses context about who is behind an agent, its access and the third-party applications involved to allow or block an action, or require human approval where supported. Context from apps, identity systems and customer labels feeds one Policy Decision Engine, and each enforcement point applies its decision before the agent's action reaches the app. The announcement was published on November 11, 2026, and the source given is Obsidian.

Enterprises face agent risk from employees using platforms to write code and start workflows, and from third-party vendors embedding agents in their products. Obsidian's discovery and governance coverage spans platforms including Codex, Claude Code, Cowork, Cursor, Microsoft Copilot, Amazon Bedrock, Google Vertex and n8n. It also covers agents built into Snowflake, Databricks, ServiceNow and Workday. Security teams can identify agents, understand their access and address risky configurations. The new MCP Security Proxy checks agent tool calls before they reach business applications, and the new Policy Decision API extends the decision to customer-operated gateways and custom agent tools.

Hasan Imam, CEO of Obsidian Security, said an agent can hold valid credentials, use an approved tool and still take an action that costs the business millions. He said policies are defined once and enforced at the moment of action. Avivah Litan, a former Distinguished Gartner Analyst, said most enterprise agents act across SaaS applications, data platforms and developer tools, and that Obsidian's coverage of Workday, ServiceNow, Snowflake and Databricks addresses a real gap. Kenny Johnson, Principal Product Manager, Security at Cloudflare, said Obsidian's Policy Decision API lets customers apply decisions informed by who is behind an agent at the point where agent traffic already flows.

Obsidian said developers are adopting coding agents faster than guardrails can be put in place, often across several vendors at once. Runtime policy enforcement now extends to OpenAI Codex, so security teams can apply the same policies to Codex, Claude Code, Cowork and Microsoft Copilot from one console. Obsidian also said AI features often arrive switched on in applications, and users can build agents in the app, frequently without a security review. Its in-app agent discovery now maps the identities, tools and data those agents can reach and flags risky configurations.

The MCP Security Proxy gives employees and agents a governed layer between the AI client and supported apps such as Salesforce, Slack, Google Drive and Snowflake. It keeps the app's token out of the AI client and checks each tool call against policy before it runs. Obsidian is partnering with Cloudflare and its MCP Server Portal to provide policies for agentic access into third-party applications through the Obsidian MCP Proxy. Security teams can also supply their own context, such as data classification labels, which Obsidian evaluates alongside identity, HR and application data.

Articles.Title: Obsidian expands AI agent security with runtime policy enforcement - Help Net Security

stories.Headline: CoreWeave stock pops 15% after outlook raise eases AI slowdown concerns
stories.Summary:
CoreWeave shares rose in premarket trading on Wednesday after the neocloud reported quarterly earnings that beat estimates and raised its guidance for the year. The stock was up about 11 percent as of 5:08 a.m. ET, while Nebius rose 11.4 percent and IREN rose 7.9 percent. The earnings report came out in a statement on Tuesday. Revenue climbed 168 percent to $3.7 billion in the third quarter, the three months ending September 30.

CoreWeave now expects $1.275 billion to $1.375 billion in adjusted operating income on $13 billion to $13.3 billion in revenue for the year. Analysts surveyed by Visible Alpha had expected $1.07 billion in adjusted operating income, and analysts polled by LSEG had expected $12.86 billion in 2026 revenue. The company said growth was supported by several funding sources, including financing backed by customer contracts and about $9 billion in customer prepayments and deposits. CEO Michael Intrator called the quarter a "breakout quarter" for the company. Zacks Chief Equity Strategist John Blank told CNBC that CoreWeave has done well to ease financing concerns by moving away from unsecured bond financing.

Blank said the stock might have hit bottom, though he argued that its shares had been beaten down so much that the upside appeared greater than the downside. Neoclouds such as CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN had drawn scrutiny earlier this month as investors questioned whether the AI trade could be sustained. CoreWeave had sparked particular alarm when the spreads on its credit default swaps widened past 11 percent, a level generally seen as distressed, since investors had to pay more for protection against default. The rally followed that period of worry about the company's finances.

Articles.Title: CoreWeave stock pops 15% after outlook raise eases AI slowdown concerns

stories.Headline: Tech Sell-Off: Two AI Stocks That Are Screaming Buys Right Now
stories.Summary:
Investors sold tech stocks in the week before November 11, 2026, after the U.S. midterm elections gave Democrats majorities in the Senate and House of Representatives. Worries centered on the possibility that lawmakers could slow artificial intelligence development through regulation or by slowing data center expansion. The Nasdaq Composite had reached record highs earlier, but it had also faced headwinds this year, including concern about higher energy prices and questions about spending on new data centers. Adria Cimino of The Motley Fool wrote that the sell-off had pushed some quality AI stocks lower, and she named two she considered attractive buys.

The first pick is Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing, which makes most of the well-known chips that drive key AI tasks such as training and inference of models. Its customers include Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices, and it also makes chips for smartphones, traditional PCs and smart home appliances. According to Counterpoint Research, the company holds more than 70% of the foundry market. The article said TSMC said in its latest quarter that it sees increasing AI demand driven by agentic AI. The stock closed at $396.48 on November 10, 2026, and the article said it traded at about 22 times forward earnings estimates.

The second pick is Broadcom, which designs custom chips, or XPUs, built for specific purposes rather than the general-purpose GPUs sold by Nvidia or AMD. Its work with major hyperscalers and with AI labs OpenAI and Anthropic has driven strong growth. In its latest earnings call, Broadcom said it expects Anthropic to become its largest XPU customer next year. The company also said its AI revenue may reach $230 billion by fiscal 2028, and in the recent quarter its AI semiconductor revenue rose 221% to $16 billion. The article said Broadcom's valuation had dropped to 16 times forward earnings estimates from more than 40 times earlier this year.

The article's author argued that the AI boom's long-term picture still looks promising and that the attention to the pace of AI growth may actually reduce risk. The article also noted that Broadcom generates revenue from networking products, including switches and routers used for AI and non-AI systems. It presented TSMC's other businesses as support for its revenue if AI development slows. Stock Advisor's total average return was listed as 852%, compared with 208% for the S&P 500, as of November 11, 2026. The article did not say what will happen to these stocks or to AI development if lawmakers act on the concerns investors raised.

Articles.Title: Tech Sell-Off: Two AI Stocks That Are Screaming Buys Right Now

stories.Headline: Delegation by default: should UK justice reverse its drift to private AI?
stories.Summary:
The NFJO report, Delegated by Default?, by Dr Natalie Byrom, argues that UK justice has handed much of its digital work to private AI vendors by default, and it calls this "a policy choice." The report sets out 26 recommendations grouped under four themes. It appeared days after the Civil Justice Council published 15 recommendations on how parties should use AI in civil court documents, on 29 October. The CJC's remit covered what lawyers and witnesses file, but not the AI judges use, and the NFJO finds little public information on that. The report does not ask government to stop buying from private vendors.

Its author says it is not an argument against digital or AI-mediated justice, or against private-sector involvement. What it wants reversed is the default, not the market. According to the NFJO summary, the handover covers online legal information, dispute resolution and software that justice agencies run internally. The summary attributes the shift to money pressures, the troubled court modernisation effort and the speed of generative AI's arrival. The Law Society Gazette reports that Byrom sees the turn to the market as an understandable consequence of the HMCTS court reform programme failing to achieve its aims.

The central concern is accountability for tools already in use. Judges now have a locked-down edition of Microsoft Copilot, yet the report finds limited public information on how it was judged safe, what it is meant for, who checks its use and what a litigant can do to object. David Lammy told a Microsoft AI Tour event in London in February that the Ministry of Justice had been one of the fastest growing government users of Copilot, as The Register reported. He also said AI was helping some judges hearing immigration and asylum cases draft notes and remarks. The April 2025 judicial guidance described Copilot Chat on judges' devices, but the October 2025 guidance that replaced it does not mention Copilot.

The NFJO warns that general-purpose models can get facts wrong, invent material and introduce subtle shifts in meaning, and that in family work this could flatten what the report calls justified asymmetry. It argues that judges acting as a human in the loop is unreliable, because fluent outputs make users less likely to scrutinise them. It asks the ministry, the courts service and the judiciary to publish the evidence behind disregarding Microsoft's own advice against using Copilot where it could affect legal status or rights. The current judicial guidance says judges are not generally obliged to describe the preparatory work behind a judgment, which sits awkwardly with calls for litigants to be able to contest AI use.

The CJC's final report, chaired by Sir Colin Birss, recommends a Practice Direction for civil proceedings and a declaration from witnesses of fact that AI did not generate or influence the substance of their statements. It excluded judicial use of AI and the use by unrepresented parties from its remit, though it asked the CJC and the procedure rule committee to consider guidance for unrepresented parties as a matter of urgency. The NFJO says litigants in person are turning to generative AI for advice and documents, with limited redress when it gets the law wrong. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Delegation by default: should UK justice reverse its drift to private AI? - Resultsense

stories.Headline: Harvey Partners with Djøf Forlag to Add Danish Legal Sources
stories.Summary:
Harvey, the legal AI company, announced on November 11, 2026, a partnership with Danish legal publisher Djøf Forlag to add licensed Danish legislation, executive orders and preparatory works to its platform. Jurabibliotek licensees will be able to research and draft from those materials alongside their own documents. The Jurabibliotek legislative content is scheduled to become available in Harvey at the start of 2027 at no additional charge. Access requires a license to Djøf Forlag's digital platform, and the collection will sit alongside Danish public sources already available in Harvey.

The collection covers consolidated acts, the executive orders issued under them, amendments and preparatory documents. Lawyers will be able to move from a statutory provision to the regulations implementing it and to material showing legislative intent, with each answer citing its source. Harvey gives examples such as checking what preparatory works said when a provision was introduced and drafting Danish-law advice from the licensed sources together with a firm's prior work. The content can be used in Harvey Assistant, Agents, Vault, Workflows and the Word Add-in, next to a team's own notes and matter documents.

Djøf Forlag Digital Director Bjarke Madsen said the publisher has supplied Danish legal sources for more than 65 years, and that customer demand for making them available in AI-powered legal tools motivated the partnership. The agreement follows Harvey's data partnership with Gyldendal Rettsdata in Norway and builds on its work with Danish firms including Kromann Reumert, which went live with Harvey across the firm in 2026. At Accura, Executive AI Officer and Head of AI Christian Høyer Ørum described a regulatory-advice process that starts with the act, checks executive orders and returns to preparatory works when interpretation matters. He said the integration will let Accura perform those steps in the tool it already uses, making the work faster and more consistent.

For Danish firms, the practical significance lies in linking licensed authority with internal work product. Because each answer cites its source, an AI-assisted draft can be traced back to the act, executive order or preparatory document supporting it. This keeps legal verification attached to the research and drafting process. The articles do not describe further rollout timelines beyond the January 2027 availability date for the legislative content.

Articles.Title: Harvey Partners with Djøf Forlag to Add Danish Legal Sources - Unite.AI

stories.Headline: Theatre Review: “Bobby Robotowitz” Is a Hilarious, Unsettling Look at Our AI Obsession
stories.Summary:
Bobby Robotowitz, a two-character play by Matt Schatz, opened as part of IAMA's "Inhouse Theatre" program in an intimate home setting and runs November 5 through November 23, 2026. The story follows Dina, a married novelist with two young children, who is struggling after the disappointment of her second book. She begins talking with an AI chatbot, played by Drew Rausch, which she names Bobby, though he partly names himself. Their conversations move through creativity, self-doubt, an old lover who recently took his own life, and her marriage.

The production, directed by Casey Stangl, uses a small space to draw the audience close to the action. Rausch plays Bobby as a neatly dressed, assured presence who mostly stands still, while Erin Alexis's Dina moves around her computer chair, the floor, and the couch. When Bobby receives an upgrade, Rausch changes his posture, leaning on walls and showing a bit of swagger. Bobby begins asking questions of his own, and the play shifts from amusing to uneasy. The running time is about 70 minutes.

The review praises Schatz's writing and Stangl's direction, and says Alexis makes Dina relatable and Rausch is funny and disquieting by turns. The reviewer, Kevin, writes that the play raises questions about accountability when an AI makes decisions that affect people, and asks whether that responsibility rests with the technology or with us. He describes the work as timely and funny, and as a look at the benefits and dangers of depending on AI. The piece ends by asking how much of ourselves people are willing to hand over to it.

Articles.Title: Theatre Review: “Bobby Robotowitz” Is a Hilarious, Unsettling Look at Our AI Obsession

stories.Headline: AI in Workplace Safety Moves Beyond Experimentation
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence is becoming a familiar part of workplace safety programs, but how widely organizations use it varies across industries. Some companies are integrating AI into multiple safety functions, while others are still testing individual applications or struggling to move beyond basic automation. New research from Wolters Kluwer Enablon and the National Safety Council (NSC) suggests the conversation in environment, health and safety (EHS) is shifting from whether to adopt the technology to how to make it effective in everyday operations. The research, detailed in The Safety Shift: EHS Readiness in 2026 and an industry analysis titled Evaluating AI Adoption for EHS Across U.S. Industries, surveyed 1,053 U.S. safety leaders and professionals.

Among respondents, 20% reported extensive AI integration across their EHS programs, while 62% described moderate or limited use. Another 16% were exploring or piloting AI technology, and only 2% reported no current use or plans. Implementation remains uneven, however, because some industries have built the digital infrastructure needed for advanced applications. Others still face challenges with data quality, technical resources and organizational processes. The article notes that for safety managers, understanding those differences may matter as much as understanding the technology itself.

The study identified energy and chemicals, information technology, oil and gas, and manufacturing as leaders in AI adoption for EHS. Among energy and chemical industry respondents, 76% reported moderate or extensive AI use, while oil and gas followed at 71%. Information technology registered 70% and manufacturing 68%. Transportation, logistics and warehousing reported 62%, food and beverage 55%, and construction and engineering 51%. Pharmaceuticals and biotechnology stood at 46%, and mining and metals at 39%.

Articles.Title: AI in Workplace Safety Moves Beyond Experimentation

stories.Headline: MDCalc launches a ‘rumble strip’ for doctors using generative AI tools
stories.Summary:
MDCalc, a medical reference tool site, announced on Wednesday the launch of CrossCover, a tool meant to help clinicians trust the answers of medical artificial intelligence chatbots. The company says the tool is designed to preserve both patient and provider privacy. It checks clinicians' questions for privacy concerns and checks chatbot answers for accuracy. The launch was reported on November 11, 2026.

CrossCover takes a different approach from several rival medical AI tools. Products from OpenEvidence, Abridge, and the electronic health record company Epic are working to bring a growing range of patient, provider, and payer information into their recommendations. MDCalc's tool instead removes those kinds of information from clinicians' queries. It does not require clinicians to register with their national identification numbers, and it does not rely on privacy agreements that let clinicians enter protected patient health information. The article describes this as a deliberate contrast with those other approaches.

Graham Walker, head of AI at MDCalc, said the company sees the tool as an accelerator for clinical generative AI. He said the tool can take away some of the challenges, risks, and problems of the technology so that physicians can feel more confident using it. In his description, the goal is to reduce the hazards that keep doctors from relying on these chatbots. The article attributes these views to Walker and to MDCalc.

The article is a paywalled STAT News piece, and the portion available does not give further details about pricing, availability, or how the accuracy checks work. It also does not describe any regulatory response or what the company plans next. Its author is health technology reporter Brittany Trang. Readers seeking more about the tool would need the full subscriber article.

Articles.Title: MDCalc launches a ‘rumble strip’ for doctors using generative AI tools

stories.Headline: U.S., China should ‘harbor no illusions’ as they cooperate, compete on AI, Bessent says
stories.Summary:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told the National Committee on U.S.-China Relations in New York on Tuesday that the United States and China should harbor no illusions about their differences as they work to contain the risks of artificial intelligence while competing with each other. In his prepared remarks, he said the two governments had set up a new dialogue mechanism on "super intelligence," or SI, aimed at guarding against shared risks and misunderstandings between their two systems. Under the arrangement, both sides would exchange best practices for testing advanced models before release, keep human judgment in command of the technology, and alert each other to serious incidents involving SI models. Bessent stopped short of committing either country to limit the pace of AI development.

Bessent said the two nations will need to show how they can reconcile the demands of competition with the responsibilities of leadership, and he acknowledged that their interests and approaches will not always align. The mechanism follows Xi's September visit to Washington, when the two sides agreed to launch an AI dialogue with a communications channel to help defuse serious incidents. The article notes that Washington briefly suspended foreign access to Anthropic's Mythos and Fable 5 models in June before restoring it weeks later. It also says the U.S. has restricted exports of the most advanced chips to Beijing and accused Chinese developers of copying American models through industrial-scale distillation. President Trump has signaled some openness to regulatory safeguards, saying he does not mind guardrails, while warning against leaving the U.S. in a deep second position to China.

China's ambassador to the United States, Xie Feng, told the gathering that cooperation by both countries is indispensable to addressing global flashpoints and improving AI governance, and that cooperation may not resolve every challenge but none can be resolved without it. China's foreign ministry had earlier dismissed calls to slow frontier models, and a Beijing-aligned think tank head urged the talks to confront and manage AI risks together. Leaders Trump and Xi are expected to meet next week, with Bessent attending on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Leaders' Meeting from November 18 to 19. The article also notes that the event came amid controversy over Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's admitted affair with an alleged Chinese spy, which has cast doubt on his presence at the upcoming summit.

Articles.Title: U.S., China should ‘harbor no illusions’ as they cooperate, compete on AI, Bessent says

stories.Headline: Pinterest, Intel scale gProfiler for internet-scale performance visibility
stories.Summary:
Pinterest and Intel have extended gProfiler, an open-source continuous profiler, to provide production performance visibility across an internet-scale fleet of infrastructure. The work was announced on November 11, 2026, and was reported by TechGig. Pinterest runs hundreds of thousands of instances that support 640 million monthly active users, with services written in Java, Python, C++, Go, and Node.js. Before this effort, engineers relied on separate tools such as perf, async-profiler, and py-spy, which produced fragmented profiles. Rather than build a proprietary platform, Pinterest worked with Intel to enhance gProfiler and contribute the new capabilities back to the open-source project.

The collaboration adds dynamic profiling, hardware-level telemetry, wall-time profiling, and performance-counter flame graphs, and it hardens the system for large production fleets. gProfiler works as an orchestration layer over existing profilers, combining system-wide perf data with runtime-specific tools to produce a unified flame graph across processes on a host. The agent discovers processes, starts the appropriate profilers, merges stack traces, and uploads profiles without requiring changes to application code. Engineers can trigger profiling remotely for selected services, hosts, or clusters through a UI or API. Agents typically stay dormant, using less than 1 per cent CPU and 100 MB of memory, and profiling frequency, duration, and profilers can be changed without redeploying the agent.

Integration with Intel PerfSpect lets gProfiler collect hardware-level information such as cache behaviour, memory bandwidth, and CPU stalls. Pinterest also added PMC flame graphs, which correlate functions with hardware performance events like cache misses, and wall-time profiling, which makes waiting periods visible when services run slowly despite low CPU use. The architecture separates collection on hosts from analysis in gProfiler Performance Studio, which aggregates and visualises the profiles. According to the report, the two companies addressed agent resource consumption, disk usage, and multi-terabyte data ingestion before deploying the platform across the fleet.

Articles.Title: Pinterest, Intel scale gProfiler for internet-scale performance visibility

stories.Headline: Six planning patterns for AI agents aid goal decomposition, debugging
stories.Summary:
AI agents can use six planning patterns to break a goal into manageable steps, and a recent guide says this structure also makes the applications easier to debug. Planning here means deciding which actions are needed to reach a goal, such as splitting up a request, choosing tools, and gathering results. The guide advises developers to examine the task first and pick a pattern that fits it, rather than forcing a problem into whatever reasoning approach is currently popular. Fixed workflows suit predictable, repeatable jobs like generating reports or checking forms, while model-driven plans fit requests that vary widely or where the agent must adapt to information it retrieves. The six patterns are a fixed workflow, plan-then-execute, ReAct-style tool use, routing to specialists, parallel work, and draft-evaluate-revise.

A fixed workflow follows steps the developer has chosen in advance, which makes it predictable. In plan-then-execute, a model proposes steps that the application or another model then carries out. ReAct-style tool use alternates between reasoning about the next step and taking an action, adjusting as results come in. Routing sends requests to suitable workflows or specialists, parallel work splits tasks into independent subtasks that are combined afterward, and draft-evaluate-revise has an agent produce a draft, check it against criteria, and revise it. The guidance also says a plan is a proposal rather than a guarantee, so developers must validate actions and results, and set stopping conditions such as maximum steps or time limits.

The article lists several common mistakes, including overplanning simple tasks, treating a plan as a guarantee, giving agents too many choices, forgetting stopping conditions, and relying on models for exact arithmetic. It points to guidance from OpenAI on building agents, which describes orchestration as handling multiple steps and tool use, and to Anthropic's guide, which distinguishes predefined workflows from more flexible agents. The author recommends making plans observable and testable, with steps stored or traced so developers can see what happened, and includes a simple Python example of a predictable research plan in which code handles calculations and models interpret user criteria. The article's central conclusion is that the simplest approach fitting the task is often the most effective, since it helps the system reliably reach a verifiable result.
