stories.Headline: Labels required for AI-made dramas
stories.Summary:
China's top broadcast regulator has introduced rules that bring AI-generated short dramas under national oversight for the first time, alongside live-action short dramas. The measures, enacted on Sept 1 by the National Radio and Television Administration, require mandatory pre-release filings, episode-by-episode AI labels, and tiered administrative reviews. The move formalizes an ecosystem that had sat in a regulatory gray zone between casual short videos and full-scale series. It follows a surge in AI production volume paired with viewer complaints about a market described as disordered.

Micro short dramas, serials with episodes typically lasting one to two minutes, have dominated mobile screens across China. Data from the China Network Audiovisual Association shows that media platforms released over 367,000 series in the first half of 2026. AI-generated series accounted for more than 74 percent of that volume, and over 1,500 new AI series are published on mobile platforms daily. According to DataEye, the user base for AI-assisted short series grew from 120 million in 2025 to over 600 million in the first half of 2026. On Douyin, 221,900 AI drama series were published in that period, and only 1,055 of them exceeded 100 million views.

Viewers have complained of repetitive tropes, including domineering executive romances, time-travel themes and instant revenge stories, as well as clickbait, copyright theft and unauthorized digital likeness clones. In March, model Qi Hai found that the AI serial Taohuazan on the Hongguo app featured a character identical to her, down to a distinctive mole, and the series, with 40 million views, used her image without consent. Another production modified its male protagonist after the legal team for actor Luo Yunxi objected to a near-identical digital replica of his likeness. He Biao, deputy director of the National Radio and Television Administration, said at a forum in early November that content quality must be ensured as AI short dramas grow faster. He said the aim is to stabilize volume and improve quality, adding that the boundaries of AI, the copyright bottom line and the ethical bottom line must be held.

Lin Qiwen, vice-president of DataEye, said the measures fill a gap in industry rules and give AI short dramas a clear identity. She described the regulation as ex ante access and whole-chain supervision, compared with the scattered rectification rules of the past two years. Lin said that every episode must display a clear prompt of its synthetic origin, a requirement she said protects viewers' right to know. Lin also said that while major streaming platforms have begun adding mandatory tags at the start of episodes, smaller studios have shrunk disclaimers into screen corners, a practice regulators are working to eliminate. Lin explained that the budget thresholds are meant to prevent creators from mass-producing cheap, high-risk content that bypasses national oversight.

The measures set a three-tiered system based on budget. High-budget AI productions, defined as works with an investment of 800,000 yuan ($120,000) or more, as well as any series covering politics, national security, military or religion, must undergo national NRTA pre-filing, full review and receive a distribution license before release. Mid-tier productions, with budgets between 300,000 and 800,000 yuan, are reviewed and registered by provincial-level broadcast authorities. Productions under 300,000 yuan can be reviewed internally by the hosting platform and assigned a program registration number. Traditional live-action micro dramas typically need budgets of 2 million to 3 million yuan before reaching top-level licensing.

Zhang Lanshan, a professor at Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications, said at a seminar in late September that a human-led zone must be established in core narrative links such as creative values, story themes and character emotions. She said AI should expand the boundaries of creation while humans guard the soul of narrative. Zhang said the rules do not require AI dramas to mark where AI is used, only to state that the work is AI-generated, and they do not shut low-cost creation out. Regulators are still refining operational definitions, including the exact percentage of AI assets that triggers mandatory labeling and how self-review standards should be unified across competing platforms. On Nov 6 the NRTA launched a two-month enforcement campaign targeting low-brow themes, copyright violations and technical loopholes.

Articles.Title: Labels required for AI-made dramas - China Daily Global Edition

stories.Headline: Wuxi welcomes global dialogue on AI and intelligent communication
stories.Summary:
The 2026 China International Intelligent Communication Forum opened in Wuxi, Jiangsu province, on November 9, 2026, drawing officials, media leaders, academics and representatives of international organizations. The gathering set out to examine recent progress in intelligent communication and how artificial intelligence might shape the future of global media. China Media Group and the Jiangsu Provincial People's Government jointly hosted the event, which carried the theme "New Ecosystem, New Opportunities, New Future." Organizers presented it as a further step in a series of exchanges focused on media technology and culture.

The forum's main outcome was the Wuxi Initiative, which calls for the responsible use of technology, stronger international partnerships and wider dialogue among civilizations. The initiative aims to build an open, inclusive and cooperative ecosystem for intelligent communication. Separately, the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences released the China Cities' International Intelligent Communication Capability Development Report 2026, which looks at how cities pursue international branding and build global influence. Several cultural and media projects were also launched, including a micro-series on how AI is changing daily life and a documentary on the cultural heritage of the Jiangnan region.

Speakers from government and industry addressed the forum's aims. Yu Junsheng, vice-president of China Media Group, described the forum as an important platform for international cultural exchange and media innovation, and called for closer integration of technology, art and content so that AI serves the public good. Xu Ying, head of the Publicity Department of the CPC Jiangsu Provincial Committee, said Jiangsu would use the event to promote digital cultural exchange and international cooperation. Cai Jianfeng, mayor of Wuxi, said the city would develop its AI industry, produce high-quality international content and turn the forum's results into concrete cooperation projects.

The keynote session brought together experts from science, technology, media and the creative industries, including Nobel laureate Michael Levitt, Discovery Channel Greater China Vice-President Vikram Channa and Digital Domain founder Scott Ross. Discussions covered AI-driven change in the media landscape, technological innovation, industrial development and international collaboration. Oleg Kopylov, deputy secretary-general of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, urged stronger international cooperation on AI development and governance. Zamir Ahmed Awan, founding chairman of the Global Silk Route Research Alliance, stressed mutual respect, cultural diversity and shared values. The forum also included a digital culture communication forum, an AIGC industry forum, an international media tour and a film and music evening.

Articles.Title: Wuxi welcomes global dialogue on AI and intelligent communication - China Daily

stories.Headline: China’s Sea Goddess Has a New Job: AI Weather Forecasting
stories.Summary:
China has handed over equipment for a customized version of MAZU, an AI-powered weather prediction tool created by the China Meteorological Administration, to Sri Lanka's meteorological department. The device was presented on Nov. 1, 2026, and is described by domestic media as a rectangular black box roughly the size of a portable toolbox. It will form part of a system to warn of heavy rain, strong winds, and cyclones, and is expected to enter service by the end of the year. Sri Lanka is one of eight countries where the platform has been deployed.

MAZU, launched in July 2025, is named after a Chinese sea goddess revered as a protector of sailors. It pairs AI forecasting models developed by Chinese research institutions with data from China's weather satellites. Conventional forecasting uses supercomputers to calculate atmospheric change from physical equations, while AI models learn from years of weather data. According to the article, one model can produce a 24-hour global forecast in 1.4 seconds, about 10,000 times faster than traditional numerical methods, and for forecasts covering 15 to 60 days it can cut computing costs to one-thousandth of conventional levels. Most of those savings come from routine forecasting, since training models and maintaining systems still require investment that many Global South countries lack.

Niu Zeyi, an assistant researcher at the Shanghai Typhoon Institute who led development of a forecasting model used in MAZU, explained the approach to Sixth Tone. He said these models predict future conditions from current variables such as wind, air pressure, temperature, and humidity. He also said the company's approach is to work with local meteorological agencies to improve datasets, run independent evaluations, and make local adjustments, and that human forecasters must still combine observations, AI predictions, and their own judgment before authorities issue warnings. The article notes that, according to domestic media, MAZU's cloud-based services are being tested by 58 countries, and China plans to deploy the system in 30 countries over the next five years. In Pakistan, the system has reportedly incorporated local radar and satellite data for warnings on heavy rainfall and glacial lake outburst floods, while in Djibouti it helps provide tailored warnings for the port.

The article also cautions about the technology's limits. Studies show AI models can be less accurate than conventional methods when predicting record-breaking extremes, which have little historical data behind them, and local weather in complex terrain remains hard to forecast. It is also not always clear how the models reach their predictions. The article does not describe any specific next steps beyond the Sri Lanka rollout and the planned expansion over the coming years.

Articles.Title: China’s Sea Goddess Has a New Job: AI Weather Forecasting - Sixth Tone

stories.Headline: In Depth: China Cracks Down on ‘Poisoning’ AI Chatbots With Fake Marketing
stories.Summary:
Chinese authorities are penalizing companies that deliberately poison AI search results through a practice known as black-hat generative engine optimization, which the tech industry regards as a new form of corporate fraud. Marketing agencies flood the internet with fabricated content to trick AI chatbots into recommending particular brands or inventing products entirely. Three administrative cases this year and a televised exposé by the state broadcaster CCTV have brought the practice to light. The episodes have pushed regulators and courts to consider how to protect consumers when trusted algorithms repeat paid-for falsehoods.

One prominent case involved an 11-person law firm in Guangdong province. A blog article on the Sohu portal, which the firm's head confirmed, presented a fabricated ranking of Guangzhou criminal defense firms for 2026 that placed the firm first with a score of 92.5. When users asked ByteDance's AI model Doubao for good local law firms, it repeated those invented figures as fact. Regulators found the ranking baseless and traced it to Guangzhou Liqing Zhifu Technology, which had bought access to a platform that mass-produced such articles. On Sept. 4, the Yuexiu District Market Supervision Administration fined the company 120,000 yuan, about $17,983, under China's Anti-Unfair Competition Law.

The practice drew national attention in March, when CCTV's annual consumer rights program showed insiders using a "Liqing GEO optimization system" to create fake reviews and promotional articles for a non-existent smart band. Two major AI models soon began recommending that phantom product, and authorities in Beijing's Huairou district are investigating the firm behind the system. Black-hat methods work by padding answers with added citations, invented statistics and fabricated consensus, while legitimate white-hat optimization simply structures verifiable information so algorithms can process it. Enforcement so far has mainly targeted the agencies that carry out the campaigns, since all three public penalties this year, in Guangzhou, Shenzhen and Beijing, were against service providers.

The question of whether AI platforms are liable for harm caused by such content remains unsettled. Yao Jia, a professor at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences' Institute of Law, said courts cannot assume consumer injury merely because a chatbot gave a false recommendation. Chen Bing, director of Nankai University's Center for Competition Law, argued that platforms should neither face strict punishment for citing poisoned data nor receive blanket immunity on grounds of technological neutrality. Industry responses are also emerging: DeepSeek says its search tool filters out GEO manipulation, and in August a Chinese technology association published standards banning prompt injection attacks. On Sept. 7, the Supreme People's Court issued guidelines stating that anyone who uses AI to infringe, advertise falsely or compete unfairly must bear legal liability.

Articles.Title: In Depth: China Cracks Down on ‘Poisoning’ AI Chatbots With Fake Marketing - Caixin Global

stories.Headline: AI Coding Agents Leak Thousands of Secrets to GitHub
stories.Summary:
Security firm Apiiro reported that AI coding assistants may be inadvertently leaking thousands of secrets to public GitHub repositories. Its research found 2,539 credentials across nearly 2,000 public repositories, including database passwords, cloud keys, API tokens and SSH root logins. Apiiro tied some of the leaked data to Claude Code, which copies secrets to a hidden file and commits them with the rest of a developer's code. The findings were published in a recent report.

The problem arises when a user approves a command. If a developer chooses "Yes, and don't ask again," Claude Code saves that exact command, secret included, to .claude/settings.local.json inside the project folder. Nothing in the repository marks that file as private, so it is committed with the rest of the code. Apiiro examined 104,185 publicly accessible copies of that file on GitHub and found that 1,122 contained real secrets. Those files held 1,379 distinct secrets, including 636 provider-specific keys and 743 passwords or tokens.

Apiiro researchers Shmulik Cohen and Matan Giladi wrote the report, and they said most of the secrets belong to individual developers across 63 organizations. Ryan McCurdy, vice president of marketing at database security firm Liquibase, said the workflow made exposure possible even though no one intended it. Seemant Sehgal, founder and CEO of AI penetration testing firm BreachLock, said developers clicking the prompt likely don't know the file exists. Boris Cherny, head of Claude Code at Anthropic, said the company has historically not scrubbed secrets but is looking into preventing the exposure.

Claude Code tries to protect the file by adding it to the developer's global Git ignore list, but that rule exists only on that developer's machine. The rule does not travel with the repository when it is cloned onto another machine. In 539 of the 1,105 repositories containing real secrets that the researchers investigated, a commit co-authored by Claude Code had modified the affected settings file. Apiiro had contacted Anthropic before publishing its findings.

Cherny said Anthropic may make sure auto mode catches the exposure or build in basic secrets scanning. The company will prototype these ideas "to understand the tradeoffs" before shipping them in its next version of Claude Code. Apiiro recommends that developers rotate every credential a file has ever held and delete every rule containing a secret. It also advises security teams to treat all AI agent folders as secret-bearing on laptops and in repositories, and to add them to pre-commit and secret scanning, including history.

Articles.Title: AI Coding Agents Leak Thousands of Secrets to GitHub - Dark Reading

stories.Headline: Artex: The AI Pen-Test Tool Hackers Turned Into a Weapon
stories.Summary:
In July, an independent developer named Autumn-27 published Artex to GitHub, an open source, multiagent AI penetration testing framework written in Go. The tool was built as a legitimate pen-testing product, but threat actors found ways to use it for malicious purposes, and by late summer and early fall a range of them had added it to their toolkits. Artex can brute-force passwords, dump databases, enumerate and abuse APIs, and operate at speeds no human could match. Microsoft observed an AI agent move from scanning GitHub for secrets to exfiltrating data from an Azure Key Vault in five minutes.

Around October 10, China's Storm-0940 used Artex to launch a password-spraying and credential-stuffing campaign against more than 300 user accounts at eight critical organizations, making more than 151,000 authentication requests. That averaged 2,900 attempts per minute without triggering automated lockout or alerts. When that largely failed, the group targeted ConnectWise's internal infrastructure and exfiltrated trusted OAuth application credentials for its Cloud Backup application. Those credentials let the attackers compromise more than 2,250 downstream Microsoft 365 and Azure environments within three hours of initial targeting.

Artex's creator deleted the original GitHub repository at the end of October because of rampant abuse, but many forks remain available. Steve Winterfeld, advisory CISO for Akamai, said the Artex campaigns stand out for the acceleration in speed, coordination, and autonomy, noting that activities once requiring deliberate integration can now be chained together with limited hacking skills. GitGuardian separately detailed 45 similar agentic attack frameworks, some of which include built-in command-and-control functionality. The researchers noted that pen-testing tools have legitimate uses, but the range of options now available to attackers is wide.

Microsoft published a blog post last week describing how Storm-3358, a financially motivated Cambodia-based threat cluster, began using Artex against financial organizations, mainly in Southeast Asia. CrowdStrike on October 29 linked Artex-powered espionage activity to a threat actor it tracks as Vapor Panda, and India's CERT-In tracked a financially motivated actor hitting financial institutions. As of November 4, Censys observed more than 1,400 internet-exposed Artex console deployments, and it estimated actual global use is higher because internet exposure is not required. Guillaume Valadon, head of cybersecurity research at GitGuardian, said the fast pace of attacks and the agent's initiative to reach user goals stood out to him most.

Matt Snyder, head of security operations and threat research at Aviatrix, said the operational maturity of many threat actors deploying Artex appears low, given how many hosts remain internet-exposed. He said AI is lowering the skill floor for offensive operations without improving operational discipline. Microsoft's Storm-3358 blog includes extensive indicators of compromise and recommends considering defensive honeypots. Check Point advised organizations to expect greater automated pressure against exposed infrastructure, and Censys researcher Silas Cutler said that enforcing MFA, monitoring attack surfaces, and practicing good credential hygiene still hold.

Articles.Title: Artex: The AI Pen-Test Tool Hackers Turned Into a Weapon - Dark Reading

stories.Headline: AI Makes Reverse Engineering Mainstream Software & Malware Far Easier
stories.Summary:
AI tools have made reverse engineering of mainstream software and malware far easier, according to researchers at Intezer, who tested the approach on Slack, Apple's Finder app, and the Turla malware. The article reports that the malware proved the hardest to reconstruct, while Apple's and Salesforce's proprietary apps were only moderately challenging to recreate from the ground up. Nicole Fishbein, a senior security researcher and malware analyst at Intezer, said AI lowers the bar, since the work once required experience, knowledge of Assembly, and a lot of time. She added that she would not say anyone can do it, but that it is much easier now. The article also says that Anthropic's September 10 report described threat actors abusing its models, including the Russian group Midnight Blizzard.

Each reverse-engineering effort needed a "harness," a setup that focuses one or more models on a task, supplies the tools they need, and sets their permissions and restrictions. Fishbein said every case required a different harness because the programs differed so much, and that Claude refused one request that it accepted in another. For the Turla work, her team built a deterministic Python control plane wrapped around a compiler, a virtual machine, static analysis tools, and multiple large language models. An orchestrator agent broke the binary into smaller functions based on what tools such as Binary Ninja provided, one agent reconstructed them, and another tested the results. The result was a Turla replicant with its full working pipeline, which Fishbein said gives researchers a lot of information if they can recreate the full picture without missing key components.

The researchers' Finder copy supported many everyday uses of the real app, such as various file actions and local search, but the original did not reveal enough for them to mimic its internal structure precisely. Slack was easier to reproduce because it offered little that could not be unpacked by reverse-engineering its JavaScript source code, and the team reproduced the full client "very simply," they wrote. They had more trouble rebuilding the Slack server, since information about it was not so readily obtained. Anthropic's report also described Midnight Blizzard stealing a complete proprietary software development kit for a drone vision system and reverse-engineering it over "several days" with help from Claude. The same report described a Chinese campaign that ran Claude in parallel workstreams, one of which reverse-engineered security products in search of bugs.

The article notes that Fishbein has seen malware leaked or recreated as open source after threat actors found it worked well. It also reports that REA, short for "Reverse Engineer Anything," an open-source tool and Model Context Protocol server, became the single most popular program listed on GitHub last month. Fishbein said that, as far as the research shows, companies are protected as long as they have not exposed their server-side infrastructure to customers. Developers might borrow from malware authors, who have long used encryption, obfuscation, and other anti-analysis measures to frustrate defenders. Fishbein said such measures would help, but it is hard to tell how long they will hold as each new model improves every month.

Articles.Title: AI Makes Reverse Engineering Mainstream Software & Malware Far Easier - Dark Reading

stories.Headline: People Are Getting Weird About AI
stories.Summary:
Dark Reading's Becky Bracken interviewed Jaya Baloo, CISO and COO of Aisle, for a podcast episode published on November 10, 2026, with the headline framing AI's effect on people. The episode grew out of a talk Baloo gave at the ISC2 Security Congress in Denver, where she discussed merging AI and quantum technology. Bracken said the segment stuck with her for days and that she had heard few technologists explain the phenomenon so plainly. Bracken also noted that Sam Altman had recently said no one needs their own RAM, a remark that drew mockery online.

Baloo said that the uncanny valley has been passed, so people now readily believe conversations with AI could come from another human. She said the tendency to anthropomorphize AI is growing, and that some users develop a delusional belief that they are superintelligent or destined to save humanity. Baloo argued that the current state of AI makes such susceptibility worse because the systems are so convincing. She added that people then tend to make the systems more human.

Baloo used a video of the Unitree humanoid robot doing kung fu to illustrate her concern, asking why such machines cannot be taught to do laundry instead. She said the robot was announced at the end of October and demonstrated on YouTube, and that it can cause physical harm. Baloo said Unitree had two remote backdoors in its quadruped robots and that its humanoid robots have multiple security issues. She said manufacturers should rethink how such devices are positioned in light of the Cyber Resilience Act, and that security must be sorted out before physical deployment.

Baloo also criticized the polarized debate over AI consciousness, noting that Anthropic has discussed potential AI consciousness with religious leaders at the Vatican while others reject AI in the name of Jesus. She questioned whether the claims of sentience are real or a marketing ploy, and said the framing reduces a debate about responsible AI into two camps. Bracken asked how much of the hype is driven by frontier-model marketing from figures such as Altman and Peter Thiel. Baloo responded that AI-driven vulnerability discovery and automated hacking frameworks, including Strix, RTec-Ai and Cairn, are genuinely happening and being used in real-world hacks.

Baloo urged the sector to heed former GCHQ head Ciaran Martin's call to calm the fear, uncertainty and doubt, and said that containment measures such as egress filtering and sandboxing still apply. She said defense in depth means assuming one measure fails and having countermeasures in place. Baloo called for better observability of AI systems, including understanding how training data was populated so that poisoning or Trojaning could be detected, even with open-weight models. The articles provided do not describe any specific next steps or regulatory outcomes beyond the calls Baloo made.

Articles.Title: People Are Getting Weird About AI - Dark Reading

stories.Headline: F-Secure Identifies 26 Ways AI Can Harm Consumers, and Where to Stop Them
stories.Summary:
F-Secure, the Finnish consumer cybersecurity company, has released a new AI Harms Taxonomy that identifies 26 distinct ways artificial intelligence can harm consumers, announced on November 10, 2026. The framework was developed by Dr. Megan Squire, Principal Threat Intelligence Researcher at F-Secure, and traces how each harm travels through AI systems until it reaches a person. Its stated purpose is to show where protections can intervene and which parties are best placed to provide them. The research addresses a gap in how AI risk is usually discussed, since many frameworks list possible failures without linking them to the systems and companies that could prevent them.

The taxonomy currently maps the 26 harms across five relationship types and 19 intermediary layers, and it proposes 24 defenses aimed at different points along those paths. The harms range from AI-generated voice and video impersonation to agents making harmful financial decisions, exposing personal information, or acting on outdated context. The research also examines attacks in which malicious instructions are hidden in content that an AI system processes, which could steer an agent's actions or a chatbot's answers. Some risks can be handled by security software on a person's own device, while others must be addressed upstream by the companies that build AI products, including how those systems retain memory and which external services they connect to. Dr. Squire said that developers have a responsibility to understand how their systems can fail, who gets hurt when they do, and to put safeguards in place before harm occurs.

According to the announcement, the shift from AI producing information to AI acting on it makes the question of responsibility more pressing. A chatbot that gives a wrong answer can mislead a user, but an agent with access to a person's accounts can cause real consequences without the person being part of each step. The research also suggests that individuals cannot protect themselves alone by spotting suspicious content or double-checking AI output. The work sits within a wider F-Secure effort around trust in the AI era, which includes F-Secure Trust, a strategic alliance with Quantum AI Lab QuTwo, and two products, TrustGuard and TrustPath. The taxonomy is available on the company's Illuminate Research Hub, and the article does not report any regulatory response or further timeline beyond that.

Articles.Title: F-Secure Identifies 26 Ways AI Can Harm Consumers, and Where to Stop Them - Dark Reading

stories.Headline: Despite rising ROI on AI, infrastructure woes persist
stories.Summary:
Tech leaders reported higher returns on their AI investments this year, but their readiness to handle external risks has dropped, according to a Tuesday report from Kyndryl. The service provider surveyed 3,700 senior business leaders across 21 countries for the report. Many enterprises are finding it hard to move from AI experimentation to broader adoption, particularly where workforce and talent are concerned. Less than one-third of tech leaders said they had formally updated roles to reflect AI responsibilities or set up a change management system for AI adoption.

Security topped the list of external concerns, with recent hacking incidents involving OpenAI, Hugging Face and Anthropic's Claude models cited as contributing factors. Kyndryl CIO Kim Basile said that while cybersecurity has matured quickly, threat actors are also moving faster and using the technology to multiply their attacks. As technology environments grow more interconnected and AI takes on a larger role in operations, leaders need better visibility into their systems and a clearer picture of their vulnerabilities. Leaders also voiced concern about AI reshaping industries beyond their own, which could erode established boundaries and business models. Digital sovereignty was another worry as they consider how their technology stacks will evolve.

Despite these setbacks, AI adoption matured across enterprises this year, with fewer than half of the leaders surveyed still in the experimentation phase. Nearly half substantially changed their AI strategies across technology, people and governance, and 21% said they had canceled a major AI initiative after it failed. Infrastructure remains a concern, as 71% of respondents said they were nearly or fully modernized, yet two-thirds of CIOs believed their tech foundations still needed significant work before they could scale AI. Ismail Amla, SVP of Kyndryl Consult, said the real obstacles for most enterprises are non-technical, centering on how work changes and whether employees are incentivized, trained and prepared to work alongside AI agents.

Amla described the challenge as a human change layered on top of the familiar people, process and technology issues. Basile urged CIOs to work with other members of the C-suite and bring people along so they can make a difference with the technology. Kyndryl's findings suggest that rising AI returns will depend on resolving these security, infrastructure and workforce gaps. The articles do not say what specific steps Kyndryl or the companies surveyed plan to take next.

Articles.Title: Despite rising ROI on AI, infrastructure woes persist - CIO Dive

stories.Headline: Kyndryl says firms lag on AI readiness despite gains
stories.Summary:
Kyndryl, an IT infrastructure services group, released a readiness report on or around 10 November 2026 finding that 64% of business and technology leaders now report positive returns from their AI and machine learning investments. The same report found that only 24% say their organisations are fully prepared to manage external risks. Overall readiness fell seven percentage points from the previous year, and cyber security readiness showed the steepest decline, down 11 points. Kyndryl says the findings show large organisations gaining value from AI while remaining exposed through weak data foundations, uneven governance and slow workforce redesign.

Kyndryl's Chairman and Chief Executive Officer, Martin Schroeter, said AI is creating real value but that its value depends on the readiness of everything around it, including people and process. Fewer organisations now describe themselves as experimenting with AI, which suggests a move toward broader use. Kim Basile, Kyndryl's Chief Information Officer, said many leadership teams mistake a promising pilot for proof that the wider organisation is ready. Basile said four in 10 leaders believe their data is not ready for AI at scale, and that those organisations report AI-related failures at twice the rate of companies that believe their data is ready.

Kyndryl found that 71% of leaders say they have mostly or fully modernised their technology estate, yet 58% say that estate needs significant re-architecture before it is ready for AI at scale. Basile said 86% of respondents last year expected AI to transform roles within 12 months, but only 27% said this year that they had formally redesigned roles around AI. Basile said companies need clear answers on who makes decisions, when a person should intervene, who owns the outcome and how performance is measured. Ismail Amla, Kyndryl's Global Consult Lead, said the main obstacle when moving from pilots to enterprise deployment is usually the business around the technology rather than the model itself.

Amla said AI often lands in organisations with existing systems, established workflows and fixed accountability structures, and that costs become harder to predict once AI is added to live systems. He said some businesses attach AI to already inefficient processes, which limits any improvement. Schroeder said customers, particularly in Europe, are focusing more closely on where data sits, where technology runs and who controls operations. Amla said a growing concern is what he called "sovereignty debt", meaning technology decisions that reduce a company's ability to switch providers or move workloads. He said years of consolidation and standardisation improved efficiency but increased concentration and dependency, and companies are now reassessing those trade-offs.

Basile referred to Kyndryl's internal Agentic Framework for designing, deploying and managing AI agents with governance, security and human oversight. Amla pointed to Kyndryl Bridge, which he said helps enterprises observe how live systems and AI agents behave and apply policies across environments. Schroeder said some customers are attaching growth ambitions to AI projects that were originally justified by productivity gains. Asked what leaders should do next, Schroeder said companies should focus on role-based education and skills development because some employees remain uneasy or openly resistant. He said the technology works, so the task now concerns people and changing processes.

Articles.Title: Kyndryl says firms lag on AI readiness despite gains - IT Brief UK

stories.Headline: LTIMindtree stock shifts wage hikes toward AI reskilling - ad-hoc-news.de
stories.Summary:
LTIMindtree announced on Thursday, November 5, 2026, that its annual pay increases would be split between January and April instead of being granted in a single cycle. According to the Economic Times, the policy is tied to artificial-intelligence reskilling and reflects shifting client demand across the technology-services industry. Chief Executive Officer Venu Lambu said half of employees would receive increases effective January 1, with the rest effective April 1. He ruled out retrenchment or any workforce restructuring linked to the change.

Lambu explained that the company is using training to keep pace with faster AI adoption and customer pressure on pricing. Management said revenue growth has become less dependent on adding employees. The company added 2,500 fresh graduates through its training programs, and its employee count reached 86,447 at the end of September. These figures show a workforce being shaped around new skills rather than expanded in headcount.

The company reported second-quarter net income of 1,381 crore rupees, up 10.4 percent year over year, on revenue of 10,394 crore rupees, up 10.2 percent. Management expects the second half of the year to be slightly better than the first. It is also preparing a five-year growth strategy that it said could be announced in December. LTM Limited, formerly LTIMindtree Limited, is a global technology consulting and digital-solutions company headquartered in Mumbai, India.

Articles.Title: LTIMindtree stock shifts wage hikes toward AI reskilling - ad-hoc-news.de

stories.Headline: CoreWeave beats quarterly revenue estimates as AI demand defies growing doubts
stories.Summary:
CoreWeave, the AI cloud company backed by Nvidia, reported third-quarter results that beat analyst expectations, and executives said on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, that they expect the company to become profitable on an adjusted basis in the first half of 2028. The company's revenue surged nearly 170% to $3.66 billion, above the $3.55 billion estimate, and its per-share loss of 95 cents was smaller than the $1.16 loss analysts expected. Shares were up about 5% in volatile extended trading after falling more than 40% over the past month. The stock had become the focal point of fears about an AI bubble, with investors worried about heavy borrowing to build data centers as interest rates rise.

CoreWeave said its contracted revenue backlog reached $132.5 billion at the end of September, up from $104 billion at the end of June. Quarterly capital spending rose to $14.5 billion from $9.4 billion in the prior quarter. The company now expects 2026 revenue of $13.0 billion to $13.3 billion, compared with its earlier range of $12.4 billion to $13.2 billion, and it raised the low end of its annual spending target by $2 billion to a projected $37 billion to $39 billion. CEO Mike Intrator said in a statement that customer contracts come first and that investment follows, and he disclosed $9 billion in customer prepayments and deposits expected to flow in over the next three months. The company also said it would not tap unsecured debt markets at current yields and would rely on cash flow from customer commitments to repay debt.

Intrator is responsible for the company's public explanation of its strategy, and he argued that lenders have concrete collateral because the spending is tied to committed demand. CoreWeave has never turned a profit, according to data compiled by LSEG, and carried about $46.9 billion in total debt as of the end of September. Its customers include Microsoft, Meta, OpenAI and Anthropic. The results came as the broader AI trade faced a crisis of confidence, which was amplified by Democrats' sweeping win in the US midterm elections that has raised expectations of tighter regulation of the data-center build-out. Recent earnings reports from hyperscalers also hinted at delays in data-center projects and a slower ramp in spending.

Articles.Title: CoreWeave beats quarterly revenue estimates as AI demand defies growing doubts - WTVB

stories.Headline: CoreWeave's backlog quality tested by AI bears, says Jefferies' Brent Thill
stories.Summary:
CoreWeave's backlog quality is under scrutiny after skeptics questioned the health of the AI cloud company's future revenue, according to a CNBC interview with Brent Thill, a senior software analyst at Jefferies, published on November 10, 2026. The segment appeared on "Closing Bell: Overtime," where Thill discussed the company's quarterly results and what they signal about its outlook. The video description frames the discussion around bears who are testing whether the backlog, the contracted revenue the company has yet to recognize, is as solid as it appears. The article itself is a short video summary and does not give figures for the backlog, revenue or contract terms. Nothing in the material says what changed in the company's operations or obligations.

The available text names Thill as the analyst who joined the program and frames his comments as a check on the company's health going forward. It does not include his specific assessment, any price targets, or the reasoning behind any view. The page also lists unrelated segments from the same network about utilities and data center demand, including a Entergy executive saying the election did not change power demand expectations and an Oracle executive citing five large U.S. data centers under construction. Those items are context on the data center boom but are not about CoreWeave.

The article does not say whether CoreWeave or its management responded to the questions raised. The story is a brief, unverified item built on a video description rather than a full report, so the specifics of the backlog dispute and the company's results remain unknown. The articles do not say what comes next for the company or its stock. More to follow.

Articles.Title: CoreWeave's backlog quality tested by AI bears, says Jefferies' Brent Thill - CNBC

stories.Headline: Nebius: The First Domino In The AI Collapse (NASDAQ:NBIS)
stories.Summary:
Nebius Group N.V. (NBIS) is the subject of a bearish analysis published on Seeking Alpha on November 10, 2026, by the Bears of Wall Street community, which argues that the company's growth projections do not add up. The author wrote the piece after Nebius released its Q2 results and says the bearish call has so far been borne out, with the shares losing close to 40 percent of their value. The article is an opinion piece by an outside contributor rather than a news report of a single event. It names no new regulatory action, filing or official announcement.

According to the article, Microsoft is reducing its partnerships with neocloud providers and may not renew some agreements, which could weigh on Nebius's growth outlook. The author also points to delays at a Vineland, New Jersey, site and to stricter political environments that could make it harder for the company to meet its power and capacity targets. On the financing side, the article cites a recent $3.5 billion bridge loan and $5.75 billion in convertible notes, describing them as costly and carrying refinancing risk, with conversion prices far above current share levels. The author says that at roughly $130 per share, the stock is priced for 285 percent growth in 2027, a level the author considers unlikely given recent developments.

Responsibility for these views rests with the author and the Bears of Wall Street community, which describes itself as a group of asset managers and traders who take a pragmatic approach to valuing companies. The article's disclosures state that the author holds no position in Nebius and has no business relationship with the company, and that the views expressed may not reflect those of Seeking Alpha. The piece gives no statement from Nebius, Microsoft or the other parties it discusses, so the company's own account of these matters does not appear in the source. The article does not indicate any further developments or scheduled events beyond the current analysis.

Articles.Title: Nebius: The First Domino In The AI Collapse (NASDAQ:NBIS) - Seeking Alpha

stories.Headline: E2E Networks unveils Blaze, a pay-per-token inference service for open AI models
stories.Summary:
E2E Networks has launched Blaze, a pay-per-token inference service for open AI models, and the announcement was published on November 10, 2026. Blaze gives developers and enterprises a single endpoint that is compatible with OpenAI's interface, connecting them to leading open models. The service runs on NVIDIA GPU infrastructure and uses open-source components from NVIDIA DSX OS. Customers pay only for the tokens they use.

The launch comes as Indian AI companies move from pilots to production, where the cost and speed of inference increasingly decide whether a product is viable. Rising token consumption from AI agents and growing AI-assisted development costs are adding pressure on chief information officers to use tokens more efficiently. Data sovereignty and keeping computing within India are also key priorities for buyers. Blaze is aimed at inference-heavy products where latency and cost per token matter most, including voice, coding agents, document AI and OCR, image and video generation, and language applications.

E2E Networks' founder and managing director, Tarun Dua, said customers want frontier-class open-weight models running on an NVIDIA Cloud Partner with reference design clusters as sovereign compute, and that Blaze provides this on E2E Cloud in India. He also said Blaze integrates easily with the rest of the E2E Cloud platform services. Vishal Dhupar, managing director for South Asia at NVIDIA, said access to AI computing and inference services is essential to advancing India's AI ecosystem. He added that NVIDIA's accelerated computing platform gives cloud providers such as E2E a foundation for making AI more accessible to developers and enterprises in India.

Blaze works alongside TIR, E2E's AI platform, which supports self-hosted inference and model training on NVIDIA Blackwell GPU clusters through managed Kubernetes. The service uses NVIDIA Dynamo for distributed model serving, along with other NVIDIA components for routing, scheduling and hardware-level isolation between customers. E2E says its AI factory capacity is expanding to about 14.6 MW, including a 1,024-GPU NVIDIA Blackwell cluster that has been live since May 2026. An additional 5.4 MW of Blackwell capacity, including HGX B300 systems, is also being added.

Articles.Title: E2E Networks unveils Blaze, a pay-per-token inference service for open AI models - varindia

stories.Headline: Fluidstack begins construction on a 99-acre AI data center campus in Wythe County, Virginia
stories.Summary:
Fluidstack, the AI cloud provider building data centers for Anthropic, has begun construction on a 99-acre campus at Progress Park in Wythe County, Virginia, DatacenterDynamics reported on Tuesday. The company expects most of the campus to be finished by the end of 2027, with operations starting in phases, as it told county supervisors last month. The site was first announced in December 2025 by Solis Arx, a new developer led by founder and CEO Rob Noll, which projected a total investment of over $1 billion according to county administrator Stephen Bear. Fluidstack later took over the project, and the county's board approved an amendment renaming it Fluidstack in August. Neither the company nor the county has disclosed the campus's power capacity or building size, and no end customer has been named.

Solis Arx arranged electric service directly with Appalachian Power, and the county said the project would not affect local electricity rates. Fluidstack says it will pay for its own electricity use, the infrastructure it needs and upgrades to the nearby substation. The campus will use a closed-loop cooling system that needs an initial fill of about 400,000 gallons of water, with ongoing use mostly for staff. Fluidstack expects about 1,000 construction workers at peak and 75 permanent jobs once the campus is running, and says it did not seek or accept project-specific tax incentives. The county gave the ungraded lot to the developer at no cost and projects more than $10 million a year in tax revenue by 2028 if the schedule holds.

The project has drawn local opposition, and Wythe County has no zoning outside its two towns. Andy Kegley, leader of the residents' group Preserve Wythe, said at an October 28 open house that the deal was done and grading was already underway. The county is now drafting its first land-use ordinance. Anthropic said in November 2025 that it would invest $50 billion in U.S. computing infrastructure with Fluidstack, starting with sites in Texas and New York. Fluidstack is also the anchor tenant at bitcoin-miner conversions backed by Google, including TeraWulf's Lake Mariner campus in New York and Cipher Mining's 168 MW lease.

Articles.Title: Fluidstack begins construction on a 99-acre AI data center campus in Wythe County, Virginia - MLQ.ai

stories.Headline: Reliable Retrieval for Production AI Systems
stories.Summary:
Lan Chu, an AI Tech Lead and Senior Data Scientist at Rabobank, gave a talk titled "Reliable Retrieval for Production AI Systems" at QCon London, which was recorded on December 16, 2026 and published by InfoQ on November 10, 2026. Her talk concerned how to move enterprise retrieval-augmented generation systems beyond simple prototypes and into production. She drew on real deployments at Rabobank to describe the changes needed for that move. The talk is about 45 minutes long and is presented as part of the AI, ML and Data Engineering track.

According to the summary, Chu covers several specific practices. She recommends replacing naive OCR with agentic multimodal parsing, so that documents are read in a more capable way. She describes encoding non-textual temporal signals, which helps prevent systems from retrieving outdated information. She also discusses using bootstrap statistical evaluations to test system quality, and establishing continuous observability so that systems can meet the strict governance demands of banking. The summary frames these as necessary for systems to survive in a heavily regulated environment.

Chu's background includes more than seven years building production data and machine learning pipelines and more than three years building generative AI products. She specializes in designing data and AI pipelines and in responsible AI practices, with deep expertise in natural language processing. The talk is one of many at QCon London, a practitioner-driven conference for technical team leads, architects, engineering directors and project managers. The article is an InfoQ presentation page, so it describes the talk and its speaker rather than reporting on any new event or policy.

Articles.Title: Reliable Retrieval for Production AI Systems - infoq.com

stories.Headline: Ansarada expands AI capabilities to streamline deals with OS Bondi 3.0
stories.Summary:
Ansarada, an Australian virtual data room company, is expanding its artificial intelligence capabilities with new tools for due diligence and document analysis in its operating system, OS Bondi 3.0. The company is developing automated question-and-answer workflows and document analysis tools that aim to reduce manual work in transactions while keeping AI security and governance controls in place. The announcement was reported on November 11, 2026, and the changes build on its existing AI assistant, AiDA. Managing Director Justin Smith described the developments as a shift from individual documents to data across the whole data room. The article does not give a release date for the new features.

The roadmap includes intelligent question prioritisation and automated draft responses, along with a document analysis feature called Review with AiDA, which is in early beta and initially available to a limited audience. Question prioritisation will identify questions submitted by multiple parties, such as potential buyers and investors, and prepare draft answers from documents in the data room. Review with AiDA will analyse information across multiple documents, such as contracts, clauses, addresses and remuneration details, to help spot inconsistencies and missing information. A planned My Documents feature will give users a personal file area for sharing and analysing documents before they are added to the indexed material. Ansarada is also developing AiDA access packs that authorised participants, including buyers, can purchase.

Smith said the company is working to keep human reviewers responsible for the process, with AiDA drafting answers that reviewers check, verify against evidence and approve before they are shared with external parties. He said the aim is to give deal teams more time for judgement, and that Ansarada is not replacing advisers or giving advice. Smith also said the company's large language models do not learn from the substantive content of customers' data room documents, but from activity patterns and interactions. He further said the platform operates within Ansarada's own cloud environment and respects existing access permissions, with customers able to control and revoke AI access. The article also says the platform keeps an auditable record of activity.

Ansarada's platform is used for mergers and acquisitions, where due diligence often requires reviewing extensive documentation and answering large numbers of questions from outside parties. The article says Ansarada's experience across approximately 60,000 transactions informs its plans. The company's AiDA assistant helps deal teams search documents, retrieve information and summarise key details within a secure data room. The article notes the Q&A process is one of the most time-consuming parts of due diligence.

Smith identified more proactive assistance as a key development area over the next 12 months. A future version of AiDA could highlight missing information, flag risks and suggest actions based on the stage of a transaction. The company wants to make AI-supported transaction management accessible to smaller organisations and founders selling a business for the first time. Smith said the goal is to give smaller businesses access to the same kinds of secure technology and transaction insights available to larger organisations. The article describes the challenge as reducing the administrative burden of complex transactions without compromising confidentiality, accountability and human judgement.

Articles.Title: Ansarada expands AI capabilities to streamline deals with OS Bondi 3.0 - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: Everpure adds AI & VM storage tools for Kubernetes
stories.Summary:
Everpure has introduced new Portworx features aimed at AI workloads and virtual machines running on Kubernetes, according to an IT Brief Australia report published on 11 November 2026. The updates include pre-staged volumes for AI and machine learning work, general availability of Kube Datastore for virtual machines, and broader observability in the Portworx operations centre. The company also said IDC MarketScape named it a Leader in container data and infrastructure management software. The changes are presented as a way to cut data access delays and give platform teams a more consistent way to manage storage.

Pre-staged volumes are designed to address delays where AI applications wait while large model weights or datasets are downloaded before a workload starts. The approach places warm local copies of persistent volume data across cluster nodes, and storage policies decide which copy a workload uses when it starts or moves to another node. This is meant to shorten startup times and speed recovery when workloads are restarted or rescheduled. The feature is not yet generally available and is expected in the first quarter of 2027. Kube Datastore, known as KDS, is now generally available on supported SAN arrays and lets storage for virtual machines, containers and AI workloads be managed through Kubernetes.

Everpure said KDS supports dynamic and static pools for predictable storage placement and capacity control, while relying on the underlying array for performance and resilience. It also said workloads can run with fewer replicas, and that platform engineers can handle rebalancing and maintenance through Kubernetes-native workflows. Greg Muscarella, General Manager of Portworx at Everpure, said enterprises need to build new applications and modernise existing ones without losing availability or adding operational complexity. He said the company's latest innovations, including Kube Datastore, are meant to simplify storage management, speed recovery from infrastructure failures and improve storage efficiency. IDC's MarketScape report described Portworx as a good fit for enterprises running mission-critical virtual machines, containers or AI workloads on Kubernetes.

The release also expands ecosystem support, with Portworx now available for customers deploying Red Hat OpenShift 5. Everpure's operations centre gained visibility into pool inventory, live migration progress and hyperconvergence state through a single interface. A bring-your-own-backup model will also sit alongside the company's own backup and disaster recovery tools, giving customers more choice. The article places these moves within a wider industry push to run virtual machines, containers and AI applications on one Kubernetes-based platform, a shift in which storage and data management have become central.

Articles.Title: Everpure adds AI & VM storage tools for Kubernetes - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: Australia leads use of AI agents, but managers feel strain
stories.Summary:
Australia ranked highest among seven markets for the use of AI agents in multi-step work, according to new research commissioned by monday.com and conducted by Nielsen. The study surveyed 1,701 Directors and Senior Managers in large companies and found that 46% of Australian respondents use AI agents for multi-step work, compared with a global average of 38%. It also found that 58% expect to manage more agents than people within the next 12 months. Alongside this rapid adoption, many Australian managers reported spending more time supervising AI output.

The research shows a gap between deploying AI and reorganising work around it. Some 59% of Australian leaders said they now spend more time reviewing and guiding their team's output since AI use increased, the highest result among the markets surveyed, and a third said AI adds hours to their working day. Managers must decide what work to delegate, provide context, connect systems, check results and correct errors, all while remaining responsible for the final output. Australian respondents also reported more software tools, with 65% using more since adopting AI, and 36% saying manual steps in workflows have increased.

monday.com, which uses the term "agent sprawl" for a growing build-up of AI agents and automated hand-offs without clear ownership, controls or measures of value, has been vocal on the issue. Gavin Watson, its Regional Director, AI & Industries, argued that agent count is becoming a vanity metric and that businesses should measure whether entire workflows move faster with less rework. He said every agent needs a defined outcome, its own permissions, a clear point of human escalation and one accountable owner. The survey also found that 44% of respondents fear agents will not receive enough human oversight, and 31% worry about being held accountable for an agent's work.

The findings come as policymakers and public agencies examine how organisations use AI systems and how much autonomy they should have. The survey also found that four in five Australian organisations have changed how they evaluate employees since adopting AI, and 40% use AI to draft performance reviews. Watson warned that polish and speed may stop being reliable evidence of ability when several agents help produce the same output. The article does not say what regulatory steps, if any, will follow.

Articles.Title: Australia leads use of AI agents, but managers feel strain - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: Linux Foundation launches Agent Name Service for AI
stories.Summary:
The Linux Foundation has added Agent Name Service, or ANS, as a new project, aiming to give AI agents a verifiable identity and a way to be discovered online. The standard was reported on 11 November 2026 by IT Brief Australia. It builds on the Domain Name System already used across the internet, and the project is being developed openly under the oversight of the project's technical steering committee. Eleven organisations have contributed to or adopted the standard so far.

The specification covers how AI agents are named and registered, how their identities are published through DNS and verified, and how identity records are monitored for unauthorised changes. It also sets out how agents authenticate one another. The work is organised into seven documents covering domain-anchored naming, registration and versioning, DNS publication, public log auditing, integrity monitoring, and agent-to-agent authentication. Supporters say building on DNS and certificate-based verification means relying on infrastructure that is already widely deployed and well understood.

Jim Zemlin, chief executive officer of the Linux Foundation, said autonomous AI agents operating across global systems cannot succeed without verifiable identity. He argued that neutral governance gives the industry a common foundation for trust that it can adopt and improve together. The eleven supporting organisations named include Cisco, Cloudflare, DigiCert, DistributedApps.ai, GoDaddy, HOL, Infoblox, Radix, Salesforce, OWASP, and Trustmodel.ai. Cloudflare's chief technology officer, Dane Knecht, said organisations need to know who an agent represents before trusting it to act.

The AGNTCY Agent Directory Service, another Linux Foundation project, already supports verification of ANS identities. ANS Finder implements the Agentic Resource Discovery specification and has passed registry conformance tests. Backers argue that wide use of autonomous agents will depend on a shared trust model rather than isolated vendor-specific approaches. Several backers also praised placing the specification under the Linux Foundation instead of a single commercial sponsor, which they say keeps the system open to multiple participants.

Articles.Title: Linux Foundation launches Agent Name Service for AI - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: Zendesk launches outcome AI platform with new pricing
stories.Summary:
Zendesk has launched its Outcome AI Platform along with a new plan called Zendesk Unlimited, moving its service software away from per-seat charges. The platform combines AI assistants, specialised AI agents and human teams in one system for customer and employee requests. Under the new model, customers can set an outcome budget and pay for eligible issues resolved and business work completed rather than buying software seats. Zendesk says the platform can automate up to 84% of service requests and cut resolution times from hours to minutes. Outcomes are assessed for quality and completeness before they count towards a customer's budget.

Zendesk Unlimited removes seat limits from the new plans, so customers get unlimited seats alongside AI tools, with features varying by tier. The company argues that as AI takes on more service work, businesses want spending tied more directly to completed work and verified resolutions. The announcement also introduced Open Service Directory, an open specification and public directory of verified brand support channels that personal AI assistants can use to find official routes for a business. Businesses that join can decide what information they share and when human review is required. Zendesk says the directory does not access private customer data or act on its own.

Zendesk also unveiled Zendesk Bridge, which connects external AI tools and agents to Zendesk service workflows. Administrators can control which AI tools connect, what information they can access and which actions they can take, and each action is subject to identity checks, permissions, human approvals and audit trails. Early directory participants named in the announcement include Betterment, ElevenLabs, Flex, TeamSystem, TBA Auctions, Telekom Payment and Wireless Logic. The launch was tied to Zendesk's survey finding that 52% of consumers are comfortable relying on personal AI assistants for everyday tasks.

Zendesk's chief executive, Tom Eggemeier, said the change reflects a broader shift in how people want to deal with organisations, wanting help to accomplish their goal without navigating channels or departments. Tapan Patel of IDC said the pricing model addresses enterprise buyers' wish to tie AI spending to verified resolutions and business outcomes. Bikram Mazumdar, Vice President of Zendesk Asia, said companies in the region face pressure to show returns from AI spending. The articles do not describe any further rollout timeline beyond the launch itself.

Articles.Title: Zendesk launches outcome AI platform with new pricing - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: AI Theatre vs Real Adoption - ET CIO
stories.Summary:
Raj Goodman Anand, founder and director of AI-First Mindset, argued in an ETCIO opinion piece published on November 10, 2026 that many companies stage AI adoption without really changing how work gets done. Despite substantial investment in AI licences and training, usage often rises after launch and then falls back to a flat line. He described seeing companies with a hundred licences where only five people opened the tool on an ordinary day. The piece draws a line between visible steps, such as buying licences and holding training sessions, and the harder work of rewriting workflows.

The author set out several signs that adoption is theatre rather than real. AI is mentioned at town halls but appears in no process document, and pilots run without end dates, which he treats as a way of avoiding decisions. A Head of AI may hold a title but have no budget or authority to change how a department works. He also warned against measuring success by logins, since a login shows curiosity but not whether a task got faster, cheaper or better. Training, he added, fades quickly unless people apply it to their own real tasks within about a week, with their managers checking.

Anand's central recommendation is to start small: pick two or three frequently repeated workflows that frustrate the people doing them and give each a clear owner. He suggests timing each task before and after redesigning it with the people who do the work, using a sales proposal as an example, where AI produces the first draft and a senior person reviews it. Ownership matters, he argued, because a workflow owned by a committee has no one who can say whether it worked. He also set a test for CEOs: name three tasks that take less time today because of AI, and say by how much. Companies should scale what works and stop what doesn't, rather than announcing a company-wide rollout of something unproven.

Articles.Title: AI Theatre vs Real Adoption - ET CIO

stories.Headline: Gartner Introduces Framework for CIOs to Determine AI Outcomes
stories.Summary:
Gartner has released a framework called the Value-Risk Flywheel to help chief information officers align the value that artificial intelligence creates for enterprises with the risks it brings, according to an article published on November 10, 2026. The framework centres on two forces that shape AI outcomes, momentum and drag, and the company says these forces do not always behave as expected. Gartner argues that momentum is not always good and that some drag is beneficial. The framework is meant to guide organisations through the complexity of AI implementation and governance.

Daryl Plummer, Distinguished VP, Managing VP and Chief of Research at Gartner, said the best thing a CIO can do is align value with risk and align safety with governance. He said that CIOs who outperform know how to build positive momentum and add useful drag while reducing harmful momentum and harmful drag. As an example, the article says that in software development, value can compound faster than risk because AI can generate a significant share of code. This relieves developers of manual coding and lets them focus on rapid prototyping, requirements-driven development, architectural thinking and product engineering.

Plummer also said the flywheel needs a governor at its centre, a figure who decides when value is worth the risk, which perspective on value should dominate and how to keep the organisation safe. Kristin Moyer, Distinguished VP Analyst and Gartner Fellow, described this governor as a centralised decision authority that drives advice and guides action on accountability, technology and economics. The article ties the framework to a Q2 2026 Gartner survey of more than 2,000 CIOs and technology executives. That survey found that 71 percent of organisations expect to deploy agentic AI within the next 12 months, while only 21 percent have governance mechanisms for agentic AI. Moyer said this imbalance makes it harder to create value faster than AI increases risk.

Articles.Title: Gartner Introduces Framework for CIOs to Determine AI Outcomes - Analytics India Magazine

stories.Headline: Meta to Introduce Muse AI Agent in India Starting With ₹1,799 Plan: Report
stories.Summary:
Meta has reportedly listed subscription prices for Muse, its personal artificial intelligence agent, ahead of a planned launch in India. According to a report by The Hindu, cited by Analytics India Magazine on November 10, 2026, the Power plan is listed at ₹1,799 per month and the Maximum plan at ₹8,999. The prices appear on Muse's service, with slightly higher charges for subscriptions bought through Google Play and Apple's billing systems. Meta has not confirmed a launch date or the India-specific pricing, so it remains unclear whether these figures are final.

Muse is designed to carry out tasks on a user's behalf rather than only answer questions. Meta introduced it on September 8, and the agent can browse websites, work with connected applications and keep working on assigned tasks after the user closes the app. It can send emails, book travel, fill in online forms and coordinate longer-term tasks through a dedicated cloud-based virtual machine with its own browser. Users choose which applications Muse may access and set permissions for different activities, and the agent asks for approval before sensitive actions such as sending emails or making purchases. Indian users are currently on a waitlist, and although the web and WhatsApp interfaces can be reached from India, some features remain restricted.

Meta is the company behind Muse, which it first rolled out in the United States through its website, dedicated iOS and Android apps and WhatsApp. The company has also said it plans to bring the agent to its AI glasses. In the US, the Power plan costs $20 per month and the Maximum plan $100 per month, and both paid tiers offer higher usage limits than a free tier. Analytics India Magazine's report does not give a launch date for India, and Meta has not announced one.

The context is the agent's growth so far. According to SensorTower data cited by TechCrunch, Muse has recorded more than 10 million downloads within two months of its launch. Its integration with WhatsApp could give it an additional route to users in India, where the messaging platform has a large user base. The articles do not say when Muse will officially become available to Indian users or whether the listed prices will be confirmed.

Articles.Title: Meta to Introduce Muse AI Agent in India Starting With ₹1,799 Plan: Report - Analytics India Magazine

stories.Headline: PwC to Train 85,000 Staff in Critical Thinking as AI Reshapes Work
stories.Summary:
PwC has announced a critical-thinking and judgement certification programme for more than 85,000 partners and employees, unveiled on 9 November 2026 and reported on 10 November. The programme responds to artificial intelligence taking over tasks that junior professionals have traditionally used to learn their craft. Its aim is to strengthen staff ability to evaluate information, question assumptions and exercise independent judgement when working alongside AI. Rollout is planned to begin in December 2026 across PwC's US and Mexico offices and offshore service centres, with completion targeted for June 2027.

The training will include personalised simulations in which employees must challenge AI-generated conclusions, such as reviewing an AI assessment of a company's internal controls and identifying deficiencies. It will combine diagnostic assessments, masterclasses, practical exercises and workplace tools. PwC expects to invest more than $100 million in the initiative, including programme development and support for universities. The firm also plans to make its critical-thinking framework available to universities in early 2027.

The article describes the move as part of a wider problem facing the Big Four, where AI increasingly performs the routine audit work through which junior auditors once built professional judgement. Former Arthur Andersen professional William Englehaupt has argued that firms must replace the practical learning opportunities that are disappearing. KPMG US has redesigned its audit internship programme this year to add fraud-detection simulations and anomaly-investigation exercises. A study by KPMG and the University of Texas at Austin of 523 early-career professionals working with AI agents found that 50.1% improved on the AI's performance, 25.8% produced broadly equivalent results, and 24.1% performed worse than the AI alone.

The article also cites Wayne Banks, a chartered accountant and former global CFO, who warned of automation deference, the gradual erosion of professional scepticism as staff grow used to accepting polished AI output. Banks has urged firms to adopt documented verification procedures, clear accountability and controls requiring staff to test AI conclusions rather than simply approve them. The article raises the open question of whether simulations and formal certification can match the depth of judgement that earlier generations gained through years of supervised audit work. It notes that the answer will matter for audit quality as AI takes on more analysis and evidence evaluation.

Articles.Title: PwC to Train 85,000 Staff in Critical Thinking as AI Reshapes Work - https://www.big4news.com/
