stories.Headline: Tallinn Digital Summit’s first afternoon finds Europe slow where AI agents are fast
stories.Summary:
Tallinn Digital Summit's first afternoon opened with a panel on competition for talent, capital and innovation, where Clark Parsons described a Berlin agentic AI company incorporated in Estonia that executed a Delaware flip for its U.S. lead investor. Mario Nava, director-general for employment, social affairs and inclusion at the European Commission, told the summit that artificial intelligence needs safeguards built in before disaster strikes. He used an elevator comparison, arguing that such systems need two ropes so that one can fail without the whole structure falling. The afternoon held two Agentic Stage sessions on the first day of the ninth summit. Parsons asked Nava to name one change in the next 12 months that would slow the flow of companies out of Europe, and Nava pointed to the skills portability initiative and recognition of skills from outside the EU, decisions he said rest with ministers in the Council.

Liina Vahtras, Estonia's minister of economy and industry, described the problem as a chicken-and-egg dynamic in which founders chase growth funding in the United States and U.S. investors want headquarters where they understand the law. She said only a truly ambitious EU company form would break that cycle. Vahtras, who led Estonia's e-Residency program before joining the government, said the original private-sector proposal for EU Inc., an optional EU-wide company form also called the 28th regime, excited Estonian officials because it tried to address taxes. She said the proposal had since gone through repeated simplification, and that the ambition was being removed with each round. Her proposal was to start with a smaller group of willing countries, perhaps 10, while others join once they see it working.

Kamal Shehadi, Lebanon's minister of the displaced and minister of state for technology and artificial intelligence, said the single market needs one capital market and one corporate market in which a company registers once and operates anywhere. He said Lebanese founders face the same pull, incorporating at home, raising money in Dubai, Abu Dhabi or Riyadh, and registering in Delaware when they have international ambitions. Lebanon has created special technology economic zones to make incorporation and visas for foreign engineers easier. Parsons said member states had capped the harmonized treatment of employee stock options at about 750 employees or 150 million euros in annual recurring revenue, a ceiling he said a fast-growing startup can pass in 18 months.

Eirini Zafeiratou, vice president of public policy at Bolt, the ride-hailing and delivery company founded in Estonia, said scaling depends on access to a single market of 450 million people and on capital. She said Bolt has had 70 percent less access to capital than its main U.S. competitor over the past decade. She put the U.S. ride-hailing market at $95 billion and the EU's at less than half that, and blamed rules she said predate the smartphone. In Italy, she said, a capped supply of professional driver licenses leaves travelers paying about 100 euros from Milan Malpensa Airport into the city. In Barcelona, she said, a Catalan rule requires private-hire cars to be 5 meters long, so drivers add bumpers, though the rule sets a minimum length of 4.9 meters.

Nava turned to AI in the workplace, saying the Commission tracks its effect on jobs and that anecdotal evidence suggests it is taking a toll on entry-level positions. He cited a Commission survey published in February 2025 finding over 60 percent of Europeans viewed AI at work positively and 84 percent said it requires careful management. He linked that demand to the Quality Jobs Act, which he said the Commission will present at the end of November or the beginning of December, including a part on algorithmic management and AI. European Commission Executive Vice President Roxana Mînzatu has said she hopes the Commission will adopt its proposal on Dec. 3. Asked what success would look like by next year's summit, Nava pointed to removing obstacles to the single market before rules are adopted and after member states add requirements on top.

Articles.Title: Tallinn Digital Summit’s first afternoon finds Europe slow where AI agents are fast - JD Supra

stories.Headline: Apple's Claris Testing 'Harbor' App for Local AI on Macs
stories.Summary:
Apple's Claris subsidiary is testing an app called Harbor, which turns Apple silicon Macs into a private AI server. The app works on a single Apple silicon Mac, and it also supports connecting multiple Macs over Thunderbolt 5 to pool unified memory for larger models. Apple added RDMA over Thunderbolt 5 with macOS Tahoe 26.2, which the article says makes clustering faster. Harbor is in early access and is not publicly available. The report was published on November 10, 2026.

Harbor is described as easy to set up, with no manual configuration required. The app automatically detects devices connected over Thunderbolt 5 to form a cluster. Users can browse, download and load open-weight models from inside the app. Harbor also pools unified memory across two or more Thunderbolt 5-capable Macs, allowing models that exceed any single computer's capacity to run. The article says the app keeps user data on the hardware, with nothing reaching the cloud.

The article identifies Claris as an Apple subsidiary known for its database platform FileMaker, which is aimed at businesses. It says it is not clear how Apple will market Harbor or whether it will be free. The Harbor sign-up page asks for a company name, which the article says suggests a business focus. An App Store listing for Harbor existed but has now been removed. Apple has not commented in the article.

The article notes that free alternatives already exist for Mac users who want a local AI server. Exo is an open-source tool for clustering Macs, and LM Studio is available for single-Mac use. The article says Harbor appears to combine LM Studio's simple interface with clustering. Commenters on the piece also raised the Claris name's history, recalling the older ClarisWorks software.

Articles.Title: Apple's Claris Testing 'Harbor' App for Local AI on Macs

stories.Headline: Many AI companies will adopt advertising: ad chief Criteo
stories.Summary:
Michael Komasinski, chief executive of the online advertising firm Criteo, told AFP on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, that many AI platforms will likely adopt advertising over time. He spoke on the sidelines of the Web Summit in Lisbon. His view is that advertising is the most scalable business model available and has funded many of the large platforms people use today, including Google, Meta and Snapchat. He also said ad formats will become more interesting and more native to conversational AI experiences.

The shift toward ads is already under way at some firms. OpenAI began testing advertising in ChatGPT in February 2026 in the United States, for free and low-cost subscription tiers, and has since been rolling ads out worldwide in cooperation with Criteo. Criteo works with OpenAI in 89 countries on advertising campaigns on AI chatbots, and Komasinski said about 3,600 brands have trialed AI advertising campaigns, noting a modest increase in their spending on ChatGPT. Microsoft has shown ads in the public version of its Copilot AI since 2023, Perplexity has experimented with ads in the United States since 2024, and Google is reportedly considering ads in Gemini. Anthropic, which is set to go public soon, has said it does not plan to put advertising in its AI tools, citing data protection concerns and the interests of its users.

The pressure behind these moves comes from the cost of building and running AI models, which requires massive investment. Investor confidence in AI-related stocks buoyed markets this year, but equity and bond investors have recently grown more wary as inflation and high interest rates make the work more expensive. Komasinski's remarks came from the Criteo chief executive himself, and he was also skeptical that AI agents could autonomously make purchases, saying that people tend not to hand important decisions to a bot. The article does not say when Google would decide on Gemini ads or how the planned Anthropic listing will affect its advertising stance.

Articles.Title: Many AI companies will adopt advertising: ad chief Criteo

stories.Headline: 45% of execs limit human AI oversight to high-stakes work, or don't have any oversight at all
stories.Summary:
Companies are placing growing trust in AI agents, and a survey of 518 U.S. executives at firms with an AI governance policy shows they differ sharply on how much human review those agents need. Zapier ran the survey between July 1 and July 7, 2026, and the article reports that 30% of executives let AI act autonomously on most tasks and step in only for high-stakes actions. Another 15% said their companies give AI full, unsupervised autonomy, while 26% approve every AI-powered action that is feasible to review by hand. The remaining executives fall in between, with 29% saying humans approve most AI-powered actions. The article, written by Lane Gillespie for Zapier and distributed by Stacker, frames the choice as a bet on whether an AI's judgment will match that of the people overseeing it.

The article presents a concrete example: an AI agent that handles vendor invoices can either pass every payment through a human or be left to pay on its own, and with no review it could wire $5,000 to a spoofed invoice. Among executives whose companies have faced problems, 38% said unsupervised AI had already cost them time, money, or reputation. Of those, 54% spent significant time correcting outputs or redoing work, 39% had delayed or lost revenue, and 36% faced legal, regulatory, or compliance consequences. The article also reports that 49% of executives at companies that had AI-related issues said their workplace has too much oversight, compared with 9% at companies without problems. The article offers two readings of that gap without settling between them.

The article recommends placing review checkpoints by risk rather than by volume. It cites three approaches: 66% of companies set approval policies around regulatory or compliance requirements, 52% base human approval on whether an action can be undone, and 49% set thresholds by dollar value or business impact. It also reports that 62% vary the policy by department or function. Executives were more willing to let AI act alone on low-stakes tasks, with 79% accepting AI updates to a customer record in their CRM without notice and 72% accepting AI scheduling a meeting with an external stakeholder. Fewer were comfortable with AI approving a budget line item under $1,000 without notice (60%) or posting to a company social media account (61%).

The survey was conducted by Centiment for Zapier and fielded between July 1, 2026, and July 7, 2026, with 518 completed surveys from directors, VPs and C-suite executives at U.S. companies with at least 100 employees and an AI governance policy. The margin of error is approximately ±4% for the overall sample at a 96% confidence level, and the data is unweighted. The article defines a formal AI governance policy as a documented, company-wide policy addressing at least one of approved or prohibited tools, data-handling rules, employee guidelines or training, or compliance and monitoring procedures. The article describes human-in-the-loop options built into the best AI tools as a way to create a clear paper trail of AI decisions.

Articles.Title: 45% of execs limit human AI oversight to high-stakes work, or don't have any oversight at all

stories.Headline: Affective and Emotion Terms Reflect Divergent AI Education Research Orientations
stories.Summary:
A bibliometric analysis of scholarly work from 2020 through 2025 has found that researchers' choice between "affective" and "emotion" terminology in artificial intelligence in education reflects systematic differences in research design. Hsiang-Ni Tsai and Sheng-Yi Wu analyzed 292 peer-reviewed journal articles indexed in the Scopus database, and published the study in the journal Discover Artificial Intelligence. The researchers used a dual-track keyword search, and the number of publications rose from 32 articles between 2020 and 2022 to 151 papers in 2025 alone. The authors concluded that the two terms do not work as interchangeable synonyms but anchor parallel research traditions. Those traditions differ in participant selection, measurement techniques and contextual settings.

The team used VOSviewer to perform keyword co-occurrence network analysis, with a minimum occurrence threshold of three appearances. After data cleaning, 138 keyword nodes remained, which the researchers consolidated into four core thematic categories. The pedagogical application category was the largest, with 47 nodes, while the technical recognition category, with 34 nodes, had the earliest average publication year. Psychological, emotional and user response research comprised 14 nodes, and generative artificial intelligence and emerging technologies formed a cluster of 43 nodes. The annual output rose sharply with the emergence of generative models, and 2025 accounted for 51.7 percent of all reviewed work.

The central empirical contribution was a five-dimensional content analysis of the 292 articles covering research purpose, measurement channel, research subject, learning environment and subject domain. Initial coding was generated by two independent large language models, after which the human researchers arbitrated discrepancies and a second independent evaluator verified reliability. Chi-square tests found statistically significant differences between the affective and emotion groups on every dimension, with Cramér's V values ranging from 0.190 to 0.311. The research subject dimension showed a moderate effect, while the other four showed small-to-moderate effects. Sensitivity analyses that excluded the 34 overlapping papers, and that reversed group assignments, preserved statistical significance across all five dimensions.

The divergences were most pronounced in the research subject dimension, where the chi-square statistic was 28.24. Among affective studies, 72.7 percent specified a clearly defined educational cohort, with higher education students making up 39.4 percent, while 46.1 percent of emotion papers left the educational subject unspecified. In the emotion group, primary and secondary school participants accounted for only 7.3 percent of studies. Real classroom settings were the largest category among affective investigations at 43.4 percent, while unspecified learning environments predominated in the emotion group at 45.6 percent. The authors suggested that many emotion studies use educational settings mainly as testing grounds for algorithmic benchmarking.

The authors proposed the Dual Knowledge Production Framework of Affective and Emotion AI Research to explain these patterns. They linked affective scholarship to the educational taxonomy traditions of Benjamin Bloom and David Krathwohl, and linked emotion research to the psychological traditions of Paul Ekman and Reinhard Pekrun. Both lineages intersect through Rosalind Picard's affective computing paradigm. The authors also outlined methodological limitations inherent to their bibliometric design, which the article details. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Affective and Emotion Terms Reflect Divergent AI Education Research Orientations

stories.Headline: AI Trade Reverses: Performance Of AI Haves And Have Nots
stories.Summary:
Baron Capital, in a segment excerpted from its Baron Small Cap Fund Q3 2026 commentary published November 10, 2026, reported that the AI trade reversed during the third quarter. The firm said stock performance this year has been heavily shaped by how the market views AI's effect on individual companies. Baron sorted its holdings into three groups, which it calls "AI Haves," "AI Have Nots," and "Other." Semiconductors, momentum, and beta all traded lower in that quarter, reversing earlier trends.

According to the commentary, AI Haves drove strong gains in the first half of 2026 but fell sharply in the third quarter. AI Have Nots lagged early in the year but rebounded strongly in the third quarter, which balanced overall fund performance. Many of the firm's Other stocks declined in the third quarter as investors worried about higher interest rates and rising fuel prices. The commentary also cited geopolitical tensions, especially in aerospace and defense, as pressure on the fund's Other holdings.

Baron Capital, an asset management firm founded in 1982 and focused on growth equity investing, is responsible for the commentary. The firm said that market-wide perceptions about AI led to sweeping reclassifications of companies and large valuation swings. It indicated that these broad sentiment shifts overshadowed bottom-up research and drove sharp price moves in both the AI Haves and AI Have Nots. The source material does not describe any further steps the firm plans to take.

Articles.Title: AI Trade Reverses: Performance Of AI Haves And Have Nots

stories.Headline: Artificial Intelligence Review Shows High Diagnostic Accuracy Across Bladder Cancer Modalities
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence tools for bladder cancer diagnosis are reported to reach sensitivity and specificity above ninety percent in many applications, according to a narrative review published in the African Journal of Urology. The review synthesized international research published between January 2015 and April 2026 and covered cystoscopic video, urine cytology, cross-sectional imaging and whole-slide histopathology. Worldwide, bladder cancer was the ninth most commonly diagnosed malignancy, with 614,298 cases in 2022 according to International Agency for Research on Cancer estimates. Accurate differentiation matters because it determines whether patients receive bladder-preserving resection with intravesical therapy or radical cystectomy with neoadjuvant chemotherapy.

Conventional methods carry known limits. White-light cystoscopy depends heavily on the operator, with detection sensitivity for flat carcinoma in situ lesions falling as low as sixty to seventy percent. Manual review of voided urine cytology missed low-grade tumors between fifty-seven and seventy-four percent of the time in prospective series. Pathologists showed interobserver discordance rates of fifteen to twenty percent when grading transurethral resection specimens. The authors describe this as an urgent need for reproducible, objective diagnostic support.

In the Cystoscopy AI Diagnostic System, developed across six hospitals in China using 69,204 images from 10,729 patients, external diagnostic accuracies reached between 97.7 percent and 99.0 percent. That platform surpassed expert urologists in identifying difficult flat lesions. In a prospective analysis of 102 cystoscopy video recordings from ninety-four patients, the HRNetV2 model recorded a per-frame sensitivity of 94.8 percent during transurethral resection. In the VISIOCYT1 trial enrolling 319 patients, the VisioCyt software reached 84.9 percent sensitivity on voided urine samples, compared with 43.0 percent for manual cytology.

The review also reports that imaging timing affects radiomic model performance. In a 2025 retrospective study by Lisson and colleagues of ninety-seven patients, restricting analysis to seventy-nine patients scanned more than fourteen days after transurethral resection raised the radiomic model's area under the curve from 0.68 to 0.80. In a multicenter lymph node analysis of 7,991 slides from 998 patients, deep learning reached a sensitivity of 0.983 for detecting metastatic spread, compared with 0.947 for senior pathologists and 0.906 for junior pathologists. The system also identified occult micrometastases in thirteen patients whose nodes had been classified as negative on manual review.

The authors stress that barriers remain before wider clinical use. Kwong and colleagues assessed fifteen outcome prediction studies with the APPRAISE-AI instrument and found only one of high quality, with most affected by small cohorts, lack of external validation and bias. Lisson's study observed lower model sensitivity in female patients, at 0.53 compared with 0.78 in men, a disparity the review says remains unaddressed. The authors say standardized reporting frameworks, multi-institutional prospective trials and formal health-economic validation remain prerequisites before algorithms can be integrated into clinical care.

Articles.Title: Artificial Intelligence Review Shows High Diagnostic Accuracy Across Bladder Cancer Modalities

stories.Headline: Taco Bell Put AI in 900 Drive-Thrus — Here’s What Happened to Sales
stories.Summary:
Taco Bell has put voice AI to work taking drive-thru orders at more than 900 of its locations, and the company reports that these stores are seeing a sales lift. According to Restaurant Business, those locations have seen about a 1.5% increase in sales from larger checks. The article says the same technology has also helped the parent company, Yum! Brands, report a 6% rise in drive-thru satisfaction and better crew retention.

Taco Bell has plans to expand the system to more than 1,500 restaurants by the end of the year. The AI system is credited with prompting customers to add items, since it always offers a side or drink, even during busy periods. KFC, also owned by Yum! Brands, is making its own changes with a new kitchen display system at its U.S. locations.

That system has made drive-thru service 8% faster and cut refunds by 12%. Delivery drivers now wait 20 fewer seconds for their orders. The article quotes Yum! Brands CFO Ranjith Roy, who said the company expects AI to be transformative to the business.

The rollout has not been without problems. Last year, the system drew attention after a customer tried to order 18,000 cups of water, a moment that spread widely online. The article's author, Jonathan Small, is an Entrepreneur staff writer who reports on the results. The article does not describe any further steps beyond the planned expansion to more than 1,500 restaurants.

Articles.Title: Taco Bell Put AI in 900 Drive-Thrus — Here’s What Happened to Sales

stories.Headline: Computable Due Process Model Establishes Legal Reasoning Standards for Judicial AI
stories.Summary:
A theoretical framework published in Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence argues that artificial intelligence systems can produce text that looks like a reasoned judicial decision without the genuine justification needed to support it. The study, written by Roberto Leonardo Cruz-Núñez, Hugo Armando Aguilar-Brito, Andherson J. Aguirre-Lanegra, and Nuccia Seminario-Hurtado, presents this as a practical concern because automated systems are already drafting court documents that judges later validate. Existing legal frameworks, the authors note, lack precise criteria for telling valid legal reasoning from superficial imitation. The paper was reported on November 11, 2026, and it is described as a hypothesis and theory study in the Technology and Law section of the journal.

To close this gap, the researchers turned the constitutional duty to give reasons into a set of formal correctness conditions. They combined legal-dogmatic analysis with formal reconstruction, placing these requirements within structured argumentation and defeasible deontic logic under a framework they call computable due process. Their formal specifications draw on Peruvian constitutional jurisprudence, which they describe as the continental tradition's most developed typology of defective judicial reasoning. The analysis maps six recognized flaws in judicial reasoning onto five conditions that any admissible argument must meet: the argument must exist, its inference must be formally valid, its premises must be justified, it must satisfy the applicable standard of proof, and it must answer every claim raised.

The required threshold varies with the gravity of the act, so a simple procedural order and a custodial criminal conviction do not demand the same justification. The authors report that current large language models fail to satisfy these conditions, citing evidence that specialized legal tools using source retrieval generate false information between 17% and 33% of the time. They also say such models are especially vulnerable when a special legal rule conflicts with a general norm, because statistical models tend to apply the norm that appears more often in their training data rather than the hierarchically correct rule. From these findings the study proposes an architectural rule for assisted judicial technology: the duty to produce inspectable justification should sit with a symbolic reasoning layer, while the final qualitative assessment stays with the human judge.

The researchers argue that this standard can separate systems that legitimately support the judicial function from those that only simulate it, and that it offers a verifiable basis for constitutional review of assisted rulings. The work comes from an institutional collaboration between the Universidad Autónoma de Chiapas in Tuxtla Gutiérrez, Mexico, and the Technological University of Peru in Lima, Peru. The authors also note that comparable requirements appear elsewhere: Brazilian statutory law sets out six equivalent grounds of defective reasoning, Spanish law grades the duty to give reasons across decision types, and European and Inter-American courts enforce analogous requirements. The article does not report any regulatory adoption of the model or any scheduled next steps beyond the publication itself.

Articles.Title: Computable Due Process Model Establishes Legal Reasoning Standards for Judicial AI - Bioengineer.org

stories.Headline: PSI is trying to make a business out of AI-driven scientific discovery
stories.Summary:
David Turturean, a recent MIT graduate on the technical staff of the startup lab Physical Superintelligence (PSI), used early access to Anthropic's Fable 5.2 model to solve an 18-year-old problem in quantum computing, the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture. The reporting was published on November 10, 2026, by TechCrunch. The solution concerns whether quantum computers can solve certain problems faster than classical ones. Scott Aaronson, one of the researchers who posed the problem, said he does not fully follow the proof but believes it is correct because it was autoformalized in Lean and checked by a team of top researchers with whom PSI shared it.

The result appears to rule out one route quantum computers could take to solve some hard problems quickly, though not all of them. PSI held the result until Anthropic's model was nearly ready for release, which gave it time to share the work with relevant experts. Turturean said the academic community will expect him to explain the result. Aaronson wrote that he was surprised the problem was missing from a recent OpenAI batch of solved problems.

PSI CEO Matt Pines said the company's model relies on specialized harnesses, tools, memory systems and simulation infrastructure to tackle scientific problems across breadth and depth. For now, the company earns revenue by using its tools to optimize data centers, simulating heat, power, water and sound. Its longer goal is converting theoretical physics breakthroughs into real technologies, which Pines acknowledged has not yet happened. He noted that AI has claimed solutions in mathematics and computer science, where results can be expressed in validated code, but physics is harder because nature has the final say.

Jim Halverson, a Northeastern University professor who advises PSI, said transparency and contacting experts are emerging best practices, and he will attend an MIT summit next week where leading physicists will discuss the new pace of science. Pines said PSI focuses on validating computational results with experiments as efficiently as possible. The startup Discovered Materials recently released a $1 million grand challenge for AI-driven research on problems such as superconductivity and heat dissipation. Participants in these new "neolabs for science" are still working out what standards will govern this work.

Articles.Title: PSI is trying to make a business out of AI-driven scientific discovery

stories.Headline: Australia Proposes New AI Rules and Criminal Penalties Following Hack
stories.Summary:
Australia's government has proposed new rules requiring artificial intelligence companies to report serious incidents immediately or face penalties for noncompliance. The proposal follows a hack targeting government systems that the articles describe as rogue and OpenAI-powered. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said on Tuesday that the government had accepted all recommendations from a rapid review into the breach. Those recommendations include mandatory reporting of misaligned behavior and cyber incidents, along with possible changes to criminal law to penalize serious misconduct.

One recommendation asks the Attorney-General's Department, the Australian Federal Police and the Home Affairs Department to consider penalties for egregious regulatory noncompliance. It also proposes a new failure to prevent offense. Under that idea, developing an AI model that causes harm could become a crime if reasonable steps to prevent the harm were not taken. The government also plans to create a new AI regulator to oversee security controls across the development and deployment of AI systems. The articles provided do not give figures, dates for implementation, or penalty amounts.

The articles do not name a specific individual or company as responsible for the breach beyond describing it as an OpenAI-powered hack. The Prime Minister is the official quoted, and he spoke on the government's acceptance of the review's recommendations. The articles do not include any statement from OpenAI or from the operators of the affected government systems. The available text is a short summary, so the wider background and any next steps beyond the proposals remain unreported in these sources.

Articles.Title: Australia Proposes New AI Rules and Criminal Penalties Following Hack - https://globalpost.com/

stories.Headline: SGLang RCE Exploit Breaches NEAR AI, Steals Data From 18 Agents and About 100 Users
stories.Summary:
An attacker exploited a remote code execution flaw in SGLang, an open-source inference engine, and ran code on one of NEAR AI's inference servers last Sunday. The attacker could also have seen requests processed on that server that day, including requests sent in confidential mode. That mode runs requests inside a trusted execution environment meant to keep them private even from the company. The company said that environment does not protect against flaws in the software running inside it, and SGLang runs there. The attacker then moved further into the company's systems.

The attacker reached an internal system behind Private Chat, a product the company had already deprecated, and downloaded account details for about 100 users, including email addresses and names. For some accounts, plan and balance information was also taken, though the company found no sign that stored conversations or uploaded files were accessed. The attacker also reached 18 AI agents on an older NEAR AI Agents deployment that did not run inside the company's trusted environment, taking chat history, settings and logs. Two customers' NEAR AI Cloud API keys were exposed in logs, and the company has revoked both. After detecting the attack, the company revoked all active sessions and administrator credentials, replaced all agent tokens, and took Private Chat offline.

NEAR AI said it deployed a fix for the SGLang flaw on all its inference servers, rotated remaining credentials, and completed a full forensic review, according to its incident report. It has restored access to its NEAR AI Cloud service and reported the flaw to the SGLang project. The company has not given a CVE number, named the affected SGLang versions, or said whether the project has released a fix. It contacted affected users directly from its security address and advised them to be wary of unexpected messages about their accounts or balances. In a follow-up post, it said users who have not heard from it need take no action.

The company has not said whether people whose requests passed through the affected server last Sunday were among those contacted. Brave, the browser maker, said in an October 15 technical write-up that its Leo assistant runs chats with one model inside a trusted environment operated by NEAR AI. NEAR AI has not said whether the affected server handled any of those chats. The articles do not say whether further disclosures are planned.

Articles.Title: SGLang RCE Exploit Breaches NEAR AI, Steals Data From 18 Agents and About 100 Users

stories.Headline: In age of AI, human touch still matters
stories.Summary:
Prime Sarmiento, a China Daily correspondent based in Hong Kong, wrote a first-person column published on November 10, 2026, after covering the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank in Bangkok, which he reached on October 12. He had expected the event to focus on the IMF's World Economic Outlook, interest rates, inflation and the energy shock, but he found that artificial intelligence came up in most discussions across the week. Some sessions were devoted to AI, including a popular panel featuring Jack Clark, co-founder of the United States company Anthropic. Participants, he wrote, felt a mix of optimism about AI's benefits and unease that its costs could outweigh the economic gains it was expected to bring.

The IMF's World Economic Outlook, released during the meetings, projected global growth of 3.1 percent in 2026 and 3.4 percent in 2027, but the gains are unevenly spread. Economies tied into the AI supply chain are better placed to absorb external shocks, while energy-importing economies outside that chain face higher import bills, exchange rate pressure and tighter fiscal room, and many of them are low-income or vulnerable countries. At a fireside chat with IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva, Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh gave no clear signal on US interest rates and instead focused on AI, including its potential to fundamentally transform monetary policy and its still-uncertain effect on jobs. Krishna Srinivasan, director of the IMF's Asia and Pacific Department, noted that since ChatGPT's launch, job postings requiring emerging AI skills have grown, roughly twice as fast in occupations highly exposed to the technology.

The author, who said he has used AI to transcribe interviews, do research, process data and copy edit, argued that AI cannot conduct interviews, build relationships with contacts or produce truly in-depth stories. He acknowledged that AI-generated content is widespread online and that producing a news report with a language model is one thing, while whether that report is worth reading is another. He concluded that only human journalists can verify questionable data, supply the context that makes facts meaningful, demand accountability and build understanding with audiences. He wrote that journalists remain relevant and have become more important in the age of AI, though the article does not describe any formal policy or institutional change arising from these discussions.

Articles.Title: In age of AI, human touch still matters

stories.Headline: Celestica Stock: Is AI Growth Worth the Risk in a Retirement Portfolio?
stories.Summary:
Celestica (TSX: CLS), which designs and manufactures networking and computing equipment for data centres, is drawing attention from investors weighing its exposure to artificial intelligence. The Motley Fool Canada analysis, published November 10, 2026, asks whether the stock's growth is worth the risk in a retirement portfolio. The article reports that the stock closed at $330.24 on the day of publication after falling about 9.2% that day. It notes that Celestica's October results showed third-quarter revenue rising 83%. Celestica's 2026 free-cash-flow outlook was reduced from US$600 million to US$460 million, while management lifted its sales outlook.

The company attributes the reduction to working-capital investment for faster growth ahead, including more inventory and receivables. The article explains that free cash flow is money left after the company's defined adjustments and capital spending. It also notes that the company has raised its 2026 revenue outlook to US$20.5 billion, according to a related Motley Fool headline. The author, Amy Legate-Wolfe, writes as a Motley Fool Canada contributor and states she has no position in any of the stocks mentioned. Her view is that Celestica suits a patient, long-term growth role rather than income.

She suggests an initial allocation of 2% of an otherwise diversified retirement portfolio, not a centrepiece holding. She also advises keeping near-term withdrawals in cash or suitable guaranteed investments. The article presents its illustrations as arithmetic, not predictions. It shows that a 40% share-price decline would reduce a whole portfolio by 0.8% at a 2% weighting, 2.0% at 5%, and 4.0% at 10%. It adds that holding the stock inside a Tax-Free Savings Account can generally shelter Canadian tax on gains, provided there is contribution room.

The article also says that Motley Fool's Stock Advisor Canada list of top TSX stocks for 2026 does not include Celestica. The article does not describe any next event for Celestica or set out a timeline for future results. It offers no forecast for the share price. The author's stated conclusion is that customer orders turning into cash would earn her confidence more than another ambitious outlook.

Articles.Title: Celestica Stock: Is AI Growth Worth the Risk in a Retirement Portfolio?

stories.Headline: Apple has new Mac app coming to make running local AI models easy
stories.Summary:
Apple appears to be developing a new Mac app called Harbor, which is designed to make running local AI models simple. The app was discovered by the leaker Aaron Perris, who shared details in a post on X on November 10, 2026. According to the post, Harbor turns a Mac into a private AI inference server that runs open-weight models on Apple silicon, so data stays on the user's hardware and does not reach the cloud. The report says Harbor is currently in a private preview under Apple's Claris brand.

Harbor is described as offering several features aimed at ease of use and scale. It detects devices connected over Thunderbolt 5 and forms a cluster automatically, without manual configuration or command-line work. Users can browse, download, and load open-weight models from inside the app, which handles model management. Two or more Thunderbolt 5-capable Macs can also be connected so that their unified memory is pooled into a single inference resource, allowing larger models or more concurrent requests than one machine could handle alone.

The information comes from Perris's discovery and his public post, and the article does not report any statement from Apple about the app. The report places Harbor within a wider trend in which the Mac has become more popular as a tool for running AI models locally on machines such as the Mac Studio and Mac mini. The article notes that budget-friendly models like the MacBook Neo have also contributed to that growth. It suggests Apple may be leaning harder into this use case, and it expects a public launch in the weeks or months ahead, though no date has been confirmed.

Articles.Title: Apple has new Mac app coming to make running local AI models easy

stories.Headline: AI usage generates a fragile codebase
stories.Summary:
Evan X. Merz, a software developer, published an essay on his blog on November 7, 2026, arguing that heavy reliance on AI coding tools produces fragile codebases. He wrote that he was laid off from Meta in May, though he could only speculate that his resistance to adopting AI tools as quickly as some peers played a part. In his final months there he generated at least 90 percent of his code with AI, the minimum for a decent rating, but he said the tools did not multiply his output and that the code his AI-reliant colleagues pushed was brittle. He now works at another large tech company and generates all of his code with AI, which he describes as the current expectation.

Merz names four failure modes. He says AI writes shallow tests, mostly trivial get and set checks and end-to-end tests that cover only already-tested paths and a single type of user, which leaves gaps that line coverage metrics do not reveal. He says AI writes overly complex code, using several helper methods where one would do and applying rules like DRY to excess. He argues that a growing reliance on AI reduces how well human developers understand the codebase, leaving them unable to spot poor abstractions. Finally, he says AI produces pull requests faster than humans can review them, so reviewers skim and small quality problems accumulate into long-term technical debt.

As symptoms of such a codebase, Merz lists more incidents over time, longer recovery times because engineers are working in unfamiliar code, errors that surface only for real users rather than in tests, and a poorer user experience. He concludes that software serving human customers needs human judgment and that the most expensive, well-regarded products will continue to be developed mainly by people. The essay is his opinion and offers no measured data on incident rates or any company's practices. It does not describe any next steps beyond his prediction that many people will come to see AI-heavy development as unsustainable.

Articles.Title: AI usage generates a fragile codebase

stories.Headline: IBM Lines Up Yen Bond Sale as Quantum and AI Tools Advance on Multiple Fronts - ad-hoc-news.de
stories.Summary:
IBM filed a preliminary prospectus supplement with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission on Monday for three series of yen-denominated notes. The filing was still subject to completion and left the principal amounts and coupon terms blank, so neither the final issue size nor the pricing had been set. Disclosures on denominations and maturities were also missing from the document. Investors therefore cannot yet see how large the sale will be or what it will cost the company. On November 5, IBM launched a joint development platform for quantum error correction with Oak Ridge National Laboratory and AMD.

According to the company, the platform connects IBM quantum computers with the laboratory's high-performance computing, which runs on AMD hardware. The effort is aligned with the U.S. Department of Energy's Quantum Genesis Mission. Four days later, on Friday, IBM joined the University of Chicago, the State of Illinois and the Illinois Quantum and Microelectronics Park to unveil an IBM Quantum System Two in Chicago. The system is initially housed in the Hyde Park Labs, runs on IBM's Nighthawk quantum processor, and the company said it is ready for operation. On the software side, IBM subsidiary Apptio announced new connectors on Monday that let enterprises track the cost and usage of their AI systems.

The offering also adds features for planning AI spending and measuring its business value, along with AI-powered analytics. The company describes these enhancements as a way to give businesses tighter control over the expense side of their artificial intelligence deployments. Separately, IBM selected four organizations for the education and workforce development track of its IBM Impact Accelerator. The chosen groups receive IBM technology and expertise as a no-charge grant, and the funding extends to quantum technology as well as artificial intelligence. The articles do not say when the bond sale will be priced or how the proceeds will be used.

Articles.Title: IBM Lines Up Yen Bond Sale as Quantum and AI Tools Advance on Multiple Fronts - ad-hoc-news.de

stories.Headline: Google-backed Tapestry completes deployment of HyperQ AI platform for PJM's Cycle 1 interconnection review
stories.Summary:
Tapestry, an energy software company backed by Google, has completed the first deployment of its HyperQ AI platform for PJM Interconnection's Cycle 1 window, the grid operator's reformed interconnection queue cycle. According to the company, the platform reviewed site control documentation for 220GW of proposed generation in less than a day. Tapestry said the same work would usually take two months to finish manually, making HyperQ about 60 times faster. The announcement was reported by DCD on November 11, 2026.

The platform produced readiness reports for 811 applications, with a median runtime of six minutes and 15 seconds per application, according to Tapestry. The company said 202GW of the screened capacity advanced into Phase 1 of the study process. Cycle 1 is the first application window under PJM's reformed process, which handles new generation requests in large, concurrent batches. Site control is the legal proof that a developer has the right to build on a specific piece of land. Tapestry said every assessment links back to the page, clause, or coordinate in the source document, giving reviewers an audit trail.

PJM said the preliminary results show a repeatable way for AI to operate under strict human governance. The grid operator said HyperQ automates intake while its own subject matter experts keep full control, and that this offers a promising basis for reaching PJM's target 12-month interconnection timeline. Tapestry said the figures cover only initial site control evaluations, not later technical or engineering studies. The HyperQ platform uses multimodal AI to analyze PDFs, maps, and legal documents, and PJM engineers make the final compliance decisions.

Tapestry said it plans to extend HyperQ into three areas once the studies are complete. The first is technical data validation, which would use AI to check engineering files such as single-line diagrams, interconnection model files, and power-flow models for errors before cluster studies begin. The second is a pre-submission interface to help developers find and fix compliance gaps before entering the queue. The third is unified model management, which would replace static grid planning files with a synchronized, interactive network model shared by stakeholders. The article notes that PJM signed a partnership agreement to deploy Tapestry's agentic AI system last April, and that Tapestry is a Google X "moonshot project" building what it calls the first unified model of the grid.

Articles.Title: Google-backed Tapestry completes deployment of HyperQ AI platform for PJM's Cycle 1 interconnection review

stories.Headline: Anthropic signs another $4.3bn in compute agreements with Microsoft
stories.Summary:
Anthropic has added up to $4.3bn in compute agreements with Microsoft, according to a new filing the AI lab made ahead of its planned initial public offering. The filing, first reported by The Information and published on November 11, 2026, shows the change to the company's cloud contracts. Anthropic disclosed the update in its prospectus as part of its preparations to go public. At the start of November, the company had reported an aggregate committed spend of about $895.4 billion, nearly all of it for compute and infrastructure.

Of that total, Google accounted for $121.3bn, SpaceX $120.5bn, Amazon $110bn, and Microsoft $44.9bn before the new agreement. The Microsoft commitment now stands at between $47.2 billion and $49.2 billion. The filing also says that the $34.9bn August 2026 agreement with Lambda, part of a larger $41.3bn commitment, can now be terminated by either party because Lambda did not secure a facility lease by a specified date. Neither side had delivered a termination notice, and Anthropic said it does not currently intend to end the deal.

Anthropic also reported a $567 million operating loss in the third quarter, compared with a $974 million operating profit in the prior quarter, which it attributed mainly to short-term compute arrangements. The company has further contracts with Nscale, Akamai, and CoreWeave. The filing sets out a planned offering of Class A common stock priced between $70 and $78 per share, targeting a valuation of $1.4 trillion. The articles do not say when the offering will take place or whether the Lambda agreement will be terminated.

Articles.Title: Anthropic signs another $4.3bn in compute agreements with Microsoft

stories.Headline: Meta wins CNCF case study contest for GitOps platform that cuts AI deployment times to minutes
stories.Summary:
Meta has won the Cloud Native Computing Foundation's End User Case Study Contest for a GitOps platform that cuts routine Kubernetes application deployments from more than four hours to minutes. The announcement was made on November 11, 2026, at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026 in Salt Lake City, where the foundation named Meta's Cloud Foundation team as the winner. The platform is built with Argo CD and Kargo and covers approximately 100 Kubernetes clusters that support AI research and inference. The team had previously used Terraform for both infrastructure and application deployment, which meant routine application updates waited on a lengthy infrastructure release process.

The new design separates application delivery from infrastructure provisioning, so Terraform continues to manage infrastructure while Argo CD reconciles application deployments against configurations stored in Git. Kargo handles release promotion across environments, allowing independent rollouts, automated health checks and versioned release records that improve traceability and recovery. Developers now describe deployment requirements in a short application definition, and the platform generates the Argo CD and Kargo configurations automatically. Application teams therefore do not have to manage complex configurations themselves. The Cloud Foundation team has more than 15 engineers and supports clusters across multiple cloud providers and accelerator families.

The Cloud Foundation team at Meta is responsible for the platform, and Phong Nguyen, a Production Engineer at Meta, said that GitOps and Argo CD give the small team a strong foundation shaped by years of community experience in Kubernetes delivery. Nguyen said the team's focus is on connecting that foundation to Meta's systems and that it hopes to share its lessons. Chris Aniszczyk, CTO of the CNCF, said Meta's approach shows how open source tools like Argo can automate application delivery, reduce operational complexity and scale infrastructure without unnecessary overhead. He described the work as an example of how cloud native technologies support the operational demands of AI at scale.

Meta plans to expand adoption of the GitOps platform and move to a centrally managed Argo CD service to reduce maintenance overhead across its Kubernetes fleet. The team is also exploring upstream contributions to improve container registry authentication and Argo CD performance in large clusters. The CNCF, which hosts Kubernetes, Prometheus and Envoy, is part of the nonprofit Linux Foundation and is supported by nearly 800 members. The full case study, titled GitOps at Meta: How We Went From Terraform on Cron to GitOps for AI Infra, is available for readers who want the details of Meta's implementation and results.

Articles.Title: Meta Wins CNCF End User Case Study Contest for Accelerating AI Infrastructure Deployments From Hours to Minutes

stories.Headline: S-1: Nvidia plans to invest ~$10B in Anthropic after its IPO, or ~10% of the total new cash Anthropic is expected to raise in November, including in its IPO (Cory Weinberg/New York Times)
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, the maker of AI software tools, began courting investors on Tuesday for an initial public offering that could value the company at up to $1.4 trillion. The filing shows that Nvidia, the chipmaker that has become the financial engine of the AI boom, plans to invest about $10 billion in Anthropic immediately after the IPO. That sum would amount to roughly 10 percent of the total new cash Anthropic is expected to raise in November, including through the offering. The deal was reported by Cory Weinberg of The New York Times, based on the investor prospectus. Anthropic said Nvidia would be among a group of AI companies investing alongside the offering.

The arrangement ties together two companies that had long kept their distance from each other despite operating in closely connected parts of the industry. For years they grew into some of the most valuable firms in the world without doing much business together. Their chief executives also publicly sparred over how the U.S. government should regulate AI technology. The new investment changes that picture, since Nvidia is now set to hold a direct financial stake in Anthropic.

Kevin S. Xu, chief investment officer of Interconnected Capital, which invests in publicly traded AI companies, said the two companies' futures are now more intertwined than ever. The article describes the timing as notable, with one company preparing for its public debut while the other faces what it calls a prolonged corporate drama that has shaken the AI industry and left investors on edge. The article does not detail the nature of that drama. It also does not say what conditions, if any, attach to Nvidia's planned investment, or how the stake would be structured beyond the roughly $10 billion figure.

Articles.Title: S-1: Nvidia plans to invest ~$10B in Anthropic after its IPO, or ~10% of the total new cash Anthropic is expected to raise in November, including in its IPO (Cory Weinberg/New York Times)

stories.Headline: Amdocs Named a Leader in the 2026 Gartner(R) Magic Quadrant(TM) for CSP AI-Enabled Marketing and Sales Solutions
stories.Summary:
Amdocs, the NASDAQ-listed software company, announced on November 9, 2026 that Gartner had named it a Leader in the inaugural Magic Quadrant for CSP AI-Enabled Marketing and Sales Solutions. The recognition was based on Amdocs' Completeness of Vision and its Ability to Execute. The company said the honor reflects its push to combine predictive intelligence with the commercial tools telecom providers need to configure, price, sell and fulfil services. Gartner's report, authored by Pulkit Pandey and Khurram Shahzad, is dated September 15, 2026.

At the center of the offering is aOS, Amdocs' agentic operating system for telecommunications, which lets predictive intelligence, agentic AI and specialized agents share customer, product and commercial context. According to the release, the platform is designed to work with any BSS environment and includes governance, traceability and human oversight. Its composable, cloud-native and API-first architecture allows providers to adopt it incrementally or as a full end-to-end platform while keeping existing investments. Amdocs says the solutions are already deployed commercially across several countries. The company also pairs the software with telecom expertise, consulting, implementation services and flexible commercial models.

Anthony Goonetilleke, Group President of Growth Horizons at Amdocs, said the company was proud of the recognition and believes it reflects both its vision for agentic marketing and sales and its ability to put that vision into practice. He stated that aOS was built to help service providers create more seamless customer experiences, govern execution, strengthen relationships and turn AI into measurable business outcomes. Gartner, for its part, said in its standard disclaimer that it does not endorse any vendor named in its research and that its publications reflect opinion rather than statements of fact. The release itself is the company's own account of the award and its product claims.

The announcement comes amid a series of recent Amdocs customer deals that the company highlighted in its newsroom. AT&T and Amdocs expanded their collaboration under an eight-year agreement to modernize operations with AI, Globe reported progress on a data modernization program on Google Cloud, and Magyar Telekom selected Amdocs for billing transformation and catalog modernization under a multi-year contract. The release also notes that the company's forward-looking statements carry risks, including macroeconomic uncertainty, competition, rapid technological change and the effective implementation of artificial intelligence. Amdocs reported revenue of $4.7 billion in fiscal 2026.

stories.Headline: The GIGABYTE AI TOP ATOM 64 GB is now available and expands the possibilities of AI development on desktop PCs
stories.Summary:
GIGABYTE has made a 64 GB version of its AI TOP ATOM desktop AI system available as of November 11, 2026, alongside the existing 128 GB model. The announcement was distributed through PR Newswire from Taipei. Both memory versions are built on the NVIDIA DGX Spark platform and share the same compact chassis design. The 64 GB version is offered with either a 1 TB or a 2 TB NVMe M.2 SSD using PCIe 4.0 connectivity, so buyers can match storage to their needs. The system is intended for local AI development, giving developers dedicated AI compute in a desktop form factor.

It supports local model inference, prototyping, data analysis, and application validation in offices, labs, and educational settings. Users can run models and process project data within their own IT environment. For supported distributed AI workloads, up to four AI TOP ATOM systems can be linked into a cluster using the built-in NVIDIA ConnectX-7 networking and NVIDIA Sync's Cluster Assistant. The announcement says this can add storage and compute resources, depending on the application and software setup.

GIGABYTE also bundles its AI TOP Utility software, which supports downloading supported models, running inference, and retrieval-augmented generation for building question-answering tools on a user's own documents. GIGABYTE's announcement says availability, sales channels, pricing, and memory configurations may vary by region. More information is available on the company's AI TOP ATOM product page. The release also notes that GIGABYTE has recently expanded its local AI lineup with the AI TOP AERO, a separate desktop built on NVIDIA's RTX Spark platform.

Articles.Title: The GIGABYTE AI TOP ATOM 64 GB is now available and expands the possibilities of AI development on desktop PCs

stories.Headline: Cisco Live Melbourne: AI agents will break today’s enterprise network, and Cisco wants to rebuild it
stories.Summary:
At Cisco Live APJC in Melbourne, Cisco Asia Pacific, Japan and Greater China president Ben Dawson said agent token consumption passed human consumption for the first time in February, and agents now consume tokens at roughly seven times the human rate. He said each agent generates far more traffic and data than a human doing the same task. Cisco's focus at the event shifted from GPUs, AI factories and data centers to the campus, the branch and the network that connects everything. Speakers argued that networks built for people will not hold up when thousands of agents work around the clock. The keynote framed the problem as a need to rebuild enterprise networking for agent behavior.

Jeff Schultz, Cisco's SVP of portfolio strategy and marketing, explained that agents still send heavy north-south traffic to reach models and context. They also generate large volumes of east-west traffic as agents talk to other agents across desktops, campuses, branches and data centers. Schultz said the architecture for campus and branch networking needs to be fundamentally reimagined. Dawson said AI will place new demands on wired infrastructure, making it more critical. Cisco's chief sales officer, Oliver Tuszik, cited IDC data showing only 9% of organizations in the region believe their networks are fully ready for new AI and digital initiatives.

He also cited research indicating 85% of organizations globally are experimenting with agents, but only 5% have deployed them to production. Cisco's product announcements covered the data center, campus and operations. Schultz highlighted 102.4 Tbps systems based on the Silicon One G300 for scale-out, and the deep-buffered Silicon One P200 for connecting data centers across metro, long-haul and transcontinental distances. Cisco is integrating ThousandEyes into its Wi-Fi 6E and Wi-Fi 7 access points at no extra cost for customers with eligible Networking Essentials and Advantage licenses. Schultz admitted ThousandEyes has been difficult to license and deploy.

Cisco Cloud Control, the company's unified operations layer, combines cross-domain telemetry, purpose-built models and both Cisco and third-party agents. Schultz said no new Cisco product will ship unless it is integrated with Cloud Control. Cloud Control is currently available only for US-based infrastructure. Cisco scheduled Australia, the EU and the UK for February 2027, followed by Japan, India and Canada in May. Schultz said the line between observing an agent and securing an agent is beginning to blur, citing an agent that suddenly deleted 10,000 files.

Cisco AI Defense is adding Anthropic's Claude Mythos to its adaptive red-teaming engine, limited to targets customers own and have registered. The model will be available to select enterprises soon, with broader availability for qualified customers later. Splunk's Tokenomics feature enters private preview in December, with general availability on AWS Marketplace in early 2027. Customers described their own deployments at the event. John Kelvie, chief digital and information officer at Asahi Beverages, described a Melbourne head office for about 1,000 employees built on Cisco's SD-Access architecture.

Asahi has since brought operational technology on its production floor onto a single IP network. Kelvie said his biggest obstacle is data, not people or technology. Yessie Yosetya, CIO of Indonesian operator XLSmart, inherited two networks after a merger, with security maturity scores of 3.2 and 1.6 on a NIST-based scale. She redesigned around five areas and reduced the company's security tools from 54 to 14. XLSmart put eight agents into production for red, blue and purple teaming, then found it could not scale them without standardization.

Articles.Title: Cisco Live Melbourne: AI agents will break today’s enterprise network, and Cisco wants to rebuild it

stories.Headline: AMD Launches Epyc SP7, Helion as AI Rack Demand Rises
stories.Summary:
AMD said on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, that its sixth-generation Epyc SP7 server processor is now generally available and that hardware makers have begun shipping servers powered by the chip. The company also said the first Helion racks for agentic AI, which hardware vendors build from an AMD blueprint, will become available throughout this month. The SP7 supports up to 256 cores and is the first of four sixth-generation Epyc CPUs to become available. AMD said the other three are expected in 2027. The broader family, much of which is code-named "Venice," is designed for enterprise, cloud, high-performance computing, and AI workloads.

AMD said it is seeing strong demand for the new chip. During the company's third-quarter earnings call last week, AMD Chair and CEO Lisa Su said early demand for Venice is the strongest AMD has seen for any new generation of Epyc processors. Su said AMD began revenue shipments of Venice during the third quarter and that hardware makers have committed to more than 240 Venice platforms, 20% more than the number committed for Turin, AMD's fifth-generation Epyc chip. Su also said Venice delivers significantly better performance per watt, per core, and per dollar than any other x86 or Arm server CPU. AMD said systems based on the SP7 deliver up to 3.7 times the performance of an Nvidia Vera CPU-based system and up to 2.2 times the performance of an Intel Xeon 6980P system.

AMD is working to capture more market share in CPUs, GPUs, and overall AI infrastructure as it competes with rivals amid surging AI demand. It is directly challenging market leader Nvidia in GPUs and rack-scale systems, while Nvidia is taking on AMD with its own CPU. Arm has also introduced an Arm-based CPU to compete with Intel and AMD's x86 processors. Cloud providers AWS, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure have built their own custom AI accelerators and Arm-based CPUs. AMD introduced Helion in October as an open rack-scale design for agentic AI, with partners that include Dell Technologies, Hewlett Packard Enterprise, Lenovo, Supermicro, and Cisco.

AMD said Helion will come in three versions. Helion Liquid is a CPU-only, liquid-cooled rack designed to operate side by side with a Helios rack for large-scale agentic AI deployments. Helion Air is a CPU-only rack designed to expand agent capacity within existing air-cooled data centers. AMD Helion Air Inference is an air-cooled rack that combines CPUs and GPUs for inference. The article notes that Helion racks are built for agentic AI and differ from AMD's Helios racks, which are designed for large-scale inference, frontier model training, and fine-tuning.

Matt Kimball, vice president and principal analyst at Moor Insights & Strategy, said Venice is an important launch for AMD and for enterprises. Kimball said enterprise CIOs have fixed power budgets and need infrastructure that supports traditional workloads today and agentic AI in the years ahead. With up to 256 cores, Venice lets companies run traditional workloads on fewer servers, freeing up space for AI infrastructure. Kimball also said that servers running sixth-generation Epyc processors are well suited to future agentic workloads because of the CPU's high core count and large cache and memory. AMD also said Meta is preparing to deploy sixth-generation Epyc platforms at scale and that Microsoft Azure's HDv2 service for AI data processing is in preview.

Articles.Title: AMD Launches Epyc SP7, Helion as AI Rack Demand Rises

stories.Headline: CrowdStrike Brings Falcon Guardian to Anthropic's Claude Cowork
stories.Summary:
CrowdStrike announced on November 3, 2026, that it is bringing its Falcon Guardian AI Detection and Response product natively into Anthropic's Claude Cowork. The announcement was made in Austin, Texas and Barcelona, where CrowdStrike was holding its Fal.Con Europe 2026 event. The integration was delivered in partnership with Anthropic in response to enterprise customer demand. The company described the move as extending Falcon protection to AI agents throughout their lifecycle. The integration places Falcon Guardian protection directly inside Claude Cowork.

The article says the protection secures agents from creation onward. It also places those agents under the Falcon platform's enterprise security control plane. The announcement describes this as an added layer for organizations that already use Claude Cowork to deploy AI agents. CrowdStrike, which trades on the Nasdaq under the ticker CRWD, is the company behind the announcement. Anthropic is the company that makes Claude Cowork and worked with CrowdStrike on the integration.

The article does not give further statements from either company beyond the announcement itself. The article does not provide further background on the history of the partnership or on prior Falcon Guardian releases. It also does not give pricing, availability dates, or the number of customers affected. The articles provide no information on next steps. The available text ends before the full announcement body, so details of the rollout are not given.

Articles.Title: CrowdStrike Brings Falcon Guardian to Anthropic's Claude Cowork

stories.Headline: CrowdStrike Extends the Agentic SOC to Detect and Stop Agent Insider Threats
stories.Summary:
CrowdStrike announced on November 4, 2026 new agentic SOC capabilities aimed at detecting and stopping what it calls agent insider threats, meaning trusted AI agents that operate under a real employee's identity and approved tools. The company says such an agent can drift without tripping an alarm when something upstream changes, such as a tampered tool or an instruction that should not be there. CrowdStrike states that AI agents touch the SOC in two ways, as the new operating unit of the SOC and as a new identity to secure. The article says current tools fall short in different ways. Most agentic SOC tools run a single LLM serially through detections without memory of prior investigations or identity, endpoint, or ownership context.

Standalone AI security tools can inventory agents and flag unusual activity but stop at detection. The article describes Agent Insider Threat Detection, slated for Q4, which is built on CrowdStrike Falcon Next-Gen SIEM. It learns the normal behavior pattern for every AI agent and the person who runs it, including the files it touches, the tools it calls, and where it sends data. It flags deviations even when no policy is violated, which the company says catches an agent that stays within its granted permissions yet is compromised. Dynamic Risk Scoring, also slated for Q4, feeds agent risk into the same 0 to 100 risk score Falcon Next-Gen SIEM builds for the agent's owner and host.

AI Ecosystem Detections, also for Q4, add detection logic for attacks on AI services, including LLM API abuse, stolen API keys, and compromise of coding assistants, MCP servers, and agent frameworks. Federated Search Expansion lets teams search related data in place without re-ingestion, with GovCloud, Dynatrace, Databricks, and Snowflake connectors generally available and Splunk, Elastic, and Cribl Lake connectors following in Q4. CrowdStrike says Multi-Agent Triage and Investigation, generally available and announced at Fal.Con US 2026, has SOC agents investigate detections end to end, with specialist agents working on shared context across endpoint, identity, and the agent's activity. In Q4, triage coverage extends to Falcon Guardian, Falcon Cloud Security, Falcon Shield, Falcon Data Security, and custom detections, including abnormal agent behavior flagged by Falcon Next-Gen SIEM. The company says investigating agents can trace a session back to what the person asked for and separate that from what the agent did on its own.

The Unified Agentic SOAR Experience, generally available and also announced at Fal.Con US 2026, handles response by coordinating stopping the agent, cutting off its access, keeping it from coming back, and documenting what happened. CrowdStrike says it is open by design and connects to any agent, model, or tool through API or MCP. The article's background is that security teams face hundreds of thousands of alerts a month, and agents add more telemetry, while an agent insider threat rarely sounds a loud alarm. CrowdStrike frames the problem as a new insider threat: not an employee, but a trusted agent acting on their behalf. The articles do not say what happens beyond the features described for Q4 and general availability dates.

Articles.Title: CrowdStrike Extends the Agentic SOC to Detect and Stop Agent Insider Threats

stories.Headline: Wesleyan Media Project: political campaigns spent ~$187M on ~300 AI-generated or AI-enhanced ads in the midterms; 90% of tracked AI ads were for GOP candidates (Loreben Tuquero/Poynter)
stories.Summary:
Campaigns in the 2026 midterm elections ran about 300 political ads that were generated or enhanced by artificial intelligence, according to the Wesleyan Media Project, which tracks political advertising. The people and groups behind those ads spent roughly $187 million promoting them online and on TV. That figure is more than 3,000 times the roughly $50,000 spent on such ads in the 2024 cycle, though it remains a small share of total political ad spending. The project also found that about 90 percent of the ads it tracked came from Republican candidates or groups backing them.

The ads ranged from deepfakes, which are fabricated videos showing people saying or doing things they never did, to subtler edits that added people to real crowd footage. Thirty-one states regulate deepfakes in political messaging, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures, and those rules are now being tested. Texas voters saw many AI-generated visuals, including ads against state Rep. James Talarico, who won the Democratic nomination for the state's U.S. Senate race. Campaigns also shaped their talking points so AI chatbots would be more likely to repeat them when voters asked about candidates and issues.

Travis Ridout, co-director of the Wesleyan Media Project, said campaigns have been cautious because of the learning curve and the risk of voter backlash. A 2025 Pew Research Center study cited in the article found that 71 percent of Americans said they would like a candidate less if they learned the candidate used AI to help write a speech they had otherwise enjoyed. Christina Walker, an assistant professor at the University of Georgia who studies AI and political information, said what voters accept about AI use is still being worked out. Cayce Myers, a Virginia Tech public relations professor, said AI content mostly confirmed opinions voters already held rather than persuading them.

Experts said it is hard to measure how much influence the ads had, since voters received many other messages across platforms. The article notes that AI may have shaped voter views more through worries about local data centers, including depleted resources, higher energy bills and effects on quality of life. Tim Harper of the Center for Democracy & Technology described many of the ads as a new medium for political cartoons. The article does not say what further rules or changes will follow.

Articles.Title: Wesleyan Media Project: political campaigns spent ~$187M on ~300 AI-generated or AI-enhanced ads in the midterms; 90% of tracked AI ads were for GOP candidates (Loreben Tuquero/Poynter)

stories.Headline: Google DeepMind launches AlphaGenome 2, trained on 100M+ cell profiles across 68 tissues to predict genetic mutation effects, for non-commercial research (Robert Hart/The Verge)
stories.Summary:
Google DeepMind has unveiled AlphaGenome 2, an AI model designed to show how changes in DNA affect different types of cells. The article was published on November 11, 2026, and reports the launch by DeepMind researchers. The model is the successor to AlphaGenome, which was released last year. It is trained on more than 100 million individual cell profiles across 68 tissues. The company says the model identifies nearly twice as many variants that can change gene expression in cells as its previous state-of-the-art model.

The model is built to predict the effects of genetic variants on individual cell types and states. Google said in a blog post on Wednesday that it offers a much finer-grained view than broader models like AlphaGenome. DeepMind says it turns static cell atlases into a predictive engine for human genetics. AlphaGenome 2 can make predictions about new cell types and biological states without being retrained. It can also identify gaps in experimental data, which may help scientists decide what to investigate next in the lab.

Google is making AlphaGenome 2 available for non-commercial research through the AlphaGenome API from the day of the announcement. Commercial research access is limited to a private preview. Adam Gayoso, a research scientist at Google DeepMind involved in the project, said the key advance is tying human genetics to cell biology. He told The Verge that the model lets researchers examine genetic variants found in large populations and connect their cellular effects to disease. Žiga Avsec, DeepMind's genomics lead, said that such specificity matters when developing drugs that target particular proteins and cell types.

Building a model like this has only recently become possible, according to Avsec, because of new technologies that capture individual cells and their states at high resolution. DeepMind is working to improve its genetics models by generating more data, including for cell states that are poorly represented today. Avsec said future versions could be trained on data across multiple species. He also said that over the longer term, such models could feed into efforts to create virtual cells, which are digital simulations of biological systems. He described AlphaGenome 2 as a successor to AlphaGenome that will not replace it soon, because its more detailed predictions are more expensive to compute.

The model sits within a wider push by Google and rival AI labs to apply the technology to science and medicine. Pushmeet Kohli, who heads DeepMind's AI for science research, has hinted that more impressive scientific results are coming. The organization is expected to open an automated materials science lab in the UK soon. The article notes that Anthropic has been experimenting with drug design and has given Claude a wet lab. It also notes that OpenAI has been solving a number of longstanding problems in mathematics and related fields.

Articles.Title: Google DeepMind launches AlphaGenome 2, trained on 100M+ cell profiles across 68 tissues to predict genetic mutation effects, for non-commercial research (Robert Hart/The Verge)

stories.Headline: Microsoft buyouts: ‘Concerned workers’ write open letter to management, urge rethink of ‘speed-at-all-costs’ AI push
stories.Summary:
A group of current and former Microsoft employees, calling themselves "Concerned Microsoft Workers," has written an open letter to company management. The letter comes as Microsoft rolls out a buyout offer to around 66,000 of its staff amid an aggressive push into artificial intelligence. According to The New York Times, which first reported it, the letter began circulating before the October 26 buyout announcement. The workers say the timing reflects growing unease inside the company about where its AI effort is heading.

The letter criticizes what the employees describe as a "speed-at-all-costs" approach to developing and deploying AI. It asks Microsoft to involve employees in decisions about how AI is built and used, and to stop tying AI use to rewards or reprimands. The writers also raise concerns about workplace conditions, job security, customer safety and the environment. They point to heavier workloads, frequent restructuring and uncertainty about the future of jobs as the company accelerates its AI investments. The letter also asks for employees to have a greater say in how the technology is developed and deployed.

The buyout itself was announced on October 26 as a Voluntary Exit Offer for eligible employees in Canada, India, the United Kingdom and the United States at level 70 and below, in participating teams. Microsoft says the offer gives eligible workers who may be considering a future outside the company a chance to make that move now, with support. Employees have until December 9 to decide, and those who accept will leave on December 31 with a minimum of eight weeks of base pay, with the amount varying by job level and tenure. The company has also cut jobs repeatedly, laying off 10,000 workers in 2023 and more than 15,000 in 2025, and in the spring offered a retirement-age buyout to about 8,600 US employees, roughly 30 percent of whom accepted.
