Microsoft's headcount peaked at 228,000 full-time employees across fiscal years 2024 and 2025 and stood at 223,000 at the end of June, as the company continues a series of workforce reductions and restructuring tied to its shift toward AI. The articles do not report a response from Microsoft management to the open letter. They also do not say whether the group plans further action or whether the company will change its AI policies. The buyout deadline of December 9 is the next date the articles identify.

Articles.Title: Microsoft buyouts: ‘Concerned workers’ write open letter to management, urge rethink of ‘speed-at-all-costs’ AI push

stories.Headline: AI pushes mid-sized IT firms to rethink sales playbook
stories.Summary:
Hexaware Technologies has replaced target-based sales incentives with commissions tied directly to the revenue its employees bring in, according to a Mint report published on 10 November 2026. The company is one of several mid-sized IT services firms changing how they motivate sales teams and reach customers as artificial intelligence reshapes client demand. Hexaware's president, Shantanu Baruah, outlined the change at the company's AI Day on 21 August. Its commission-based plan removes several performance thresholds that previously determined payouts, and the commissions are separate from employees' variable pay.

LTM Ltd is offering separate incentives for AI-native deals, while Coforge Ltd is turning to external deal advisors to access new opportunities. The article says firms with $1-5 billion in annual revenue face the challenge of finding new sources of growth as AI changes technology spending, while competing against larger rivals. Hexaware ended the July-September quarter with $412 million in revenue, up 2% sequentially, and does not disclose its order intake. LTM ended the September quarter with revenue of $4.76 billion, up 1% quarter-on-quarter, and order intake of $1.26 billion, down 25%. Coforge ended its last quarter with $652 million in revenue, up 10%, and order intake that rose 51% to $1.04 billion.

Vikash Kumar Jain, chief financial officer of Hexaware, described the commission shift on a post-earnings analyst call on 29 October and said the company expects it to work out well. Venu Lambu, chief executive of LTM, said on a post-earnings call on 16 October that the company uses different sales commission structures to encourage salespeople to sell AI-native deals, describing it as a change management exercise. John Speight, president and executive director of Coforge, said on a call on 23 October that the company has started using advisory channels that have brought in deals it had never had before. Saurabh Goel, Coforge's chief financial officer, said advisory costs sit under sales or other sales and marketing expenses. An email sent to LTM seeking more detail on its commission structure went unanswered.

Traditionally, Coforge relied on sole-sourced deals rather than competitive bids. The article also notes that larger peers, including Tata Consultancy Services Ltd and Infosys Ltd, said they were investing in their sales processes but did not elaborate. Peter Bendor-Samuel, founder of Everest Group, said a more attractive commission structure helps firms attract better sales teams in what he called a moribund market. Namratha Dharshan, chief business leader for India Research at ISG, said the new incentive systems could also help firms retain key account personnel whose client relationships matter in winning business.

Articles.Title: AI pushes mid-sized IT firms to rethink sales playbook

stories.Headline: AI was supposed to kill this industry. So why is it still growing?
stories.Summary:
The Philippines' outsourcing industry, long expected to be among the first casualties of artificial intelligence, is still growing. According to the IT and Business Process Association of the Philippines, the information technology and business process management sector employed about 1.9 million people and generated US$40 billion in revenues in 2025. Its contact centre and business process management segment added roughly 60,000 workers, bringing that segment's employment to 1.68 million. The figures were reported in June, and the article's author, J.C. Punongbayan, a visiting fellow at ISEAS and an assistant professor at the University of the Philippines School of Economics, argues they do not suggest the industry is being wiped out.

The article notes that growth in headcount does not rule out displacement, since firms can cut some roles while adding others, and totals alone cannot isolate AI's effect. It cites a 2025 study finding that AI assistance raised customer support productivity by 15 per cent, measured by issues resolved per hour, with less experienced workers benefiting most. The author says the Philippines' opportunity lies in more specialised services such as complex customer support, financial analysis, healthcare administration and supervising automated processes. A revised best-case target of 2.14 million workers by 2028 implies annual growth of roughly 4 per cent, close to the 3.7 per cent growth reported for 2025, against the original 2.5 million target that would have required about 9.6 per cent a year.

Punongbayan writes that AI is not the only pressure on future hiring. He points to US initiatives to discourage offshoring, including the bipartisan Keep Call Centers in America Bill and proposals from the US Federal Communications Commission, which he says could lead clients to delay Philippine expansion even before any rules take effect. He also cites an August Stanford study finding that employment among US workers aged 22 to 25 in AI-exposed occupations lagged behind peers in less-exposed jobs, largely because of weaker hiring, which the authors present as early, descriptive indicators rather than causal estimates. The author calls for policymakers, government agencies and the IBPAP to identify the tasks employers need and tie publicly supported training to demonstrated demand, measuring success through placement, retention and earnings. He also urges employers to keep paid apprenticeships and supervised routes into skilled work, warning that automating simpler entry-level tasks could weaken how the industry trains its future workers.

Articles.Title: AI was supposed to kill this industry. So why is it still growing?

stories.Headline: Google SWE points 48 AI agents at NASA Lidar, finds unmapped Maya pyramid in 72h
stories.Summary:
An independent researcher says he used 48 AI agents to scan public NASA lidar data of Mexico's Maya lowlands and flagged a previously unrecorded archaeological site in about 72 hours. The lidar strips cover roughly 1,200 square kilometres of jungle, and the agents examined them image by image, looking for pyramids, platforms and plazas while filtering out natural hills, sinkholes and roads. The researcher then wrote a report with the site's details and sent it to Mexico's National Institute of Anthropology and History, known as INAH. In a written reply, INAH said its records showed no registered archaeological site at the location he gave.

The site, as the author describes it, includes a levelled plaza, an oval pyramid at least 8 to 12 metres tall, a raised courtyard attached to it and a flat-bottomed hollow that may have been a water reservoir. The researcher checked the raw point cloud to confirm the shapes sat on the ground rather than in the tree canopy. He also reports that a later update, dated 11 November, says the same site had already been mapped in a 2025 study by Estrada-Belli and colleagues, which the agents missed while searching the literature. In that case the find is a rediscovery rather than a new one, though the site was not yet in INAH's register. The author notes that none of this is official yet.

The researcher, who says he is not an archaeologist, presents the work as evidence that agentic AI can contribute to scientific fields beyond coding, mathematics and physics. He describes the origin of the project as an idea he had while travelling in Peru, prompted by the story of Hiram Bingham and Machu Picchu. He also reports that he consulted several AI tools during planning and that he translated his report into Spanish with their help. He says he offered INAH help with a field check, and notes that under Mexican federal law any fieldwork at an archaeological site requires INAH's authorisation. The decision on whether to send a team rests with the local INAH centre, and the author says he will post an update if one goes.

The author's own interpretation is speculative: he suggests the site may be a small Classic-period Maya civic centre dating roughly from AD 250 to 900, with the pyramid as a temple and the courtyard as a possible residence for a local ruler. He acknowledges this is conjecture drawn from a long conversation with the agents. For further context, the author points to earlier lidar work in the region, including a 2024 discovery of a Maya city in Mexico by Auld-Thomas and colleagues and a 2025 study by Estrada-Belli and colleagues estimating population in the Maya lowlands. Whether the site is confirmed, and whether INAH sends a team to verify it, are still open questions the articles do not answer.

Articles.Title: Google SWE points 48 AI agents at NASA Lidar, finds unmapped Maya pyramid in 72h

stories.Headline: Applied Digital And Harwood: A Teaching Moment For AI Data Centers?
stories.Summary:
Tech giants are reportedly set to spend about $9 trillion on the U.S. artificial intelligence buildout over the next six years, and that spending is now running into resistance at the local level. On Nov. 3, more than 250,000 voters across 10 states cast ballots on local measures that would restrict or allow data centers. The article reports that a strong 73% of the voters weighing in took part in these decisions. The piece frames these votes as a possible teaching moment for the companies building AI data centers.

The article's central point is that data center developers can no longer treat local opposition as a minor hurdle to clear. Governors facing reelection have been putting obstacles in the way, and voters have now weighed in directly on whether these facilities should be restricted or permitted. The measures on the ballot covered a wide range of communities, showing that the question of where data centers go is becoming a matter of public decision. The source text is cut off before it lays out the specific rules or limits each measure would impose.

The article does not name a single party responsible for the ballot measures, and it does not attribute specific statements to the companies or officials involved. Its framing points to the large technology firms driving the buildout as the parties that now face the pressure. Beyond the overall trend, the piece describes voters and governors as the forces pushing back. The available text does not provide direct quotes from any of them.

The context offered is a broader shift in which AI infrastructure is moving from a purely corporate and financial question into one shaped by local politics. The article's headline and summary suggest that developers will need to respond to these voter signals as they plan future projects. The text provided does not say what concrete steps companies or regulators will take next, so further developments remain unclear. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Applied Digital And Harwood: A Teaching Moment For AI Data Centers?

stories.Headline: Anthropic says a key AI safety alarm has been triggered, days before its IPO
stories.Summary:
Anthropic said on Tuesday that one of its key AI safety alarms has been triggered, in the same amended prospectus that set a price range for its record-setting IPO. A week earlier, the company had told would-be investors that AI speeding up its own research might "imminently" trigger the alarm. The filing said the threshold has now been met, and the company wrote that it made the determination "rather than on what we have observed from current models." The safety threshold is part of Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy, which sets out tougher safety measures as its AI grows more powerful. It is triggered when AI does enough of Anthropic's research to roughly double how fast its models improve.

The policy says that pace would fit two years of AI progress, measured at the 2018-2024 rate, into a single year. Crossing the line brings more safeguards, not a shutdown, and the filing says AI "has already been accelerating our research and development." Anthropic set its IPO price range at $70 to $78 per share on Tuesday as it began its roadshow, valuing the company at as much as about $1.4 trillion. Trading could start as soon as Nov. 19, according to reports.

Nvidia and Google are each buying $10 billion of Anthropic stock at the IPO price, part of a $26 billion private placement that also includes AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft and Taiwan Semiconductor. Anthropic says humans remain in charge and that it does not expect to safely use Claude "to fully autonomously design and build successive generations of frontier models without meaningful human supervision or understanding." The filing says the company is weighing policy changes "to keep humans in control." METR, an independent nonprofit that tests AI systems, estimated last week that Anthropic's models have been improving nearly twice as fast since October 2025, and in a separate review called Anthropic's August argument that it was still below the threshold "overstated."

The filing also changed some terminology. Anthropic swapped in "super intelligence" for "AI" in places, citing President Trump's Sept. 29 executive order telling federal agencies to use the term, and mentions of "AI" fell by about a quarter from the Nov. 2 version, by Yahoo Finance's count. Anthropic said it is still weighing what crossing the threshold means and will release further reports. It also warned that "our organization may lose visibility across certain processes" as it increasingly uses Claude to accelerate progress within the company.

Articles.Title: Anthropic says a key AI safety alarm has been triggered, days before its IPO

stories.Headline: Takaichi seeks international AI cooperation at France-hosted meeting
stories.Summary:
Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi on Monday urged the international community to work together on security issues tied to artificial intelligence. She joined a meeting hosted by the French government online, which started at 10 p.m. that day. French President Emmanuel Macron also attended, along with leaders, government institution representatives and AI-related business officials from interested countries. The article does not state the exact date of the meeting beyond Monday, and it was reported on November 10, 2026.

Takaichi said that advanced AI is creating new security problems, including its use in cyberattacks and the risk of losing control over it. She argued that because the effects of AI cross national borders, international cooperation is essential. She also called for deeper international discussion on how to encourage innovation while managing risks at the same time. The Japanese government, she said, aims to host an AI summit at an early date and hopes to help advance international cooperation under an evolved free and open Indo-Pacific.

Takaichi faced criticism at home for skipping an online summit of the Group of Seven major nations held on Oct. 2. At a news conference on Tuesday, Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said the French government had informed Tokyo of the schedule for Monday's meeting in the second half of the previous week. He said the prime minister chose to take part because it was important to communicate Japan's stance and efforts to the international community. The article does not say whether the French government confirmed any outcomes from the meeting.

Articles.Title: Takaichi seeks international AI cooperation at France-hosted meeting

stories.Headline: Why is Vietnam’s To Lam in Japan? AI, chips and nuclear power
stories.Summary:
Vietnam's leader To Lam visited Tokyo this week to widen trade and investment ties with Japan, with a focus on technology. The trip came as uncertainty continues over the future direction of American policy. After talks with Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi on Monday, the two leaders pledged to speed up public-private cooperation on critical minerals. A joint statement called economic security a top priority in the relationship and promised deeper cooperation on defence and investment.

The two governments also stressed the need to bring Japanese-funded liquefied natural gas and gas-fired power projects online quickly. They reaffirmed their plan to introduce nuclear power to Vietnam. Hanoi is seeking to build domestic industrial strength through these partnerships. The agenda covers artificial intelligence, semiconductor chips, critical minerals, LNG projects and defence ties. Each of these areas is tied to the broader aim of strengthening Vietnam's economy.

Responsibility for these commitments rests with the leaders of both countries, who issued a joint statement after their meeting. Takaichi and To Lam framed economic security as central to the bilateral relationship. The articles do not give further detail on specific figures or timelines for the projects. Officials from both sides are expected to carry the agreed cooperation forward, though the reporting does not specify who will lead each track.

The visit reflects Vietnam's effort to diversify its partners at a time when its traditional economic ties are being tested by shifting policy in Washington. Japan offers capital, technology and energy expertise that Hanoi wants for its industrial plans. What happens next depends on how quickly the announced projects move from pledges to construction and operation. The articles do not say when specific agreements will be signed.

Articles.Title: Why is Vietnam’s To Lam in Japan? AI, chips and nuclear power

stories.Headline: Japan to create defense research hubs at universities for AI, space tech
stories.Summary:
Japan plans to set up research hubs by fiscal 2031 at universities and other institutions to develop technologies that can be applied to defense equipment. The move was reported by Nikkei Asia on November 10, 2026, and it is aimed at helping the country respond to new forms of warfare in areas such as artificial intelligence and space. The hubs are part of an effort to strengthen Japan's defense research base in fields that are changing quickly. The article notes that Japan has lagged behind the United States and China in next-generation defense research. The initiative represents a shift in how Japan organizes its defense science, with academic institutions being brought more directly into military-related technology work.

Its stated purpose is to give the country a longer-term perspective as the security environment changes rapidly. Japan's government has been under pressure to keep pace with rivals that are advancing in these areas more quickly. The article presents the hubs as a way to build capacity over the coming years rather than respond only to immediate needs. The article attributes the plan to the Japanese government in Tokyo, and reporter Ryota Ogata wrote the report. Its headline frames the initiative as Tokyo's response to rapid changes in the security sector.

The piece does not provide direct quotations from named officials in the portion available. It also links to related Nikkei coverage on Japan's plans to reorganize defense research around AI and cyber issues. Taken together, the report describes a government effort to build long-term defense research capacity inside universities. It points to growing competition in advanced military technology as the backdrop for the decision. The available text does not provide further details on budgets, the specific universities involved, or how the hubs will be governed, so those points remain unclear from this report.

Articles.Title: Japan to create defense research hubs at universities for AI, space tech

stories.Headline: China’s Singles’ Day turns 18: bye coupon math, hello AI tokens
stories.Summary:
Singles' Day, China's annual online shopping festival also known as Double 11, marked its 18th year this season with a noticeably different tone. Shopper Sunny He, a 32-year-old from Shanghai, bought a 12,000-yuan iPhone 18 Pro Max on Alibaba Group Holding's Tmall marketplace, using a 300-yuan voucher to lower the price. He told the South China Morning Post that the event felt less lively than before because she had less spare cash. Her selective approach, the article says, mirrors a wider change in how Chinese consumers are spending during the sale.

The article frames the season around a pivot away from complicated coupon schemes toward simpler, straightforward pricing. Retailers appear to be moving to clearer discounts, and the article notes that the shift is aimed at keeping shoppers in a domestic market that has become increasingly saturated. Newer elements such as AI-driven shopping features are also part of what the headline describes, though the excerpt available here offers limited detail on how they work. Shoppers are generally becoming more cautious, and the article ties this to a sluggish economy. Buyers are choosing to purchase items they had previously avoided at full price rather than spending freely across the board.

The reporting attributes the analysis to unnamed analysts, who link the pricing change to the goal of retaining customers. Ann Cao, the reporter, covered the story from Shanghai and published it on November 10, 2026. The excerpt does not give further figures, company statements, or forecasts for sales results. Readers should look to the full article for any additional data on the scale of the shift or the specific AI tools being introduced.

Articles.Title: China’s Singles’ Day turns 18: bye coupon math, hello AI tokens

stories.Headline: Integration among ASEAN, China, Japan, South Korea boosted by AI boom
stories.Summary:
The artificial intelligence boom is accelerating economic integration across Southeast Asia, China, Japan and South Korea, according to Yasuto Watanabe, director and CEO of the ASEAN+3 Macroeconomic Research Office (AMRO). He made the remarks in Bangkok on Nov. 10, 2026, as reported by Nikkei Asia. He said the technology will boost trade and investment within the region. The report centers on his outlook for regional ties. Watanabe's comments came at a time when the private sector is driving closer links among these economies.

The article says AI demand is pulling companies into deeper cooperation across borders. It does not give specific figures on trade volumes or investment totals in its excerpt. Nor does it set out any new policy requirements or formal agreements tied to his remarks. Watanabe, who leads AMRO, is the source of the outlook described in the report. The article attributes the bullish view to him and does not report any dissenting official view.

He is quoted at an event held during the International Monetary Fund and World Bank annual meetings, which the article places in Bangkok on Oct. 14. The photo caption describes him speaking at that gathering. The surrounding coverage points to a region where AI and related supply chains are reshaping business ties, though the excerpt provided does not spell out the details. Other stories listed alongside the article cover electric vehicle competition, chip-related supply chain pressures and regional trade frictions. The articles provided do not say what steps AMRO or governments will take next.

Articles.Title: Integration among ASEAN, China, Japan, South Korea boosted by AI boom

stories.Headline: India's electronics firms face PCB squeeze as AI demand drives up costs
stories.Summary:
India's electronics manufacturers are facing high costs and supply constraints for printed circuit boards as an increasing share of capacity is captured by booming demand for artificial intelligence hardware. Nikkei Asia reporter Ananta Agarwal reported the story from Bengaluru on November 10, 2026. Printed circuit board makers worldwide are diverting more production toward advanced and specialized boards for demanding AI applications. That shift is squeezing India's traditional users in the electronics industry, which rely on more ordinary boards. The article says that prices for these materials have risen by as much as 350 percent.

Manufacturers in India are passing those higher costs on to their customers. The article gives no further figures on the size of the increases or on the period over which they occurred. The article does not name a specific company or official who is responsible for the squeeze. It describes it as a result of market forces, with global board makers choosing to put their output into AI-related work.

The article gives no statement from any named industry figure, government body or board maker on the situation. The article does not describe any policy response or a timeline for relief. Its headline frames the squeeze as the outcome of rising AI demand, and the body text points to the same cause. The piece gives no outlook for how long supply will stay constrained.

Articles.Title: India's electronics firms face PCB squeeze as AI demand drives up costs

stories.Headline: QSAN and JetStor to Showcase 3U60 NVMe All-Flash Storage for On-Prem AI at SC26
stories.Summary:
QSAN Technology Inc. announced on November 11, 2026, that it will take part in SC26 (Supercomputing 2026), held November 15 to 20 at McCormick Place in Chicago, Illinois. Together with its U.S. distribution partner, JetStor, QSAN plans to show its 3U60 NVMe All-Flash Array, which uses an OCP card-based design. The companies present the showing as part of QSAN's work on on-premises AI infrastructure. The announcement was issued from Taipei, Taiwan.

The 3U60 array accommodates up to 60 NVMe SSDs within a 3U chassis, which the article says maximizes storage capacity while minimizing data center footprint. The OCP card-based design is described as a modular approach that allows high-density hardware integration and greater architectural flexibility. The platform is also described as offering low-latency, high-throughput data access for AI data pipelines, large datasets and HPC applications. QSAN says selected NVMe platforms support NVIDIA GPUDirect Storage.

The article also lists uses for its broader NVMe portfolio, including retrieval-augmented generation, vector databases, and enterprise data protection. QSAN describes the array as a product of its in-house hardware engineering, and the partnership with JetStor is described as combining that engineering with JetStor's established U.S. market presence. JetStor is described as a U.S.-based provider of enterprise data storage solutions that brings QSAN's technologies to customers across the United States. Steven Lin, General Manager of QSAN Technology Inc., said that storage infrastructure must evolve to deliver greater density, performance, and efficiency as enterprises bring AI workloads into their own data centers.

QSAN invites enterprise AI architects, HPC professionals, system integrators, and IT decision-makers to meet its representatives at SC26 through one-on-one consultations. The article describes SC26 as the largest international HPC conference, attracting more than 18,000 attendees from around the world. Separately listed event details say Women in HPC will host a full-day workshop, a Rising Stars early-career program, and a networking reception at SC26 on November 16 in Chicago. The article gives no further background on QSAN's prior conference activity or on how the array has performed in deployments.

Articles.Title: QSAN and JetStor to Showcase 3U60 NVMe All-Flash Storage for On-Prem AI at SC26

stories.Headline: Sakana AI may go public in 2027
stories.Summary:
Sakana AI, a Japanese artificial intelligence company, may go public in 2027, according to media reports. Nikkei broke the news, saying the firm is weighing a listing on the Tokyo Stock Exchange, Nasdaq, or both for its initial public offering. The company's market value could exceed that of Mercari, which is valued at ¥680 billion ($4.3 billion), and would put Sakana AI among Japan's most valuable startup listings. Goldman Sachs has reportedly been hired as an adviser for the process.

Sakana AI responded in an X post on Monday, saying it has no near-term plans for an IPO. The company said its priority is building a generational AI company that serves as Japan's national AI champion. The reports come as AI companies worldwide face problems with valuations, local resistance to data centers, and doubts about how useful the technology is. AI shares fell sharply after the U.S. midterm elections, as investors worried a Democratic-controlled Congress would tighten AI rules and slow data center construction. The Nasdaq is about 9% below its all-time high, partly because of the retreat in AI stocks.

The company has raised ¥32 billion ($200 million) in Series B funding from backers including Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group, Google and Citi, and Nvidia took part in an earlier Series A round. Earlier this year, Sakana AI introduced Sakana Namazu, its first large language model, which was built on Kimi 2.6, an open-weight model from China's Moonshot AI. Concerned about overreliance on Chinese and U.S. models, Japan has made developing its own language models a priority, and it has reportedly invested $6 billion in an AI effort through Noetra, a consortium that includes Sakana AI, SoftBank and Sony. On Oct. 26, Sakana AI said it was training its own model from scratch, and its planned Sakana Sawara series will include a large and a small model.

Articles.Title: Sakana AI may go public in 2027

stories.Headline: SK hynix Rides the AI Data Center Boom and HBM4 Ramp-Up
stories.Summary:
SK hynix, the South Korean memory chipmaker, is drawing attention as demand for artificial intelligence applications and data center expansion grows. Its high-bandwidth memory and conventional DRAM are both expected to benefit from this shift, since more complex AI workloads require high-performance memory. The company began mass production and shipments of its next-generation HBM4 chips in the third quarter of 2026. It expects HBM4 to surpass HBM3E in both shipment volume and revenue contribution in the fourth quarter of 2026.

A Zacks Investment Research analysis cited in the Yahoo Finance piece says large cloud service providers are expected to raise capital expenditures by 60% or more in 2027. The AI data center buildout is expected to grow about 40% per year through 2030. The analysis puts SK hynix at a forward 12-month price-to-earnings ratio of 3.51X, below the industry average of 9.47X. It also notes that the Zacks Consensus Estimate for the company's 2026 earnings has not changed over the past seven days.

The company's shares have fallen 8.5% over the past three months, compared with a 19.6% decline for the industry. Zacks gives SK hynix a Zacks Rank of #3, meaning Hold. Lattice Semiconductor and Micron Technology are also named as companies expected to benefit from continued AI data center buildout. Micron is described as a maker of DRAM and NAND flash memory.

A separate Tech Insider report, citing CNBC analysis and Ballotpedia, says voters in 10 states considered 41 data-center-related measures in the 2026 midterms. Voters opposed data centers in 40 of the 41 measures. The one exception was in Harwood, North Dakota, where voters rejected a proposal requiring additional review of industrial projects. The measures ranged from outright bans to limits tied to water use and electrical load, such as a Kansas moratorium covering facilities using more than 100,000 gallons of water per day or peak loads above 10 megawatts.

Bloomberg's November 8, 2026 video, with Brody Ford, David Gura and Christina Ruffini, frames the results as a signal about the physical infrastructure behind AI, including land, power and water. The Tech Insider report says local voters, rather than federal regulators, delivered the verdict through zoning rules, moratoriums and bans. Tech Insider describes the results as a pattern rather than isolated votes, given their number and the 40-to-1 split. The article also notes the reporting does not name specific companies or projects affected by the measures in most cases.

Articles.Title: SK hynix Rides the AI Data Center Boom and HBM4 Ramp-Up

stories.Headline: Deux revives late Kim Sungjae's voice with AI for new album
stories.Summary:
Legendary Korean hip-hop duo Deux is set to release a full-length album, "4th Deux," on November 21, 2026, and will use artificial intelligence to recreate the vocals of the late Kim Sungjae. The album arrives more than 30 years after the duo's previous record, "Force Deux," which is widely regarded as one of the best albums in K-pop history. The pair split barely three months after that release, and each went on to a solo career. Kim was found dead in a Seoul hotel room in November 1995, one day after his solo debut, and the case remains unsolved.

The upcoming album has nine tracks, and Lee led its production and wrote "The Future," one of two focus tracks. The other main track, "I Want You," features Dynamic Duo, another well-known hip-hop pair. Lee described the song at a pre-listening session in Seoul on Saturday, saying it sounds like what Deux might have produced had it taken a new jack swing number a step further. Under Lee's wishes, a portion of the album's proceeds will go to Kim's family. The articles do not say how the AI was used or how the vocals were produced.

Lee is the person the article ties most directly to the project, as he led production and wrote the focus track. The article reports his remarks at the pre-listening session and his request that proceeds go to Kim's family. It gives no further statements from the duo's partners or from Kim's family. The article also notes that the two musicians parted ways after their last album and later released two albums, a live recording and a best-of set, in 1995 and 1997. It does not report any further developments beyond the album's release plans.

Articles.Title: Deux revives late Kim Sungjae's voice with AI for new album

stories.Headline: When AI writes, what remains human?
stories.Summary:
Philippe Jaenada, who was named winner of France's Prix Goncourt on November 3, 2026, has admitted using AI three times while writing his prize-winning novel, "L'inconnue du quai de Javel." The admission came amid a wider dispute in France over AI in literature, which the opinion piece links to the removal of Haitian Canadian writer Thélyson Orélien from the shortlist in September after allegations of AI use. Orélien denied using AI, while Jaenada acknowledged his actions voluntarily. Social media critics have questioned whether Orélien, a writer of color, was treated more harshly than Jaenada, a white man.

Jaenada said he had inserted a ChatGPT-generated sentence to "play with the reader" and included an AI-generated section to show how unreliable the tool could be on technical questions. The author of the column says his explanations are hard to judge for sincerity. The dispute has also produced a new literary award, the Pascal Prize, which accepts only works created with AI and requires applicants to submit a technical dossier naming the large language models used and the prompts that started the work. Its jury is chaired by futurist Jacques Attali. The organizers first proposed a Goncourt AI Prize, but the Goncourt rejected that idea, saying it honors books written by humans, not machines.

The column draws two lessons for Korea. First, the Goncourt remains France's most prestigious literary award, so an AI controversy there carries real weight. Second, the French debate has split into acceptance of the technology on one side and insistence on purely human authorship on the other, and the writer argues Korea would gain little by copying that rigid division. Publisher L'Observatoire plans a label called "Sanctuaire" to certify fully human-authored works, which the column presents as part of that polarization.

The column argues that AI use is already spreading through Korean writing, translation and research faster than these debates are moving. Lee Eun-hye, head of the publisher Geulhangari, wrote on Facebook that she has received noticeably more translation proposals from master's and doctoral candidates, and that some of the samples are suspiciously polished. She told the columnist she strongly suspects some of those samples were prepared with AI. The column also cites Kim Seong-woo's 2024 book, which describes how AI can let researchers write while relying on machine summaries instead of reading the original papers. The author ends by asking what distinguishes human intellectual work once machines can write, summarize and translate, and says it is time to reconsider what it means for writing to be entirely human.

Articles.Title: When AI writes, what remains human?

stories.Headline: Hitjis and Jenus music videos will be created through an AI video contest
stories.Summary:
MindSpark is running the generative AI video contest "The 3rd Korea AI Advertising Awards," accepting entries from November 9 through midnight on November 30. This year's biggest change is a music video category that uses unreleased new songs from two idol groups, the five-member girl group Hitjis, who debuted in April of last year, and the five-member boy group Jenus, who debuted in April of this year. Entrants can pick a track from either group and make a music video with generative AI. MindSpark will choose one standout work per track and give each winner 1 million KRW.

The category is meant to ease a real burden on rookie idols, since sets, filming crews, and equipment quickly push production costs up. Several creators can interpret the same song through different videos, letting Hitjis and Jenus review multiple versions of a music video for one new track. Entrants also get hands-on experience making videos for newly debuted idols. The organizers present it as a chance to see how far AI video can extend beyond advertising into music content.

Alongside the music category, the contest is running brand advertising briefs from 14 companies across finance, beauty, food, and robotics. Samsung Securities wants ads that make pension products approachable for younger audiences, while JB Financial Group seeks ads that present its group image with an MZ-generation sensibility. Entrants may submit a horizontal AI Video Ad (16:9, 30 seconds) or a vertical AI Short-form Video (9:16, 30 seconds to 1 minute), with one work per category and the option to try several brands. Anyone aged 14 or older can enter individually or as a team, and a new corporate division has been added for production companies and studios.

The contest has grown quickly, with entries rising from 725 in the first edition in May last year to 999 in the second in December, a 38% increase in seven months. The total prize pool has also grown from 47 million KRW to 50 million KRW and now 53 million KRW this year. According to a Ministry of Science and ICT report, 44.5% of people have used generative AI, up 11.2 percentage points in one year. Judging is 80% expert panel and 20% public YouTube vote, and some winning works will be shown on the M-CITY billboard at the Euljiro-ipgu Station intersection in Seoul. A MindSpark representative said AI advertising is no longer an experiment but a production method that brands actually use.

Articles.Title: Hitjis and Jenus music videos will be created through an AI video contest

stories.Headline: Dartmouth provost resigns over undisclosed AI use
stories.Summary:
Dartmouth Provost Santiago Schnell has resigned and is leaving the university after a faculty-led committee found he used artificial intelligence in his writing without properly disclosing it. President Sian Leah Beilock announced the resignation on Oct. 28 in an email to the campus community. She wrote that the decision was Schnell's own and was made out of respect for his colleagues and the institution. Beilock had formed the committee on Sept. 25 after news reports questioned his AI use, including an August Semafor article about AI-written opinion pieces that named his Washington Post column.

The committee's report, dated Oct. 27, concluded that Schnell used AI in ways that broke at least one publication's disclosure rules and that he was not forthcoming about it. It did not use AI detection tools, relying instead on his logs from Dartmouth's enterprise tool, Claude, and his emails. In one journal paper, it found he used Claude to substantially edit a manuscript, troubleshoot code and generate figures without the disclosure the journal required. Schnell told Semafor he used ChatGPT to refine arguments and check grammar in a Post submission, which the committee called a clear violation of the paper's policy. The report also said he did not provide logs of his personal AI accounts when asked, though he did hand over his Dartmouth laptop.

The committee was led by former provost David Kotz and included Hany Farid, Peter Orner, Lindsay Whaley and Odette Harris. It said it was not recommending any disciplinary action. Schnell did not respond to a request for comment, and Dartmouth's media relations director did not immediately reply. Beilock wrote that leaders must model the transparency and human judgment expected of students and scholars. History professor Matthew Delmont will serve as interim provost through June 2028.

Articles.Title: Dartmouth provost resigns over undisclosed AI use

stories.Headline: The AI industry's week from hell
stories.Summary:
Anthropic announced on Tuesday, November 11, 2026, that it plans to raise as much as $64.4 billion in an IPO that targets a valuation of up to $1.4 trillion. The offering fell short of earlier expectations, as the valuation sits roughly $600 billion below what investors envisioned just months ago. Slowing revenue growth, soaring infrastructure costs and a sharp market selloff all contributed to the lower target. The article describes the move as one of the largest IPOs in history, and the timing added to a difficult week for the wider AI industry.

The reset came after a series of setbacks for AI companies that began with last week's midterm results. Voters in 40 of 41 local ballot measures nationwide favored restrictions on data-center development. Congress will also gain AI-skeptical Democrats who may use subpoena power to look into the industry's safety record and political influence. Nvidia has shed more than $1 trillion in market value since New York Times reports on October 29 linked CEO Jensen Huang to an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, and the FBI, the company's board and Congress are investigating. The Nasdaq also lost $2.5 trillion in value on Thursday, its worst session since April 2025.

Anthropic's own figures show the strain. Its annualized revenue reached $81 billion in October, but its long-term commitments to chips, data centers and computing infrastructure have climbed to nearly $901 billion. Other financial warning signs appeared as OpenAI scaled back its fundraising ambitions and SoftBank reported a $3.7 billion write-down on U.S. data-center equipment. The article also notes that lenders are growing wary of financing the industry's infrastructure spending. Still, Google, Nvidia and other technology giants have committed another $26 billion in private investment alongside the public offering.

The article suggests the outcome will depend on whether Anthropic can post a strong debut and keep its share price up after trading begins. It points to SpaceX, whose stock surged after its record June IPO but later fell below its offering price within weeks. If Anthropic completes the offering, the company could bring in roughly $85 billion in net new capital. The article argues that even a valuation of $1 trillion or $1.5 trillion may not reassure investors who expected as much as $2 trillion only weeks ago.

Articles.Title: The AI industry's week from hell

stories.Headline: Enticed by massive GPU sales···The AI chip ‘backdoor’ market reexamined amid the Jensen Huang affair
stories.Summary:
Reporting from Korea's Kyunghyang Shinmun on November 10, 2026, describes how an adultery scandal involving Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang has drawn renewed attention to a practice in which China has reportedly obtained advanced AI chips through Southeast Asia despite US export controls. The woman involved, Alice Huang, is a former executive at Megaspeed, a Singaporean firm suspected of illicitly exporting graphics processing units. According to industry sources cited in the article, Megaspeed has grown into the largest buyer of Nvidia GPUs in Southeast Asia. Bloomberg reported that from 2023 through November 2025 the company procured at least 4.6 billion dollars in Nvidia equipment and leased computing capacity to Chinese companies, including Alibaba.

The article also reports that the US Commerce Department had been investigating allegations that Megaspeed illegally exported GPUs, citing the New York Times. In August of last year, Nvidia's top legal officer reportedly asked to meet Commerce officials and said he had secured the approval of a deputy secretary, after which the inquiry was halted. This has prompted allegations that Nvidia tried to influence the probe to protect its GPU sales. US short seller Culper Research estimated in May that more than 20 percent of Nvidia's computing revenue in fiscal 2026 came from Chinese demand routed through Southeast Asia and other regions, and its founder, Christian Lamarco, said he had identified at least six more firms with similar warning signs. Separately, Bain & Company reported that data center capacity in Southeast Asia rose 45 percent in half a year, from 4 gigawatts at the end of last year to 5.8 gigawatts in the first half of this year, and the Institute for Progress estimated that about 75 percent of AI compute Chinese firms access remotely from overseas is concentrated in the region.

The article explains that US policy has largely allowed remote leasing of chips while blocking physical smuggling. The Biden administration's AI Proliferation Rule, which would have restricted exports to places such as Malaysia and Singapore, was rescinded by the Trump administration two days before it was to take effect after industry objections. More recently, Nvidia has required overseas cloud providers to sell at least 51 percent of their services to customers outside China, and on the 4th it emerged that Oracle, under US government pressure, canceled a GPU leasing deal with Tencent. On the 9th, Republican Representative Jim Banks and Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren called for tougher export controls on AI chips bound for China, and supporters of a Chip Security Act pressed for mandatory location tracking of GPUs overseas. A domestic AI industry source quoted in the article said that chip purchases through routes such as Malaysia had long been an open secret, and that confirmed violations could cause serious damage to the industry.

Articles.Title: Enticed by massive GPU sales···The AI chip ‘backdoor’ market reexamined amid the Jensen Huang affair

stories.Headline: Dot-Com lessons for the AI bubble
stories.Summary:
Chi Onwurah, a Labour Party member of the U.K. Parliament and chair of the House of Commons Science, Innovation and Technology Committee, published an opinion piece on November 10, 2026, in The Korea Times, distributed by Project Syndicate, arguing that the current artificial intelligence investment boom may be a bubble and that the late-1990s dot-com crash offers warnings. Drawing on her own experience as an engineer at a telecoms infrastructure company that collapsed in the early 2000s, she describes how that boom ended with the loss of her job and visa. She notes that firms such as Global Crossing and WorldCom filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy, while Nortel Networks and Lucent lost about 99 percent of their stock value. She says the infrastructure providers of that era relied heavily on debt and on "vendor financing," in which suppliers helped their own customers pay for products, and she sees similar circular arrangements in today's AI sector.

Onwurah points to specific examples of this circularity. She cites Anthropic buying compute capacity powered by Nvidia chips from a company in which Nvidia is a major investor, and Microsoft investing more than $13 billion in OpenAI while also selling it cloud services through its Azure division. She also writes that justifying the trillions of dollars being spent on AI infrastructure would require more than $2.5 trillion in annual revenue by 2030, and that this revenue would likely have to come from customers cutting costs, mainly salaries. Her view is that such cuts could cause societal upheaval, and that a financial crash could follow either from that process or from markets concluding that AI firms cannot repay their debts. She argues that today's scale of debt is far larger than in 2001 and closer to the run-up to the 2008 financial crisis, and that the technology, media, and telecommunications sector now accounts for nearly half of the broader U.S. large-cap equity market, up from one-fifth during the 2008 crisis.

Onwurah says booms end when lenders stop funding them, pointing to American Express suspending her former company's credit cards months before its bankruptcy filing. She asks whether money withdrawn from AI could flow into productive investment elsewhere, such as in Newcastle or in youth unemployment, or instead into safe assets like gold, and says she does not know the answer. She concludes that with the U.K. placing AI at the center of its ambitions during its 2027 G20 presidency, the country's agenda should include security, standards and planning for a possible crash. The article does not describe any formal government action or response to her arguments.

Articles.Title: Dot-Com lessons for the AI bubble

stories.Headline: Inside AI-powered fight against digital sex crimes
stories.Summary:
The National Center for Digital Sexual Crime Response in Korea is using artificial intelligence to detect suspected child sexual exploitation material and speed up takedown requests. The center's AI system collects posts around the clock using about 220 keywords, analyzes text and images together, and presents its findings to staff for review. Once a staff member approves a report, the system prepares the information the relevant platform or authority needs, and each takedown request now takes about a minute or less to process. The center's director, Kim Mi-soon, said the system handles most of the process without human intervention at every step, and she said it is also detecting deepfakes that are hard to spot with the naked eye. The Korea Times reported these details in a November 10, 2026 article.

The center says the AI has greatly increased its output. The average number of cases each worker processes per day rose from 20.8 in 2025 to 202.1, roughly a 9.7-fold increase. From April to September 2026, the center processed 96,210 cases, more than twice the 45,438 handled in all of 2025. Automation also limits staff exposure to disturbing images, since images are now blurred by default and revealed only when needed for a reporting decision.

The center plans to expand monitoring from 14 platforms to 139 by 2027. It is also developing technology that looks at how conversations unfold, in order to detect online grooming, and an AI chatbot that will send vulnerable young people information about support services. Officials at the center described the grooming problem in plain terms. A staff member at a demonstration for reporters on Tuesday said comments on a teenager's video, such as compliments or questions about age, can look harmless but may be used to build trust and move a child toward private contact.

The center's official said keyword searches alone cannot catch this because individual words are not suspicious by themselves. Kim Mi-soon said she hopes these tools will curb digital sex crimes, which fall most heavily on teenagers and people in their 20s. The center supported 10,637 victims in 2025, up from 4,973 in 2020, and that group made up 77.6 percent of those supported last year. Park Kwang-soo, head of the Women's Human Rights Institute of Korea, which oversees the center, credited the gains to staff expertise and said that people remain necessary at many points in victim support.

Faster detection does not guarantee removal, and the center reported that 28.5 percent of its takedown requests went unfulfilled in 2025. Among websites whose server locations it could identify, at least 95.5 percent were hosted overseas, which complicates enforcement. Officials said technical gains must be paired with international cooperation, stronger platform accountability, and efforts to cut off the revenue that sustains illegal sites. The article does not describe any specific steps scheduled to address these gaps beyond the planned expansion and new tools.

Articles.Title: Inside AI-powered fight against digital sex crimes

stories.Headline: "AI has caused an insane inflation in the number of games; it’s becoming harder to capture a player's attention."
stories.Summary:
AI has caused what Anat Horvitz, a director at Google Israel, called an insane inflation in the number of games, making it harder than ever to capture players' attention. She said this during a panel at the Gaming Conference hosted by Calcalist, Google, and Playtika, where Eitan Reisel, managing partner at investment fund vgames, also spoke. The panel was moderated by Meir Orbach of Calcalist, and the discussion took place on 11 November 2026. The two discussed how artificial intelligence has made game development faster and cheaper while intensifying competition for players' attention. Horvitz described an 11% decline in game downloads over the past year, although revenue rose 1.5% this year, the third consecutive year of revenue growth.

She said the industry once focused on attracting new customers, but the battle is now centered on market share and retaining existing players. Reisel said games can be released much faster but still require significant capital. He cited five-person teams building games that generate hundreds of millions of dollars in annual revenue. Horvitz said the bottleneck has shifted from production to attention, since tools such as those provided by Google let even small studios produce games in days. She projected 136,000 new games would be released in 2026, a massive increase over 2025.

She said only 6% of total playtime goes to games released within the past year, with the rest going to older titles. Winning attention, she said, requires AI, creative strategy, and in-depth data analysis. Reisel said that where a $5 million seed investment once bought two attempts at casual games, he now expects a company to launch 12 games with the same amount, which reduces risk. He added that faster production does not make running a gaming company easier, because companies must constantly create new content and invest heavily in marketing. Horvitz said studios now want to determine quickly whether a game's economics work, and Reisel said competitors' ability to clone games has reached an extreme level.

Reisel described vgames' financing model, which has raised $500 million with backing from The Phoenix and in partnership with General Catalyst. The fund covers user acquisition costs and is repaid from revenue generated by the users it helps acquire, rather than taking equity. Horvitz said similar financing is emerging among companies that fund smaller studios, and that M&A activity is high because companies can acquire existing titles instead of developing every game themselves. Reisel said his portfolio company is generating 800 creative assets a week, and Horvitz said Israeli companies think globally from day one. More to follow.

Articles.Title: "AI has caused an insane inflation in the number of games; it’s becoming harder to capture a player's attention."

stories.Headline: Anthropic’s I.P.O. and the Clubby Business of A.I.
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, the artificial intelligence company, has begun the roadshow for its initial public offering, a move that has drawn major attention in the A.I. industry. Investor demand for the stock offering is reported to be robust so far. The company's latest I.P.O. prospectus disclosed a $26 billion private share sale, which has drawn scrutiny for what it reveals about how money moves through the sector. The figures in the filing also showed which investors stand to gain the most if the listing succeeds.

The $26 billion private share sale is worth close attention because it highlights circular financing, a pattern in which money flows among companies that also depend on one another as customers or backers. Reporting on the filing suggests this kind of arrangement underpins much of the A.I. economy. The story was reported by Sri Muppidi, and the newsletter that carried it framed the offering as among the biggest recent stories in artificial intelligence. Earlier in the same coverage, attention had been on the scrutiny facing Nvidia's chief executive, Jensen Huang, before the Anthropic roadshow took center stage.

The articles do not identify any individual or executive held responsible for the financing structure, and they do not supply direct statements from the company on the circular financing point. The newsletter is written by a team of DealBook reporters and editors, led in this edition by Andrew Ross Sorkin. Beyond the roadshow and the prospectus, the material leaves open how the offering will price and how the investors named in the filing will be affected. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Anthropic’s I.P.O. and the Clubby Business of A.I.

stories.Headline: Plurai wants to help AI agents work better using the same approach that helped get self-driving cars to roads
stories.Summary:
Plurai, a startup, has raised $13 million in seed funding to build simulation tools that aim to make AI agents more reliable. The round was led by Team8, with participation from U&I, Velocity and Mercer, and the announcement came on Wednesday. Co-founders Ilan Kadar and Elad Levi previously worked at Nexar, which develops autonomous driving technology. Kadar had worked with Waymo to simulate and evaluate its end-to-end deep learning driving software.

The company's approach creates a digital twin of a business's electronic systems, including the knowledge base and tools an agent will use in production. It maps the possible flows an agent could take and uses that map to prepare the model for edge cases. The platform works alongside existing agentic tools such as Claude Code, Codex, Copilot and Cursor. Plurai also uses the data it gathers to post-train small, open-weight models tailored to individual customers.

Kadar described the core problem as the gap between a demo and a product that is both reliable and cost effective. Tests done with Nvidia and Nebius showed Plurai's models outperforming mid-tier frontier models at lower cost, according to the article. Reah Miyara, a Google DeepMind researcher who backed the company as an angel investor, said its edge comes from understanding failure modes in production and generating synthetic data to tune models. Kadar argued that general models will not know a particular business's policies.

The article gives background on agent reliability, citing LiveBench 2.0, where Claude Fable 5.2 and ChatGPT-6 Astra succeeded on 82.9 and 75.6 out of 100 tasks. A test by the AI infrastructure company EON in a simulated corporate environment found the top model, Claude Opus 4.8, reached 76.8% accuracy. The article notes that agents booking travel can ignore spending policies, and that combining data from multiple sources or long customer conversations can cause errors. It also compares this to the simulation methods used to bring self-driving cars to roads.

Meta's Muse agent, launched in early September, drew 10 million downloads in the U.S. within 40 days, with buying as its most popular task and average purchases above $200. OpenAI followed with its own always-on agent, Dots, a few weeks later. Amazon blocked Muse almost immediately and had already spent a year in court fighting Perplexity's shopping agent. Walmart announced a system giving each agent its own profile with purchase approval or spending limits, while JPMorgan said it would not let outside agents into customer accounts.

Articles.Title: Plurai wants to help AI agents work better using the same approach that helped get self-driving cars to roads

stories.Headline: Don’t just prompt AI — architect it: Introducing the Professional Agentic Architect Certification
stories.Summary:
Google Cloud has announced a new certification called the Professional Agentic Architect, aimed at proving skill in building production-ready AI agents. The announcement was published on November 11, 2026, by Gary Eimerman, managing director of Google Cloud Learning. The certification is the latest step in the company's Gemini Agent Ready initiative, which nearly one million developers are already using to learn about agents. It was first used internally, where Google trained thousands of forward deployed engineers and strategic partners over the past four months, and is now being opened to the wider developer community and partner ecosystem.

The certification uses a hybrid format rather than a traditional multiple choice test. The first part is a proctored multiple choice exam that tests system design choices, architectural standards, cost optimization, and security governance. The second part is a set of hands-on labs on Google Skills, where candidates build, test, and debug live agentic workflows in an active cloud environment. The curriculum covers building agents with low-code tools, using coding agents for application development, developing custom agents on the Gemini platform with open source frameworks, evaluating and deploying agentic workflows, and securing and governing them. Candidates who pass both parts receive a digital badge.

The announcement was written by Gary Eimerman, who presents the program as a response to enterprise demand for agentic workloads, which the article says has skyrocketed. Google says its forward deployed engineers and partners work directly with customers worldwide, and that standardizing training ensures its own teams follow the same standards it recommends. The article also cites research with Ipsos, reporting that 82% of learners using Google Skills say listing Google Cloud certifications on a resume draws more recruiter responses, and that 90% of cloud professionals say such credentials give them verified know-how for in-demand roles. Ravi, the vice president who manages Google's forward deployed engineers, is also named as a contributor to the program's rollout.

Developers can get started by registering for Gemini Agent Ready, which offers 35 free monthly learning credits on Google Skills. Google Cloud customers can join a no-cost, cohort-based guided certification journey called Get Certified, while partners can register for Partner Certification Kickstart. Candidates are directed to review the exam guide, learning path, and sample questions, complete the hands-on preparation modules, then take the multiple choice exam and the lab requirements. The article does not state the exam fee, pass thresholds, or the number of participants who have completed the certification so far.

Articles.Title: Don’t just prompt AI — architect it: Introducing the Professional Agentic Architect Certification

stories.Headline: Microsoft Warns a New Trade Crackdown Could Derail America's AI Boom
stories.Summary:
Microsoft has urged the Trump administration to drop a planned restriction on Chinese-made optical transceivers, according to a November 10 Reuters report cited by GuruFocus and Yahoo Finance. The company has lobbied administration officials against an import ban being developed by the Federal Communications Commission. The move was reported on November 10, 2026. The dispute centers on components that connect servers, networking switches and other equipment through high-speed fiber-optic cables.

The proposed ban would restrict these devices because the administration worries that Chinese-made components could enable espionage, malware installation or disruptions to critical American infrastructure. The article notes that China accounts for roughly two-thirds of the global optical transceiver market, according to Counterpoint Research. American manufacturers Coherent and Lumentum offer competing products but currently lack sufficient production capacity to replace Chinese suppliers. One possible compromise would restrict only advanced transceivers capable of transmitting 3.2 terabits per second, which are not expected to enter large-scale production until 2028. The article identifies the FCC's final decision as the most important near-term catalyst.

Microsoft is the company pressing the issue, and the article says it raised supply-chain concerns during September meetings with White House and National Security Council officials. The company has 35 data centers under construction across the United States and another 134 planned, according to market intelligence firm Cleanview. Microsoft's position is that a broad ban could increase construction costs and delay AI deployments. The administration's stated concern, as described in the article, is national security.

The article places the dispute within a broader vulnerability, since large technology companies' AI investments still depend on Chinese components that domestic manufacturers cannot quickly replace. Investors are told to watch whether restrictions target existing products or future generations, and how Azure revenue growth and data center utilization respond. The article suggests a narrowly targeted restriction could preserve Microsoft's expansion plans while broader restrictions could leave expensive AI processors underutilized. The FCC's final decision on the matter is still pending, and the article does not say when it will be issued.

Articles.Title: Microsoft Warns a New Trade Crackdown Could Derail America's AI Boom

stories.Headline: Commvault CEO on AI security, Nvidia, data recovery
stories.Summary:
Commvault CEO Sanjay Mirchandani appeared on CNBC's "Power Lunch" on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, in an interview that ran from 2:42 p.m. Eastern time. The segment covered AI agents that have gone rogue, the company's partnerships with Nvidia, and data recovery. The video listing identifies the interview only by these topics and does not describe any specific incident or event involving the company.

The article gives no further detail on what the rogue AI agents did or how Commvault's Nvidia partnership works, so those points cannot be filled in from the material provided. The listing also includes a list of other videos from the same program, mostly featuring executives from utility and energy companies discussing electricity demand and data center growth. Those related segments are not about Commvault and do not add facts about its products or customers. No new requirements, dates for changes, or regulatory actions are stated in the article.

Mirchandani is responsible for the remarks in the interview, and the article presents him as speaking for Commvault. The listing does not include any paraphrased or quoted statements from him, so his specific views on AI security or recovery are unavailable here. The CNBC description frames the discussion as a conversation about AI agents and data protection, rather than reporting a confirmed breach or outage. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Commvault CEO on AI security, Nvidia, data recovery

stories.Headline: Agent substrate: how Kubernetes became the foundation for AI
stories.Summary:
Kubernetes, the container orchestrator, has grown into what enterprises now rely on to run artificial intelligence agents, according to a SiliconANGLE report published on November 11, 2026. The article frames this as a shift in which Kubernetes acts as the agent substrate, a change that revives older security ideas such as the network perimeter. It also raises the importance of moving workloads smoothly between clouds. The story centers on remarks made at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America, where Broadcom unveiled two open-source initiatives.

Broadcom is pushing two main efforts to make the platform simpler to deploy and safer to run. The company's approach is security in depth, which uses its vDefend firewall at the network perimeter and deeper inside the system to cut off network access when rogue agents appear. Broadcom also isolates agents inside compute boundaries called vSphere Pods, which are micro virtual machines that create a secure runtime. On the portability side, the company is co-chairing a new working group on Kubernetes workload conformance, which aims to end separate validations for each distribution.

Dilpreet Bindra, senior director of engineering in the VCF Division at Broadcom, is the main voice in the report. He said that KubeCon blew open the doors on a project that some had considered stable and less active, because Kubernetes has become the foundation for AI. Bindra also said Broadcom wants Kubernetes to work the same way wherever it runs, so that users do not need separate validations for VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service and other distributions. He described the company's contribution of its VM API project to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation as a way to bring virtual machines into Kubernetes as first-class citizens.

The article places this discussion within a wider debate about how agents change cloud infrastructure, and it notes that the interview was sponsored by Broadcom, which had no editorial control over the content. The report does not describe specific timelines for when the working group will produce results or when the VM API project will reach a particular milestone. It likewise does not say how widely the security approach has been adopted by customers. The piece appears as part of SiliconANGLE and theCUBE's coverage of the conference, with the full video interview included.

Articles.Title: Agent substrate: how Kubernetes became the foundation for AI

stories.Headline: Nvidia scandal adding to investor caution over AI
stories.Summary:
Fox Business senior correspondent Charlie Gasparino and New York Post columnist Miranda Devine discussed a scandal involving Nvidia on the program Kudlow, broadcast on November 10, 2026. The discussion centered on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's alleged relationship with a suspected Chinese spy. The segment was framed as a factor adding to investor caution over artificial intelligence. The articles provide no details of any new rule, requirement, or change arising from the matter.

They do not name any regulator, filing, legal action, or policy response. The only specifics available are the date of the broadcast, the names of the two commentators, and the nature of the allegation as described by them. The allegation concerns Jensen Huang, whom the segment identifies as Nvidia's chief executive. The articles describe the relationship as alleged and the individual as suspected, and they do not report any finding, charge, or statement from Nvidia or Huang in response.

The account comes solely from the broadcast summary and does not attribute any further claims to specific sources. The articles offer no further context about the wider investor reaction or the company's share price. They also do not say what, if anything, will happen next. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Nvidia scandal adding to investor caution over AI

stories.Headline: AI-native applications need distributed cloud, not just GPUs
stories.Summary:
Vultr, a cloud provider operating under the legal name The Constant Company LLC, has been arguing that enterprises building AI-native applications need more than raw GPU capacity. The position was laid out by Kevin Cochrane, chief marketing officer of Vultr, in an interview recorded at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA and broadcast on theCUBE, with John Furrier and Rebecca Knight of theCUBE Research. The article is dated November 11, 2026. Vultr sponsored the segment, a disclosure the article states plainly.

Cochrane said the early wave of so-called neoclouds focused on building large GPU clusters for a small set of buyers, often reselling that capacity to hyperscalers. In his view, the sector lost sight of the fact that companies still need a full cloud to run their workloads. He said the architecture has drifted back toward centralized systems and that the longer direction of computing is toward decentralized, distributed systems built on open standards and open source. The article also says distributed inference is a focus, with Vultr working with partners such as Vast Data Inc. on a global namespace that shares KV cache across nodes. Cochrane argued that networking between data centers, including private networks isolated from other tenants, is the main obstacle to enterprises adopting GPUs from newer cloud providers.

Vultr is also backing the open-source community, according to the article. The company has joined the Cloud Native Computing Foundation as a platinum member and highlighted its Open Source Credits Program, which provides infrastructure to maintainers of new CNCF projects. Cochrane said maintainers cannot be expected to fund compute themselves, and asked how a major CNCF project can be built without it. The article notes that the views are Cochrane's and that neither Vultr nor other sponsors have editorial control over theCUBE content.

Articles.Title: AI-native applications need distributed cloud, not just GPUs

stories.Headline: QuEra, Harvard and Anthropic Use AI to Reduce Quantum Circuit Resource Requirements
stories.Summary:
Researchers from QuEra Computing, Harvard University and Anthropic reported on November 10, 2026 that AI can design quantum circuits that need fewer computational resources. The team used Claude to design circuits for eight computational building blocks, and in seven of them the AI-designed circuits reduced both gate counts and qubit requirements compared with baseline designs. The research preprint, titled "Discovering state-of-the-art quantum circuits with large language models" (arXiv:2610.22367), was led by Andi Gu as part of Anthropic's STEM Fellows Program. The eighth building block produced a new approach that offers additional trade-offs between qubit requirements and gate counts. The work was announced in a press release from QuEra.

The researchers paired Claude with an independent automated evaluator that checked each design for correctness and scored it on Toffoli-gate count and qubit count. The Reed-Solomon decoder, the most expensive step in decoded quantum interferometry, went from 5.1 million Toffoli gates to about 440,000, with fewer qubits used. The Coulomb potential calculation saw a 9.9-fold reduction in its combined resource metric, with Toffoli gates falling from 6,355 to 1,140 and qubits from 252 to 142. A fixed-point Gaussian function showed a 39-fold reduction in the combined metric, with Toffoli gates dropping from about 24,000 to 1,583 and qubits from 362 to 139. The combined metric multiplies Toffoli-gate count by peak logical qubits, so these figures are not speedups, and the results are resource estimates rather than hardware runs.

Beyond improving existing designs, Claude helped discover a new reversible approach to modular inversion, an arithmetic operation central to elliptic-curve calculations. In the complete point-addition benchmark, one design required about 17 times fewer gates than the prior design using the fewest qubits, while using about 12 percent more qubits. Mikhail Lukin, Co-Founder and Chief Science Officer at QuEra and a professor at Harvard, said AI guided by a rigorous evaluator found circuit structures that work more efficiently within the constraints of reversible computing. Alek Kemeny of Anthropic said the evaluator made the work possible because every design was independently checked and scored. Takuya Kitagawa, President of QuEra Computing, said AI-driven reductions in resources expand what future fault-tolerant systems can deliver.

The findings build on an earlier pilot between QuEra and Anthropic in which Claude developed and validated laser-control software. In that pilot, the software recovered the correct laser lock in 695 of 700 trials, in seconds rather than the 5 to 10 minutes a human expert needs. The article notes that successive advances reduced the estimated Toffoli-gate count for one widely studied FeMoco simulation by roughly 150,000 times over eight years. The new elliptic-curve circuit approach came from a 53-hour search guided by researcher-defined requirements and an automated evaluator. QuEra says it is building fault-tolerant quantum computers, with its Libra system targeted for availability on Amazon Braket in 2028.

Articles.Title: QuEra, Harvard and Anthropic Use AI to Reduce Quantum Circuit Resource Requirements

stories.Headline: OpenAI Acquires Odessia, the AI Travel Agent From Sonder’s Co-Founder
stories.Summary:
OpenAI has acquired Odessia, the AI travel agent startup founded by Sonder co-founder Francis Davidson, less than a year after its launch. Davidson announced the deal on Tuesday, November 10, and said he will join OpenAI to focus on the future of travel. Terms of the deal were not disclosed. Davidson did not say whether Odessia will keep operating as a standalone company. He wrote that OpenAI will have more to share on the shape of the future soon.

Davidson unveiled Odessia in June with a team of eight in San Francisco and about $6 million in seed funding led by Sequoia Capital. The product plans and books flights, hotels and itineraries through a single conversation. It opened to the public on October 14 as a free concierge that users reach by text. Odessia holds IATA accreditation as a travel agent, which gave it access to private hotel rates and perks such as free breakfast and room upgrades. The startup also wrote guides to hundreds of thousands of hotels, ranking each on factors such as street noise and gym quality.

According to Skift, the deal brings OpenAI capabilities that its partnerships with Booking.com and Expedia do not provide. Skift reported that Booking.com and Expedia were among the first apps inside ChatGPT when OpenAI opened its app platform in October 2025. PYMNTS reported that Odessia was built on OpenAI's GPT 5.5 and Codex models and processed about $60 million in travel volume during its first year. Davidson previously founded the hospitality company Sonder, which PYMNTS said grew to $600 million in revenue. In his announcement, Davidson said Odessia had planned over $60 million of travel over the summer for tens of thousands of early adopters.

Shares of major online travel agencies fell on Tuesday after the acquisition was reported, according to PYMNTS, which cited Seeking Alpha. Expedia Group dropped nearly 4 percent, Tripadvisor fell more than 3 percent and Booking Holdings fell more than 2 percent. PYMNTS reported that investors were concerned about possible disruption to established booking platforms.
