PYMNTS also reported that Odessia, unlike conventional aggregators that redirect consumers to supplier websites, handles trip planning and reservations inside its own conversational interface. The same report said nearly 25 percent of consumers in PYMNTS Intelligence research reported feeling comfortable delegating travel itinerary planning to artificial intelligence.

Skift reported that OpenAI has been building travel advertising and booking into ChatGPT so users can buy without going to a merchant's site. PYMNTS reported that traditional booking intermediaries such as Booking Holdings and Kayak have added conversational tools and native checkouts to protect their transaction volumes. Skift also reported that Davidson launched Odessia with capital from Sequoia, individual angel investors and commercial travel partners. Skift said Davidson's experience running a lodging company, which included hotels and short-term rentals for a decade, was part of what OpenAI acquired. Skift stated that Odessia's IATA accreditation gives OpenAI a capability its partners lacked.

Articles.Title: OpenAI Acquires Odessia, the AI Travel Agent From Sonder’s Co-Founder

stories.Headline: Microsoft stock falls as Anthropic takes aim at Excel and workplace software
stories.Summary:
Microsoft shares fell about 2% on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, after Bloomberg reported that Anthropic was preparing a suite of AI-powered workplace tools aimed at Microsoft's Excel and Google's Sheets. The new products were expected to be unveiled at an Anthropic event that day. Among them is Claude Sheets, a spreadsheet service that closely resembles Excel and Google Sheets but builds Anthropic's AI capabilities directly into the application. The package also includes a video-call assistant and a data dashboard tool. The launch is seen as a possible expansion of competition for Microsoft, which has been adding AI to its Office products through its Copilot platform.

Anthropic is also widening Claude's role as a platform for third-party software, announcing a way for businesses including Adobe, Atlassian and HubSpot to embed versions of their applications within Claude. This positions Claude as an alternative interface through which customers can reach business applications, while Anthropic builds competing products of its own. The company's revenue run rate reached $81 billion as of October 31, up $10 billion from the end of September, according to its IPO filing. Anthropic is seeking a fully diluted valuation of about $1.4 trillion in its planned public offering. Its push into workplace software is therefore closely watched as investors judge its ability to compete beyond its established strength in AI-assisted software development.

The tension is complicated by Microsoft's own ties to Anthropic. According to the company's latest filing, Microsoft is among the companies taking part in a separate $26 billion private placement tied to Anthropic's IPO, alongside Google, Nvidia and AMD. Anthropic product leader Nicholas Lin told Bloomberg that Claude Sheets is still a relatively basic product and is not designed for sophisticated financial modeling or advanced enterprise workloads. He said the company believes its integrations with existing spreadsheet software will remain more effective for those tasks. Even so, the move signals Anthropic's ambition to capture a larger share of corporate productivity spending, an area dominated by Microsoft and Google.

Articles.Title: Microsoft stock falls as Anthropic takes aim at Excel and workplace software

stories.Headline: Work at the Frontier: AI’s effect on freelance work
stories.Summary:
Researchers at OpenAI, working with the online freelance marketplace Upwork, published new findings on November 10, 2026, on how AI is changing freelance work. The study compared freelance job postings on Upwork with the tasks people carry out directly in ChatGPT, covering ChatGPT data from January 2025 through June 2026 and Upwork data through the first half of 2026. The authors found that demand is shifting, with some familiar services losing market share while AI-related projects bring together different capabilities. They also found that these projects tend to carry larger budgets and more hours of work. The report was released as part of OpenAI's Work at the Frontier series.

The research does not describe a new rule or requirement, but it does document several changes in the market. Writing made up a much larger share of ChatGPT use than of freelance requests, while video and animation accounted for larger shares of Upwork postings. Of 63 work categories analyzed, 43 followed the pattern in which activities common in ChatGPT use lost share on Upwork, while 20 showed the reverse. Between early 2023 and late 2025, the mix of tasks in AI-related postings became 45% more diverse, roughly the equivalent of an increase from about 15 equally common tasks to about 21. Although hourly rates were similar for AI-related and other work, AI-related projects had larger fixed-price budgets and involved more hours of work.

OpenAI's Economic Research Team and Upwork are the parties behind the findings, and the authors are careful about what their data can show. They say that ChatGPT use alone does not explain changes in freelance demand, and they point to a gap they call the capability overhang, meaning the difference between how people currently use ChatGPT and the wider range of tasks AI can support. The authors also argue that the findings do not point to a simple substitution story, since the pattern of lost share was not uniform. They suggest that AI may be shifting both what clients seek from freelancers and how they assemble projects.

They further note that freelance postings can reveal changes sooner than economy-wide employment statistics because contracts are short and clients revise requirements with each posting. The context the articles provide is that Upwork's 2026 Future Workforce Index found 38% of skilled U.S. knowledge workers freelance, and an earlier Upwork study estimated that freelance knowledge work generated $1.5 trillion in U.S. earnings in 2024. The articles do not describe any further steps, follow-up studies or policy responses that are planned. They describe the work as an early view of changes that are still developing.

Articles.Title: Work at the Frontier: AI’s effect on freelance work

stories.Headline: Imperial Heritage Caviar doubles time saved on administrative tasks by adding AI to its Dynamics 365 Business Central platform
stories.Summary:
Imperial Heritage Caviar, a family-owned Belgian caviar house, has added custom AI agents to its Dynamics 365 Business Central platform so that it can take and process orders more quickly. The company had already been saving an hour a day on administrative tasks with Business Central, and with the agents that time savings has more than doubled, which the company says amounts to hundreds of hours a year. The agents were built by the technical partner Deltanexx, took just a few weeks to develop, and were announced in a Microsoft customer story dated November 11, 2026. The company's owner, Elisabeth Colman, said the agents have turned data entry into a conversational process.

The agents were built because orders arrive through WhatsApp, email, SMS and phone calls, and Imperial Heritage wanted one system that could handle them all. Deltanexx built two agents, one on Microsoft Copilot Studio and one on Anthropic's Claude, so employees can use the tools they prefer. Both connect to Business Central through its MCP server and carry out three skills: creating sales orders, setting up new customer records and preparing weekly customer follow-up reports. For sales orders, the agent turns a plain-language request into customer and item records, presents them for review and asks for confirmation before creating the order. Administrators must also grant consent for the Claude connection, which is registered in the company's Microsoft Entra ID tenant, and Business Central's MCP configuration defines which operations the agent can use.

Colman estimates that manual order entry previously took one to two hours a day and now takes less than 30 minutes, with routine order preparation taking just a few seconds. She also said the agent has virtually eliminated the errors that came from entering large, complex orders quickly. Deltanexx managing partner Dhia Athmini said the agents were shaped specifically to Imperial Heritage's workflow processes. Colman said that employees can now begin preparing deliveries at the start of the day rather than first entering the orders received overnight. The company serves about 500 active customers, including three-star Michelin restaurants and a privately owned cruise ship.

Imperial Heritage is planning to extend the agents further, according to the article. Vendor and purchase order APIs are already included in the MCP configuration, which would allow Deltanexx to develop additional purchasing skills. The company wants to build on the follow-up skill to identify customers who normally order weekly or monthly but have not yet placed their next order. It is also exploring how the agent could help manage supplier price increases while limiting the effect on margins. Colman summarized the company's aim as giving staff more time to serve customers and build relationships.

Articles.Title: Imperial Heritage Caviar doubles time saved on administrative tasks by adding AI to its Dynamics 365 Business Central platform

stories.Headline: Detecting sleeper agents hiding in AI model neurons
stories.Summary:
Microsoft Research has released threat research, reported on the Microsoft Security Blog on November 10, showing how a capable agent model could be turned into a sleeper agent. According to the research, editing fewer than 10 neurons is enough to inject a short payload into the model. The sleeper agent passes all evaluations, but when a trigger string appears in its context, the agent runs an attacker's command. Because agents now frequently run unattended with privileged system access, the article says the integrity of model weights is a security concern for both third-party and internally developed models.

The article says the attack needs only inference-only compute, since a machine with enough RAM to run a model has enough resources to weight-space backdoor it. A backdoored model runs the command with whatever access the agent has in its environment. Microsoft says it has not observed any threat actors weaponizing this technique. The article notes that the research aligns with similar recent work by Anthropic and MIT on agentic backdoors and weight-space programming, respectively. Claude Code with Opus 4.5 discovered most of this threat autonomously, according to the post.

Microsoft Research is the group behind the findings, and the post is published under Microsoft Threat Intelligence. The article states that Microsoft Research found the threat is detectable by frontier agents, which can identify anomalous weight edits. It also says Satya Nadella recently outlined an approach of independent observability and other controls for AI models and agents, in a blog post the article links. The article describes the research as demonstrating a process in which agents surface new security problems and human researchers then systematize, study, and mitigate them.

The article's mitigation guidance recommends diffing every checkpoint against its declared base model before deployment and after each update. It says implanted neurons tend to change a few weight vectors by a large amount, while legitimate fine-tunes change weights broadly and diffusely. The guidance also recommends using frontier AI agents as auditors in the model intake pipeline, and treating every third-party model as untrusted until it is audited. Microsoft further advises running agents with least privilege, executing agent-generated code only in isolated sandboxes, and requiring human approval for high-impact tool calls. The article lists Microsoft Defender tools, Azure Machine Learning registries, and Microsoft Entra Agent ID among the products it names for these controls.

Articles.Title: Detecting sleeper agents hiding in AI model neurons

stories.Headline: Stifel CEO: Using Anthropic's AI tools made us realize we need more positions
stories.Summary:
Stifel CEO Ron Kruszewski spoke on Fox Business's "The Claman Countdown" on November 10, 2026, about his firm's use of Anthropic's AI tools. He described integrating Anthropic's Claude AI into the workflow of Stifel's financial advisors. The discussion also covered Anthropic's amended S-1 filing, which offers 825 million shares ahead of its planned Nasdaq debut. The clip was published by Fox Business that morning.

Kruszewski said the experience of using Claude inside the firm led Stifel to conclude that it needs more positions. The articles do not spell out which roles would be added or how many. They also do not say how the firm measured the change in advisor productivity. The amended filing, as described in the segment, is the company's step toward listing its shares publicly on Nasdaq.

The 825 million figure is the number of shares in that offering. Kruszewski is the chief executive of Stifel, and the articles attribute the comments about AI and hiring to him. Fox Business's description of the segment says he discussed both the Claude integration and the S-1 amendment. The articles contain no statement from Anthropic or Stifel beyond what was said on air.

They also contain no response from regulators or other parties. The context here is a financial firm reporting that adopting a specific AI product changed its staffing outlook, at the same time that the AI developer prepares to go public. The articles do not say what happens next, such as the timing of the Nasdaq listing, the offering price, or any further hiring announcements by Stifel. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Stifel CEO: Using Anthropic's AI tools made us realize we need more positions

stories.Headline: ByteDance Builds Assistant to Take on US AI Labs
stories.Summary:
ByteDance, the Chinese technology company, is reportedly developing an artificial intelligence agent similar to Meta's Muse, according to a Bloomberg report published Wednesday, November 11. The effort could help ByteDance narrow its gap with AI labs in the United States in the coming years. The report cites unnamed sources saying that ByteDance co-founder Zhang Yiming described the plan to the company's AI team at a meeting. He reportedly said ByteDance can compete with Anthropic and OpenAI, though he thinks that will take until at least 2029 or 2030.

The new agent would serve a function similar to Muse, which Meta debuted in September and which the report describes as a success for its creator. Meta has begun adding Muse to hardware such as its smart glasses, and it plans an upcoming device called Muse Charm built around the agent. The report says it is unclear whether ByteDance also intends to pair its agent with hardware. Zhang reportedly focuses on data, and the report notes that ByteDance's Seed AI models are pre-trained on datasets smaller than those used by its frontier competitors.

Meta's own push has been significant, as PYMNTS reported on October 21 that Muse had become a new centerpiece of the company's AI ambitions. Chief executive Mark Zuckerberg pointed to the assistant on the company's third-quarter earnings call as evidence that the strategy was working. More than 10 million people in the United States and Canada set up Muse within six weeks of its launch, and about 25% use it daily. The broader competitive picture shows that these assistants are gaining traction with users, which raises the stakes for newcomers like ByteDance.

Consumer attitudes toward AI agents also set limits on what such products can do, according to a PYMNTS Intelligence report released in October. That report found that 63% of consumers would let an AI agent help with credit by comparing offers, but only 49% would let it complete and submit an application. It also found that 79% said it is very important or essential for an agent to explain in plain language why it chose a particular offer or action. The articles do not say how or when ByteDance's agent will be released, or whether it will address these concerns.

Articles.Title: ByteDance Builds Assistant to Take on US AI Labs

stories.Headline: HP, EdgeRunner AI Partner on Domain-Specific AI for Defense, Federal Agencies
stories.Summary:
HP and EdgeRunner AI have announced a collaboration to bring EdgeRunner's domain-specific artificial intelligence software and agents to HP's AI personal computers and workstations used by the military, federal agencies and other critical industries. The announcement came from EdgeRunner AI, which said the effort was revealed on Tuesday. The companies are working to adapt EdgeRunner's software to run on HP hardware and to link it with systems that warfighters already use. The reporting is dated November 11, 2026.

The work covers EdgeRunner's specialized AI models, agents and edge harness, which are meant for compatible HP AI PCs and HP Z Workstations. The software is designed to handle conversational AI, language translation, document analysis and agent-based workflows. HP and EdgeRunner are still deciding which systems, configurations and use cases to validate. The companies plan to announce specific features, purchasing options and availability once that validation is complete.

Tyler Saltsman, co-founder and CEO of EdgeRunner AI, said demand is rising for AI that understands how specialized users work and can run wherever they are. He said the company's military-tuned models center on defense use cases and local execution, and that the HP partnership gives it a way to bring those capabilities to high-performance computing platforms. Todd Gustafson, president of HP Federal and head of U.S. public sector at HP, described the effort as a way to move high-performance, domain-specific AI closer to the edge for critical industries. He said the goal is to identify validated configurations that can support local AI workloads in demanding customer environments.

The collaboration builds on HP's earlier federal work, including its June 2024 acquisition of CyberCore Technologies, a Maryland company, for an undisclosed sum. Matt Barry, chief operating officer at HP Federal, has stressed endpoint security by design for government and contractor systems and has pointed to HP Wolf Security and HP Sure Admin as tools to reduce attack surfaces. EdgeRunner AI has its own government record, including a 2025 agreement with Carahsoft to offer its Athena platform to agencies. This year the company released WarClaw, won a Space Force contract to develop AI agents for acquisition modernization, and teamed with the Army's Artificial Intelligence Integration Center on an Army-specific model. The Navy also granted EdgeRunner OS an Impact Level 6 Authority to Operate.

Articles.Title: HP, EdgeRunner AI Partner on Domain-Specific AI for Defense, Federal Agencies

stories.Headline: AntiFox AI Pentesting Platform Linked to Attacks That Accessed AWS Production Secrets
stories.Summary:
AntiFox, an emerging agentic penetration testing platform, has been used in intrusions that stole Amazon Web Services credentials and moved laterally into compromised environments. Cybersecurity researchers disclosed the campaign on November 11, 2026, and Arctic Wolf Labs reported that Alibaba Cloud systems hosting AntiFox interfaces were tied to confirmed malicious actions against internet-facing web services. The activity chained web exploitation with web shell deployment to support configuration discovery, credential validation, cloud-service enumeration, secret access and storage operations. AntiFox is available on GitHub and describes itself as an AI-driven autonomous penetration testing platform. At the time of writing, the project had been forked 251 times and starred 474 times.

According to Arctic Wolf, some initial access ran through a compromised internet-facing Internet Information Services application. The attackers used that access to create an ASPX web shell through the IIS worker process, w3wp.exe, and ran operating system commands from it. Those commands identified the execution context, enumerated the application directory, checked permissions and tested whether files could be written into the web root. The same activity attempted to connect to an internal production database using a credential extracted from the application configuration. The precise vulnerability used to gain code execution on the IIS server is not known.

In other attacks, the threat actor reportedly began with a valid AWS credential obtained through means yet to be determined. Using valid IAM identities, the actor tried to enumerate dozens of services, including IAM, EC2, S3, Lambda, Secrets Manager, KMS and Amazon Bedrock. Most of these cross-service requests returned an "AccessDenied" error, but some discovery and secret-access operations succeeded. In at least some instances, the activity advanced to a successful GetSecretValue request against a production secret. Elsewhere, a valid AWS identity was used for S3 discovery and object operations.

Arctic Wolf said agentic frameworks such as these make penetration testing techniques more accessible to threat actors while increasing the speed and consistency with which the techniques can be applied in live attacks. The report notes that the disclosure comes as threat actors increasingly weaponize AI-powered penetration testing tools such as ARTEX to run broad-scale attacks. Check Point Research identified 2,557 systems that hosted ARTEX, including 10 misconfigured instances exposing their full databases. Censys counted 1,465 hosts running an exposed ARTEX console as of November 4, 2026, and the article notes that not every instance is necessarily malicious. ARTEX-linked attacks mostly aim to siphon cryptocurrency, steal Apple code-signing certificates, compromise gaming accounts and conduct denial-of-service attacks against gambling websites.

Tools like AntiFox and ARTEX belong to a broader set of about 45 open-source agentic attack frameworks, which connect to a large language model and can act on its outputs autonomously. GitGuardian said each framework has public source code and wires a model into a loop that runs tools and acts on their output. It warned that agentic tools hand the agent a shell and web access, letting the model assemble a pipeline at runtime. The article does not say what further action, if any, the affected companies or researchers have taken, and it does not describe any next steps.

Articles.Title: AntiFox AI Pentesting Platform Linked to Attacks That Accessed AWS Production Secrets

stories.Headline: J. Crew debuts new AI shopping tool that’s designed to think like a stylist
stories.Summary:
J. Crew on Wednesday, November 11, 2026, announced Style Advisor, a consumer-facing AI shopping tool that runs on a collection of Anthropic's models. The tool was trained on data from thousands of outfit pairings from the company's photo shoots, along with J. Crew's styling principles and its outfit and accessory pairings. It will debut on J. Crew's desktop website and is expected later to be added to the retailer's mobile app. Style Advisor asks questions to understand a shopper's intent, so a customer seeking a wedding outfit in Miami, but not too formal, would get recommendations based on those details.

Style Advisor runs on several Claude models. Fable 5.1 handles the more complex and ambiguous judgment behind the stylist-like responses, while Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 4.5 support the speed of back-and-forth replies. Claude Opus 5.5 was used by J. Crew's team to build a working prototype. In the future, the tool will also draw on a consumer's past purchase history to make more personalized recommendations. J. Crew also built a back-end observation layer that lets the retailer monitor costs.

Danielle Schmelkin, chief information officer at J. Crew, said the goal is to recreate online what stylists offer in stores, which is more than just the item a shopper picked up. Lauren Collett, Anthropic's enterprise go-to-market leader, said the company must decide the experience it wants shoppers to have and then map the right models to deliver it. Schmelkin said the retailer wants to keep refining the models in the right way for both customer outputs and scalable efficiency. The tool was conceptualized by a J. Crew digital product designer who built a working prototype before engineers joined.

According to the article, more than 50% of global consumers have used AI to buy goods in the past three months, and new shopping tools have come from Meta Platforms, Amazon, Lowe's, Ulta Beauty, and Macy's. McKinsey found that 56% of consumers use AI chat or search tools such as Claude or ChatGPT, but only 27% use retailer-created AI shopping assistants. J. Crew's internal efforts include an AI fluency program that advances up through vibe coding. An internal AI lab called "Second Thread" began with the tech team and has broadened to all corporate employees. For four years, J. Crew has also run a two-day tech summit with workshops, hackathons, guest speakers, and vendor presentations.

Articles.Title: J. Crew debuts new AI shopping tool that’s designed to think like a stylist

stories.Headline: Study evaluates AI tools for making medical documents easier to read
stories.Summary:
A team of researchers from the Universidad Carlos III de Madrid evaluated several artificial intelligence language models for simplifying medical reports into clearer language for non-expert readers. The work was published in the journal Scientific Reports. The researchers said many people struggle to understand their own medical documents, which affects how well they can manage their health. Their approach uses language models to produce one version of a report for clinicians and another for patients, explaining abbreviations and complex phrasing. The study is one of several efforts aimed at improving communication between doctors and patients.

The timing matters because Royal Decree 707/2026 takes effect on January 2, 2027. It was published in the Official State Gazette on September 3 and sets the first rules on basic cognitive accessibility conditions. The decree requires documents, administrative procedures and services to be easier for citizens to understand. It applies to public administrations in areas including justice, healthcare, employment, digital services and transport. The researchers describe plain language as a structured method that makes information easy to find, understand and use, rather than just shortening sentences.

The team tested 50 medical reports drawn from clinical cases supplied by the Andalusian Society of Family and Community Medicine. Each report had three adaptations written by cognitive accessibility experts following the international standard ISO 24495-1:2023, producing 150 adapted texts. The researchers compared four model families, including Llama 3.2 at 1B and 3B, Salamandra at 2B and 7B, RigoChat-v2 at 7B and Medical-mT5 at 3B, across simplification, accuracy, readability and environmental impact. They found no single model performed best in every area. Llama-3.2-3B gave the most balanced results, while RigoChat-v2-7B scored highest on output quality and readability.

The researchers also identified three recurring errors across all model families: oversimplification that removes clinical details patients need, invented or altered data, and incoherent sentences. Paloma Martínez, a co-author, said human oversight remains essential in healthcare because of these errors. The team has released its models, dataset and prompts as open-source material on GitHub and Zenodo so others can reproduce and extend the work. The research was carried out under the HumanAI project, funded through Spain's State Plan for Scientific, Technical and Innovation Research.

Articles.Title: Study evaluates AI tools for making medical documents easier to read

stories.Headline: "We're building the organization of the future, where AI agents will talk to one another."
stories.Summary:
Nir Korczak, chief marketing officer of Playtika, told the Gaming Conference hosted by Calcalist, Google, and Playtika on November 11, 2026, that the company is building an organization where AI agents communicate with one another and carry out tasks on their own. He described the shift as moving toward an ecosystem in which agents talk to each other, rather than employees using AI tools in isolation. According to Korczak, Playtika reached a new milestone in recent weeks in this effort. The change reaches into daily marketing work.

One system analyzes campaign performance and recommends ways to improve results, and although employees still approve some recommendations, the goal is to expand automation over time. Playtika has linked its internal marketing system, called "Samurai," to other systems so that decisions are documented and new capabilities can be added to the workflow. A second tool, an AI agent named "Corey" that acts as an organizational analyst, connects to agents and data sources across the company and is built into Microsoft Teams, where staff and executives can ask it complex business questions. Korczak said Corey is, for all intents and purposes, an employee.

Korczak also said the creative process is being transformed. He said that this year, with a smaller workforce, the company produced three times as much output, and that tasks that once required substantial video production budgets can now be handled by marketing staff with the click of a button. He stressed, however, that quantity alone is not the goal, so the company still employs creative professionals to develop original ideas that set it apart from competitors. In his view, AI is no longer limited to producing advertising content and is changing nearly every role in the marketing department.

Korczak framed these changes against a competitive backdrop in which barriers to game development are falling and the number of publishers is growing by about 30 percent a year, raising the cost of advertising and user acquisition. Other entertainment segments, led by short-form drama series, are competing for the same ad inventory and users. He also described a broader shift in which consumers increasingly rely on AI agents, so that brands may eventually communicate agent to agent with consumers. He concluded that if companies learn to use AI capabilities and build agent-based organizations, they will be able to construct the new marketing system for 2027.

Articles.Title: "We're building the organization of the future, where AI agents will talk to one another."

stories.Headline: Databricks’ new AI agent tells CEO Ali Ghodsi the unvarnished truth
stories.Summary:
Databricks on Wednesday unveiled an updated version of its AI agent Genie, which can now carry out multi-step jobs that take extended work to finish. The agent works through an ontology that Databricks built to give it context from the information customers store on the Databricks platform. The company says corporate leaders can assign it a wide range of tasks, and it will complete them without supervision. To demonstrate, CEO Ali Ghodsi showed TechCrunch how he uses the agent internally, walking through his actual recent chats and charts rather than a scripted product demo.

Ghodsi showed how the agent analyzed the parts of an employee satisfaction survey where the company scored poorly, and how it helped him rate and discard fixes that some executives had proposed. He also showed how it summarized a large sales pitch to a prospect that went badly, including the features the prospect said it needed before buying. In addition, the agent reviewed his past podcast appearances to develop likely interview questions. During the conversation, he even had it suggest what he should say to the reporter, and its advice was not bad.

The article describes Ghodsi using Genie to surface the information he is now unlikely to hear as a senior leader, a source of candid feedback about what was going wrong. He pointed to Dunbar's number, the theoretical limit of about 150 people with whom humans can maintain stable relationships. In a small startup, a CEO knows everyone and employees feel safe delivering bad news directly. With roughly 12,000 employees, Ghodsi acknowledged he cannot know everyone, so a salesperson may not confess a failed call and an HR manager may not admit a satisfaction idea will likely fail. He said that companies with more than 150 employees could get value from this kind of agent.

Databricks is now pitching Genie as an always-on agent for business leaders, in part because Ghodsi uses it internally and in his personal life, which the company calls dogfooding. He believes the tool can do for business work what AI agents and harnesses are doing for programmers. On cost concerns, he said spending can be controlled through Databricks' Unity Gateway product, which lets companies set usage limits and swap in less expensive open-weight models. The article notes that the company's approach is framed around these controls as agents take on more work.

Articles.Title: Databricks’ new AI agent tells CEO Ali Ghodsi the unvarnished truth

stories.Headline: Carahsoft’s Mike Adams on Turning Government AI Pilots Into Mission Outcomes
stories.Summary:
Carahsoft, a Reston, Virginia technology provider, has been helping AI companies enter the public-sector market, and program executive Mike Adams described that work in an interview with ExecutiveBiz published November 11, 2026. Adams, who has been with Carahsoft since September 2007, said the company onboards and vets new technology partners and connects them with contracts, resellers and integrators. He said agencies are now evaluating agentic AI, AI governance tools and AI infrastructure, including servers and GPUs. Carahsoft's role, he said, includes helping customers identify solutions that deliver measurable mission outcomes.

Adams said many AI companies lack government-procurement experience, so Carahsoft invests in helping them through the contracting process, including proposal development. He said a provider needs a meaningful U.S. presence, local personnel and a clear security and compliance strategy, including progress toward FedRAMP when applicable. Carahsoft also looks for offerings that complement its existing ecosystem and help agencies get more value from current investments. Adams said the most effective providers focus on outcomes, such as processing more requests in a day or reducing wait times.

Adams cited several examples of agencies moving from pilots to operational use. He said the Department of Veterans Affairs is using AI to help veterans access benefits more quickly and to support fraud detection. He said Treasury and the IRS are using automation to process taxes, claims and refunds while identifying cases that may need further review. He also named state and local activity in Pennsylvania, Texas, New York, Florida, Virginia and Maryland. Adams added that AI-enabled cybersecurity technology will be a major use case in national security.

Adams said successful adoption requires more than access, since users must understand which model fits a task and how to use it responsibly. He said agencies need processes for safeguarding data and monitoring use, and that Carahsoft offers introductory and advanced webinars, hands-on boot camps and training with frontier model providers. He said consumption-based models let agencies pay for what they use and test use cases without long-term commitments. Controls such as token limits, notifications and usage monitoring can help agencies manage costs, according to Adams.

Carahsoft was founded in 2004 by President Craig Abod and describes itself as The Trusted Government IT Solutions Provider. The company closed 2025 with $22.5 billion in bookings and $125 billion in lifetime bookings, according to Virginia Business, and it counts more than 4,000 employees and more than 1,000 technology vendors. Adams has championed Carahsoft's work with Anthropic under the GSA OneGov agreement, which extends Claude access to government organizations at every level. The article provides no further timeline for the company's next steps.

Articles.Title: Carahsoft’s Mike Adams on Turning Government AI Pilots Into Mission Outcomes

stories.Headline: Study planning is better served by Monte Carlo simulation than AI-generated participants
stories.Summary:
The article is an opinion piece in Communications Psychology, published on nature.com on 11 November 2026, arguing that Monte Carlo simulation is a better basis for research planning than "silicon samples," which are AI-generated synthetic participants built from demographic profiles. The author contends that the two approaches differ in how transparent their assumptions are. A Monte Carlo simulation specifies a data-generating process, plausible effect sizes and error terms, and then repeatedly simulates experiments to estimate power, so its conclusions are conditional on stated assumptions. A silicon sample, by contrast, treats the output of a large language model as evidence about humans, and the researcher can adjust the prompts and demographic inputs but cannot inspect or alter the mechanism producing the data.

The article describes a thought experiment in which two researchers plan the same study. The first runs a Monte Carlo simulation generating 10,000 complete datasets for each combination of effect size, variance and sample size, and chooses a sample size offering at least 80% power across plausible scenarios. The second prompts a large language model to respond 10,000 times, each time with a distinct demographic persona, then uses the observed effect size to motivate a power analysis. The author argues the first approach offers the more defensible basis for planning. The author notes that the Nature paper that sparked the discussion found LLM-derived predictions correlated strongly with treatment effects across 70 nationally representative survey experiments, while systematically overestimating their magnitudes.

The author places the debate in the context of a growing body of work suggesting silicon samples could help with research planning, and acknowledges that even sceptics might accept their use for cheap pretesting. The article states that silicon sampling assumes not only a data-generating process but also which demographic variables matter and how prompts should be formatted, with no general method for either. It says formatting choices irrelevant to the phenomenon, such as prose versus bullet points, can substantially shift outputs. The author adds that a silicon sample's accuracy may not generalise across contexts, since a configuration may recover one feature of human data well and another poorly, and that results depend on the model chosen, hyperparameters such as temperature and the prompt content.

The article's central claim is that the model-human gap in silicon sampling does not shrink with more generated answers, unlike finite-sample error, which falls roughly tenfold when 100 times as many responses are generated. The author argues a Monte Carlo approach states conditional claims openly, while a silicon sample approach presents its conditional result as if the assumption were established. The article also notes that Monte Carlo simulations model sources of variation such as measurement error explicitly, for example through an error term with a stated variance, whereas silicon samples vary in ways that are harder to specify. The piece does not describe any further steps, responses from the authors of the cited work, or any forthcoming changes to practice.

Articles.Title: Study planning is better served by Monte Carlo simulation than AI-generated participants

stories.Headline: Microsoft data center in Washington state brings "a kind of boom" despite growing AI pushback
stories.Summary:
Microsoft has run its Columbia Data Center in Quincy, Washington, for about 20 years, and the town says the facility has brought a kind of boom to the area. Quincy's mayor, Paul Worley, told CBS News that additional tax revenue from the project helped fund a new high school and a hospital. He also said it has improved other critical services in the community. The reporting comes as opposition to data centers grows across the country.

Microsoft president Brad Smith described the company's pledges to the communities where it builds and runs data centers. He said Microsoft will put the community first and will not take steps that raise neighbors' electricity rates. The company also says it will replenish more water than it uses. Smith added that data centers power everyday actions like using a phone app, and he argued the industry needs to explain that role better to its critics. Microsoft says it employs roughly 700 people, which it puts at almost 9% of Quincy's roughly 8,000 residents.

Not everything has gone smoothly, according to the article. Electricity rates per kilowatt-hour in the area have risen by roughly 55% over the past 20 years, based on figures from the Grant County public utility. That increase is smaller than the rise in Washington state, where rates climbed 107% over the same period, and the national rise of 66%. The article also notes that some residents have been asked to leave their homes to make room for the roughly two dozen data centers that have arrived in the area. Smith said managing growth and its effect on residents' utility costs is the company's fundamental responsibility.

The context includes political pressure on the industry, since opposition to data centers helped Democratic candidates who pledged to stall new construction win in last week's midterm elections. More than half of voters said artificial intelligence and data centers were a significant factor in their votes, according to a CBS News exit poll. Smith said he wants a chance to make the case to residents, but he also said the people they have elected will make the final decisions. Yale professor Kenneth Gillingham has suggested that communities ask developers about their cooling technology, the facility's size and how it will generate electricity.

Articles.Title: Microsoft data center in Washington state brings "a kind of boom" despite growing AI pushback

stories.Headline: AI Heart MRI Measurements Improve Mortality Prediction
stories.Summary:
A study of more than 27,000 heart MRI patients found that artificial intelligence measurements of heart function predicted mortality slightly better than measurements made by clinicians. The retrospective, multicentre research was published online on 2 November 2026 in The Lancet Digital Health, and it was reported by EMJ on 11 November 2026. The study covered 27,382 patients who had cardiac MRI scans in the UK and the USA, with most scans coming from Barts Heart Centre in London and an additional cohort from the University of Pittsburgh Medical Centre. Researchers applied AI segmentation to the scans and compared the prognostic value of automated and clinician-derived left-ventricular ejection fraction. Over a median follow-up of 5.6 years, 3,458 patients died.

After adjusting for age and sex, the AI measurements gave a C index of 0.781, compared with 0.777 for clinician measurements, a difference the articles describe as modest. The AI-derived figures also offered a better statistical model fit. The researchers said automated analysis took roughly two to three seconds per patient, while earlier work by the team found expert clinician analysis typically took around 13 minutes. Ejection fraction guides decisions on heart failure treatment and implanted devices, so more consistent and efficient measurement could matter across imaging services. The articles stress that this time comparison was not a direct measure of time saved across a whole service.

The researchers, Joy G and colleagues, stressed that human oversight remains necessary, since automated errors were uncommon but clinicians still need to verify measurements and interpret them within the wider clinical picture. The articles say the study shows AI measurements were more closely associated with later mortality, but they do not show that adopting the tool changes treatment decisions or helps patients live longer. The authors and commentary call for prospective evaluation to see whether the small statistical gain translates into better care and how automated measurements perform alongside clinician review in routine workflows. For radiology teams, the findings give a reason to evaluate AI as an initial measurement tool, with its clinical value depending on quality assurance and evidence that faster analysis supports effective patient management.

Articles.Title: AI Heart MRI Measurements Improve Mortality Prediction

stories.Headline: Weil's Head of AI Looks to Rehome Halted Summer Associate Tech Program
stories.Summary:
Weil, Gotshal & Manges has halted a planned ten-week summer associate program focused on artificial intelligence, a program that was shuttered before it could begin amid the firm's ongoing collapse. The initiative was designed by chief AI and innovation officer Andrew Simon and was meant to place first-year law students alongside the firm's Lawyer Augmented Solutions Engineering and Research team, known as LASER. According to the report, the program would have replaced a conventional 1L summer experience. Reporter Tony Thompson covered the development in a Law.com article published on November 10, 2026. The program was built around hands-on technical training rather than traditional summer work.

Participants would learn Python, build neural networks, and then apply those skills to developing technology for use on real legal work. Those who completed it were expected to receive offers to return for Weil's 2028 2L summer, which would have made the program an alternative first-year route into the firm. Simon has said the goal was not to produce expert coders but to train lawyers who understood AI well enough to build and scrutinize tools effectively. The article describes the effort as an attempt to rethink how the next generation of lawyers might be trained on emerging technology.

Simon, who leads the firm's AI and innovation work, has said he intends to take the training model with him to wherever he lands next. The article presents this as his plan for the concept rather than any announced arrangement with another employer. The report does not specify what Simon will do next or name any firm that has agreed to host the program. It also does not detail how many students had been selected or what the program's budget was.

The piece frames the halted program as one of the lesser-known casualties of Weil's collapse. The article does not say what happens next for the program itself. Beyond Simon's stated intention to carry the model forward, the report offers no timeline, plans for the students who had expected to participate, or statements from the firm about whether any part of the initiative will continue. Readers seeking those details will need follow-up reporting.

Articles.Title: Weil's Head of AI Looks to Rehome Halted Summer Associate Tech Program

stories.Headline: Honeywell boosts Forge capabilities, says other AI enhancements coming
stories.Summary:
Honeywell Technologies on Monday unveiled AI-powered building intelligence, fire and life safety, and security upgrades to its Forge Cognition platform. The upgrades, called EBI One, build on the agentic AI and simulation features the company added in October. Honeywell also announced low-level carbon monoxide monitoring and fire safety tools, including incident command software and a system sensor detector that can tell fire signatures apart to cut down on nuisance alarms. The company says these moves show how it is rolling out AI across its technology stack, as it positions itself as a building-technology organization following the spin-off of its aerospace business earlier this year.

The combined EBI One and Forge Cognition offering adds several features for building operators. Alarm assist uses machine learning to interpret and classify alarms, while AI assist is a conversational tool that pulls building insights from operational data and documentation. An open integration network lets users build low-code or no-code applications on site, and a redesigned architecture speeds upgrades and reduces the risk of data loss. A browser interface also lets operators use EBI One Command and Control on the go. EBI is a building management system that unifies HVAC, security, fire and life safety, lighting and energy management in one centralized interface.

Honeywell also said it will release several upgrades to its fire and life safety products in early 2027. The LenelS2 Adaptive Intelligence Suite will provide AI-weighted alarm management, alarm contextualization, natural-language reporting, anomaly detection and guided workflows meant to reduce alarm fatigue. The suite will start by layering contextual AI onto LenelS2 OnGuard. The company also expects to release Niagara 5, the next generation of its framework, which lets systems from different buildings and vendors connect across HVAC, fire, security, access control, lighting and energy. Chief executive Vimal Kapur has said the company is leaning more heavily on LenelS2, which it acquired two years ago as part of its purchase of Carrier Global Corp.'s Global Access Solutions business.

Honeywell Technologies said the Forge platform is central to its growth, and that its building automation segment revenue rose 8 percent year over year in the third quarter of 2026. Growth was driven by double-digit gains in fire and security products and a stronger product introduction cycle, the company said on its earnings call. Forge Cognition launched on October 14 as a self-contained agentic AI and simulation platform for facility operations, developed alongside Nvidia and Dell Technologies. In its release, Honeywell said the combined trusted view of building assets and Forge Cognition intelligence should reduce engineering and commissioning work and help owners and operators move toward more autonomous building operations.

Articles.Title: Honeywell boosts Forge capabilities, says other AI enhancements coming

stories.Headline: North Smithfield man accused of creating AI-generated child sexual abuse material - WJAR
stories.Summary:
A former gymnastics and dance instructor from North Smithfield, Rhode Island, has been arrested and charged after federal prosecutors alleged he filmed a child and created artificial intelligence-generated child sexual abuse material. The Rhode Island U.S. Attorney's Office said 38-year-old Joseph Mello faces charges of attempted production of child pornography, receipt of child pornography, possession of and access with intent to view child pornography, and production of obscene visual representations of the sexual abuse of children. Mello was previously an instructor and participant at gymnastics, dance and cheerleading facilities in Rhode Island and southeastern Massachusetts, according to authorities. Prosecutors allege he tried to film a child in a bathroom and changing area at a dance studio where he took classes. He was arraigned on Monday and held temporarily pending a detention hearing scheduled for this Thursday.

Officials said Mello photographed multiple children at the facilities where he worked and allegedly used those photos to create AI-generated images and videos depicting child sexual abuse. Investigators also allege he possessed other child sexual abuse materials. Federal prosecutors said there may be additional victims and witnesses connected to the investigation. Parents who believe their child had close contact with Mello, or who are aware of him photographing children or contacting them, were urged to contact Homeland Security New England Victim Assistance at the email address given in the U.S. Attorney's Office news release.

First Assistant U.S. Attorney Charles C. Calenda said the case shows how quickly technology can be misused to exploit children. He said the defendant allegedly used artificial intelligence and other digital tools to create sexually explicit depictions of real children. Calenda said each image represents a child victim whose safety, privacy and dignity were violated. He said the office, with its law enforcement partners, is committed to protecting children, identifying victims and holding accountable those who use any technology to facilitate child exploitation.

Articles.Title: North Smithfield man accused of creating AI-generated child sexual abuse material - WJAR

stories.Headline: CoreWeave beats on revenue and lifts guidance, easing AI slowdown concerns
stories.Summary:
CoreWeave reported its third-quarter 2026 results on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, beating analyst expectations on revenue and raising its full-year guidance. The company posted revenue of $3.66 billion against an expected $3.55 billion, a jump of 168% from about $1.36 billion a year earlier. It posted an adjusted loss of 95 cents per share against an expected loss of $1.16, while its GAAP net loss was $709 million, or $1.27 per share. Its shares rose in extended trading, though the stock had lost more than 40% of its value over the prior month.

The company now expects 2026 adjusted operating income of $1.275 billion to $1.375 billion on revenue of $13 billion to $13.3 billion, up from its August forecast of $960 million to $1.15 billion and $12.4 billion to $13.2 billion. It is targeting $37 billion to $39 billion in full-year capital expenditures and still expects 1.85 gigawatts of active power by the end of 2026. Its revenue backlog reached $132.5 billion, up from $104 billion in June. Chief executive Michael Intrator said most of the capital needed for 2027 will come from client prepayments and hardware partner financing, with a limited amount of new raising. Finance chief Nitin Agrawal said the company does not intend to issue more parent-level unsecured debt through 2027 at current yields and projects under $5 billion in parent-level debt financing through that year.

Intrator said the company does not expect the recent regulatory setbacks for data center development to affect it, since nearly all of its power is online or permitted and under construction. He said CoreWeave has chosen not to sell all of its available capacity to buyers in its queue, preferring to bring infrastructure to market when it is further along. Agrawal said that if the company focused only on committed backlog, 2027 capital spending would stay in line with 2026 while revenue and EBITDA grow significantly. Analysts quoted in the article described the result as encouraging demand news while noting that the cost and availability of capital remain critical concerns.

The wider backdrop includes rising interest rates that have pushed lenders out of the market, with some CoreWeave bond yields topping 16%, and a broader slide in AI infrastructure stocks. Nvidia, which supplies GPUs and capital to CoreWeave and similar providers, has dropped nearly 10% to start the week after its board said it hired outside counsel to investigate chief executive Jensen Huang over an alleged affair with a suspected Chinese spy. Anthropic, a key CoreWeave customer, is scheduled to debut on the Nasdaq next week, and its updated prospectus suggests a valuation of around $1.4 trillion. Neocloud peer Nebius reports earnings Thursday.

Articles.Title: CoreWeave beats on revenue and lifts guidance, easing AI slowdown concerns

stories.Headline: How AI, computer vision, and augmented reality are transforming flour mills
stories.Summary:
I can't write this as a breaking news story, because the article is a feature piece and not a report of a news event. It describes how AI, computer vision and augmented reality could be used in flour mills, and it gives no dated event, no named actor who did something, and no official response. There is no single incident to report on, so the "what happened, who did it and when" structure you asked for has nothing to attach to. What the article does contain, drawn from its own text, is the following. Written by Prof. Dr. Farhan Alfin, an independent milling consultant, and published by Miller Magazine on 10 November 2026, it argues that three technologies can work together in flour mills.

Computer vision lets computers interpret camera images to identify machinery and read gauges. AI analyzes that information alongside sensor data and historical records to diagnose problems and predict failures. Augmented reality displays instructions and diagnostic data over real equipment through tablets or smart glasses. The article gives a few specific examples. A bearing temperature reading of 72°C is shown alongside a moderate failure probability and a recommendation to relubricate within 48 hours.

Computer vision is described as able to assess incoming wheat for foreign seeds, stones and insect damage. The article also lists challenges to adoption, including reliable wireless communication, dust-resistant cameras, cybersecurity and integration with existing control systems. The article offers no new deployment, no regulatory change and no company announcement. It does not report any mill that has adopted these tools, and it does not quote any reaction from industry bodies, regulators or manufacturers. If you want, I can write a 650 to 850 word feature-style summary in five paragraphs of four to five sentences each, covering the article's arguments and examples, while keeping its authorship and date clear.

Articles.Title: How AI, computer vision, and augmented reality are transforming flour mills

stories.Headline: Researchers Explore Quantum Inspired AI Repair
stories.Summary:
Researchers from QDeep and ITMO University have developed Tree-Ising, a method that repairs repetitive reasoning in small language models by making targeted changes to their internal weights. The work is described in a preprint posted to arXiv, and the main repairs ran on conventional graphics processors. One solver uses simulated bifurcation, a quantum-inspired method that runs on classical hardware. A separate quantum experiment tested only a small part of the problem and did not show any quantum advantage.

The method targets reasoning loops, in which a model keeps repeating parts of its answer instead of reaching a conclusion. Rather than retraining the whole model, Tree-Ising searches for selected edits to the weights, the numerical settings that shape a network's responses. It represents these edits as decision trees and converts them into Ising problems, a mathematical framework for choosing among interacting options. Computer solvers then pick which edits to apply. The reported gains are specific to test conditions, and the researchers say broader use will depend on scaling and practical validation.

Reported results include 55.1% accuracy on the MATH-500 mathematics benchmark for the Qwen3.5-0.8B model, compared with 51.7% for an earlier AI-agent repair under the same protocol. For Qwen3.5-2B, accuracy on the GSM8K benchmark rose from 21.6% to 69.4% under greedy decoding. In the quantum experiment, the team ran an eight-variable repair subproblem on an IBM Heron processor using the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm. That run tested whether a small piece of the problem could execute on quantum hardware, not whether a full model could be repaired that way.

The study was led by Hadi Salloum of QDeep in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, and Ammar Ali of ITMO University's Lab for Efficient AI and Data. Salloum said in the accompanying release that the results show targeted model repair can be framed as an optimization problem, and that the IBM experiment is an initial proof of concept. He added that if the approach can be scaled and deliver practical benefits, it could become a promising direction for quantum computers to help improve large language models. The article notes that arXiv preprints have not undergone formal peer review, so the findings remain unverified by that process.

Articles.Title: Researchers Explore Quantum Inspired AI Repair

stories.Headline: The Company That Published Fake Journalists in Sports Illustrated is Collapsing Dramatically After Massive AI Rebrand
stories.Summary:
Paradium.AI, the company formerly known as The Arena Group, reported steep third-quarter losses on November 9, 2026, and its shares fell about 14 percent that day. The company posted a net loss of $3.6 million for the third quarter of 2026, a sharp reversal from the same quarter a year earlier, when it earned a $6.9 million net profit and its revenue was around 30 percent higher. Its stock now trades around $0.077, placing it firmly among penny stocks. The results were the first the company released since it rebranded in August from The Arena Group to Paradium, a move it described as a shift toward becoming a publicly traded AI company.

As part of that rebrand, Paradium bought InfoSentience, an AI firm whose product it describes as turning live structured data into accurate, on-brand stories at scale. It also launched Cutter Studios, an AI-powered video editing and distribution tool. The company's portfolio includes Parade, TheStreet, Athlon Sports, College Spun Media, and Men's Journal, among others. In its press release, Paradium blamed industry-wide problems, including weaker referral traffic and distribution struggles, many of which the company tied to AI's effect on the digital world. It also cited a $1.3 million reversal of an employee retention tax credit asset that was disallowed, and said its advertising revenue fell as traffic dropped.

Paradium's chief executive, Paul Edmondson, said in a statement that the company sees major opportunity in the age of AI and is fully committed to it. He argued that its real momentum comes from tools like Cutter Studios and InfoSentience, which he said are already raising output and efficiency. Paradium also highlighted that it used AI to produce 15 percent more articles than in the prior quarter, and pointed to an upcoming AI task management system called Tablation. The company's embrace of AI stands in stark contrast to its past, since in November 2023 a Futurism investigation found that The Arena Group had published AI-generated articles bylined by fake writers on Sports Illustrated's website.

That scandal led to the firing of several executives, including then-CEO Ross Levinsohn, and the company eventually lost control of the Sports Illustrated brand. The articles note that the AI content had come from a third-party contractor, AdVon Commerce, which supplied similar material to other publishers. Paradium is not alone in struggling with an AI-focused strategy, as BuzzFeed also reported weak third-quarter results while its own AI push has yet to pay off. The articles do not say what further steps Paradium will take beyond the launch of Tablation.

Articles.Title: The Company That Published Fake Journalists in Sports Illustrated is Collapsing Dramatically After Massive AI Rebrand

stories.Headline: AI Needn’t Be Trustworthy, Teens Say. It Just Has to Be Less Risky Than People
stories.Summary:
Researchers at The Rithm Project, a nonprofit focused on human connection in the age of AI, released a new report on how young people are turning to AI for emotional support. The report follows a March survey of 2,383 people ages 13 to 24, which found that 18% use AI for personal and emotional support and 15% talk to AI characters and personas. Researchers then conducted in-depth interviews, analyzing 29 conversations with participants ages 16 to 24. The researchers caution that these interviews are not representative and rely on a self-selected group, so the results are case studies rather than a statistical portrait.

The report describes a pattern in which users begin with mundane uses such as homework help, grammar checks, translating an MRI report or chatting with an anime character. In nearly every case, the shift came at what the researchers call a "gateway moment," typically a rupture in a human relationship, such as a friendship ending, a boyfriend forgetting a birthday or a sibling argument. One young woman who was not asked to homecoming turned to AI and asked whether she was lovable and pretty. Alison Lee, the group's chief research and development officer, describes large language models as "omnibots" that can handle many tasks, and says each use gives the model more context, making its answers feel more personal. By the time a crisis arrives, she said, AI has become the go-to advisor.

Lee said the young people interviewed are not naive about chatbot flaws, which they can list, including sycophancy, hallucinations and a tendency to tell users what they want to hear. They keep using AI because it does not have to be trustworthy, only less risky than a real person, and they see its biases as predictable and fixable. Michael Robb, head of research at Common Sense Media, said the finding rings true, adding that teens "only have to trust it more than an alternative at that moment." He said teens are acutely sensitive to what friends think, and that AI carries no such social threat, which makes it appealing to them. Robb also questioned how much control young people really have, noting that many features of AI products are built in and hard to avoid.

The report also finds that teens often hide their AI use from parents out of fear of judgment. One 16-year-old named Meghan said she tells her parents she uses ChatGPT for school and decision-making but not as a therapist, because she does not want them to think it is unsafe. Whether AI draws young people closer to others or pushes them apart depends largely on what they ask it, the subjects told researchers. Those who asked it to help them see another person's point of view often returned with more confidence, while one 21-year-old named Aaron said he sometimes showed his girlfriend AI responses that sided with him as "leverage." Lee said adults give young people little guidance, offering only advice to avoid AI or to go all in on it.

Articles.Title: AI Needn’t Be Trustworthy, Teens Say. It Just Has to Be Less Risky Than People

stories.Headline: New framework grades AI jailbreaks across capability gains, scope, and how easy they are to deploy — Frontier Model Forum proposes CVSS-style rating system for new AI models
stories.Summary:
The Frontier Model Forum, an industry group whose project began in 2023 with four founding companies (Anthropic, Google, Microsoft, and OpenAI), has released a Jailbreak Rating Framework that tracks how easily an AI model can be pushed past its safeguards. The framework also estimates how much collateral damage a jailbroken model could cause if it were used for cyber-attacks across the internet. The published document is a rough analog to the CVSS security rating system, aimed at classifying the type and severity of large language model jailbreaks across several axes and multiple frontier providers. Version 1.0 is a work in progress, and the group is accepting comments and suggestions until December 21. The article notes that relying on the system before then is inadvisable.

The framework has four scoring components split across two categories: severity, which measures how serious a jailbreak technique is, and likelihood, which measures how easy it is to find and weaponize. Each component is graded from zero to three, and the two category scores combine into a final rating from low to critical. Capability gain is described as the most important dimension, acting as both a floor and a ceiling for the other scores, so a jailbreak that offers nothing beyond existing means is treated as meaningless in the grading. A zero rating does not mean a flaw is harmless, only that it should be handled through standard practices such as platform policies and conventional cybersecurity ratings. The baseline also shifts as models evolve, so a zero in 2026 would not necessarily mean the same thing in 2028.

Capability scope rates whether a jailbreak works for only one action or target, with zero meaning it is a one-trick pony and three meaning it can, without specific redesign, drive work across at least two unrelated categories of cyber-warfare. Ease of deployment considers how much human expertise and steering a jailbreak needs, with a three meaning a novice can use it with little effort to run an automated cyber-warfare task. Ease of discovery measures how hard the jailbreak is to find, with a zero requiring heavy spending on inference tokens, elevated access, or specialized infrastructure, and a three meaning anyone can look up and use the technique. The article gives a denial-of-service example in which a jailbreak offers little advantage because black-market services and other models with fewer safeguards already exist.

The article draws a comparison with Anthropic's safeguard-breakage classifiers, which the company proposed in July 2026 after an incident that led to Claude Fable 5 being temporarily unavailable. That proposal also used a moving baseline and considered only jailbreaks that improve on cyber-warfare capabilities already available, and the article describes the two documents as strikingly similar. Because Anthropic is an FMF founding member, it may have helped develop the new standard, though the article says there is no confirmation either way. The article itself also opens by noting recent high-profile headlines about AI models letting loose from their safeguards.

Articles.Title: New framework grades AI jailbreaks across capability gains, scope, and how easy they are to deploy — Frontier Model Forum proposes CVSS-style rating system for new AI models

stories.Headline: Everybot, a physical artificial intelligence (AI) service robot company, announced on the 11th that
stories.Summary:
Everybot, a physical AI service robot company, announced on November 11 that it had run a second robot field demonstration at VL LeWest, a premium senior residence in Magok District, Seoul. The residence was built by Lotte Engineering & Construction and is operated by Lotte Hotel & Resort. The aim was to test whether the robots could realistically be introduced into an operating facility. The event followed a first field demonstration held on October 8.

The second demonstration went beyond simple functional checks and examined a robot operating model tied to real service needs. The areas reviewed included convenience for residents, support for movement, and guidance and patrol tasks inside the building. VL LeWest offers residential units, restaurants, a fitness center, a sauna, and a lounge. Everybot said the results would guide its plans to seek commercial supply of service robots at the residence.

An Everybot official described the event as a step to check the application plan for service demand and operating conditions with actual installation in mind. The official said the company would keep upgrading its robot solutions and expand commercial opportunities by reflecting the needs and conditions of users in the field. Everybot also plans to extend its business into other business-to-business markets, such as silver towns and elderly-friendly housing, in response to population aging. The articles give no figures on contract value, deployment timing, or the number of robots involved.

stories.Headline: UPF Summit to Address Digital Infrastructure and AI in Fez-Meknes
stories.Summary:
The University of Fez (UPF) will host a regional digital summit in Fez-Meknes, titled "Fez-Meknes Smart & Sovereign Region 2030," with the article published on November 10, 2026, indicating the event is set for the following day. The summit will bring together representatives of public institutions, businesses, universities, and technology experts to present four projects meant to strengthen the region's technological infrastructure, improve digital healthcare, and support artificial intelligence research. The organizers say the discussions will follow Morocco's Digital Morocco 2030 strategy. The four projects are the Fez-Meknes Regional Micro Data Center, the Fez-Meknes Digital Health Living Lab, the Regional SOC / Cybersecurity Hub, and the Fez-Meknes Digital Innovation & AI Lab.

The Micro Data Center would provide local, high-availability data hosting for regional digital services, critical data storage, and new AI applications, and it would serve as the base for the other initiatives. The Digital Health Living Lab would bring together healthcare professionals, researchers, and technology companies to test and develop digital health tools, including telemedicine and clinical AI. The cybersecurity hub, linked to the data center, would monitor and protect critical infrastructure and local authorities against cyber threats through security operations, threat intelligence, and incident response. The Digital Innovation & AI Lab would offer computing and prototyping resources to teachers, students, and startups, aiming to turn research into practical applications. The article does not give budgets or completion dates for any of these projects.

The summit will open with speeches from representatives of UPF, the Fez-Meknes regional administration, and several government bodies, including the Ministry of Digital Transition and Administrative Reform, the Ministry of Industry and Trade, and the Ministry of Higher Education, Scientific Research and Innovation. Speakers from the Regional Council, the Digital Development Agency (ADD), Maroc Data Center, and Rwadtech are also scheduled to take part. According to the organizers, the event will close at 6 p.m. with a summary of the discussions and the signing of partnership agreements, though the article does not name the parties to those agreements.

The initiative sits within Digital Morocco 2030, a national strategy launched in September 2024 to position the country as a digital hub, expand public service digitization, develop digital skills, and strengthen the digital economy. The government has set a target of creating 240,000 direct jobs in the digital economy by 2030. UPF said the summit aims to connect public institutions, academic institutions, and businesses to identify areas of cooperation and link scientific research with regional economic priorities. The article does not say what follows the summit beyond the signed agreements.

Articles.Title: UPF Summit to Address Digital Infrastructure and AI in Fez-Meknes

stories.Headline: AI scanners at rental car lots are ‘definitely not perfect,’ watchdog says - WDAM-TV
stories.Summary:
Several rental car companies are now using AI scanning systems to check vehicles for damage, and a consumer watchdog says renters should document the car themselves to avoid a surprise bill. The scanners work like a car wash at pick-up or drop-off, with cameras taking photos and videos from different angles to look for damage. Teresa Murray, consumer watchdog director with the U.S. Public Interest Research Group, said the technology has both benefits and drawbacks. Her main concern is that artificial intelligence can make errors that matter in a rental setting, and she said it is definitely not perfect.

Murray gave examples of how the system could go wrong. She said a splotch of dirt could be mistaken for a dent, and a shadow could look like significant damage. Her advice is the same whether a company uses AI or an employee inspects the vehicle, which is to take a few minutes to look the car over closely before leaving the lot. She recommends taking pictures of every part of the car and recording a walk-around video, including crouching down to check the wheels, hubcaps, interior, trunk and glass. She said renters should allow 5 to 10 minutes for this, depending on whether a live worker is present or not.

Murray also recommends doing the same inspection before and after the trip if a company uses an AI scanner. Having personal photos gives a renter a way to challenge a charge if a damage bill arrives later. The article does not describe any specific company's response or any regulatory action. It also does not say how widely the scanners are being used or whether any renters have already disputed charges. The piece is a consumer advice report focused on what renters can do to protect themselves.

Articles.Title: AI scanners at rental car lots are ‘definitely not perfect,’ watchdog says - WDAM-TV

stories.Headline: Why does AI visibility matter for furniture stores?
stories.Summary:
Jake Freedman, CEO of Dovr Media, is urging home furnishings retailers to address how their businesses appear to AI shopping assistants, according to a Furniture Today article by Spencer Musick dated November 10, 2026. He made the remarks at High Point, where he argued that a retailer left off an assistant's recommendations becomes invisible to the customer, regardless of how long it has been in business. Freedman said longevity is not a strategic plan. He framed the immediate issue as whether a retailer's online presence gives an assistant enough clear, consistent information to recommend its products. Freedman said AI assistants give consumers one, two or sometimes three recommendations, which he described as usually significantly better than what a Google search would return.

The article notes that this shorter list makes inclusion decisive, since a retailer cannot explain its value to a shopper it is never shown to. Freedman listed the details he said matter: product data, category page data, site health, return policy, shipping policy, delivery and financing. He called having these details built out a trust indicator between retailers and AI platforms. He said doing this work alone is challenging. Freedman said retailers once gated their websites to keep bots out and withheld prices, but he now wants as many bots crawling their sites as possible.

He said the fidelity and quality of product information separates good from great, and he pointed to thin listings, limited photography, missing descriptions and non-standardized information as weak spots. He also cited an old Yelp listing with a differently formatted address as an example of inconsistency across websites. Freedman recommended outside expertise for this work, comparing it to electrical wiring that a store owner should not attempt alone. The article reports that most of his company's time is now spent on this work. Freedman drew a comparison with earlier technology shifts, recalling that some retailers ten years ago refused to build websites, saying they had survived 60 years without one.

He said AI-native entrants in their early 20s, some still in college, are entering home furnishings with AI-first strategies. He said some of these competitors do not pay rent, carry tenured salespeople or pay six-figure annual software costs. Freedman tied the argument to meeting customers where they shop, naming radio, television and the Internet as earlier examples. He said that now means AI. The article does not report any regulatory action, stated timeline or specific planned changes beyond these remarks.

Articles.Title: Why does AI visibility matter for furniture stores?

stories.Headline: Artificial Intelligence Models Reshape Receptor Structure Prediction and Molecular Pharmacology
stories.Summary:
