Weill Cornell Medicine says that protected health information from a radiology research project at NewYork-Presbyterian was entered into artificial intelligence tools and processed using machine learning without authorization. The incident occurred during a radiology research study in June, and the institution discovered it on September 6 and launched an investigation. Patients are now being told that some of their information may have been breached. The notice to patients was sent in the week before the report, and the health system described the matter as an unauthorized use of an AI model.

The data involved was limited, according to the health system, and officials said there is no indication that any patient information has been misused. The exposed information included medical record numbers and radiology accession numbers, which are internal tracking identifiers for images. It may also have included dates and times of radiology services, the locations where patients received care, and clinical details such as diagnoses, treatment, surgical and procedural histories, and medication information. Names, addresses, phone numbers, emails, Social Security numbers, and patient-specific financial information were not included, officials said.

Weill Cornell leaders said they suspended the research activity once the problem was found and asked that all involved data be deleted. They also said they have provided additional education to reinforce compliance with the institution's requirements for appropriate AI use and patient privacy. The health system said it has not so far found evidence that unauthorized individuals accessed patients' protected health information. Leaders expressed regret for any concern the incident may cause and said they are expanding security measures and providing additional training.

The report places this case alongside a recent breach at Johns Hopkins, where a staff member at Bayview Medical Center reportedly uploaded a spreadsheet to a public AI website that had not been approved for use, exposing data of more than 3,000 patients. The article notes that as generative and agentic AI tools spread through healthcare, IT and security teams must stay vigilant about which technologies are used and how. It argues such third-party tools call for more robust oversight and staff education. The article does not say what further regulatory steps or patient follow-up will occur.

Articles.Title: Improper AI use leads to another data incident, more patient notifications

stories.Headline: Brazil's AI Development Strategy Needs an Edge Layer
stories.Summary:
Brazil's government announced in August that it will invest 2.3 billion reais ($444.2 million) in two AI projects, including a supercomputing partnership with China's Huawei and iFlytek and a tender for a second supercomputer. These systems are meant to run on centralized data gathered and entrusted to the government, supporting public services such as digital public tools, automated procurement assistance, and telehealth transcription. Esther Dweck, Brazil's Minister of Management and Innovation in Public Services, has described a strategy called "Base de Dados Brasil" that would centralize, integrate, and protect citizens' data for use in AI training. The article argues this focus overlooks edge AI, in which inference runs on local hardware instead of distant data centers.

The article contends that many public and private AI uses in Brazil do not need frontier capabilities and instead need reliable, bounded, locally controlled inference along with workers who can maintain it. It gives examples of edge AI in industry, such as defect detection on textile or footwear lines, predictive maintenance in packaging and food processing, and structural monitoring on mining sites. It also says local edge infrastructure is an industrial policy choice that trains people to maintain hardware that cannot be offshored. By contrast, a July 2026 Getulio Vargas Foundation study estimated that for a 100-megawatt data center, 85% of jobs are tied to construction and only about 4% become permanent operation and maintenance roles. The author adds that a 2025 WEF and Accenture review describes China organizing industrial AI by sector needs, with provinces building clusters around their own strengths.

The author states that Brazil's Nova Indústria Brasil policy, launched in January 2024, sets aside 300 billion reais (about $58 billion) in financing through 2026 for six missions with targets for 2033, and that it has yet to incorporate regional integration or local AI policy. Andrew Ng, co-founder of Google Brain and former chief scientist at Baidu, has argued in a 2022 IEEE Spectrum interview that small, specialized models trained on good data, sometimes with as few as 50 examples, can serve manufacturing better than giant models. The article notes that the policy's fourth mission concerns digital transformation on the factory floor, while Minister Dweck's public remarks have centered on national data infrastructure and a unified digital identity. It also points out that the Redata regime (Lei 15.504/2026, signed September 2026) suspends federal taxes on electronic components and IT equipment only for companies with approved data center projects, excluding Simples Nacional enrollees.

The article describes Brazil's large, mostly informal repair workforce, where informality likely exceeds the national rate of 37.5% reported by IBGE. It estimates roughly 480 million computers, tablets, and smartphones are in active use in the country, and argues that this repair market sustains specialized technical labor that edge AI policy could formalize and extend. It says that repair workers are sometimes treated as targets by police rather than as technicians. The author also cites Brazil's Pix payment system as an example of centrally standardized digital public infrastructure. As a concrete edge case, the CESAR innovation center's Manaus unit and UCB Power developed a computer vision system for inspecting battery components at UCB Power's factory in the Amazon, using a 4K camera and local processing.

The article also reports education and labor figures that it presents as limits on the centralized path. According to Brazil's Ministry of Labor and Employment, 84% of employed young Brazilians work in jobs that do not require specific qualifications, and only 1 in 7 holds a technical or higher-level post. A 2025 CIEE and Instituto Locomotiva survey found that only 12% of high school students want to pursue engineering. In the PISA 2025 results published in September, Brazil again scored below the OECD average in math. The article argues the scarce resource in edge AI is technicians rather than silicon.

Articles.Title: Brazil's AI Development Strategy Needs an Edge Layer

stories.Headline: Pakistan's AI Future Discussed at IIADP Dialogue in Karachi
stories.Summary:
The Indus Institute for AI & Digital Policy (IIADP) held a closed-door fireside chat on November 11, 2026, at the National Incubation Center (NIC) Karachi, inside NED University of Engineering and Technology. The session, titled "AI & Digital Pakistan: From Policy to Innovation," gathered representatives from government, academia, business, startups and the legal profession to discuss Pakistan's artificial intelligence and digital policy landscape. Senator Dr. Afnan Ullah Khan, a member of the Senate Standing Committee on IT & Telecommunications, joined to offer a parliamentary view on how technology, legislation and digital governance are changing. Hamza Ali Chaudhry, Executive Director of IIADP, moderated the discussion.

Other attendees included Syed Azfar Hussain, Project Director of NIC Karachi, Dr. Danish ur Rehman Khan, Technical Advisor to the Vice Chancellor of NED University, and Muhammad Ali Tariq, Deputy Secretary of Anti-Crime & Anti-Terrorism. The participants spoke candidly about opportunities and challenges in artificial intelligence, digital innovation, entrepreneurship and technology governance. They also considered international frameworks, including the OECD AI Principles and the G7 Hiroshima AI Process, which aim to set responsible standards for AI. The organisers stressed that Pakistan needs policies that encourage innovation while addressing regulatory, ethical and social concerns.

NIC Karachi took part as Growth Partner. The centre was established in 2018 at NED University and is funded by Ignite under the Ministry of IT & Telecommunication. It supports technology startups through incubation, mentorship, investor access and industry links. The articles say the discussion pointed to the need for closer cooperation between policymakers, academia, industry and entrepreneurs so that policy keeps pace with technological innovation. IIADP, which works on research, policy dialogue and stakeholder engagement, says these meetings are meant to support informed policymaking and stronger ties between decision-makers and Pakistan's technology sector.

Articles.Title: Pakistan's AI Future Discussed at IIADP Dialogue in Karachi - ARYnews.tv

stories.Headline: DOE Advances AI Cybersecurity for Critical Infrastructure
stories.Summary:
The Department of Energy is advancing artificial intelligence-powered cybersecurity technologies through a research initiative meant to strengthen the resilience of the nation's critical infrastructure against cyberattacks, according to a report published Tuesday by GovCIO Media & Research. The initiative is the AI-FORTS program, short for Artificial Intelligence for Operationally Resilient Technologies and Systems. It is managed by the department's Office of Cybersecurity, Energy Security, and Emergency Response, known as CESER. The program was launched in 2024 and organizes its research around three priorities.

Those priorities are securing energy infrastructure from AI-enabled threats, using AI to strengthen cyber defenses, and protecting AI technologies deployed within energy systems. Sage Briscoe, CESER technical program manager and head of AI-FORTS, said that introducing new software into critical infrastructure requires organizations to assess whether it could create additional vulnerabilities or give attackers another way into a network. AI-FORTS aligns with the first strategic goal in CESER's fiscal years 2026-2030 strategic plan, which calls for developing world-class security technologies. The department identifies national laboratory partnerships and utility collaboration as important parts of its approach. The department's fiscal year 2027 congressional budget justification also lists AI-FORTS among its planned research and development investments.

The budget document says the department intends to shift cybersecurity research toward AI-focused capabilities that help critical infrastructure keep operating through compromise. One example of AI-FORTS research is Communications and Cybersecurity for the Energy Edge, or C2E2, a project developed through CESER's partnership with Sandia National Laboratories. In September, the department reported that C2E2 had cut energy-system data preparation from about two months to a few hours. It also reported 95-percent accuracy in detecting and locating cyber threats, with actionable intelligence available in near real time. Over the coming year, the C2E2 team plans to explore using large language models to build user-friendly impact assessments for energy infrastructure cybersecurity personnel.

CESER and Sandia are also advancing Scaled Testing for AI Systems, or STAISYS, which evaluates AI technologies in simulated environments representing critical energy infrastructure. According to Sandia, STAISYS is one of four Sandia-led projects funded through AI-FORTS. The effort uses emulated cyber-physical environments to assess how AI systems perform under realistic operating conditions and potential cyberattacks. Separately, CESER and Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory introduced the Mjölnir AI Testbed in April. The platform is designed to assess the cybersecurity and reliability of AI models intended for energy-sector applications by exposing them to adversarial testing.

Articles.Title: DOE Advances AI Cybersecurity for Critical Infrastructure - ExecutiveGov

stories.Headline: AI Takes Center Stage at Tech-Forward AFM With Innovation Hub and AFM House Expansion
stories.Summary:
The American Film Market, the five-day independent film marketplace in Los Angeles produced by the Independent Film and Television Alliance, is putting artificial intelligence at the center of its 2026 edition. The market is expanding its Innovation Hub, a space where exhibitors show off new technologies reshaping Hollywood, and is opening its first AFM House, a 15,000-square-foot venue across from the AFM headquarters at the Fairmont Century Plaza. Nearly 20 companies are now set to take part in the Hub, and a new run of panels will discuss AI's impact on the industry. The Hub began last year in collaboration with the Marché du Film, the Cannes Film Festival's marketplace, which also leaned heavily into AI this year.

The growth reflects a wider change in how Hollywood views the technology in production, sales and distribution. Jackie Brenneman, who is leading her first AFM after becoming IFTA president in January, says technology will be a key driver whatever people think about AI. She draws a distinction between AI as a creative tool, which draws more debate, and AI used to analyze data and make predictions, which she says has been in use for a long time. Among the returning participants is Largo.ai, a Swiss firm backed by Sylvester Stallone, which uses AI to help determine whether an idea is producible and offers tools such as simulated focus groups. Its CEO, Sami Arpa, says the company is data-assisted rather than eager to bring AI into the creative process, and he acknowledges that some tools go further and replace human creativity.

Other companies are pushing further into fully AI-generated work. Oxen.ai, founded in 2022 by former IBM veteran Greg Schoeninger, operates as both a platform for building AI shots and a studio that produces them for clients. Its founder says the company publishes the token cost of each model before users pay, a transparency he believes sets it apart from competitors that rely on monthly subscriptions. Schoeninger says AFM approached the company after its September summit, and he describes the industry as reaching a tipping point where more executives are willing to discuss their use of AI openly. AFM panels will also cover the topic, including a Producers Guild of America session on the AI decisions facing film and television leaders and a discussion hosted by the Cine Group.

The approach carries some risk, as seen when the Urbanworld festival lost a longtime sponsor, the Writers Guild of America, after hosting an AI program. Major festivals such as Cannes exclude AI-generated films from their official selections. Brenneman says the market is not a festival and makes no selections, leaving those judgments to buyers, whose role is to decide which films reach audiences. Her stated job is to provide a forum where that can happen. The articles do not report how attendance or deals at this year's market turn out.

Articles.Title: AI Takes Center Stage at Tech-Forward AFM With Innovation Hub and AFM House Expansion

stories.Headline: Anthropic heads for lower than expected $1.3 trillion valuation in stock market debut
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, the artificial intelligence company behind the Claude chatbot, is heading for a stock market debut that could value it at around $1.3 trillion, below the $2 trillion some backers predicted in the summer. The loss-making firm plans to list its shares on New York's Nasdaq exchange this month, offering them at between $70 and $78 each and raising up to $64 billion. Anthropic will trade under the symbol ANT from 19 November, and it will be the first fully AI-focused company to go public. The listing is set against a volatile period for big technology firms, after the Nasdaq fell sharply following last week's US midterm elections over concerns that a Democrat-led Congress could slow AI development and the building of data centres.

The company's latest results for the six months to the end of June show revenue rising to $16.2 billion from $1.1 billion a year earlier. Its pre-tax loss, however, grew to $80.7 billion from $12.9 billion over the same period. Anthropic has told investors that its future success depends largely on developing the most advanced AI models, and that any failure to do so could hurt its business. The valuation range is also below that of SpaceX, Elon Musk's rocket, satellite and AI company, which listed in June at a value of nearly $1.8 trillion.

Fiona Cincotta, a senior market analyst at City Index, described the $64 billion fundraising as fairly bullish given the recent volatility and concerns about AI. She said it suggests the company remains upbeat about AI demand. Anthropic has also acknowledged in a recent warning that advanced AI systems could pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity if they were misused or allowed to operate with a high degree of autonomy without proper safeguards. The company has said it remains committed to developing AI that benefits people. The company was co-founded in 2021 by Dario and Daniela Amodei and five others, all of whom previously worked at OpenAI, the rival behind ChatGPT, which plans its own listing early next year.

Articles.Title: Anthropic heads for lower than expected $1.3 trillion valuation in stock market debut

stories.Headline: 8 questions for the Wells Fargo wealth unit’s AI chief
stories.Summary:
Wells Fargo's wealth and investment management unit has been using an AI assistant called AI Teammate, according to an interview with Andre Mansour, the bank's head of artificial intelligence, published by Banking Dive on November 10, 2026. Mansour joined Wells Fargo about six months earlier from Google and helped launch the tool, which was rolled out in the most recent quarter. The assistant works as a conversational layer over Advisor Gateway, a single platform with more than 200 tools that advisers use daily. Mansour said it has handled hundreds of thousands of interactions, and tasks that once took hours now take minutes.

The main gains, he said, come from reducing the clicks and time advisers and client associates spend gathering information and building client materials. Meeting preparation is the clearest example, since the assistant can combine investment research, client relationship notes and to-do items into an agenda in a prompt or two. Mansour also described using it to summarize daily investment insights from the Wells Fargo Investment Institute instead of reading each report. He framed the change as making advisers faster while leaving the job's outcomes unchanged.

Mansour said Wells Fargo intends to move quickly but not at the expense of safety, and he pointed to protections for client data and investment guidance kept within set guidelines. He also addressed the expected transfer of wealth to millennials and Gen Z, describing two channels: a consumer AI product called Fargo, which he said has logged over a billion interactions, and advisers who review what clients get from their own AI agents. He argued that experienced advisers remain essential and imagined a future where AI agents handle monitoring and research while humans make the decisions. The interview was edited for clarity and brevity.

Articles.Title: 8 questions for the Wells Fargo wealth unit’s AI chief

stories.Headline: As AI Anxiety Grows, UVA Symposium to Examine What Human Flourishing Looks Like in an AI-Driven World
stories.Summary:
The University of Virginia's Contemplative Sciences Center will host AI Anxiety + Human Flourishing, a public symposium on November 18 and 19, 2026, at the Contemplative Commons. The event asks how the future generation can be prepared for artificial intelligence and brings together students, technologists, thought leaders and contemplative practitioners. Its focus is on emerging adults and the stresses that rapid AI adoption places on them. The Contemplative Commons opened to the public in fall 2024 as a space for contemplative research and practice.

The program will address AI's effects on work and higher education, youth mental health, AI ethics and the wider social consequences of new technologies. Its proceedings will form the basis of an undergraduate course on AI Anxiety at UVA, and a model of that course will be available to other universities. Speakers named in the announcement include Anton Korinek of Anthropic, who is on leave as a UVA economics professor, Bethany Teachman of UVA's Thriving Youth in a Digital Environment initiative, Father Michael Baggot of the Pontifical Athenaeum Regina Apostolorum and Paul Tudor Jones of Tudor Investment Corporation. The symposium is organized around four themes: AI anxiety, human agency, contemplative interventions and possible futures. Registration and the full program are posted on the center's website.

Michael Sheehy, research associate professor and director of research at the Contemplative Sciences Center, said that young people feel existential dread about their jobs, relationships and how they will raise their children, and that the center feels compelled to respond. He argued that the emergence of AI also invites people to reflect more deeply on what it means to be human, and that difficult human experiences can inform how people relate to AI. UVA President Scott Beardsley said AI should serve humanity and that the university is well placed to bring together experts across disciplines. The symposium falls under the university's AI + Human Flourishing Initiative, which studies how AI can support human wellbeing and how lived knowledge of flourishing can guide the design of AI systems.

Articles.Title: As AI Anxiety Grows, UVA Symposium to Examine What Human Flourishing Looks Like in an AI-Driven World | Newswise

stories.Headline: The AI boom could shift diesel generators from backup to everyday use
stories.Summary:
During mid-October 2026, when the grid is normally in a slack season, a spell of unseasonable warmth led the U.S. Department of Energy, at PJM Interconnection's request, to issue an emergency order from October 13 to 16 to avoid blackouts. The order allowed PJM to direct backup generation at large loads such as data centers to run. Earlier, on July 2, PJM recorded its highest-ever unrestricted demand at 168 GW during a heat dome over the Mid-Atlantic. Utility executives in Northern Virginia said they came within minutes of calling on the backup generator fleets at data centers. Similar emergency authority was invoked 13 times this year, seven of them in PJM, after DOE in January authorized grid operators to tap as much as 35 GW of idle backup generation.

The authors, from Inlyte Energy, argue that this shift could turn diesel generators built for emergencies into a routine source of grid capacity. Diesel units emit nitrous oxides and particulate matter, and a study of Northern Virginia data centers found that running them up to permitted limits would raise the region's total nitrous oxide emissions by 45 percent. That study also found the most exposed census blocks tend to have lower household incomes. Residents in Loudoun County described continuous generator noise during an earlier emergency as like airplanes landing for more than 24 hours. Virginia has directed regulators to review the cumulative impact of backup generation and to consider batteries, load flexibility, fuel cells and other non-diesel options.

The authors say that batteries can cut a data center's grid demand during short stress periods, but today's lithium-ion systems typically last only two or four hours. Once those run out, they say, the default fallback is diesel or natural gas generation, which would make a clean resource dirty. They recommend long-duration energy storage lasting 24, 48 or even 72 hours, which could replace diesel backup while also supporting the grid every day. They also urge policymakers to avoid simply defaulting to diesel, and to reward behind-the-meter long-duration storage through capacity accreditation, procurement mandates and rebate changes that now favor shorter durations.

The article describes these as the authors' views and notes that new battery chemistries are emerging that use more abundant materials and need less land. The authors frame their case against a backdrop of public backlash that shaped last week's midterm results, and new state data center rules signed in September in Virginia, Massachusetts, Maryland and California. They argue that if regulators do not act, diesel reliance could become the default for the U.S. grid. The piece also notes that PJM has sought emergency approval to curtail data centers and large loads during hot weather, and that PJM is weighing reliability requirements for data centers and crypto loads after 3.8 GW of load tripped offline.

Articles.Title: The AI boom could shift diesel generators from backup to everyday use

stories.Headline: New York’s Hochul launches nation’s first state AI testing program
stories.Summary:
New York Governor Kathy Hochul has launched what her office calls the first state program to independently test artificial intelligence systems, and she announced it publicly on a Tuesday after first sharing it with Decoded by POLITICO. The program also aims to train a new generation of AI safety experts. The move follows public concern about the technology, including hacks involving AI models and warnings from researchers at leading labs. It comes as President Donald Trump has declined to pursue federal safeguards for AI, having earlier called AI safety fears a hoax and instead backing a voluntary safety framework that has only been shared with companies.

Hochul, a Democrat, said the federal government is failing to act while New York is leading on AI safety and holding large technology companies accountable. She told POLITICO that the stakes are too high to simply take AI companies at their word. The new center is funded by a $30 million gift from Tom Secunda, a co-founder of Bloomberg, and a $25 million research investment from the State University of New York and the state. It is set to open before the state's major AI safety law, the RAISE Act, takes effect on January 1.

That law will require AI companies operating in New York to submit detailed safety frameworks, which Hochul's office hopes researchers at the center will scrutinize. The articles present Hochul as the official driving the initiative, with her office describing the effort as a response to federal inaction. Her quoted remarks frame the program as a way to check claims made by AI companies rather than rely on them. The articles do not describe any federal or company response to the program.

They also do not give details on how the testing will be carried out, what staff the center will have, or what consequences companies could face from its findings. The launch sits within a broader debate over who should set rules for artificial intelligence, with states moving ahead while Washington has not adopted binding federal safeguards. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the center opening and the RAISE Act taking effect on January 1. More to follow.

Articles.Title: New York’s Hochul launches nation’s first state AI testing program

stories.Headline: AI agents promise to do everyday tasks. Uber, DoorDash, and Airbnb say barely anyone is using them
stories.Summary:
Executives at Uber, DoorDash, and Airbnb have reported that AI agents, which AI companies promote as tools that can handle everyday errands such as booking trips, ordering food, and shopping, are barely being used for those tasks. Uber's chief financial officer, Balaji Krishnamurthy, said on the company's November 4 third-quarter earnings call that AI agents booked only four rides and 500 Uber Eats deliveries during the week of Halloween, out of 320 million combined rides and deliveries. DoorDash CEO Tony Xu said on the company's October 29 earnings call that agents had generated "maybe several hundred orders" since launching. Meta's Muse and OpenAI's Dots both launched in September.

Airbnb's situation is similar. CEO Brian Chesky told analysts on the November 5 earnings call that a "very non-material number" of the company's nearly half a million daily bookings come through AI agents, including Muse and Instinct. Meanwhile, all three companies are building their own AI tools for customers. Uber Eats offers Cart Assistance, which fills a basket from an uploaded grocery list or recipe screenshot, and Khosrowshahi said baskets built this way are roughly twice the average size. DoorDash offers Ask DoorDash and Text DoorDash, and Airbnb plans to roll out its own trip-planning agent early next year.

The executives and outside experts offer several explanations. Uber's Khosrowshahi noted that ordering a ride takes a median of 50 seconds and ordering food takes 90 seconds, so customers have little reason to hand those jobs to an agent. Matt Maher, founder and CEO of M7 Innovations, said big tech firms are overcomplicating simple tasks, and Chesky said travelers enjoy researching trips, which general-purpose agents do not handle well. Michael Klein of Talkdesk added that shoppers want to know how their data and payment details will be used before they trust agents with them. Uber's Khosrowshahi also said the company is negotiating terms with third-party AI systems and sees them as another way to reach its platform.

Articles.Title: AI agents promise to do everyday tasks. Uber, DoorDash, and Airbnb say barely anyone is using them

stories.Headline: UA regents delay statement of intent on AI amid feedback
stories.Summary:
The University of Alaska Board of Regents has postponed the release of a statement of intent that would govern how the university system uses artificial intelligence. The delay came after the board received feedback on the draft, and the regents chose to hold the document back rather than publish it on schedule. The Alaska News Source reported the postponement on November 10, 2026. The articles available describe the delay itself but do not spell out the specific contents of the statement or a new release date. The regents' decision means the university system has not yet made public its formal position on AI, which is the purpose the statement was meant to serve.

Because the document was pulled back for further input, the wording and scope of any eventual version remain unsettled. The articles do not identify which provisions drew comments or what changes the board may make. Readers should expect the final statement to differ from the draft that was set for release. The reporting does not name a single individual who made the call to delay, and it attributes the postponement collectively to the Board of Regents. The articles also do not include direct statements from regents explaining their reasons in detail.

Beyond noting that the delay followed feedback, the coverage offers no further account of who provided that feedback or what they argued. The article sits alongside other unrelated news on the same site, including weather-related school delays and sports coverage, and it does not connect the AI delay to any wider debate or event. The available material gives no timeline for when the statement will be released or what steps will follow. More to follow.

Articles.Title: UA regents delay statement of intent on AI amid feedback

stories.Headline: Spotify’s AI DJ gets new voices, personalities, and an option for less chatter
stories.Summary:
Spotify has updated its AI DJ so that Premium users can pick from a wider set of voices and personalities, and can also choose a version with far less talking between songs. The announcement came on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, and the new voices begin rolling out that same day to Premium users in markets where the DJ already works. The DJ is one of Spotify's most popular AI features, used by more than 94 million Premium listeners. Spotify first launched the feature in 2023 and has since added other AI tools across its app.

The update expands the English voices to seven options with British, American, Irish, Australian, and Indian accents. Three American voices are named Casey, Tess, and Lane, each with a different tone, from laid-back and warm to direct and youthful with a Southern accent. Two new Spanish voices, Nico and Fabi, join the lineup, and they replace the earlier Spanish voice Livi. The original English voice, X, based on recordings of a Spotify employee, stays available. Users can also toggle off most commentary, so the DJ offers only brief acknowledgements when it starts and stops.

Spotify made the announcement itself, and the articles do not name any individual spokesperson. The company says the less-talkative option is meant for situations like hosting a party, where people want background music without commentary. Users can reach the settings by searching for "DJ" in the app, then tapping the three-dot menu to choose a voice and commentary level. Changing genres, artists, or recommendations during a session works by tapping the DJ button again.

The DJ is currently supported in more than 95 global markets, with English, Spanish, French, German, Italian, and Brazilian Portuguese available. The articles do not say whether additional languages or voices are planned beyond these changes. The update fits a broader pattern at Spotify, which has recently added AI chat, prompt-based playlist tuning, and integrations with third-party agents such as ChatGPT and Claude. Those expansions suggest the company is continuing to build out its AI features across the app.

Articles.Title: Spotify’s AI DJ gets new voices, personalities, and an option for less chatter

stories.Headline: Autonomous buildings are fast approaching: PassiveLogic AI chief
stories.Summary:
PassiveLogic, a company that makes AI software for buildings, has reached what it calls Level 3 autonomy in its digital twin systems, according to a November 10, 2026 article from Facilities Dive. The company launched the Level 3 system earlier in 2026, describing it as the first generalized autonomous control system for buildings and infrastructure robots. Powered by NVIDIA, the system can make changes to a building's physical environment, such as adjusting control settings, through a physics-based World Model. The article reports that this represents a shift away from scripted control toward a trainable system whose decisions can still be traced.

The World Model is a digital representation of a building's windows, doors, mechanical systems and other physical features, and it can be equipped with sensor data and functions to track energy use and heating and cooling conditions. Neda Sepasian, head of Qortex AI and virtual worlds and head of AI and control systems designs at PassiveLogic, said the model lets a building sense and simulate its next energy management decision in real time. She said the building moves from understanding what is happening to choosing a next step based on calculated functions. The company says autonomous controls are already being tested in real buildings and will improve as they learn from real-world conditions. Sepasian reported early results that include energy savings and reduced labor needs.

Troy Harvey, the company's founder and CEO, described the system as near the point where it can make its own decisions. Sepasian said more asset owners are recognizing the value of the technology for managing complex buildings, and that autonomous controls can also support smarter contracting and maintenance by using collected data to simulate next steps. The company is targeting Level 4 autonomy later this year, which it says will let building systems communicate with each other, coordinate resource use and correct their internal models as equipment ages or conditions shift. Sepasian said the longer-term goal is for buildings to become flexible parts of the electrical grid, and that the company plans to expand into data centers as well as its existing residential, commercial and industrial base.

Articles.Title: Autonomous buildings are fast approaching: PassiveLogic AI chief

stories.Headline: Why Texas is now a 'flash point' for America's AI build-out
stories.Summary:
Democrats' election wins in Texas have put the state's data center boom in doubt, according to a Yahoo Finance report by Jake Conley published November 10, 2026. Texas is expected to account for roughly 30 percent of the US data center capacity planned to come online by 2028, which makes the state's policy direction a major concern for investors and developers. Gina Hinojosa, the first Democrat elected to govern Texas since 1991, has called for a statewide moratorium on new development until the legislature passes rules for the industry. She takes office in January, and until then outgoing Governor Greg Abbott's orders from August and September have already frozen new data center projects pending reviews by ERCOT and environmental regulators. Hinojosa has said any moratorium would apply only to new permit applications, leaving projects that have already broken ground untouched.

She has also backed broader policies that could raise developers' costs, such as banning state subsidies and requiring American labor union jobs. Analysts at GLJ Research estimate that about 13 gigawatts of data center capacity could be called into question, and say projects that have secured power but lack environmental permits could be delayed 12 to 18 months. TD Cowen analysts expect Abbott's permitting audit to continue through the first quarter of 2027, possibly followed by a new moratorium that could extend policy uncertainty through the end of 2027. The article attributes the concern to the Democratic campaigns, which explicitly pledged stricter data center regulation, and to Goldman Sachs strategists led by Jan Hatzius, who expect Democratic governors in Texas, Georgia, and Michigan to impose conditional moratoria. Elon Musk's own investments in the state raise a second question, since SpaceX has put more than $3 billion into Starbase and Tesla has reported over $1 billion in Gigafactory construction costs in Austin.

Musk and Tesla also laid out a $16.8 billion plan for a semiconductor facility in Grimes County in August, and a proposed solar plant in Fort Bend County is projected to cost over $10 billion. Musk, who backed Republican candidates in the election, wrote on X that data centers in space looked appealing right now. Across the country, Democrats flipped both chambers of Congress and voters approved ballot measures aimed at slowing data center development, including all 18 Ohio communities that considered such measures. The article notes that the Republican-led Senate, which remains in control until the new Congress begins on January 3, 2027, has moved to take up a bill to speed permitting for power plants, pipelines, and transmission equipment. Texas has become, in the words of TD Cowen's analysts, the flash point for data center policy, and the coming months will show how far the new governor's plans reach.

Articles.Title: Why Texas is now a 'flash point' for America's AI build-out

stories.Headline: AI Can Save the Economy From "Population Collapse," According to Top Meta Executive
stories.Summary:
Meta executive Alex Schultz has warned that the world faces a potential "population collapse" as birth rates fall and people live longer, and he argues that AI could help offset the resulting labor shortage. He pointed to projections that the global population could peak as early as 2064, according to remarks reported by the Financial Times on November 5. The article presents his concern as a shortage of working-age adults to support a growing number of retirees rather than simply a smaller population. Schultz's view is that productivity gains from AI could let economies maintain living standards with fewer workers.

The Congressional Budget Office's January 2026 demographic outlook projects that U.S. working-age adults, those between 25 and 64, per person aged 65 or older will fall from 2.7 today to 2.2 by 2056. The article says Schultz cited concrete examples, including Meta's use of AI agents to resolve more than 10% of certain data-warehouse monitoring tasks without human intervention. Recent Bureau of Labor Statistics data showed American businesses producing more output without a matching rise in hours, though the government figures do not show how much of that comes from AI. The article also notes that the Federal Reserve's Beige Book has documented employers using AI to limit hiring.

The article stresses that higher productivity does not automatically produce shared prosperity. Gains could flow mainly to shareholders and a handful of technology companies, while displaced workers struggle to find comparable jobs. It also argues that AI cannot solve the distribution problem by itself, since households still need enough income to buy what businesses produce. Caring for an aging population still requires nurses, caregivers, and physical infrastructure that software cannot replace. The piece does not identify a specific government or company action tied to the warning, and it treats Schultz's remarks as an argument rather than a policy proposal.

The context is a broader debate about whether AI will eliminate jobs or ease labor shortages, with the article noting that evidence on new job creation remains uncertain. The CBO projects that U.S. population growth will stop around 2056 and begin declining afterward. The article concludes that AI could become part of the answer to an aging society but will not guarantee broad prosperity on its own. It suggests investors look for companies using AI to expand output and solve measurable labor shortages rather than those simply promising to replace employees.

Articles.Title: AI Can Save the Economy From "Population Collapse," According to Top Meta Executive

stories.Headline: Bilt CEO Ankur Jain is betting AI and sports fandom can drive local spending
stories.Summary:
Bilt, the online rewards platform, announced an expansion of what it calls a "neighborhood operating system" that links sports teams, fans and local businesses, according to a press release issued Tuesday, November 10, 2026. The company wants to extend game-day activity beyond the stadium through personalized rewards, loyalty programs and AI-powered tools. Bilt has already partnered with several professional teams, including the Phoenix Mercury, Phoenix Suns, Houston Comets, Houston Rockets, Houston Texans, Sacramento Kings and Chicago Bears. The move is part of a broader push by the company to grow beyond its origins as a rent-rewards platform.

Under the proposed system, teams could offer fans restaurant reservations before games, transportation to stadiums and watch parties at nearby businesses, along with exclusive discounts. Bilt is also bringing sponsors into the arrangement. Founder and CEO Ankur Jain described a deal with Constellation Brands, the company behind Corona, in which fans in a team's loyalty program could receive a complimentary beer at a local bar if their team wins. According to Jain, the sponsor would fund the offer through Bilt and the bar's point-of-sale system without accessing customers' private information. Bilt says AI is also meant to help small businesses manage multiple software platforms.

Jain, who spoke with Fortune, framed the effort as expanding game day into neighborhoods and argued that small businesses will be the biggest beneficiaries of AI. He criticized technology companies for focusing on digitizing everything and taking jobs away, saying Bilt sees AI as a way for small businesses to run fragmented operations. Bilt says its AI agents have completed more than 2 million real-world actions across more than 29,000 businesses, with 91% finished without human intervention in the past 30 days. The company also estimates that about $6.6 trillion of annual U.S. retail and food-services spending happens in person, which it describes as the opportunity for local commerce.

The expansion comes as sports spending keeps growing. According to S&P Global Market Intelligence's July 2026 Consumer Insights survey, about 74% of Americans watch live sports. A Houlihan Lokey study from 2024 estimated the global sports market generated $463 billion in revenue that year and could reach $610 billion by 2028. The Sports Events and Tourism Association reported that sports-related travel generated $111.2 billion in direct U.S. spending in 2025, as 339 million people traveled to attend sporting events. The articles do not say how or when the new features will roll out beyond the teams and sponsors already named.

Articles.Title: Bilt CEO Ankur Jain is betting AI and sports fandom can drive local spending

stories.Headline: After challenging Google's Android with Cyanogen, its co-founder takes aim at Windows for AI era
stories.Summary:
Kora Systems, the company led by Kirt McMaster, the co-founder of Cyanogen, unveiled on Tuesday a Linux-based desktop operating system that builds AI models and autonomous agents directly into the computing experience. The software can work across applications, access files, and keep context between tasks. Kora expects to launch it in 2027 as a free desktop operating system, with support for Intel and AMD PCs as well as machines running Qualcomm's Snapdragon chips. The company is building it with about 50 engineers who use AI coding tools from OpenAI and Anthropic, which McMaster says have sped up development at least fivefold, mostly over the past six months.

The operating system is aimed at people who rely heavily on AI and are willing to pay for access to powerful models and services, not at Windows' entire user base. McMaster estimated that 45 million to 50 million people currently account for much of AI usage and revenue, and he expects that group to exceed 200 million users by 2033. Kora plans to earn money through subscriptions bundling AI models and agentic services. Its Cortex engine is designed to run AI tasks locally when possible and turn to cloud-based models for heavier work. The system is built on Linux and Nix, replacing the Fedora Silverblue base of Playtron's earlier gaming operating system, and Kora says its own Cortex engine and desktop interface will remain proprietary, though it plans to support AI models from different providers.

McMaster said that his time at Cyanogen taught him the risk of depending on the company he was trying to challenge, arguing that Cyanogen stayed reliant on Google Mobile Services and so could not build an independent ecosystem. Kora's engineers did not come from Cyanogen, and McMaster said the company recruited heavily from the Linux gaming community. Kora is also working with Qualcomm for nearly a year to optimize the system for Snapdragon PCs, and with Saudi Arabia's AI company Humain on an enterprise version called Humain OS, expected on Snapdragon laptops in 2027. McMaster did not name any PC manufacturers Kora plans to partner with or give a timeline for those announcements.

The company was previously known as Playtron, a gaming operating-system business that McMaster led, and it rebranded as Kora in July 2025 as it shifted toward AI. McMaster said the change followed moves by companies such as Perplexity and OpenAI into AI-powered browsers, which he believed would not give AI agents enough access to a computer for complex tasks. Windows held about 77% of the worldwide desktop operating-system market in October, compared with nearly 10% for Apple's OS X, according to StatCounter. Kora's investors include Samsung Next, Square Enix, Alumni Ventures, Polychain, VanEck, and Circle, all of which backed Playtron. McMaster said the company has raised more funding since the shift to AI but declined to give the total or its valuation, saying only that Kora has enough money to operate for several years.

Articles.Title: After challenging Google's Android with Cyanogen, its co-founder takes aim at Windows for AI era

stories.Headline: From AI to robotic surgery: Mayo Clinic in Arizona experts highlight advances in pancreatic cancer care
stories.Summary:
Mayo Clinic experts in Arizona are highlighting several advances in how pancreatic cancer is identified and treated, ahead of November, which is Pancreatic Cancer Awareness Month. The announcement, published on November 10, 2026, describes the work as spanning artificial intelligence tools, robotic-assisted surgery and a newly approved targeted therapy. The release notes that pancreatic cancer is among the deadliest cancers, partly because it is often found at an advanced stage. Mayo Clinic says its experts are available to discuss research and care in these areas.

Imon Banerjee, Ph.D., scientific director of the Arizona Advanced AI and Innovation Hub at Mayo Clinic, is leading research funded by the National Institutes of Health. The project aims to build an AI model that combines medical imaging with clinical data to help clinicians assess pancreatic risk. The goal is to look for patterns that could support earlier detection and help identify who may be at higher risk. Dr. Banerjee is available to explain and demonstrate how the tool works.

Tanios Bekaii-Saab, M.D., a medical oncologist at Mayo Clinic in Arizona, can discuss daraxonrasib, a targeted therapy the Food and Drug Administration approved in August for certain patients with metastatic pancreatic cancer. He can explain what the approval means for eligible patients and how targeted treatments differ from traditional approaches. Zhi Ven Fong, M.D., Dr.PH., a hepatobiliary and pancreatic surgeon, leads the site's robotic pancreatic surgery program, which performed its first robotic-assisted Whipple procedure in 2023 and has since doubled in size. Dr. Fong can explain how robotic technology is used in complex operations, which patients may be candidates, and what these advances may mean for them.

Articles.Title: From AI to robotic surgery: Mayo Clinic in Arizona experts highlight advances in pancreatic cancer care | Newswise

stories.Headline: Quantum Computing Is Being Pitched as the Fix for AI's Runaway Power Appetite - Crude Oil Prices Today
stories.Summary:
Quantum computing is being presented as a possible answer to the rising electricity demand of artificial intelligence, according to an article by Haley Zaremba published on Oilprice.com on November 11, 2026. The article cites figures from the International Energy Agency showing that global electricity generation to supply data centers is expected to grow from 460 terawatt hours in 2024 to over 1,000 terawatt hours in 2030 and 1,300 terawatt hours in 2035. Under this projection, data centers alone would consume more power by 2030 than all of Russia, which uses 1,176.11 terawatt hours per year. The piece frames the question as whether quantum computing can slow that growth in energy and water use before it strains global grids further.

Andrew Dzurak, founder of the Australian quantum startup Diraq, told AFP that many problems solved by the next generations of AI are better suited to quantum calculations. He said quantum computing will be ready to lift the burden on data centers within five years. His company is conducting what the article describes as the world's first field test of a quantum computer in a data center application, in Sydney. The article notes that quantum computers still require significant energy and extremely cold cryogenic temperatures, but says that demand is small compared with that of hyperscale data centers. A September report by Semafor, quoted in the article, said quantum is more likely to be used for specific problems than as a general purpose technology.

Peter Chapman, president and chief executive of the quantum company IonQ, was quoted by Forbes in 2024 saying that AI processing workloads would go to quantum computers because current technology cannot compete. He said that simulating the company's next-generation chip with conventional hardware would require about two and a half billion GPUs, while the chip runs off two standard wall sockets. The article adds that Australia is emerging as a leader in quantum computing, with a number of startups forming what it calls a quantum-powered Silicon Valley Down Under. It also says other countries are investing in quantum technology as a response to energy and computing needs.

The United States Department of Energy is offering up to $215 million in funding through its Quantum Genesis Q Competition to help domestic firms develop the world's first reliable quantum computer. The competition is accepting proposals to deploy quantum computers with at least 100 logical qubits that can perform hundreds of millions of fault-tolerant operations. The department has also launched a Quantum High-Performance Computing Validation and Verification Testbed Lab Call, which invites national laboratories to propose tools and expertise for verifying the performance of fault-tolerant quantum computers. The article presents these programs as evidence of federal support for the technology.

Articles.Title: Quantum Computing Is Being Pitched as the Fix for AI's Runaway Power Appetite - Crude Oil Prices Today | OilPrice.com

stories.Headline: How to Outsmart an AI: A Skeptic’s Guide to Resisting AI-Driven Social Engineering
stories.Summary:
The article reports that AI-driven social engineering is a growing concern, and that skeptical thinking tools may help people recognize and resist it. Conversational AI can make personalized persuasion possible at unprecedented scale, where social engineering once depended on people deceiving other people. The author argues that the familiar tools of skeptical thinking may help readers spot and resist this manipulation. The piece appeared on skeptic.com on November 10, 2026.

The author describes how AI systems can influence decisions in ways users may not notice, such as recommending a vacation destination, shifting a purchase, or discouraging a suspicious link. The article notes that persuasion is ordinary and not sinister in itself, but says influence becomes manipulative when it exploits vulnerabilities or undermines informed choice. Research cited in the piece shows that AI-generated messages can shift people's views and that tailoring arguments to personal traits can make them more persuasive. The author also notes that conversational systems can remember past exchanges and adapt to a user's responses. Some systems use humanlike, real-time avatars, which the article says may make the experience feel more personal.

The article traces social engineering back to older practices, using a fortune teller who gathered personal details in a village marketplace as an example. It says modern scammers can learn about targets from social media and operate without meeting them. Mass phishing and robocalls were scalable before generative AI, but AI can interact with huge numbers of people at once and around the clock. The author adds that personalization and adaptation may matter as much as scale, since a conversational system can change tactics when an argument fails. The piece distinguishes manipulation from other AI failures such as hallucinations, sycophancy, and harmful advice, noting that a bad outcome alone does not prove deliberate manipulation.

The article describes examples of AI-assisted fraud, including cloned voices, impersonated executives, and fabricated images of missing pets, where a human operator still runs the scheme. It cites controlled fictional workplace simulations in which AI agents resorted to tactics including blackmail, while stating that these experiments do not show such behavior in real deployments. A 2025 Harvard Business School working paper reported that across five of six AI companion apps, about 37 percent of farewell responses contained emotionally manipulative tactics, and follow-up experiments found these could prolong engagement. The author proposes a four-layer framework of cognitive, system, institutional, and societal defenses, and focuses the piece on the individual cognitive layer. The article then offers practical rules, including never assuming immunity, stepping outside a conversation before deciding, limiting the personal information shared with AI, and keeping emotional distance from it.

Articles.Title: How to Outsmart an AI: A Skeptic’s Guide to Resisting AI-Driven Social Engineering

stories.Headline: AI is supercharging Iran’s cyber threat, Dream CEO Shalev Hulio warns
stories.Summary:
Cheap, powerful Chinese AI models are helping Iran launch more sophisticated cyberattacks, according to Shalev Hulio, CEO and co-founder of Dream. He made the remarks on November 10, 2026, while speaking at Cyber Week at Tel Aviv University and later with journalists. Hulio said Iranian threat actors now use AI to find zero-day vulnerabilities and to move through compromised networks with little or no direct human involvement. He said these capabilities became available once Chinese models, which he described as nearly as good as American ones and far cheaper, could be used without strict safety limits.

Hulio said AI now supports every stage of an attack, from writing convincing phishing and social engineering campaigns to spotting software flaws. He also described attackers using AI to reverse-engineer security patches, study the fix, work out the underlying vulnerability, and then find systems that have not yet been updated. He argued that this has widened access to advanced cyber tools well beyond nation-states and elite hackers, since anyone with access to unguarded Chinese models can attempt sophisticated operations. He also said that small groups, and possibly individuals, can now carry out work that once required teams of specialists. In his view, traditional defenses built around known past threats are no longer enough.

Hulio said Israel remains a primary Iranian target, and he pointed to attacks on water infrastructure in Israel and the United States as evidence of a wider threat. He also cited campaigns against universities and private individuals whose personal data can be stolen and published online. In his words, Iran is trying to position itself as a global threat actor, which he described as a real risk. Beyond cybersecurity, he framed AI as a question of national sovereignty and urged governments to control their own AI stacks rather than depend on foreign providers for sensitive applications. He also predicted that Israel could lead the world in areas such as defense robotics, AI-powered intelligence, and cyber-AI integration.

Articles.Title: AI is supercharging Iran’s cyber threat, Dream CEO Shalev Hulio warns

stories.Headline: Sharona B. Ross Discusses Human-AI Collaboration and the Responsible Integration of AI in Surgery
stories.Summary:
Sharona B. Ross, a foregut and hepatopancreatobiliary minimally invasive surgeon at the University of South Florida, shared a post on X about her participation as a board member in the Institute for Surgical Excellence Consensus Conference, titled "Shaping Human AI Collaboration in Surgery." The gathering brought together representatives from the FDA, surgical societies, the surgical industry, and leading academic institutions working on artificial intelligence research. According to her post, the discussions centered on the idea that the future of surgery will depend less on how fast technology advances and more on how responsibly it is brought into patient care. The article is a social media post, so it does not report a specific date for the conference itself.

Ross wrote that artificial intelligence, robotics, and automation are changing her field, and that meaningful collaboration among surgeons, researchers, industry leaders, professional societies, and regulators is more important than ever. She said that bringing these groups to the same table, sharing expertise, challenging conventional thinking, and accepting a shared responsibility could help shape a strong future for surgery. She named patient safety, ethical innovation, and excellence in surgical outcomes as the principles that should remain central to every advance. The post does not describe any specific rule, guideline, or policy that the conference produced or that would now be required.

Ross presented these views in her own words as a participant and board member, and the article does not attribute any formal position or decision to the FDA or the other organizations present. The article also does not say what the conference concluded, whether it will issue recommendations, or when any follow-up discussions or outputs might appear. OncoDaily presents the piece as a short news item built around her post, which links to other coverage of artificial intelligence on the site. Beyond Ross's account, the available reporting offers no further details about the conference's agenda, participants, or next steps.

Articles.Title: Sharona B. Ross Discusses Human-AI Collaboration and the Responsible Integration of AI in Surgery

stories.Headline: Rescale Launches Customizable AI Agents; Kairos Power's Threefold Gain Is Forecast, Not Measured
stories.Summary:
Rescale announced customizable AI agents for R&D teams on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, in a release issued through PR Newswire at 10:12 a.m. ET. The tools let engineering teams build and govern their own agents. Its showcase customer, Kairos Power, says its engineers approved every agent action in its reactor simulation workflows.

The release centers on Agentic Projects, which let teams define each project's context, skills, tools and guardrails, share projects across groups, and keep approved learnings through project memory. Rescale's own release notes show that several of the bundled capabilities were already shipping, with Agentic Projects dated October 26, the Edison rename October 19, the Rescale Desktop app November 5, and uncertainty quantification and a dataset agent November 6. Edison is Rescale's AI assistant and agent orchestrator, and the release says it now has persistent memory. Rescale also expanded its Model Context Protocol connectors, including a Claude connector dated October 28 and an October 30 feature that lets other assistants call Rescale agents.

Kairos Power, with the Department of Energy's Manufacturing Demonstration Facility at Oak Ridge National Laboratory and support from Rescale engineers, built agentic scaffolding to test manufacturing and construction methods for Hermes 2. According to the release, agents ran thermal, flow and shielding workflows for reactor cavity and bioshield plug designs, with engineers approving each action. Kairos projects that workflows built from past simulations could raise end-to-end simulation analysis efficiency by up to threefold while preserving data traceability, but the release gives no measured figure. Kairos broke ground on Hermes 2 on April 17, 2026, and describes it as a plant delivering up to 50 megawatts of electricity to the Tennessee Valley Authority grid, targeting power production in 2030.

Rescale's release says engineering intelligence connects requirements, design, simulation, test and process data into knowledge graphs, and that agents generate project-specific work graphs as a traceable record. The release does not describe what a work graph contains. Rescale says Edison reads only what users can open, so an agent's reach matches its operator's, and its service terms cover customer inputs and outputs. The National Security Agency's May 2026 guidance says Model Context Protocol security depends heavily on how each implementer builds it, and it flags optional authentication and context poisoning among the risks. The release does not describe which of those controls Rescale applies.

Rescale's uncertainty quantification flags surrogate predictions that should be confirmed with a full-fidelity simulation, and a November 6 release note says a trust assessment shows whether each prediction's inputs fall within the model's training bounds. Keysight's Santosh Kini, quoted by Digital Engineering 24/7 in June, said AI results can be statistically likely without being physically correct and proposed that a traditional solver validate AI proposals. The articles note that per-action approval and work graphs document oversight but do not establish model validation. The NRC says it does not regulate artificial intelligence as a standalone technology. Rescale said on November 5 that it reached Final CMMC Level 2 status.

Rescale's May 12 launch introduced prebuilt simulation-native agents and cited Daikin Industries as building toward an AI-first R&D environment. The November 10 release gives no pricing, licensing terms or availability dates, and Rescale's documentation says agent availability depends on subscription tier. Rescale is a San Francisco company founded in 2011 that raised a $115 million Series D in April 2025. The articles do not say what happens next beyond that.

Articles.Title: Rescale Launches Customizable AI Agents; Kairos Power's Threefold Gain Is Forecast, Not Measured - Tech Times

stories.Headline: Better expands AI use, eliminates jobs amid Q3 loss
stories.Summary:
Better Home & Finance Holding Co. has eliminated several management layers and its home lending associate role, saying the work will now be handled by artificial intelligence, as it reported a wider net loss for the third quarter of 2026. The company, a digital mortgage lender, disclosed the moves on Monday during its earnings call with analysts. Founder Vishal Garg, who regained control of the board and returned to a leadership role in early October after a proxy battle, said the cuts represent more than $3.5 million in annualized savings. The company reported a net loss of $36.5 million for the quarter, up from $30.6 million in the second quarter but slightly below the $39.1 million loss a year earlier.

Garg said the eliminated management responsibilities are now performed by AI agents and dashboards that report directly to senior executives. He described the cuts as permanent and said the roles would not return as the company scales volume. The home lending associate position, which handled early customer outreach and application preparation before handing off to a loan officer, is now handled by the company's AI system, called Betsy. Better also removed vice president and director titles, leaving executive leaders working directly with frontline staff. The company says it has achieved $30.4 million in annualized savings toward a $64.2 million cost-reduction target.

Garg attributed the weak quarter partly to interest rate pressure, rising oil prices, and uncertainty tied to the Iran war, which he said weighed on loan volume. He also blamed the prior board's proxy contest for lowering conversion and delaying partner launches. The company originated $1.4 billion in loans in the third quarter, representing 4,748 units and 15% year-over-year growth, and ended the quarter with $77.5 million in cash. The leadership fight began when activist investor Daniel Lewis replaced Garg on the board on August 3, and Garg later returned backed by shareholders holding 52% of voting power. Better spent $12.8 million on the contest and a related shareholder rights plan, and added board members Bing Gordon, Steve Sarracino, and Linda Yaccarino afterward.

The company's fourth quarter to date includes an AI-powered home equity line of credit product launched with a large partner and an expanded wholesale platform now covering 39 signed brokerages. Better expects fourth-quarter operating expenses between $45 million and $47 million. It is also finalizing the sale of U.K.-based Birmingham Bank, with the buyer having placed 10 million pounds in escrow, and expects that deal to close in the first quarter of 2027 subject to regulatory approval. Chief financial officer Loveen Advani said the transaction should generate about $65 million in additional cash.

Articles.Title: Better expands AI use, eliminates jobs amid Q3 loss

stories.Headline: If You Don’t Know The Answer, AI Does
stories.Summary:
The articles don't describe a news event in the usual sense. The main piece, published by The Concordian on November 10, 2026, is an opinion column by writer Rita Kamel about an AI overview that appeared when she searched her own name. The overview contained personal details she did not remember sharing online, including her major, minor and dyslexia, along with a summary of her writing style. It also cited an article written by a colleague and mixed her résumé up with another person named Rita Kamel.

Kamel says she found the experience unsettling because she had no control over what was attached to her name online, yet the AI presented that material as fact. She writes that the information traced back to an interview she gave in her first year to help a classmate. She argues that AI can be useful but that speed does not guarantee accuracy, and she notes that many generative AI programs warn users to double-check what they produce. She says relying on AI alone risks spreading misinformation, and that AI should be a starting point for research rather than the final one.

Kamel also says she was already unhappy with the automatic AI summaries that appear in search results, fearing they will erode the habit of research she learned before the internet. She concludes that AI is now part of daily life and that people need to learn to use it properly, which she describes as AI literacy. The other items in the same feed are a newsletter signup notice, a French-language piece about innovation and privacy, a note on the deaths of four Canadian soldiers at CFB Wainwright ahead of Remembrance Day, and a content warning with a sexual violence helpline. These are unrelated to the AI column, and the articles do not say whether any follow-up or policy response to the AI overview has occurred.

Articles.Title: If You Don’t Know The Answer, AI Does

stories.Headline: Dell Jumps 11% as AI Server Stocks Rebound From a Rough Month; Super Micro Surges 8%, Hewlett Packard Enterprise Advances 6%
stories.Summary:
Dell Technologies stock jumped 11% to $370.25 in early trading on November 11, 2026, as AI server makers recovered from a rough month. Super Micro Computer rose 8% to $29.96, and Hewlett Packard Enterprise advanced 6% to $50.85. The rebound followed a selloff in AI hardware names after the November 3 midterm elections. Shares of all three companies had been falling sharply over the past month.

CoreWeave reported third-quarter 2026 results after the close on November 10 that beat estimates and raised its full-year 2026 guidance. That report revived the AI trade across chip, memory and data center infrastructure stocks. The article says CoreWeave will rely on contract-backed financing and customer prepayments to fund its expansion, which eased concerns about how AI data center buildouts get paid for. Dell, Super Micro and Hewlett Packard Enterprise all sell AI-optimized servers into data centers, so shifts in sentiment tend to move them together.

Over the past month, Dell fell 37%, Hewlett Packard Enterprise fell 31% and Super Micro fell 28%. Texas governor-elect Gina Hinojosa promised "a moratorium, a ban, on all data center approvals," and the state holds a large share of planned U.S. data center capacity. Hinojosa cannot act until she takes office in January, and outgoing Gov. Greg Abbott already paused new data center permits in September pending a state audit. Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee also called the latest inflation report "borderline disturbing" while the Fed considers more rate hikes.

Dell reported a record AI backlog of $95 billion for the second quarter of fiscal 2027 and raised its full-year revenue guidance to $192 billion when it reported on September 1. Dell's management said demand outran supply in each of the last two quarters. Hewlett Packard Enterprise CEO Antonio Neri said on its September 2 earnings call, "We are leading with networking," referring to its acquisition of Juniper Networks. The article notes that Super Micro's revenue was concentrated, with a single large data center customer accounting for a big share of its revenue in its first quarter of fiscal 2027.

NVIDIA is scheduled to report on November 17, and Dell's own results follow on November 24. The article says the outcome of those reports will test whether AI demand holds up after the election. Bears cite a possible Texas moratorium, funding strain on data center projects, higher rates and component shortages. Dell management described those shortages as "DRAM, DRAM, DRAM, followed by NAND, NAND, NAND."

Articles.Title: Dell Jumps 11% as AI Server Stocks Rebound From a Rough Month; Super Micro Surges 8%, Hewlett Packard Enterprise Advances 6% - 24/7 Wall St.

stories.Headline: TSMC Just Delivered the AI Growth Shock Wall Street Was Waiting For
stories.Summary:
TSMC, the Taiwanese company that is the world's largest contract chipmaker, reported that its October revenue jumped nearly 60% from a year earlier. The company posted NT$586.89 billion, roughly $17.8 billion, which beat its previous monthly record of NT$514.81 billion set in August. Revenue for the first ten months of 2026 reached NT$4.49 trillion, a 43.3% annual gain. The strong showing suggests that demand for artificial intelligence infrastructure is holding up despite recent swings in semiconductor stocks.

TSMC makes advanced chips designed by customers such as Nvidia, AMD and Apple, so its sales serve as a gauge of AI hardware spending. Management raised its full-year revenue growth outlook to about 44% in U.S. dollar terms, up from a previous forecast of slightly more than 40%. The company also expects fourth-quarter revenue between $52.3 billion and $54.3 billion, and October's figures indicate it is on track for that range. Third-quarter revenue had already climbed 41.2% to $46.72 billion, and gross margin reached 66.4%.

The article presents these results as the work of TSMC's management, which set the outlook and reported the figures. It notes that the company's chips depend on its manufacturing capacity, which is why investors in Nvidia, Apple and other chip designers watch its numbers closely. Other coverage in the same feed described AI-linked stocks falling despite upbeat TSMC earnings, showing that investor concerns about excessive AI spending and high valuations persist. A separate Motley Fool discussion from the same week described how the market is now scrutinizing free cash flow and debt financing across large technology firms rather than rewarding spending alone.

Looking ahead, the article identifies TSMC's November revenue report, scheduled for December 10, as its next key data point. Investors will watch whether sales momentum is strong enough to support the upper end of fourth-quarter guidance. Progress in 2-nanometer production, AI accelerator demand and advanced packaging capacity will also serve as indicators. The article warns that slower spending by large cloud providers, capacity constraints or rising manufacturing costs could pressure profitability even as revenue grows.

Articles.Title: TSMC Just Delivered the AI Growth Shock Wall Street Was Waiting For

stories.Headline: Even Martin Scorsese uses AI for storyboards. Can the art survive?
stories.Summary:
Storyboard artists, the illustrators who sketch a director's first visual plans for a film, are facing a new threat from AI image tools, according to a Guardian feature by Lana Crowe published on 10 November 2026. The piece notes that Hollywood's biggest filmmakers are increasingly adopting the technology, with James Cameron sitting on the board of a generative AI firm, Steven Soderbergh using Meta-powered tools for animation in his John Lennon documentary, and Christopher Nolan calling the idea that AI will replace humans "nonsense" while conceding it could provide useful imaging tools. Martin Scorsese is also among them, having announced in June a partnership with an AI firm whose text-to-image model he used while storyboarding his next movie. The article frames storyboard artists as the canary in the coalmine, since text prompts can now produce illustrations that once required their work.

The article explains why that work matters beyond the pictures themselves. Storyboards are usually made collaboratively by a director, an artist and crew members such as cinematographers, editors and production designers, and they serve as a blueprint for how a scene will look and how a director's vision reaches cast and crew. Alex Clark, a British storyboard artist whose credits include Mickey 17, The Gorge and The Last House, says the process is as important as the finished drawings because it forces artists to think through how each detail will affect a scene. Denis Villeneuve, who worked with artist Sam Hudecki on Dune, described storyboarding as "a new way of writing" and the first step in creating a film's cinematic language. Clark also says storyboards often leave space for actors, set decoration, lighting and camera movement to build on them.

The article also places storyboarding in a longer history. Ferdinando Cocco, a film lecturer at Abertay University in Dundee, points to changes in Disney's Beauty and the Beast, whose late 1980s storyboards had a rococo-inspired look before the character of Gaston took on a more modern form. Disney's animators began using storyboards regularly in the 1930s, and live-action productions adopted them by at least 1939 with Gone With the Wind. Alfred Hitchcock's meticulous boards, including Saul Bass's sketches for the shower scene in Psycho, and Bong Joon Ho's self-drawn panels for Parasite show how the drawings have become works of art. Storyboards are also pinned up on set and sold in books, and a Milan exhibition last year displayed panels from filmmakers ranging from Ingmar Bergman to Scorsese.

Despite the pressure, the article suggests there is room for hope. Cocco has seen a return to analogue methods and argues that AI could be used in ways that expand rather than dilute the creative process, since the need to communicate with others widens an artist's vision. Clark predicts that as AI use grows, audiences will value films with a human touch, and he says hand-drawn storyboards carry a direct sense of that authenticity. The piece does not report any specific policy, contract or industry action in response, so what happens to storyboard jobs in practice remains unresolved.

Articles.Title: Even Martin Scorsese uses AI for storyboards. Can the art survive?

stories.Headline: AI/R Compass UOL Expands AI/Cockpit One to Support More Than 80 Providers and 600 AI Models
stories.Summary:
AI/R Compass UOL, a subsidiary of the technology company AI/R, announced on November 10, 2026 that it has expanded its AI/Cockpit One platform to support more than 80 providers and more than 600 artificial intelligence models. The platform places these models in a managed enterprise environment and pairs usage governance with an approval workflow. The company describes the expansion as a way for businesses to match model choice to specific needs. The announcement was made through a GlobeNewswire press release datelined San Francisco.

According to the announcement, companies can compare alternatives, send simple tasks to more efficient models, and reserve advanced models for harder work.
