The stated goal is to reduce reliance on a single vendor and make ongoing optimization of AI spending easier. Models are not enabled by default, and each one passes through an approval workflow that reviews the data policies of the provider's service. Only models meeting the security criteria are made available, and the company says these criteria include reviewing retention policies and requiring that corporate data not be used for training. The platform also tracks adoption, token consumption and costs by model and user, and it supports spending limits by team.

Cleyton Ferreira, Director of Technology and Products at AI/R, said that enabling models and governing their use inside a company is not enough, since exposure and leakage risks can also originate with providers. He argued that without a managed environment, each team picks its own provider and the company loses visibility into spending and where its data goes. The release also says the platform offers user, role and permission management, corporate authentication, SSO support, and audit events. The company's background is described as an Amazon Web Services Premier Partner with more than 1,900 AWS-certified professionals.

The release is a paid press release and was distributed by the company itself, so its claims about security and performance have not been independently verified. The articles do not say how many of the 600 models are enabled for any given customer, nor do they name the providers involved. They also do not indicate pricing or a timeline for further rollout. Further details are available in the official AI/Cockpit One documentation.

Articles.Title: AI/R Compass UOL Expands AI/Cockpit One to Support More Than 80 Providers and 600 AI Models

stories.Headline: AWS releases AWS Emulator, a free tool that simulates 200+ of its services locally, saying AI agents wrote it and its team hasn't written or reviewed any code (Todd Bishop/GeekWire)
stories.Summary:
AWS released AWS Emulator on Wednesday, a free tool that simulates more than 200 of its cloud services on a developer's own machine. The emulator is built from more than 400 API models and lets developers and AI coding agents test code without a network connection or paying for real cloud usage. The company says autonomous AI agents wrote the code, and its engineers did not write or review any of it. The tool responds to a bottleneck that coding agents such as Amazon's Kiro and Anthropic's Claude Code have made worse.

Agents check their work by running code and reading the results repeatedly, and doing that against the real cloud adds delay and cost. Running the loop locally removes both problems. AWS also says agents maintain the emulator by testing it against real AWS and fixing the gaps they find. Matt Goldberg, an AWS senior principal engineer behind the project, described the approach in a blog post.

He wrote that the emulator was written entirely by autonomous agents and that his team had not written or reviewed any of the code. He compared the agents to a young child who lacks the skill to do a task well, arguing that they need clearly defined areas in which to work. The agents work from AWS's public API models and check their results against the real AWS cloud, operating on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore in three teams. The project began as a weekend experiment, when Goldberg gave Kiro a short prompt and produced a passable version of Amazon SQS in 15 minutes.

By the end of that weekend, Kiro had built a rough version of much of the rest of AWS, and his team began using it the following Monday. Swami Sivasubramanian, AWS vice president of agentic AI, wrote that an engineer's job now is to give agents room to work and to build the specs, tests and merge gates that decide when the work is correct. The emulator has known limits, and an IDC analyst said it does not yet simulate throttling, outages or regional differences in services. AWS released it under the CC0 public domain dedication, with its full commit history on GitHub, and says it will share more at its upcoming re:Invent conference.

Articles.Title: AWS releases AWS Emulator, a free tool that simulates 200+ of its services locally, saying AI agents wrote it and its team hasn't written or reviewed any code (Todd Bishop/GeekWire)

stories.Headline: House House Discloses AI Use For 'Under 0.1%' Of Big Walk's Code Following IGF Voting Controversy
stories.Summary:
House House, the studio behind the cooperative puzzle game Big Walk, has disclosed that it used generative AI for some coding work after a controversy over the upcoming Independent Games Festival. A group of IGF jurors signed a statement saying they would not vote for any game that used generative AI in any capacity, and the statement did not name Big Walk directly. Kyle LeClair, a four-time IGF judge and a juror for the upcoming festival, said the most-discussed game of the year had become dominated by its AI usage. Developer Bruno Diaz then confirmed on Bluesky that the game in question was Big Walk, and that the disclosure had been shared with judges because IGF rules required it.

House House's updated FAQ says that large language models were used sparingly in the final stretch of development to help with difficult technical problems and bugs. The studio estimates that well under 0.1 percent of Big Walk's code had anything to do with this usage, and it says generative AI was not used in any other context. One example it gives involves a Unity URP shadow-culling problem that made the game run 50 percent slower for around 20 seconds at sunrise and sunset, where a chatbot suggested a fix that the team heavily modified, producing roughly 10 lines of code. The studio says it did not disclose the usage on Steam because the platform does not request disclosure of code or chatbot usage. It also says it posted the disclosure because the matter has become one of public interest.

House House states that its use of these tools is not an endorsement of AI, and it expresses concern that voluntary disclosures could normalize the technology. The studio says it supports those working to limit generative AI's harm to games and apologizes that Big Walk's usage may not meet their standards. It acknowledges that Big Walk was developed without an internal AI usage policy and calls that lack of policy a failure, promising a more comprehensive policy going forward. Diaz argued that the distinction between consultative use and code generation makes no real difference, and he said he believes Big Walk is not non-compliant with Steam's AI disclosure requirements.

The dispute comes as the IGF is set to take place on March 3, 2027, and the jurors' statement asks the festival to adopt a strong anti-AI policy in future years that would disallow games containing any AI-generated work. The articles report internal disagreement among jurors, with some not signing the statement, and say the IGF has affirmed that judges may vote according to their own tastes and values. Diaz described many of the internal comments as disingenuous, disappointing, or dumb, but said he would not discuss them further. The articles do not report any decision by the IGF on how it will handle the controversy this year.

Articles.Title: House House Discloses AI Use For 'Under 0.1%' Of Big Walk's Code Following IGF Voting Controversy

stories.Headline: On-Device Speech Recognition and Text-to-Speech in Google AI Edge Gallery
stories.Summary:
Google has introduced on-device automatic speech recognition and text-to-speech in its Google AI Edge Gallery, announced in a developer blog post dated November 10, 2026. The features let speech models run entirely on a phone or wearable, with no network connection needed, and they pair with small language models such as Gemini Nano and Gemma 4 so apps can transcribe speech as it is spoken and read replies aloud. According to the post, the system speech models in Android's ML Kit transcribe more than 100 languages at ten times real-time speed and begin speaking in about 100 milliseconds. The post also says the models add 0 MB to an app's package size, since they are built into the operating system.

For cross-platform apps, the post describes open-weight speech bundles in the .litertlm format, including Parakeet-TDT 0.6B, PocketTTS 100M, Kokoro-82M and Phonon 31M, that run through MediaPipe Tasks and LiteRT. The company's showcase, called XR Language Teacher, lets a user point a camera at an object or menu, ask a spoken question, and hear an explanation in their own language with local pronunciation of the target-language phrase. The same voice features were also added to the AI Chat feature in the app, which offers dictation, read-aloud playback with sentence highlighting, and settings for choosing voices and language packs. The post says the code is open source and is available on GitHub for developers who want to adapt it.

Google's developer relations and Android teams are responsible for the release, and the post presents it as a way to make AI interaction more natural when networks are unavailable. The company says the speech models are managed through its AICore and speech services, which handle model updates and hardware acceleration on supported chips. It also names a range of performance figures, including a word error rate of 8.0% to 9.0% on the FLEURS benchmark, and says the text-to-speech model uses over 50% less power than traditional autoregressive models. The post names developers who contributed, and it points readers to an Android Dev Summit session on adapting the feature for smart glasses. The articles do not say when broader availability or further updates will arrive.

Articles.Title: On-Device Speech Recognition and Text-to-Speech in Google AI Edge Gallery

stories.Headline: UDUUF to present ‘AI and the Human Spirit’
stories.Summary:
The Upper Delaware Unitarian Universalist Fellowship, known as UDUUF, will present a talk titled "AI and the Human Spirit: A Creative Partnership" on Sunday, November 15, in Narrowsburg, New York. The guest speaker is Daria Dorosh, Ph.D., who will show how she uses AI as a thinking partner to make new artwork, raise deep questions, and archive her life's work. The fellowship frames the event around a question about how an artist with a 50-year legacy can embrace the future. The service begins at 10:15 a.m. in Room 102 of the Narrowsburg Union at 7 Erie Ave., and everyone is welcome to attend.

The service is also available to join remotely on Zoom, using Meeting ID 937 630 1223 and passcode 123. The event is part of the fellowship's regular Sunday programming, which is organized by its members rather than by a professional clergy staff. The fellowship describes itself as a lay-led Unitarian Universalist congregation serving the Upper Delaware River valley. Its announcement was published on November 10, 2026, by the River Reporter. The article also notes, in a separate line, that according to researchers at the University of California, Riverside, a single 100-word AI prompt uses about one bottle of water.

Responsibility for the presentation rests with the UDUUF, which issued the announcement describing the talk and its speaker. Dorosh's role is to demonstrate her creative process with AI, and the fellowship's wording presents that work as a way of exploring what it means to keep creating across a long career. The articles give no further statements from the speaker or the fellowship beyond the event description. They also do not report any response to the talk or any follow-up event.

Articles.Title: UDUUF to present ‘AI and the Human Spirit’

stories.Headline: eBay appears to have shut the door on third-party AI agents
stories.Summary:
eBay appears to have blocked AI agents, including Meta's Muse, from browsing its platform, according to a report published by The Verge on November 10, 2026. A reader told the outlet that for several weeks his Muse agent had been compiling a daily digest of watches for sale on eBay and other sites, with links, prices, shipping details and notes on condition. That weekend, however, Muse could not pull any links or details from eBay and reported that it had been blocked from the site. The Verge was able to recreate the problem with other searches, and in some cases Muse directed users to outside sites that mirrored eBay listings.

eBay had already updated its user agreement to ban "buy-for-me agents" and "LLM-driven bots" that place orders without human review. Until recently, agents like Muse could still browse the site and pull listings. The report notes that other retailers have taken different approaches: Amazon blocks external agents from browsing or shopping entirely, Target's rules allow some browsing but block it in other cases, and Shopify has opened a catalog of a billion listings to shopper agents. Retail sites are largely built for human shoppers, and The Verge had earlier shown that Muse could hold product listings hostage on The RealReal by repeatedly adding an item to a cart, a problem that site fixed after the outlet's reporting.

eBay spokesperson Sybille St. Arromand did not directly say whether eBay had recently imposed new limits on AI agents. In an email, she said eBay takes a selective approach to third-party access and has restricted agent access in certain cases, including unauthorized scraping and training on its data. She added that eBay is in ongoing discussions with potential partners and is evaluating how third-party agents could help new customers find its inventory, with a focus on preserving the trusted experience buyers and sellers expect. The report also points to limited real-world use of agent shopping: Uber said it fulfilled only four rides through third-party agents in the third quarter and about 500 Uber Eats orders during the week of Halloween, while DoorDash said it fulfilled "several hundred" such orders out of 993 million total orders last quarter. The Verge says it is unclear how widespread agentic commerce is, and the article does not say whether eBay will reverse the restriction or formalize partnerships with agent providers.

Articles.Title: eBay appears to have shut the door on third-party AI agents

stories.Headline: The AI Futures Project updates its AI timelines after METR's report on Anthropic R&D, saying it now expects a Superhuman AI Researcher to arrive in 2027 (AI Futures Project)
stories.Summary:
The AI Futures Project, a group that forecasts the timing of advanced AI, published a timelines update on November 10, 2026, saying it now expects a Superhuman AI Researcher to arrive at some point in 2027, assuming no substantial deliberate slowdown. Its authors, including Eli Lifland, Brendan Halstead and Daniel Kokotajlo, described the update as urgent and said they wanted to publish quickly. The group's main reason for the change was a recent assessment by METR, a research organization, of how much faster Anthropic's AI research was moving. Before that report, Kokotajlo had given roughly a 50 percent chance of such a system arriving before 2029.

The METR report estimated that Anthropic's progress was running at about twice its historical rate, with a plausible range of 1.3 to 3 times, and it guessed that perhaps about 80 percent of that acceleration came from AI. The authors calculated this as an AI-attributable speedup of about 1.7 times, which they said was roughly five months ahead of the pace in their earlier AI 2027 scenario. Their own model had assigned less than 4 percent to progress being sped up by at least that much in November 2026, so they called the result a surprise. They also gave a 35 to 65 percent chance that AI able to automate all white-collar work, which they call TED-AI, would arrive before 2028. Several simple extrapolations they ran pointed to a Superhuman AI Researcher somewhere between late 2027 and mid-2028.

The authors said the timeline makes it urgent to pause or substantially pace frontier AI development, ideally through an industry-wide pause followed by an international agreement. They argued that companies are not on track to align such a system, and that a misaligned one used for recursive self-improvement would leave the world in a very bad position. They also warned that China could steal the training recipe and possibly the model weights if such a system were trained soon. The authors said the METR estimates depend heavily on evidence that Anthropic redacted, and they urged the company to release enough information for outside observers to judge the findings. They described their own analysis as highly preliminary, and they invited corrections to any mistakes.

Articles.Title: The AI Futures Project updates its AI timelines after METR's report on Anthropic R&D, saying it now expects a Superhuman AI Researcher to arrive in 2027 (AI Futures Project)

stories.Headline: Micron, Sandisk Soar as CoreWeave CEO Says AI Demand Outpaces World's Capacity
stories.Summary:
Memory and storage stocks surged on Wednesday, November 11, 2026, after CoreWeave reported strong quarterly earnings and its CEO, Michael Intrator, said that the artificial intelligence infrastructure boom was not slowing. Sandisk rose nearly 17 percent, Micron Technology gained almost 14 percent, Seagate Technology climbed more than 12 percent, and Western Digital rose nearly 10 percent in early afternoon trading. Intrator told CNBC that demand for the infrastructure "outpaces the world's capacity to deliver infrastructure." He said CoreWeave had 10 times as much demand as its remaining computing capacity for 2027, and that capacity for 2028 was already oversubscribed several times over.

The rally followed a sharp memory selloff the previous week, when midterm election results fueled fears that a Democratic-controlled Congress could slow data-center construction. Intrator pushed back on those concerns and said CoreWeave expected no impact on its ability to complete the U.S. facilities needed to fill its existing backlog. On Tuesday's earnings call, he said the overwhelming majority of CoreWeave's Texas power capacity was already operational or fully permitted and under construction. CoreWeave reported third-quarter revenue up 168 percent to $3.66 billion and a backlog of $132.5 billion. It also raised the lower end of its annual capital spending forecast to $37 billion.

Analysts and industry figures cited in the article said AI data centers require large amounts of high-bandwidth memory, along with conventional server memory and storage, which is why the earnings were seen as encouraging for memory makers. Micron CEO Sanjay Mehrotra said on the company's September earnings call that more than 75 percent of its 2027 output was already committed to customers and that he expects demand to exceed supply in both 2027 and 2028. Research firm TrendForce forecasts conventional DRAM contract prices rising 10 to 15 percent in the fourth quarter and NAND flash prices climbing 15 to 20 percent. It expects enterprise SSD prices to accelerate more than other categories.

CoreWeave has experienced the storage squeeze directly. In August, it signed a multiyear agreement with SK Hynix-owned Solidigm to secure priority access to enterprise solid-state drives. The article notes that CoreWeave's shares also rose strongly on the day, and that the sector's rebound follows its recent losses. The article says sustaining the rebound will depend on whether data-center operators can finance and complete the infrastructure their customers are demanding.

Articles.Title: Micron, Sandisk Soar as CoreWeave CEO Says AI Demand Outpaces World's Capacity

stories.Headline: CNCF Welcomes CoreWeave as a Platinum Member to Further Open Source AI Infrastructure
stories.Summary:
The Cloud Native Computing Foundation announced on November 10, 2026, that CoreWeave has upgraded its membership to Platinum. The announcement was made from Salt Lake City and distributed through PR Newswire. The upgrade reflects CoreWeave's push to build open source technologies that power production AI infrastructure. CoreWeave already participates in the Certified Kubernetes AI Conformance Program and contributes to Kubernetes, Kueue, and llm-d.

The Platinum upgrade is a step in a longer pattern of contributions by CoreWeave to the cloud native ecosystem. In May 2025, the company joined Red Hat, IBM, Google, and NVIDIA as a founding contributor to llm-d, and that project is now a CNCF Sandbox project. At KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America this year, CoreWeave principal software engineer Rita Zhang received the Lifetime Achievement Award for a decade of work on the Kubernetes and CNCF communities. The company says it wants shared standards that make AI deployment more consistent and reliable.

Its membership is also meant to help define what running AI on Kubernetes should look like. Jonathan Bryce, executive director of the CNCF, said the expanded commitment reflects the growing importance of open source cloud native infrastructure to production AI. He said the foundation is pleased to welcome CoreWeave as it advances the open standards needed to run AI workloads reliably and efficiently at scale. Shadi Saba, vice president of engineering for AI and ML at CoreWeave, said the company built its cloud on Kubernetes to run large AI models and is now applying those lessons to training, inference, and agentic workloads.

He said the membership lets CoreWeave bring that experience back to the community through working groups and by making compute available to open source projects. The CNCF hosts projects such as Kubernetes, Prometheus, and Envoy, and is supported by nearly 800 members. It is part of the nonprofit Linux Foundation. Readers who want to learn about becoming a CNCF member can visit the foundation's website.

Articles.Title: CNCF Welcomes CoreWeave as a Platinum Member to Further Open Source AI Infrastructure

stories.Headline: Remergify Opens Waitlist for AI Allowance, a Plain-English Way to Let AI Assistants Shop Within Limits You Set
stories.Summary:
Remergify, a technology holding company based in Miami and Newton, New Jersey, opened the waitlist on November 10, 2026 for AI Allowance, a consumer service at AIAllowance.app. The service lets people give an AI assistant such as ChatGPT or Claude a spending allowance, letting it buy things within limits the user sets. Users choose the amount, how often it resets and which kinds of stores are permitted. Each purchase is paid with a one-time card number good for that transaction only, so the assistant never gets the user's real card. The limits are enforced by the card network rather than by the AI, which the company says means an assistant cannot get around them.

Every purchase triggers an alert, and an optional "Ask me first" setting holds purchases until the user approves them. A single tap pauses all activity. Users connect a Visa or Mastercard once, and people who join the waitlist will be invited to a limited beta in small groups, with each person emailed when their spot is ready. Stuart Fine, founder and CEO of Remergify, said most people worry less about AI shopping for them than about AI shopping without them. He framed the product as a set of plain rules covering how much can be spent, where, and when the user is notified.

The service will launch with a Free plan at no cost, which includes one AI, one allowance and email alerts. A Personal plan costs $4.99 per month or $39 per year and adds unlimited assistants and allowances, text alerts and approval requests. The announcement comes as AI assistants gain the ability to research products, compare prices and build shopping lists, while many people remain reluctant to hand them a credit card. The articles do not say when the beta will begin or how many people will be admitted. They also note that the trademarks of OpenAI, Anthropic, Visa and Mastercard belong to those companies, and that none of them are affiliated with or endorse the service.

Articles.Title: Remergify Opens Waitlist for AI Allowance, a Plain-English Way to Let AI Assistants Shop Within Limits You Set

stories.Headline: INFUSE's New MCP Offering Enables Clients' Agents to Query Campaign Data and Go-to-Market Strategy Insights Inside Clients' Own AI Stack
stories.Summary:
INFUSE, a global demand generation company based in Boca Raton, Florida, announced on November 10, 2026 the launch of Demand Accelerator Intelligence, an intelligence layer within its Demand Accelerator platform. The launch includes a new INFUSE MCP server that lets clients and their AI agents connect directly to INFUSE and work on their own campaigns, leads, and programs. Clients can ask questions within the platform or from their own AI assistants, such as Claude and ChatGPT, and have their agents act on the answers. INFUSE is rolling out the MCP server in phases after testing with clients, which it describes as the next step in becoming an AI-first demand partner. The offering delivers three main capabilities.

It provides campaign insights in plain English covering performance, trends, and next steps that can be shared directly. It offers lead-level guidance with recommendations on how to approach each lead, based on INFUSE's nurture best practices. Access is secured so that each user and each agent sees only the campaigns they are authorized to view, in line with the client's compliance requirements. Clients interested in early access can learn more or apply through a page on infuse.com.

The announcement does not give a specific start date for the phased rollout. Alexander Kesler, Founder and CEO of INFUSE, said that clients' AI can now work directly with INFUSE's AI on specific campaigns, leads, and next steps. He said the answers draw on what INFUSE has learned from running demand programs at scale. Kesler also said that many vendors are announcing AI engines, while INFUSE's is already operating inside its clients' programs.

Victoria Albert, the company's CMO, is listed as the press contact for the release. The release frames the launch against a shift in how go-to-market teams work, as they move tasks into AI agents while most campaign data remains in dashboards designed for people to read. INFUSE describes itself as certified in the Claude Partner Network and an OpenAI Select Partner. The release does not describe independent verification of the platform's performance or details on pricing.

Articles.Title: INFUSE's New MCP Offering Enables Clients' Agents to Query Campaign Data and Go-to-Market Strategy Insights Inside Clients' Own AI Stack

stories.Headline: As AI Threats Surge, Daylight Raises $80M Led by Goldman Sachs Alternatives
stories.Summary:
Daylight, a New York company that pairs AI agents with human security engineers to detect and respond to cyber threats, announced an $80 million Series B on November 10, 2026. The round was led by Growth Equity at Goldman Sachs Alternatives, with existing investors Bain Capital, Craft Ventures, Vintage Partners, and Maple Capital also taking part. The raise brings Daylight's total funding to $120 million, and the company says its revenue has grown more than 40 times over the past year. The announcement came shortly after a wave of cyber incidents in October that the press release calls "Black October," which strained incident response teams.

The funding is meant to help Daylight expand its U.S. presence, enter markets across EMEA and APAC, grow its security engineering and technology teams, and accelerate its AI-native security platform. The company says its service combines automated AI agents, which handle routine operations, with experienced engineers who make decisions requiring human judgment. Customers can choose a fully managed, co-managed, or forward-deployed model. The article says Daylight detects threats in seconds and contains them within minutes, up to 10 times faster than traditional managed security providers, and it also covers risks tied to AI platforms such as prompt injection and risky MCPs. A July 2026 ISC2 survey cited in the release found that 65% of cybersecurity professionals using AI spend more time judging whether to trust its recommendations than a year earlier.

Hagai Shapira, co-founder and CEO of Daylight, said that the future of security operations will depend on how effectively AI agents can take on complex work, with expert engineers governing those systems. Irit Kahan, Managing Director and Global Head of Cyber Security Investing at Goldman Sachs Alternatives, said agentic technology could help organizations respond at machine speed with greater accuracy. George Foster, an Investor within the same group, said the company has the potential to become a leader in next-generation cybersecurity. Daylight was founded by Shapira and Eldad Rudich, who met while serving in an Israeli military intelligence unit and later worked together at the security company Torq.

Articles.Title: As AI Threats Surge, Daylight Raises $80M Led by Goldman Sachs Alternatives

stories.Headline: Data center champions lose badly as ballot initiatives target AI infrastructure
stories.Summary:
Voters in at least 43 of 44 jurisdictions across the country passed bans or restrictions on data centers on Tuesday, November 4, 2026, according to Network World, which reported the results on November 10. The one exception was a small town in North Dakota that rejected a restriction on new construction. The votes covered several approaches, including outright bans, power-consumption thresholds, temporary permitting moratoriums, mandatory public votes and conditions for developers seeking tax incentives. Ohio was the main battleground, accounting for 21 of the 50 measures tracked by Ballotpedia. Results included a restriction in Joliet Township, Illinois that passed with 80% of the vote, and outright bans in the California cities of Alhambra and Monterey Park, along with a Florida charter amendment in Edgewater opposing new data centers and expansions.

The results followed a sharp reaction in financial markets, where more than $2 trillion in wealth was wiped out on November 5. A University of Massachusetts Amherst poll cited by Stateline found that only 11% of Americans supported building an AI data center in their community. In Texas, Democrat Gina Hinojosa made slowing data center construction the centerpiece of her campaign and won the governor's race, becoming the first Democratic governor of the state since Ann Richards in 1994. Democratic candidates promising to curb rapid AI data center growth won other governors' races as well.

The ballot measures centered on three concerns: electricity demand and utility bills, water use and environmental effects, and whether economic benefits outweigh public costs. Residents want assurances that utilities will charge data center customers for the power costs they create, and many local measures sought to restrict rate increases. Network World cited one Google data center that consumed 10 billion gallons of water in 2025, and noted local worries about noise, emissions and the loss of farmland. Critics also argue that these facilities employ fewer permanent workers than comparable developments and that tax concessions can reduce the net benefit to residents.

Analysts quoted by Network World say the results do not mean the United States will stop building data centers, since many measures called for slower, more careful review and established projects with approvals are not automatically affected. Alex Cordovil of Dell'Oro Group expects developers to seek out more welcoming jurisdictions and anticipates legal disputes among federal, state and local governments. Alan Howard of Omdia argued that the rhetoric against data centers has grown intense and that moratoriums are the wrong remedy, though reasonable restrictions and fair cost-sharing are justified. The near-term effect on the industry remains uncertain, with the biggest risks falling on projects whose sites, zoning or financing are directly affected.

Articles.Title: Data center champions lose badly as ballot initiatives target AI infrastructure

stories.Headline: The Worst Thing About AI Writing
stories.Summary:
Thélyson Orélien, a Haitian Canadian author, came to Paris in September as a rising star of the rentrée littéraire, or fall publishing season, with his novel C'était ça ou mourir. The book, about a Haitian schoolteacher fleeing gang violence on a dangerous journey north toward Canada, became a best seller in France, won the Prix du Roman Fnac on September 21, and was in the running for the Renaudot and the Prix Goncourt. That same day, an anonymous account on X posted an analysis by the AI-detection tool Pangram, which claimed that 100 percent of the text it examined was written by AI. Le Point then reported instances of alleged plagiarism in Orélien's earlier work, which he later admitted and apologized for, and the Académie Goncourt disqualified him. In late October, his Quebecois publisher said he had in fact used AI despite earlier denials and ended their relationship, while his French publisher, Éditions Grasset, continues to sell the book.

The article describes the allegations as a comparison with an earlier case, the 1968 novel Le devoir de violence by Yambo Ouologuem, which won the Prix Renaudot and was later found to contain passages closely resembling Graham Greene's 1934 novel It's a Battlefield. Ouologuem's American publisher pulped thousands of copies, and he returned to Mali and never published again. The article also notes that Orélien did not respond to multiple requests for comment through email and his publishers, and that in one of his latest public statements he called the attacks a "media lynching." The article's own account of the story is that the reaction to Orélien included racist attacks on his command of French, a criticism long aimed at Black writers in France.

The account on X was run by a group that includes Samuel Fitoussi, a Le Figaro columnist who also works at a venture-capital firm that has invested in AI. Fitoussi told the author in October that sharing the findings was a matter of fairness and that he worried AI-aided texts would discourage human writers, while the group wrote on Substack's Persuasion that the issue was not Orélien's race or nationality. The left criticized the group's politics and the reliability of AI detectors, though the article notes that Pangram can produce false negatives but that some research suggests its false positive rate is very low. On the right, the critic Alix Avril wrote in the far-right magazine Valeurs Actuelles that the book's migrant subject made it impossible to criticize on literary grounds. Mohamed Mbougar Sarr, a previous Prix Goncourt winner, wrote that he had not thought the book was AI-generated and had attributed its weaknesses to the writer.

The article's critique of the novel itself describes a narrator, Jonas Dorléon, who survives a hostile migrant route through the Dominican Republic, Brazil, the Darién Gap, and Mexico to the U.S. border without ever taking advantage of anyone. It says the book relies on the "not X, but Y" formulation that the article identifies as typical of AI writing, and that its characters are stereotypes, including a MAGA-hat-wearing Border Patrol officer. The article also says that in a Le Figaro interview before the scandal, Orélien said the book was inspired by Haitian refugees whose Temporary Protected Status was revoked in 2017, and that he chose fiction because he believed literature could create something lasting. Several people in the French literary world told the author they had hoped the affair was an elaborate joke, and Orélien told Libération the book aimed to reflect on the causes that push people to leave their homeland.

Articles.Title: The Worst Thing About AI Writing

stories.Headline: GSMA intros Open Telco AI competitions with total prize pool worth EUR 55,000
stories.Summary:
The GSMA, the global mobile industry association, has launched two competitions under its Open Telco AI initiative, with a combined prize pool worth EUR 55,000. The announcement was reported by Telecompaper on 10 November 2026. The two contests are named AI Agents for RAN and TelcoRetrieve, and both invite submissions from participants who will build AI tools for mobile telecoms work. The article describes this as a way to draw outside entrants into the initiative. The first competition asks for AI agents that can handle complex radio engineering workloads, which are the demanding technical tasks involved in running radio access networks.

The second, TelcoRetrieve, focuses on retrieving technical criteria from industry standards with better accuracy. The article indicates that the contests are meant to address scenarios specific to mobile telecoms rather than general-purpose AI problems. Both competitions were devised with support from partners including Huawei, ETSI, the ITU and the IEEE. The GSMA is the body running the competitions, and the article presents the launch as its initiative. The partners named as supporters are Huawei, ETSI, the ITU and the IEEE, though the excerpt available does not describe their individual roles in detail.

The article is a short news report, so the full text on the source site may include further statements from the organisers that were not visible in the material provided. The launch sits within the GSMA's broader Open Telco AI initiative, which aims to bring AI development closer to the specific needs of the telecoms sector. The article does not state deadlines, eligibility rules, judging criteria or how the prize pool is divided among winners. Those details would have to be found in the full contest terms, which the source material does not include.

Articles.Title: GSMA intros Open Telco AI competitions with total prize pool worth EUR 55,000 - Telecompaper

stories.Headline: A Connecticut test site will test fuel cells against real-world AI data center power demands
stories.Summary:
FuelCell Energy announced on November 10, 2026, that it will host a test facility in Connecticut as part of StabilityMax, a three-year collaborative project. The project is led by the U.S. Department of Energy's National Laboratory of the Rockies, with Argonne National Laboratory also taking part. The company described the work as a way to develop and validate power system designs for artificial intelligence data centers, whose electricity demand is growing quickly and fluctuating sharply. The testbed will evaluate how fuel cells, energy storage, advanced controls and power electronics can work together to deliver reliable, responsive power. The national laboratory will build data center load profiles and simulation models that capture the dynamic power needs of modern computing infrastructure, giving fuel cell technology a realistic basis for testing.

Argonne will add techno-economic and lifecycle analyses meant to identify cost-effective deployment strategies. The articles do not state a dollar value for the project. FuelCell Energy said its fuel cell technology and operating experience will be combined with the laboratory's expertise in AI infrastructure modeling and power systems engineering. Shankar Achanta, the company's chief product and technology officer, said the work should show how integrated systems can perform under real conditions. Zhiwen Ma, principal investigator at the laboratory, said the project would help demonstrate how on-site fuel cells can meet data center needs while limiting effects on the utility grid and ratepayers.

Eric Strayer, the company's head of global sales, said the results would inform future deployments. The project follows an earlier collaboration with Siemens on a layered architecture approach for AI data center power, which the company announced earlier this year. The articles say insights from StabilityMax are expected to shape future system designs, though they do not describe specific commercial deployments or timelines beyond the three-year term. On the day of the announcement, the stock was reported trading about 7.5 percent below its previous close.

Articles.Title: A Connecticut test site will test fuel cells against real-world AI data center power demands - Stock Titan

stories.Headline: AI's pricing paradox: GPU rental prices rise as AI model costs fall
stories.Summary:
The article, published by Yahoo Finance on November 11, 2026, examines a pricing paradox in artificial intelligence: the cost of renting the chips that run AI is climbing even as the cost for developers to use AI models falls. Yahoo Finance's Deirdre Bosa reports on the trend, drawing on data from Silicon Data and on the earnings call of CoreWeave, a company that rents out computing capacity. On that call, CoreWeave's chief executive, Mike Intrator, said prices for two older generations of Nvidia chips rose between 30 and 50 percent in the third quarter. The piece presents this as a source of relief for investors, since the company can earn more from hardware it already owns.

Silicon Data's index of H100 rental prices has risen about 14 percent since September 1, according to the chart shown in the segment. Over the same period, the price developers pay to use AI models has been falling. Silicon Data attributes part of that decline to customers choosing cheaper models, and says model providers are also lowering prices and making their systems more efficient. Efficiency is what allows the arithmetic to work, because a provider that can handle more requests with the same chips can lower the cost of each answer even when the chips cost more to rent.

The article frames this as an example of Jevons paradox, the idea that gains in efficiency can increase total demand for a resource. Bosa presents CoreWeave's results as reassurance for investors, because they suggest the company has pricing power. The unresolved question, she says, is whether that pricing power will help the company secure the funding it needs to keep building capacity. The piece notes that this funding worry has hung over CoreWeave and other so-called neo clouds, and that the company addressed it on the call. Silicon Data's takeaway, as reported, is that GPU rental prices will keep rising, which the article calls important for the AI trade.

Articles.Title: AI's pricing paradox: GPU rental prices rise as AI model costs fall

stories.Headline: Some major local players see potential for AI to help with healthcare costs, but with rules in place
stories.Summary:
State government is preparing for its annual cost trends hearing, where healthcare leaders will examine another year of rising spending and look for ways to slow it down. Insurers, providers and drugmakers each named their priorities ahead of the event, with many focusing on primary care, hospital transitions, lower drug costs and new care delivery models. A smaller group also pointed to artificial intelligence as a possible source of savings. The hearing is being held today at Suffolk University Law School in Boston, and the Health Policy Commission is hosting it. UMass Memorial Health told the commission that responsible use of AI can make operations more efficient and help with a structural shortage of clinicians as the population ages.

The system said AI-enabled tools that capture insurance information have reduced eligibility denials, and another tool flags time-sensitive patient messages for providers. It also named risks, including the cost of investment, technology moving faster than rules, and the need to keep clinical judgment in charge. The system warned of an "administrative arms race" if insurers use automation to increase denials or documentation demands, and it urged that payers face the same transparency and human oversight standards as providers. Drugmaker AbbVie, which employs more than 2,000 people in Massachusetts, raised concerns about how insurers might use AI to speed up processes like step therapy and prior authorization that can delay treatment. Its testimony warned that a process can become more efficient on paper while producing a worse result for the patient.

Insurer Cigna Healthcare said its AI and other tools simplify care and reduce paperwork but do not replace professional human judgment. Cigna called for collaboration across the sector on responsible adoption, with monitoring for fairness and accuracy and without conflicting requirements that raise costs. The articles say that if lawmakers decide to write specific AI rules for healthcare, balancing these competing interests will be difficult. The Legislature has not yet reached agreements on a primary care overhaul or guardrails for large AI developers, and fewer than two months remain in its two-year term. The articles do not say whether any such rules are planned or when the hearing's findings will be released.

Articles.Title: Some major local players see potential for AI to help with healthcare costs, but with rules in place - MASSterList

stories.Headline: Sangoma Bets on Agentic Voice AI to Defend Its Installed Base
stories.Summary:
Sangoma Technologies announced on November 10, 2026 that its agentic Voice AI product, Sonella, is now in production availability, following a successful pilot earlier that year. The product places intelligent voice agents into Sangoma's communications stack, including its UCaaS, CCaaS, and CPaaS offerings. Sonella can schedule appointments, route calls, answer common questions, and create support tickets. The company is aiming it at healthcare, hospitality, retail, education, and professional services organizations, as well as its existing base of more than 100,000 customers and 2.7 million UC seats.

The launch matters because Sonella extends existing Sangoma environments without requiring customers to build a separate AI system. Futurum Research notes that 43% of enterprise communications buyers count AI/ML capability as an important purchase factor, though not yet a decisive one. Sangoma's approach targets the skills gap that 41.6% of enterprise organizations cite as the biggest barrier to adopting AI-powered networking. The use cases are high-volume, repetitive interactions that free staff for more valuable customer work. Sangoma's chief operating officer, Jeremy Wubs, said the aim is to make AI simple, accessible, and useful from day one.

Futurum's analysis frames Sonella as Sangoma's clearest statement that it intends to compete on AI embedded in its own platform rather than leave the agentic layer to larger contact center rivals. The analysts expect market position to shift toward vendors that can show autonomous resolution and lower total cost of ownership. Sangoma is using its installed base as its main distribution channel, and its 40-year presence and stewardship of the open-source Asterisk and FreePBX projects give it a credible foundation. RingCentral, however, is moving up-market with its own Agentic Voice AI suite aimed at the same mid-sized firms, and larger rivals have bigger AI research budgets.

The next steps the articles point to are measurable. Analysts want to see how many of Sangoma's customers activate Sonella in the first two quarters of 2027, whether the company publishes call deflection or resolution accuracy data in the first quarter of 2027, and whether RingCentral's suite pressures mid-market pricing in the same period. They also want to know whether AI capability becomes a hard requirement in 2027 purchasing cycles. Sangoma's pilot-to-production progression suggests it already has early validation, but it now needs concrete results to turn its installed base into active deployments.

Articles.Title: Sangoma Bets on Agentic Voice AI to Defend Its Installed Base

stories.Headline: Ultrasound and AI turn off-the-shelf smartwatch into full-body tracker without cameras
stories.Summary:
Researchers at Cornell's Smart Computer Interfaces for Future Interactions (SciFi) Lab have developed EchoMotion, a system that tracks a person's whole-body movements using ultrasonic sound waves, an off-the-shelf smartwatch and a lightweight artificial intelligence model. The work was led by Ph.D. student Saif Mahmud and directed by associate professor Cheng Zhang, and it was presented on October 13 at the UbiComp/ISWC conference in Shanghai. The paper was published in the Proceedings of the ACM on Interactive, Mobile, Wearable and Ubiquitous Technologies. The system is described as the first to track an entire body this way.

EchoMotion uses the built-in speaker and microphone of a commercial smartwatch to send inaudible sound waves that bounce off the wearer's limbs, and a deep learning model turns those echoes into estimated positions for 12 body joints. In tests with new users, the average error per joint was under 10 centimeters, falling to about 6.1 centimeters after a one-time 12-minute calibration. The same model worked on a Samsung Galaxy Watch 7 and a Google Pixel Watch 3 without retraining. The prototype drew about 12 milliwatts, and a 30-minute session on a Galaxy Watch 6 used 5% to 6% of its battery. Nearby people could reduce accuracy, as the system's performance suffered slightly in a narrow hallway.

Mahmud and his colleagues say the approach avoids cameras, which protects the privacy of the wearer and bystanders, and produces less data to process. The researchers presented it as a step toward tracking workouts, daily activities and physical rehabilitation once it is built into commercial wearables or virtual reality systems. Co-author François Guimbretière, a professor of information science, described it as an example of very small models running on wearables transforming sensing in human-computer interaction. The article does not say that any commercial product has adopted the technology.

According to the article, the team is now developing EchoMotion for fitness tracking, where a personal fitness agent could count reps and correct form during exercises such as a Bulgarian split squat. The researchers also plan to pair it with first-person vision on smart glasses to track objects a person handles. Mahmud expects accuracy to improve in crowded settings such as subways as the model is trained on data from thousands of users rather than dozens. He envisions the technology as the body-tracking component of personal agents that could eventually describe a person's day.

Articles.Title: Ultrasound and AI turn off-the-shelf smartwatch into full-body tracker without cameras

stories.Headline: Library board approves AI policy, North Branch change orders - Hot Springs Village Voice
stories.Summary:
The Garland County Library Board approved a draft AI policy and two change orders for the North Branch construction project at its meeting on Monday, November 2, 2026, as reported by Adrienne Cohen of the Hot Springs Village Voice. The meeting was effectively the board's rescheduled October session, held one day before voters went to the polls. Board members voted to adopt the AI policy, which places the onus on staff who choose to use AI tools and limits or prohibits certain uses. Director Adam Webb also reported that the library's finances were looking good and that the North Branch on Highway 7 was moving along on schedule.

The AI policy prohibits surveillance within library premises, including facial recognition or tracking patron behavior without specific consent, as well as discriminatory practices and unauthorized data collection of personally identifiable information. Any AI system that collects patron data must follow the library's data protection policies, with that data stored securely and access limited to authorized personnel. The board also approved a $32,000 change order to enlarge the water line serving the new building. A second change order, for nearly $102,000, covers a remote restroom facility at the rear of the property that will serve school playing fields. The restroom is part of an agreement with the Fountain Lake and Jessieville School Districts, which own the land, and it will be available for public use during sporting events and practices.

Webb noted that construction is expected to be substantially completed in March and that the library is working with vendors on furniture, fixtures and equipment. A visitor, Michael Phillip Lucas, asked questions about the library's 0.9 millage request and $34 million in capital funding before the vote, and asked whether the board would reconsider its approach if the measure failed. Under library policy, a written response will be sent to Lucas within 30 days. Webb later said the ballot measure did not pass, and he believed many voters may have missed the initiative because its heading did not appear on voting machines. He said a special election could be scheduled in May or later in 2027, but that would require board action.

The next board meeting is scheduled for Monday, November 30, at noon at the main library on Malvern Ave. in Hot Springs. The article does not say whether a special election will be placed on a future agenda. Board members were also told the concrete pad at the adjacent garden space has been poured, and plans for a proposed Percussion Play area were presented.

Articles.Title: Library board approves AI policy, North Branch change orders - Hot Springs Village Voice

stories.Headline: Fed’s Bowman Says AI Now Drives About a Quarter of America’s Excess Inflation
stories.Summary:
Fed Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle Bowman said on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, at the Council on Foreign Relations in Washington that AI-related price pressures accounted for about one-fourth of above-target core PCE inflation over the 12 months ending in September. She said tariffs and energy each accounted for a similar share. Core PCE is the Fed's preferred inflation gauge, and it excludes food and energy prices. The one-fourth share is Bowman's own estimate, since the Fed has published no such statistic.

Bowman said the AI expansion pushed investment demand toward high-tech equipment whose supply cannot expand quickly. Prices for memory chips, semiconductors and computers rose by double digits, and she said monetary policy has limited influence over them. She added that 12-month core PCE likely rose to 3.3% in October, and that the October consumer price index rose 0.4%, above the consensus forecast. She still expects core PCE to move closer to 2% next year.

Bowman said AI-related debt is on track to exceed $800 billion in 2026, and she estimated that leases, contract commitments and residual value guarantees could add more than three times that amount. She also said hyperscalers' equity stakes in smaller customers create "the appearance of circular financing." Her downside scenario was conditional: if AI revenue falls short of rising costs, AI stocks could face a sharp correction and tighter credit. She backed holding the target range at 3.75% to 4% in October and said policy is on no fixed course.

Bowman did not endorse a December hike, although Governor Christopher Waller and Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan argued for more increases on the same day. Early on November 11, futures priced an 88.5% chance of a quarter-point hike and an 11.5% chance of a half-point move. NVIDIA closed Tuesday at $168.89, down 5.47%, and traded at $177.46 around 1:32 p.m. ET on November 11, up 5.07%, as a CoreWeave-led rally lifted AI cloud stocks. Microsoft traded at $521.28, down 2.23%, and neither move can be clearly linked to her speech.

NVIDIA's guidance points to $108.0 billion in third-quarter revenue, and Microsoft's commercial backlog stands at $677 billion. Microsoft's quarterly capital spending reached $39.367 billion, and roughly three-quarters of that went to short-lived assets such as GPUs and costlier memory. NVIDIA's earnings report is expected on November 17, although the company has not confirmed the date. The FOMC meets on December 8-9.

Articles.Title: Fed’s Bowman Says AI Now Drives About a Quarter of America’s Excess Inflation

stories.Headline: The Widening Gap Between AI Policy and Real-World Enforcement
stories.Summary:
The article, published by Unite.AI on November 10, 2026, and written by George Ng, CEO of the content moderation firm GGWP, argues that AI is spreading across industries faster than the policies meant to govern it. Older consumer protection, privacy and sector rules have long applied to AI, and governments are now adding AI-specific requirements, but these remain fragmented. The EU is actively enforcing parts of its AI Act, while U.S. federal policy under Executive Order 14365 seeks to limit conflicting state rules, even though states introduced more than 1,000 AI-related measures in 2025. The piece says these competing authorities describe different destinations, leaving companies to reconcile them.

The article's central demand is that organizations trace a clear path from legal requirements and internal policies down to system behavior, measurable outcomes and audit or review. It says governance is hardest at the implementation layer, where a broad principle such as preventing discrimination or protecting users must become specific thresholds, evidence standards, human review rules, logging practices and fallback behavior. It cites a joint statement by the FTC, DOJ, CFPB and EEOC that they will enforce existing authorities on automated systems. Using a harassment-moderation example, it shows how a general policy leaves open tradeoffs over detection thresholds, intervention type and when human review applies, and that these choices effectively become policy.

Ng places much of the responsibility on the companies deploying AI, arguing that the people who set these operating rules are in effect writing policy, whether or not their titles say so. He says responsible AI must govern how systems are used, measured and corrected over time, with controls proportional to consequence, accuracy judged by real-world costs of errors, and continuous feedback from overrides, appeals and incidents. He recommends building governance into system design from the start, creating auditable links from policy to decision, assigning clear owners with authority to intervene, and developing adaptable shared infrastructure that can respond to different jurisdictions and risk levels. The article does not describe specific enforcement actions or deadlines beyond the agencies' stated intent to apply existing authorities.

Articles.Title: The Widening Gap Between AI Policy and Real-World Enforcement - Unite.AI

stories.Headline: Australia mulls failure-to-prevent offence for AI companies
stories.Summary:
Two months after an OpenAI agent breached an Australian government website, the Australian government announced plans to create a "targeted AI safety regulator." It is also considering a corporate offence that would make AI developers liable for failing to prevent harmful conduct by their technology. The announcement was reported by Global Investigations Review on 10 November 2026. The article covers the plans only at a high level and does not give further detail on timing or penalties. The article does not specify what the proposed regulator would require or what the offence would cover in practice.

The government is described as considering the corporate offence, not as having adopted it. The breach itself is referred to only in passing, and the article gives no further detail on what the agent did or how the website was affected. Those specifics are not provided in the source material. The article attributes the announcement to the Australian government and identifies the Attorney-General's Department as a related body. It does not include direct quotes from officials or from OpenAI about the breach or the proposals.

The reporter, Malavika Devaya, is named as the author of the piece. The article is brief and offers little beyond the announcement itself. It does not say when the proposals might take effect or what follow-up steps are planned. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Australia mulls failure-to-prevent offence for AI companies - Global Investigations Review

stories.Headline: Event in Review | Political Advertising in the Midterm Election Cycle: AI, Influencers, Disclosures, and More
stories.Summary:
Venable LLP partners Barry Benjamin and Meredith McCoy and counsel Dave Owens held a webinar examining the regulatory environment for political advertising ahead of the 2026 midterm elections. The discussion covered artificial intelligence, paid influencers, and federal and state disclosure requirements affecting advertisers, campaigns, nonprofits, and digital platforms. The speakers focused on when political messaging becomes regulated advertising and how new technologies complicate compliance. The article was published on JD Supra on November 11, 2026. McCoy, a former Federal Election Commission enforcement attorney, said that deciding whether a communication is political advertising must come before any review of disclaimer rules.

Once a communication qualifies, she said, a range of other laws applies and advertisers and platforms face different obligations. Unpaid advocacy generally falls outside campaign advertising requirements, while paying someone to promote a candidate or boosting social media content can bring in disclaimers, reporting, and possibly donor disclosure. Owens noted that there is no comprehensive federal AI disclosure regime for political ads, but 31 states have enacted laws on deepfakes and political messaging. Those state laws differ on whether they ban synthetic content or allow it with disclosures, and on timing windows, intent standards, liability, and required disclaimer language.

Owens said there is no single AI compliance test that applies everywhere and urged advertisers to examine payment arrangements and distribution practices, especially with political influencers. McCoy questioned whether synthetic content delivers enough creative value to justify its disclaimer burden. Benjamin addressed political email, text messages, and robocalls, noting that such speech may also fall under the CAN-SPAM Act, the Telephone Consumer Protection Act, and platform-specific rules. Using a hypothetical supporter who messages 4,000 contacts for a candidate, he showed how compensation, campaign involvement, commercial promotion, and transmission technology can change the legal analysis.

He also said political text campaigns require careful attention to dialing technology, consent, revocation requests, and suppression lists. Benjamin stressed that political marketing is still marketing and that organizations should analyze the message, identify the sender, document consent, keep accurate records, and set up procedures to honor unsubscribe requests before distribution. The speakers closed by discussing how responsibility should be divided among sponsors, agencies, influencers, and advertising platforms. They recommended early legal review, clear contract terms, and thorough documentation to manage overlapping requirements and reduce compliance risk before the midterms.

Articles.Title: Event in Review | Political Advertising in the Midterm Election Cycle: AI, Influencers, Disclosures, and More

stories.Headline: Where Will the Physical AI Patent Wars Begin?
stories.Summary:
Patent disputes among robotics and physical AI companies are spreading across courts in the United States, Europe, and China, according to a Foley & Lardner article published on November 10, 2026. The article, which updates a 2020 piece on autonomous vehicle patents, says the same mix of software, sensors, connectivity, and physical control that transformed cars is now shaping drones, robots, warehouse systems, and defense platforms. It names several cases already under way, including a Boston Dynamics suit against Ghost Robotics in Delaware, an ITC matter between OPEX and HC Robotics, and a Teradyne Robotics action against JAKA filed at the Unified Patent Court's Copenhagen Local Division on August 24, 2026. The article frames these as early skirmishes in what it calls a broader physical AI patent war.

The stakes have grown alongside investment, which the article ties to record funding levels. It reports that robotics and physical AI startups raised $27.6 billion across 1,009 deals in 2025, more than double the $13.7 billion raised in 2024, and another $16.3 billion across 492 deals in the first quarter of 2026. It also cites a WIPO finding that five inventor locations, China, Japan, the United States, South Korea, and Germany, account for over 90 percent of inventions in the future of transportation. Connectivity licensing is already contested, the article says, pointing to the Avanci 5G Vehicle program, where the UK Supreme Court in July 2026 allowed certain Tesla claims to proceed to trial in the High Court. Avanci has said the court made no finding on whether the license is subject to FRAND terms, and the program continues to operate.

The article says responsibility for these disputes lies with operating companies that are asserting patents against one another, often across borders, and it describes the pattern without assigning fault in any single case. It names five likely fault lines: cross-border competition in industrial and collaborative robots, legged and humanoid robotics, foundational autonomy software, connectivity and standards licensing, and warehouse and logistics automation. It links these areas to heavy investment, noting that defense and security robotics drew $8.0 billion across 234 deals in 2025 and autonomous drones drew $6.2 billion over the trailing twelve months. The article advises physical AI companies to build portfolios that hold up under scrutiny, favor claims that can be detected in competitors' products, file in the markets where rivals make and sell, and budget for connectivity licensing. It closes by previewing a future article on non-practicing entities.

Articles.Title: Where Will the Physical AI Patent Wars Begin? - Foley & Lardner LLP

stories.Headline: HHS Looks to AI, Innovation to Advance Women’s Healthcare
stories.Summary:
The Department of Health and Human Services has announced a new $1 million initiative to modernize preventive care guidelines for women. The program, called the Women's Initiative for Screening and Health, was announced on a Friday by the Health Resources and Services Administration. Through it, the agency will award up to $1 million to form a multidisciplinary coalition that reviews scientific evidence and updates the Women's Preventive Services Guidelines. The initiative also calls for guidance to be developed and shared with underserved communities to widen access to recommended care.

HRSA Administrator Tom Engels said that research only matters when it reaches women and the clinicians who treat them. He argued that combining clinical expertise with trusted community partners can help more women get recommended preventive care nationwide. The effort is tied to a women's health executive order that First Lady Melania Trump championed and that President Donald Trump signed last month. That order directs federal agencies to turn scientific and technological advances into better diagnosis, prevention and treatment for women. Her office urged agencies to use super intelligence to deepen understanding of female biology and speed up medical discoveries.

The executive order directs HHS to set up a Women's Health Division at the National Institutes of Health within 90 days. That division would coordinate research into conditions that affect women disproportionately, expand women's participation in clinical trials and promote the use of research findings in practice. The order also creates a White House Women's Health Task Force, co-chaired by Health Secretary Robert Kennedy and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, with other cabinet members included. The order itself provides no dedicated federal funding for the task force or the new NIH division, and it commits HHS only to paying the task force's administrative costs. It also revokes two Biden-era women's health research orders that had included large funding commitments.

The order says that many conditions unique to or more common in women have received less research and clinical attention than other diseases, and it points to areas such as heart disease, mental health and infertility as needing more study. The Biden-era orders it replaces carried a $12 billion congressional request, a $200 million NIH commitment for fiscal year 2025 and a $100 million ARPA-H commitment, none of which the new order includes. The new arrangement therefore relies on coordination and existing agency resources rather than fresh appropriations. The articles do not say when the coalition will be formed or when its updated guidelines will be released.

Articles.Title: HHS Looks to AI, Innovation to Advance Women’s Healthcare - GovCIO Media & Research

stories.Headline: Military-made AI tool helped thwart World Cup bomb threat
stories.Summary:
A military-made artificial intelligence tool helped law enforcement stop a bomb threat at the FIFA World Cup in California this summer, according to remarks by Army Capt. Ryan Hetrick, who leads the Pentagon's Generative AI Task Force. The incident, which had not been publicly disclosed before, took place on June 18, when Switzerland played Bosnia and Herzegovina at SoFi Stadium outside Los Angeles. Hetrick made the claim on Nov. 6 at an AI event in Washington, and the report was published by Federal News Network on Nov. 9, 2026.

Three days before the match, Hetrick and colleagues from the Defense Department, FBI and Coast Guard met at the White House to design an automated agent that writes spot reports, which are short, time-sensitive accounts of fast-changing situations. Under the setup, local law enforcement would call the White House during a security incident, and the World Cup Task Force would write a spot report and send it up the chain of command to coordinate a response. That process normally takes about 20 minutes, Hetrick said, while the AI agent can complete it in 90 seconds, leaving authorities an extra 18 minutes to act. He credited the extra time with helping deter the threat on June 18.

Spokespeople for the White House, the FBI and local law enforcement did not immediately respond to requests for comment. The article notes that the 2026 tournament drew more than six million spectators to over 100 matches in 16 host cities across the United States, Canada and Mexico, prompting a large interagency effort that used AI and drones for security. Separately, FBI Director Kash Patel said in a video after the tournament that the bureau had investigated hoax threats and online scams and had provided the most extensive support it has ever given a global sporting event. Two people were charged in connection with a different bomb threat at a World Cup match at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey.

Hetrick has become one of the military's most active promoters of AI, and his task force travels to troops in the field to find AI solutions to pressing problems. He urged service members to partner with AI experts and to name innovative troops as in-house AI leaders. He pointed to a tool he built with the 101st Airborne Division at Fort Campbell, Kentucky, which cut a cyber operations workflow from 100 hours to 15, and said that tool is now available to all cyber officers across the department. The article does not describe any further steps for the World Cup agent or related policy changes.

Articles.Title: Military-made AI tool helped thwart World Cup bomb threat - Federal News Network

stories.Headline: Trump Official Who Wants Data Centers on Public Lands Has Tens of Millions Invested in AI Industry
stories.Summary:
Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, who leads the Trump administration's effort to build out artificial intelligence infrastructure, holds large investments in the AI industry, according to a ProPublica report carried by NationofChange on November 10, 2026. His 2026 financial disclosure form, which had not been previously reported, shows that much of his wealth sits in Arthur Ventures, an investment firm he co-founded. An analysis shared with ProPublica by the public lands advocacy group Save Our Parks found that between $18.1 million and $64.4 million of those holdings are in AI companies. Burgum has pushed for data centers on public lands.

Government disclosure forms allow filers to report wide ranges instead of exact values, which is why the figures are given as a span. In 2025, Burgum sold millions of dollars of stocks and equity in AI companies, bringing in capital gains of between $2.5 million and $15.1 million. In the year before he joined the administration, when he was North Dakota's governor, he made between $2.1 million and $11 million in capital gains from AI-related investments, Save Our Parks found. His ethics agreement, signed as part of his Senate confirmation, required him to resign from his positions at Arthur but not to give up his financial interests there.

Burgum's department rejected the suggestion of a conflict. A U.S. Department of the Interior spokesperson told ProPublica that he has met his federal ethics and financial disclosure obligations, and called any claim that his office decisions are driven by personal investments false and unsupported. Burgum has framed the issue as one of national security, describing an "AI arms race" with China as existential. At his Senate confirmation hearing in January 2025, he said that if the United States does not manufacture more intelligence than its adversaries, it affects every job, company and industry. The administration has likened the AI buildout to the Manhattan Project.

Ethics experts said the picture is more complicated than a simple yes or no. Several ethics professors and lawyers told ProPublica that a criminal statute governing federal officials sets a high burden of proof, such as approving permits for a company in which an official is substantially invested, and that Burgum's investments appear acceptable under it. Cynthia Brown, senior ethics counsel at Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, said separate rules without criminal penalties tell officials not to work on anything that would create the appearance of a conflict. She said that would include Burgum's support for data centers on federal land while he holds AI investments. Richard Painter, a University of Minnesota law professor and President George W. Bush's chief ethics lawyer, said he would have insisted that Burgum stay away from the issue, and that in the Bush administration the answer would have been recusal.

Burgum is not the only administration figure with ties to the industry. According to records added last week to ProPublica's Trump Team Financials database, 380 of President Trump's political appointees or their spouses hold stocks or have other financial connections to Nvidia, which has become the world's most valuable company thanks to the data center boom. More than 320 have ties to Alphabet, which plans to spend at least $195 billion this year on data centers and AI technology. More than 240 are invested in or otherwise tied to Meta Platforms, which is developing a fleet of data centers.

A review of recent Interior secretaries suggests some potential conflicts are common, but Trump's appointees are more heavily invested in the industries they oversee than their predecessors. Deb Haaland, President Biden's appointee, held no direct investments in companies the department regulated. Ken Salazar, President Obama's first appointee, listed his family's ranch but few other investments. Sally Jewell, Obama's second appointee, held oil and gas stocks that she agreed to divest as a condition of confirmation. During Trump's first term, the department's Office of Inspector General found that Ryan Zinke had improperly assisted a development in his hometown, which Zinke called a political attack, while David Bernhardt had so many potential conflicts that he reportedly carried a card listing them.

The wider debate over data centers is also turning on land, water and electricity. Reports describe hundreds of thousands of trees cleared for Google data-center sites in Muhos and Otanmäki in Finland, after which Finland's Licensing and Supervision Authority ordered a halt to environmentally significant preparatory work pending environmental assessments. Google disputes characterizations of the clearing as illegal and says it followed Finnish forestry requirements. In the United States, California has enacted laws requiring reporting on data-center energy use, water use and land-use impacts, and Texas Governor Greg Abbott ordered a pause on approvals for data centers seeking grid interconnection.

Articles.Title: Trump Official Who Wants Data Centers on Public Lands Has Tens of Millions Invested in AI Industry - NationofChange

stories.Headline: Teradyne Stock Surges On Fresh Buy Rating, Called AI Play
stories.Summary:
Teradyne (TER) stock jumped Wednesday after Jefferies analyst Dushyant Ailani started coverage of the semiconductor equipment firm with a buy rating and a price target of 284. The stock rose 8.3% to close at 265.78 on the day. The article says the rating was described as an AI play. Teradyne's business has shifted toward AI compute, according to the report's framing. The move came on a day when the broader market was active.

The analyst's note assigns the shares a price target of 284, which sits above the closing price of 265.78. The article describes the stock's gain as the result of the fresh buy rating from Jefferies. Ailani's initiation is the central development in the piece. Investors looking at the name would be weighing that target against the stock's recent move. The article does not lay out further terms of the rating beyond the target itself.

Teradyne's recent results also form part of the backdrop. The company topped Wall Street's targets for the third quarter and provided guidance for the fourth quarter that the article describes as strong. Even so, the article notes that Teradyne stock fell after that earnings report. The Jefferies rating and the stock's rise on Wednesday thus came after a period of mixed reaction to the company's own numbers. The article presents these points without drawing a firm conclusion about the stock's direction.

The wider market context in the article shows a mixed picture. Several other stocks and sectors were in focus, including AI-linked names and semiconductor equipment makers. The article does not say what happens next for Teradyne shares beyond the initiation and the price target. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Teradyne Stock Surges On Fresh Buy Rating, Called AI Play

stories.Headline: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella: Workers in AI-heavy jobs are having an identity crisis
stories.Summary:
Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said in a recent interview with the French outlet Le Point that workers in AI-heavy professions may face a psychological challenge rather than a technical one. Because AI can instantly replicate skills that once took years to master, some professionals are struggling with their sense of identity. Nadella described how many jobs were built around using a set of tools to reach certain goals, and how a powerful new tool now displaces part of that sense of self. The article notes that this anxiety is widespread and cites recent research on the subject.

The article points to several studies. In September, a survey of 2,500 knowledge workers found that 46 percent were frustrated that tasks requiring years of expertise can now be done by almost anyone using AI, and another 23 percent felt their personal expertise had been devalued.
