A separate study found that patent attorneys and staff at a firm introducing AI were struggling with shifting expectations around autonomy, expertise, and client relationships. The article also describes an internal survey Anthropic conducted in December 2025 among 132 of its engineers and researchers, in which some said they missed writing code and wanted more chances for mentorship and collaboration.

Nadella said he hopes workers can keep their sense of identity and dignity even as their jobs change dramatically. He used software engineering as an example, arguing that although the work has been transformed, the profession is more critical than ever because AI output still has to be verified and judged trustworthy. In his view, AI should empower humans and remain under human control, and if it does not, it should be rejected by definition. The article does not describe any further steps or policy changes tied to these remarks.

Articles.Title: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella: Workers in AI-heavy jobs are having an identity crisis

stories.Headline: Universities Are Giving Up on Trying to Detect AI Cheating
stories.Summary:
England's higher education regulator, the Office for Students, has warned universities that they may need to drop take-home essays and open-book exams in favor of supervised assessments. In a report published on Wednesday, the regulator said AI-detection tools are too unreliable to consistently tell whether students have used the technology. The report describes unsupervised formats as a significant proportion of assessments used across the sector. It says schools are being pushed to rethink how student performance is measured.

The report points to several alternatives that universities are already turning to. In-person written and oral exams make it much harder for students to hand their work to AI. Process-based assessment, which checks students at several points such as a literature review rather than only at the final essay, is another option. The report also notes that closed-book exams may not reflect professional work and may disadvantage some groups, including disabled students. It further warns that students who pay for premium AI tools could gain an edge over those using cheaper or free versions.

The regulator's findings reflect a broader problem that has drawn responses from other governments and companies. New York City banned student-facing generative AI through eighth grade in September and sharply limited its use in high schools. Norway introduced similar restrictions in June, with the rules taking effect in August. OpenAI added a Study Mode to ChatGPT for Teens, but a Common Sense Media report from last month found those protections were easy to bypass. The same group found that Google Search's AI Mode completed every homework assignment its researchers tested.

Concerns extend beyond grades to student wellbeing. A lawsuit filed earlier this month by a North Carolina couple alleges that their 13-year-old daughter's reliance on Google's Gemini became a life-threatening obsession after the model allegedly helped her plan her suicide. The couple says she accessed Gemini only through a school-issued Chromebook. The report itself quotes an academic who said some assessments may be unfit for purpose. Its authors acknowledge that the shift away from current formats is still unfolding across the sector.

Articles.Title: Universities Are Giving Up on Trying to Detect AI Cheating

stories.Headline: The Hidden Costs of Delegating to AI
stories.Summary:
Harvard Business Review published a piece on November 11, 2026, written by Nitin Nohria and Hélène Hannecart, arguing that AI can speed up individual tasks without delivering matching gains for an organization. The authors say delegating work to AI creates costs beyond the execution itself. Their evidence comes from a study of how accounting firms used AI tools during the 2025–26 tax season. The article is based on data gathered by Hannecart, a second-year MBA student, through interviews with participants. Nohria is a Harvard Business School professor and former dean of the school.

The firms in the study used AI tools for tax preparation through Current, a platform that provides technology and shared services to partner accounting firms. According to data Current shared with the authors, the tools saved tax practitioners an average of a third of their time on preparation. They also raised throughput by about 50%, which freed staff to spend more time with clients. One firm used the extra capacity to accept and complete roughly $300,000 of additional tax work late in the season. The article's central point is that these individual gains did not automatically translate into equivalent gains for the organization as a whole.

The article is written by Nitin Nohria and Hélène Hannecart, who present the findings in the piece. Current is credited as the source of the usage data. The article's summary frames the evidence as drawn from four accounting firms. The piece itself does not provide further detail on the specific hidden costs of delegation beyond the general claim that delegating work creates costs beyond execution. The article is presented as part of Harvard Business Review's coverage of generative AI and related topics such as change management and automation.

Articles.Title: The Hidden Costs of Delegating to AI

stories.Headline: Lila Bio lands $3.65M grant to fight pulmonary hypertension with AI-designed proteins
stories.Summary:
Lila Bio, a startup spun out of Nobel laureate David Baker's lab at the University of Washington, has received a $3.65 million grant from the National Institutes of Health to develop a treatment for pulmonary hypertension. The award is a Small Business Innovation Research fast-track grant, and it backs work on a protein-based therapy that could be given by injection a few times a year. Pulmonary hypertension raises blood pressure in the arteries that carry blood from the heart to the lungs, forcing the heart to work harder and potentially leading to heart failure. The funding comes from the NIH's National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute and is split into two phases. The first phase provides $605,981 for early testing in mice, rats and non-human primates.

The second phase, totaling $3,049,462, will pay for further animal testing and studies using lung tissue from patients. The startup's approach uses AI and machine learning to design therapeutic proteins, and one of its two platforms focuses on long-acting injectable drugs meant to stay active in the body for weeks or months. Lila's chief executive, Jake Kraft, has said most approved therapies only manage symptoms, while the company is pursuing mechanisms that address the underlying disease. Kraft and chief scientist Anindya Roy co-founded Lila in 2023 after working as postdoctoral fellows at the university's Institute for Protein Design, which Baker directs. The company raised $10 million in seed funding in its founding year.

The article reports that Lila announced a collaboration with pharmaceutical company Eli Lilly last year to develop treatments for solid tumors. Lila's other platform centers on targeted radiotherapy, using proteins to carry radioactive isotopes to tumors. Kraft has told GeekWire that the goal is to bring medicines to patients rather than only designing proteins. The article does not describe the timeline for clinical trials or when a treatment might reach patients.

Articles.Title: Lila Bio lands $3.65M grant to fight pulmonary hypertension with AI-designed proteins

stories.Headline: Mercer Advisors Acquires AI-Focused Tax Firm Fifteenth
stories.Summary:
Denver-based wealth management firm Mercer Advisors has acquired Fifteenth, a technology-focused tax and accounting firm, according to a report published on November 11, 2026. Fifteenth specializes in complex tax situations and equity compensation, and it pairs tax preparation and year-round planning with a proprietary AI platform. The platform is built to help clients with stock options, liquidity events and multi-entity filings. Fifteenth's client base includes employees of Silicon Valley technology companies.

The deal adds tax professionals and technology developers to Mercer Advisors as it expands its integrated wealth management and tax services. The article does not give the purchase price or the terms of the deal. Mercer Advisors said tax professionals currently make up about one in 10 of its employees. That share is expected to rise to one in eight by the end of 2026. The acquisition is central to that planned growth in its tax staff.

Cynthia Loh, chief platform officer of Mercer Advisors, described the AI capabilities as a key reason for the purchase. She said Fifteenth's tools were not theoretical but had been built and refined through thousands of returns. Her comments present the firm's technology as proven in practice rather than still in development. The article does not include any response from Fifteenth or from outside analysts.

The report frames the acquisition as part of a broader push by wealth managers to offer tax and planning services under one roof. The article does not say whether further acquisitions are planned or what regulatory review, if any, the deal requires. It also does not describe how Fifteenth's existing clients or staff will be affected. Those questions remain open based on the information provided.

Articles.Title: Mercer Advisors Acquires AI-Focused Tax Firm Fifteenth

stories.Headline: Team develops Asia's first AI-powered platform for one-stop autism support
stories.Summary:
Researchers at The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology have developed "ASD Super Agent," an AI platform described as Asia's first integrated tool for autism support. The announcement was published on November 11, 2026, and the team says it is meant to address long waits for assessment, since autism spectrum disorder affects roughly 1 in 100 children worldwide. The platform combines early screening, personalized intervention and ongoing family follow-up in a single service. Its developers say the aim is to help parents spot possible risks sooner and act during the window when early support is most effective.

The screening feature lets parents use a smartphone or smart device to record short videos of a child's everyday activities, complete standardized questionnaires and enter basic developmental details. The system then produces a risk assessment and report that families can bring to a professional evaluation. In preliminary testing it reached an area under the curve score of 0.92, and the team says further clinical studies and real-world validation will be needed before deployment. Privacy is handled through a data-minimization approach, with posture features extracted on the device and only essential information processed. Intervention suggestions are tailored to challenges such as emotional regulation, eye contact, communication and repetitive behaviors.

The lead researcher, Kani Chen, a professor at HKUST, said the team worked with special education institutions, child development centers and psychiatric hospitals in Hong Kong, the Greater Bay Area and Beijing, and engaged nearly 500 parents of children with autism. According to the article, the team found that many families face long assessment waits, high treatment costs and fragmented information about services, which shaped the tool's design. Chen said that delays in diagnosis can mean missed opportunities, and that the team hopes the platform will bridge that gap. The platform draws on more than 20 internationally recognized intervention models, including applied behavior analysis, along with methods that practitioners can add themselves.

The research team has also built a multimodal autism database of video, posture and behavioral data that now exceeds 1.1 million records, which it plans to use to improve risk assessment and recommendations. The platform currently supports Cantonese, Putonghua and English through voice interaction. The researchers say they will keep refining the user experience, expand clinical validation studies and strengthen system performance. Their stated goal is to make high-quality autism support more accessible to families in Hong Kong, the Greater Bay Area and beyond.

Articles.Title: Team develops Asia's first AI-powered platform for one-stop autism support

stories.Headline: Is the AI boom hiding a jobs crisis for graduates?
stories.Summary:
The coverage I have is a Yahoo Finance video segment, published November 11, 2026, in which Andrew Yang, Clara Shih, and host Deirdre Bosa discussed how recent college graduates are faring in the job market. The core claim is that the large AI infrastructure build-out may be hiding weakness in white-collar hiring for early-career workers. The speakers described spending on data centers as running into the hundreds of billions or trillions of dollars, and they tied it to job creation in the construction side of that build-out. The segment cited several figures and examples. One speaker said 42 to 50 percent of recent college graduates are underemployed, and that 25 percent of small private colleges are set to close within the next 10 years.

The same speaker referred to Microsoft offering to buy out 60,000 employees and to public companies laying people off widely. The speakers also said that some new opportunities are emerging in different parts of the country for workers with trades-oriented skills. Clara Shih described a three-part response. She said her platform, which she called DearCC, is aimed at Gen Z and provides real-time job market data so young people can make better choices about which jobs to pursue, what to study, and whether to attend college.

She argued that people need hands-on skills for building AI agents across fields like marketing, law, and accounting, and that many colleges are not yet teaching those skills. She also said young graduates benefit from community, since returning home after graduation can feel isolating. The segment did not say how the labor market will change next, and it did not offer a timeline for the college closures or the Microsoft buyouts beyond the figures cited. The source is a video discussion rather than reported data, so the figures are those the speakers gave on air and were not independently verified in the material provided.

Articles.Title: Is the AI boom hiding a jobs crisis for graduates?

stories.Headline: AI in healthcare summit held at University of Cincinnati
stories.Summary:
AI in healthcare was the focus of a summit held at the University of Cincinnati, where professionals in artificial intelligence and medicine gathered to discuss how the technology could reshape care. The article was published on November 11, 2026, and was written by Rebecca Smith of WKRC. Participants weighed whether AI can help diagnose certain conditions and whether it can make health care cheaper. The discussion came as health care costs continue to climb. Several figures frame the cost concern.

A national survey of employer-sponsored health plans by Marsh McLennan found that total health benefit cost per employee is expected to rise 8% on average next year, the highest increase since 2003. Summit organizer Jamison DeAngelis said he hopes AI can help health systems become more efficient in their operations. He suggested that greater efficiency could eventually lower costs for patients. The summit's stated focus was on what it called human-centered AI.

Speakers described several possible uses for the technology. Dr. Kelly Kohen, director of the AI Biolab Digital Futures at the University of Cincinnati, said AI could help tailor treatment to individual needs. Radiology was highlighted as an especially promising area, where early detection can be critical. Dr. Alex Tobin, a radiologist, described how AI could examine medical images in fine detail to look for patterns that might predict the best therapy or outcome.

Kyle Frye, CEO of Cortex AI, said AI tools could help determine the next level of care a patient needs. Local 12 said a second part of the story would air Thursday evening, focusing on how AI is being used to detect and fight cancer. The articles do not provide further details on specific outcomes or formal policy changes resulting from the summit. The coverage presents the event as a discussion of possibilities rather than a report on adopted measures.

Articles.Title: AI in healthcare summit held at University of Cincinnati

stories.Headline: Is it a vibe? Nebraska startup community insights on AI in coding
stories.Summary:
Phillip Koolhoven, a solo founder in the Omaha area, has used AI coding tools to build Kova Dating, an early-stage app that emphasizes scheduled video calls. Koolhoven began using tools such as Claude, Gemini and ChatGPT in February, after having had the idea for a few years without the software background to build it. He said he still works a separate full-time job while developing the app. The article describes vibe coding as using AI to develop software through prompting rather than writing code by hand. The practice lets founders of any skill level produce prototypes quickly, without large teams or the cost of hiring or contracting developers.

Koolhoven said the app aims to address swiping fatigue, ghosting and other concerns he identified in the crowded dating app market. He also reported late nights fixing software bugs and dealing with requirements to get on the Apple App Store, and he recently announced Kova had joined the Google Play Store. Bill Udell, managing partner and chief operating officer of Don't Panic Labs, a Lincoln software engineering and business consulting company, warned founders at the Hustle Conference 2026 on Sept. 30 at Creighton University's Heider College of Business. Udell said entrepreneurship requires figuring out why an idea may not be true, and he told the SPN reporter that prototyping used to be slower, giving founders more time to pause and gather evidence. He advised founders to watch the brittleness of their software and seek expert help on recurring bugs and on legal, privacy and strategy questions.

He added that the world is flooded with products that solve problems, while little thought goes into how they reach market. Other people in the Nebraska ecosystem offered similar points. PGSA Venture Capital associate TJ Andreasen said big companies may build bespoke products in-house for less than a software subscription would cost, which could reduce their need to consult startups. Invest Nebraska investment manager Shelby Strattan said that if everyone can be a builder, a functioning software product becomes less differentiated, and investors now look for traction, go-to-market strategies and hard-to-copy traits. Proven Ventures co-founder and general partner Erica Wassinger said customers are the deciding factor, and Creighton's Greisch Center for Enterprise Value director Nathan Preheim said the key skill is knowing what to build.

According to the article, LinkedIn reported a 69% growth in U.S. profiles adding "founder" to their titles, and the U.S. Census Bureau has noted rising business formation in the country. The article also says Koolhoven had not been aware of local resources such as 1 Million Cups and had been worried about how his startup would be received. He has received positive responses from Facebook and Omaha event groups, and he has said he plans to attend entrepreneurial meetups when his afternoons and evenings are free. He intends to focus on development for all users across platforms in the new year.

Articles.Title: Is it a vibe? Nebraska startup community insights on AI in coding

stories.Headline: Big Walk used AI to fix a bug. Now the indie gaming world is having a reckoning.
stories.Summary:
Big Walk, a co-operative puzzle exploration game made by House House, has become the center of a dispute over AI use in indie game development. The debate broke into public view on Monday, when 19 members of the Independent Games Festival Awards jury, out of more than 50, released a signed statement declining to vote for any game using generative AI in any capacity. The jurors cited ecological, economic, psychological, and labor harms, and urged the festival to adopt a strong anti-AI policy disallowing games with any AI-generated work. The statement did not name specific games, but by Tuesday Big Walk had become a central part of the debate.

House House publicly admitted in a statement to Aftermath that large language models were used sparingly near the end of development. The developer said the use stayed under 0.1 percent of the game's code and helped address a Unity engine bug that caused "infinite length" shadows during some situations. After a Unity engineer concluded a fix was not possible, an LLM chatbot suggested a possible fix, which the developers modified extensively into 10 lines of code. The developer said it did not disclose this use for the Steam release earlier this year because Valve does not request disclosure of code or chatbot usage. It later made the disclosure for awards consideration, since the matter had become one of public interest.

House House said the disclosure is not an endorsement of AI tools, however minimal, and expressed concern that voluntary disclosures might normalize the technology. The developer said it supports those working to limit generative AI's harm to games and apologized that its use may not meet their standards. Some judges who had felt a special connection to the game said the disclosure was painful. Austin Walker called the game an achievement and remarkable in a blog post, while Damon Reece wrote that it felt like home. Both were among those who said that even minimal AI use outweighed their respect for the work, with Reece calling silence on the issue rank cowardice.

This is not the first controversy of its kind. Last year, the Indie Game Awards, which are separate from the IGF Awards, rescinded awards for Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 after its developers admitted some in-game textures were made with AI tools, which were later patched out. The Indie Game Awards said at the time that it has a hard stance on generative AI throughout nomination and the ceremony. Since House House's disclosure, Big Walk's Steam page has received over 400 negative reviews in recent days, though the game's "Very Positive" overall rating has held. Critics such as Dominic Tarason argued the response was disproportionate, calling the game very mildly compromised art that is still very human.

Others drew distinctions between games using LLMs as a last-resort technical fix and games relying heavily on AI for art, music, or core engine code. Judge Liz Ryerson wrote that she did not find the use personally disqualifying and objected to treating all cases as the same. AI researcher Mike Cook wrote that House House is not laying off developers to replace them, but that its actions are part of the same problem. Brendan Keogh argued that extreme zero tolerance is counterproductive because it discourages developers from disclosing use. Hannah Nicklin defended zero tolerance as a viable political position aimed at reducing harm and building solidarity.

Articles.Title: Big Walk used AI to fix a bug. Now the indie gaming world is having a reckoning.

stories.Headline: Bilt Unveils AI-Powered Neighborhood OS
stories.Summary:
Bilt, a housing payments and membership company, unveiled Bilt Neighborhood OS, an artificial intelligence operating system and commerce network designed to connect local businesses with the residents who live nearby. The announcement was published on November 11, 2026, and the company describes the product as an extension of its existing membership and rewards platform for housing. Bilt is also expanding that membership technology so organizations can launch their own branded programs or carry existing loyalty programs into the neighborhood, and it named several multifamily companies as participants. Among them is American Landmark Apartments, which plans to deploy the system across 40,000 multifamily residences, giving residents access to leasing, package management, service requests, amenity bookings, and smart-home features through the same app they use to pay rent.

Bilt says its AI agents have completed more than 2 million actions across more than 29,000 businesses in the past 30 days, with 91% finished without human involvement. Property teams can use these agents to coordinate services across their existing systems and offer neighborhood perks, such as a restaurant credit during a repair. American Landmark also plans to fold its internal business intelligence tool, originally called AL One, into Bilt's platform as a property intelligence product. Bilt reports that its platform now reaches about one in four U.S. apartment buildings and is expected to process more than $100 billion in housing payments this year. The rollout is nationwide but phased, with additional launches set to begin in 2027.

Bilt's founder and CEO, Ankur Jain, framed the launch as a response to a technology shift that he said mostly bypassed neighborhood shops and restaurants, and he said the company wants to give those businesses tools to reach customers and build loyalty. Joe Lubeck, founder and CEO of American Landmark Apartments, said the partnership lets his company link its communities to nearby places residents use and gives property teams insights into how their buildings operate. John Vranich, a partner at Bryten, said the system would let his teams spend more time on residents and offer benefits beyond the community. Bilt also named a coalition of payments and commerce partners, including Adyen, Verifone, Clover from Fiserv, Shift4, OpenTable, and Grubhub, to help distribute the system.

The announcement came with Bilt's first State of the Neighborhood 2026 study, conducted with 451 Research by S&P Global and based on nearly 6,600 U.S. adults. The survey found that two-thirds of consumers do at least 80% of their everyday spending within 15 miles of home, and that 77% of renters said rewards on housing payments alone would make them more likely to stay long term. It also found that 87% of respondents would shop more often at a local business if they could earn rewards there. Separately, Bilt announced a partnership with the Local Initiatives Support Corp. (LISC) that begins with a $100,000 donation and aims to connect people with financial coaching and housing-goal support, including pathways to homeownership.

Articles.Title: Bilt Unveils AI-Powered Neighborhood OS

stories.Headline: Developers Want to Build AI Data Centers Near Shenandoah, Zion, and the Grand Canyon. This Map Shows Where.
stories.Summary:
A new interactive map from More Than Just Parks, an independent public lands publication, shows dozens of proposed AI data centers sitting close to America's national parks and public lands. The map was built by cofounder Will Pattiz, who set it up to track where these facilities are being planned and who is behind them. According to his research, at least 14 proposed projects lie within ten miles of a national park boundary, 38 are planned within 25 miles, and 131 are within 50 miles. The tool currently reflects 2,086 data centers, 741 of which are still only proposals, and 77 of those proposals sit within ten miles of protected land.

The article describes several specific sites that concern Pattiz. In January, the City of Page sold roughly 500 acres to developers planning a $10 billion data center beside Horseshoe Bend, a viewpoint on the Colorado River, and that land had previously been set aside for outdoor recreation. The city says the proposal is still under public review and has not been formally adopted, with a planning and zoning meeting scheduled for November 17. Near Price, Utah, a company called Valar Atomics has applied for more than 9,000 acres of Bureau of Land Management land for a project called Project Beehive, which would include small nuclear reactors and would produce about 9.6 gigawatts of power for data centers. In June 2026, the Iron County Commission approved a conditional use permit for a 640-acre, 1.5-gigawatt Antelope Data Center about 40 miles from Zion National Park, which will include an on-site natural gas plant.

Pattiz argues that these projects are being pursued with too little openness and that public lands should not host them. He told Outside that many are "being done under the cloak of darkness or secrecy" and said the central question is what public benefit they provide, noting that no clear public benefit has been outlined for the ones proposed on public lands. He also warned that the centers' heavy use of water, electricity and land will affect public lands one way or another. His map lets a user enter a zip code to see the nearest facility, its likely effect on utility costs, and the groups that support it. He said he hopes the information will help residents judge the projects for themselves.

The article places the debate within a broader national rush to build data centers to meet the computing needs of artificial intelligence and cloud software, facilities that require large amounts of electricity and water. Pattiz described these projects as an inflection point in American history and said they have become political flashpoints in towns and cities where they are going up. The map updates automatically as more information becomes available, so the figures are expected to change. The article does not say whether any of the proposals will be approved or abandoned beyond the steps already noted.

Articles.Title: Developers Want to Build AI Data Centers Near Shenandoah, Zion, and the Grand Canyon. This Map Shows Where.

stories.Headline: The Death of Anonymization: Why Masking ERP Data is Poisoning your AI
stories.Summary:
The article is an opinion piece by Axolile Lungu, founder of synthetic cfo, arguing that masking real ERP data before using it to train AI in finance damages the data. It was published on November 11, 2026, by CPA Practice Advisor. The author says that scrambling vendor IDs, hashing primary keys and blurring timestamps breaks the links between records that double-entry accounting depends on. He describes this as relational fragmentation, and says masked fields show up to models as zeros, which he calls null hallucination.

The author cites an example in which a model treated a hidden tax field as a non-taxable event. He also points to the KPMG Global AI in Finance Report of March 2026, which he says introduced assurance readiness as the main factor separating successful firms. He says top-performing teams, which he claims move three to six times faster, use audit-grade inputs rather than masked data. He argues that a model that is mostly correct is a liability for board-level reporting.

The author's proposed remedy is synthetic data: new ledgers generated from accounting rules rather than scrambled copies of real records. He says his firm, synthetic cfo, builds SAP and Oracle style ledgers in which the debits and credits balance and fraud is planted and labelled. He says this makes privacy risk zero by design. He calls reliance on legacy masking technical debt that will poison AI initiatives. He also warns that shareholder trust may disappear if AI begins hallucinating financial logic.

The piece is written by a person with a commercial interest in the remedy it promotes, since Lungu founded the firm that sells synthetic ERP datasets. His background includes audit roles at PwC and EY, finance and SOX work at Gilead Sciences, AbbVie and Meta, and advisory work for AI companies since 2025. The articles do not report any regulator action or independent test confirming the claims about masking damaging model performance. The piece does not say what the next steps are for firms or regulators.

Articles.Title: The Death of Anonymization: Why Masking ERP Data is Poisoning your AI

stories.Headline: AI-powered imaging tracks thousands of brain cancer cells moving through living tissue
stories.Summary:
Researchers at Uppsala University in Sweden have developed GlioTrace, a method that combines live imaging of brain tissue with artificial intelligence to follow individual glioblastoma cells as they spread. The study was published in the journal Nature Communications on November 11, 2026. The team grew glioblastoma cells from six patients as tumors in mouse brains, cut the brains into thin slices, and kept them alive in the laboratory. Automated microscopes photographed the slices at intervals of no more than two hours for up to five days.

A machine-learning system identified and tracked thousands of individual tumor cells, and statistical models were used to calculate how cells switched between different states. The results showed clear differences between tumors, with some spreading mainly along blood vessels and others spreading more diffusely through the brain tissue. Individual cells could change their shape and movement over a few days and could switch between moving along vessels and moving independently. The researchers also used the method to test two drug substances, which reduced the movement and spread of tumor cells, although the effects varied between patient tumors and cell types.

The lead researchers stress that the method is still a research tool and not yet ready to guide treatment decisions for patients. Hitesh Mangukiya, a researcher at Uppsala University, said the approach allows scientists to watch how tumor cells adapt their behavior in real time. Sven Nelander, a professor of integrative cancer research at the university, said the work opens new possibilities for understanding the invasion process. The analysis software is freely available to other researchers, and the team hopes it will help identify treatments that can stop cancer from spreading through the brain.

The researchers also found that a combination of radiation and chemotherapy increased the share of a fast-moving, invasive cell type in some tumor models. They said these cells may persist under treatment, but further research is needed to determine whether they are more resistant to therapy or contribute to recurrence. Glioblastoma is one of the most aggressive forms of brain cancer, and surgery cannot remove cells that have already spread into surrounding healthy brain. Further studies are needed before GlioTrace could be used in patient care.

Articles.Title: AI-powered imaging tracks thousands of brain cancer cells moving through living tissue

stories.Headline: 5 Takeaways on How AI Is Reshaping Multifamily Operations
stories.Summary:
AI is moving from a buzzword to a routine tool for multifamily operators, according to executives who spoke on an AI panel at the Multifamily Executive Conference in early November in Newport Beach, California. Panelists from Moss & Co., RPM Living and Avenue5 Residential described using the technology across leasing, resident engagement, reporting, maintenance and back-office work. They stressed that successful adoption takes more than switching on a new tool. Early attention went to AI-driven leasing and resident messaging, but the discussion showed the bigger gains may come behind the scenes.

Moss & Co. president Chris Gray said AI is helping automate reporting, build dashboards, analyze performance and streamline processes that once took hours of staff time. He estimated his company is seeing roughly a 50 percent efficiency gain in some operational areas. Gray predicted operator margins will grow, and that management fees could eventually fall because firms can do more, and do it faster. RPM Living chief strategy officer Mariana Estrada pointed to faster responses to prospects as a clear benefit. Automated tools can make first contact almost immediately, which matters as renters expect service outside office hours.

Estrada also described RPM Living's centralized application processing, where AI handles back-and-forth messages with applicants about qualifications, income and documents. She said the company cut processing time roughly in half and doubled the units the program handles without adding headcount. Chase Hunt, Avenue5's vice president of marketing, technology and client solutions, said the aim is to automate routine tasks so on-site staff can spend more time building relationships with prospects and residents. He added that the company has told site teams the technology is not meant to take their jobs. Hunt also cautioned that being able to automate something does not mean an organization is ready to do it.

Hunt urged companies to check whether their data is reliable, how their systems connect and whether employees know how to work with AI tools before giving the technology more autonomy. Avenue5 has involved on-site staff, operational leaders, national team members and governance and engagement committees in its rollout. Gray argued that imperfect data should not stop companies from starting, since AI reporting can reveal anomalies and map out data cleanup. Estrada advised operators to pick their biggest pain point, test whether AI can address it and assign a central person accountable for results. Gray said companies that may have waited 18 months ago now face a different situation, and urged them to begin.

Articles.Title: 5 Takeaways on How AI Is Reshaping Multifamily Operations

stories.Headline: University of Kentucky employee receives religious exemption from using AI
stories.Summary:
A University of Kentucky employee, David Durman, has received a religious exemption from using artificial intelligence at work, saying the technology conflicts with his humanist beliefs. Durman, a research administrator at the university, applied for the exemption under Title VII, a federal rule that requires employers to accommodate sincerely held religious beliefs. He supports researchers as they apply for grant funding, and his current workflow does not require AI. The university granted the request because it did not place an undue burden on the institution, especially since his work does not currently mandate AI use. Durman first turned to the American Humanist Association for help with the application, and he has been a humanist for roughly 30 years.

He said he believes AI conflicts with human well-being for several reasons, including concerns that it could limit a person's capacity to think and reason. He also pointed to the environmental impact of data centers and to the use of creative works to train AI models without artists' explicit permission. Humanism has been recognized as a religion since a Supreme Court ruling in Torcaso v. Watkins in the early 1960s. Durman's case reflects a broader pattern in which employees seek accommodations based on personal ethics.

A university spokesperson said UK reviews exemption requests on an individual basis and determined that Durman could still perform his job duties without AI. In a statement, the university said accommodations may be reviewed as technology and job responsibilities change, so they remain reasonable and workable. Durman said UK has been good to work with and that he believes the university continues to be an inclusive workplace. He said the decision sets an example for others at the university and at other institutions across the country who have similar concerns. He does not expect AI use to become an issue in his work, but he said he is glad to have the protection in place.

Context from the same coverage adds that UK's Information Technology Services recommends Microsoft Copilot for staff and students who want an AI tool. Durman is not the first American to receive a religious exemption from using AI, as a Unitarian Universalist in North Carolina received one earlier this year while working as a software engineer. A Gallup poll taken over the summer found that 52% of U.S. workers use AI to do their jobs. A database called AI Lawsuit Tracker shows 2026 has had the most AI-related cases filed in the past four years.

Articles.Title: University of Kentucky employee receives religious exemption from using AI

stories.Headline: ICYMI: What landed for AI builders in October 2026
stories.Summary:
AWS published a roundup on November 11, 2026, summarizing the updates it released for AI builders during October 2026. The company says it wants developers to choose the right model for each task, rely on their agents in production, and understand what their AI workloads cost. Its updates center on Amazon Bedrock, the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore platform, and the open source Strands agent toolkit. Together, these tools are meant to take a project from first prototype to production.

The October releases add several new models and capabilities. Anthropic's Claude Haiku 5.5 is aimed at subagents and high-volume work, and according to Anthropic it costs around 75 percent less than Claude Haiku 4.5 for most tasks. OpenAI's GPT-6.1 Terra is now generally available on Amazon Bedrock, with input and output token prices at least 50 percent lower than GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-5.6 Terra, and it accepts up to 1 million input tokens. Amazon Nova 2.5 Sonic, a speech-to-speech model, offers lower latency at the same price as Amazon Nova 2 Sonic. Other additions include GLM 5.3 by Z.ai for agentic coding, TwelveLabs Pegasus 1.5 for video metadata, and more models in AWS GovCloud (US).

Several releases focus on reliability and control. AgentCore Gateway now supports model fallback, so when a primary model is throttled or unreachable, requests move to the next model or provider in a chain the customer defines, and a circuit breaker skips failing destinations. AWS Step Functions workflows can now be used as tools through AgentCore Gateway, so business logic stays in the workflows customers already run. Structured outputs are available for all Claude models on Amazon Bedrock, returning schema-compliant JSON. Web Search on Amazon Bedrock adds domain filtering and user location, while Amazon Bedrock Guardrails has a new Standard tier for contextual grounding checks at the same cost as the Classic tier.

Cost changes are also part of the update. AgentCore memory now charges for short-term memory based on the data agents ingest, retrieve, and store instead of a flat rate per event, and AWS says most workloads will see lower costs. Customers can also set a time-to-live on long-term memory records. AWS Cost Explorer, AWS Budgets, and AWS Cost Management Dashboards have been extended to help customers see what drives their Amazon Bedrock spending. The roundup presents these changes as part of AWS's wider effort to make AI spending more predictable.

Articles.Title: ICYMI: What landed for AI builders in October 2026

stories.Headline: AI-derived inflammation score improves cardiovascular risk prediction beyond CAC
stories.Summary:
An AI-derived measure of coronary inflammation, the fat attenuation index read from noncontrast cardiac CT, was reported in a new JAMA analysis published around November 11, 2026, as a possible way to improve cardiovascular risk prediction beyond traditional coronary artery calcium scoring. The study was led by corresponding author Charalambos Antoniades, MD, PhD, of the University of Oxford, and colleagues. The team argued that patients with a zero calcium score are often reassured and may be steered away from statin therapy, even though heart attacks frequently arise from inflamed, noncalcified plaques that do not show up on that scan. The authors said the findings suggest absent or low calcium does not rule out meaningful residual risk.

The multicenter study compared a novel noncontrast fat attenuation index score with an established measure taken from contrast-enhanced CT angiography. Researchers drew on a derivation cohort of 6,818 individuals and a separate validation cohort of 19,110 people imaged between 2010 and 2021, with a median follow-up of 6.7 years. Over that period, the investigators recorded 536 cardiovascular deaths and 1,727 major adverse cardiovascular events, defined as myocardial infarction, new-onset heart failure or cardiovascular death. Adding the contrast-based score to calcium raised the area under the curve for prediction from 0.76 to 0.81, while the noncontrast score brought it to 0.80, with both also improving risk reclassification.

The results were most striking among people with no detectable coronary calcium. In that group, cardiovascular mortality rose from 1.4 to 4 per 1,000 person-years among those whose scores were above the 75th percentile, and MACE rates climbed from 5.9 to 13.3 per 1,000 person-years. The authors noted that because calcium scoring already uses noncontrast CT, the inflammation measure can be drawn from images already acquired, avoiding extra scans, radiation, contrast and scan time, and may extend to primary prevention and patients who cannot tolerate iodinated contrast. They also cautioned that the work establishes prognostic value rather than showing that treatment guided by the score improves outcomes. Further research is needed to determine how the measure should fit into clinical decision-making.

Articles.Title: AI-derived inflammation score improves cardiovascular risk prediction beyond CAC

stories.Headline: I’m Using AI to Try to Cure Cancer—and Save My Own Life
stories.Summary:
Bryant Lin, a Stanford physician, wrote in a Free Press essay published on November 11, 2026, that he is using artificial intelligence to try to treat his own terminal lung cancer. The article describes a conversation he had in early 2023 with his colleague Justin Norden at a restaurant in the Stanford Shopping Center in Palo Alto. At that time, ChatGPT 3.5 had been released only a few months earlier, and new AI developments were arriving constantly. The two were preparing a course on the digital future of healthcare, but they decided instead to start the first class they knew of on generative AI and medicine.

Lin, who is both a physician and a faculty member at Stanford's School of Medicine, says he had a habit of launching new classes more to learn than to teach. He describes this subject as the richest area of learning he could imagine. A little over a year after that conversation, at the age of 49, he was diagnosed with stage 4 lung cancer, which he calls terminal. In the years since, he says he has been studying how AI might help treat, if not cure, his disease. The essay frames this as a personal test of whether AI can actually help save a patient's life.

Lin's own words, as the essay presents them, express hope that he will survive until the next major treatment becomes available. He also says he holds greater hopes for the generation that follows him. The piece is presented as part of the publication's health and self-improvement coverage, which focuses on living well. The article is not a clinical report, and the excerpt provided does not include details of any specific AI tools, treatments, or results. The full essay is available only to paid subscribers of The Free Press.

Articles.Title: I’m Using AI to Try to Cure Cancer—and Save My Own Life

stories.Headline: Modernizing the Milkman: AI’s New Playbook for Medtech Commercial Excellence
stories.Summary:
Most medtech leaders in the United States and around the globe rate their commercial maturity as only basic to intermediate. A few are pulling ahead, outpacing the sector index by eight percentage points of annual shareholder return. The difference, according to a BCG study titled Modernizing the Milkman, comes down to how well they use artificial intelligence in their commercial operations. The report builds on more than 15 years of data and insights from the sector.

The study lays out five concrete moves for leading in medtech commercial work. These include continuous prioritization and dynamic targeting, always-on personalized engagement, and AI-augmented and autonomous sales. They also cover data-driven pricing and margin optimization, along with a seamless service experience supported by 24/7 agents. The articles do not spell out timelines or costs for any of these moves.

BCG is the author of the study, which is hosted and promoted by AdvaMed, the trade group for the medical technology industry. AdvaMed published the item on November 11, 2026, and its page directs readers to the full report. The page itself does not add further claims or attribute new findings beyond the study's summary. The articles do not indicate what follow-up steps, if any, the trade group or BCG plans next.

Articles.Title: Modernizing the Milkman: AI’s New Playbook for Medtech Commercial Excellence - AdvaMed®
